title: As a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Content: Lab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East in Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APView image in fullscreenLab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East in Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APOpinionInfectious diseasesAs a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victimDevi SridharRussia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheldMon 12 Oct 2026 10.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTShareInpandemic preparedness work, scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning.The World Health Organization(WHO), for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritise emerging disease threats and collect theevidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation.As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that thedeath of a single lab workerin Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwideevery month. But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened – and ongoing concern about biological weapons research.The 28-year-oldlab workerdied after developing severe pneumonia. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, established in 1934, which studies plague and other dangerous pathogens including anthrax and cholera, and is rumoured to be involved in biological weapons research. Prof Ashish Jha, who was the US White House Covid-19 response coordinator, and who co-chaired an Ebola commission with me,wrote on social media: “US intelligence assess that Russia’s scientists continue developing biological weapons capabilities. Those programmes operate in secret. Nobody outside inspects them and nobody inside has much incentive to admit when something goes wrong.”On top of that, initial local media coverage suggested that she had died from pneumonic plague after a lab accident, possibly a broken test tube. Pneumonic plague is caused by a bacterium (Yersinia pestis), and can spread through respiratory contact and isalways fatal if untreated. If antibiotics are given in the first 24 hours after symptoms, or even before onset of symptoms post-exposure, it is largely treatable. If she knew she had been exposed, why was treatment not given in time? (Pneumonic plague is a different disease to the more common bubonic plague, which transmits through flea bites.)Despite Russian health authorities denying that it was a case of plague and insisting it was pneumonia of unknown origin, they quickly placed about 200 contacts of the lab worker under quarantine. The authorities reported that no high-threat pathogens were detected and monitoring had ended. The WHOreleased a statementnoting a potential second linked case, but Russia denied this. The cause of death remains unconfirmed.The WHO has pushed the Russian government for more information – including confirmation of the diagnosis and details of the investigations, the reason why it put so many people in quarantine and more information on the second case – but it has not yet received this information.On the one hand, if this infection was spreading further, additional cases would have emerged by now. The lab worker died on 2 October, and the testing of contacts and release of those in quarantine indicates that any spread has been contained so far. However, given that theincubation periodcan be one to three days, continued monitoring is important.There are three hypothetical scenarios if we assume the illness was pneumonic plague. The first is that the lab worker was accidentally exposed to thebacterium while doing research, and either didn’t know, or didn’t tell anyone out of fear – and therefore didn’t ask for treatment immediately. So when she became sick, her window of treatment had been missed.Second, the lab worker was exposed to an antibiotic-resistant strain. This may sound like a conspiracy theory, but senior academics have raised concerns given thehistory of the Soviet biological weapons programmeand the potential for pathogens to be engineered for hostile purposes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYou have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi SridharRead moreThird,Dan Singer(the former White House director for countering biological threats) has suggested that this lab worker might have been given an outdated vaccine, which is only available in Russia as it is not approved by the WHO or most other countries. This is a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning a weakened version of the bacteria is given, but it doesn’t always provide protection and sometimes can cause disease.In short, we don’t know what happened because there is insufficient information from the Russian authorities. To understand what happened, investigators would need access to laboratory and clinical evidence, including genomic sequencing, pathogen identification and details of the worker’s research. Without this, we are left with speculationwhen only scientific certainty will do.As a member of the WHO, Russia has an international legal obligation to share information with the agency. The WHO’s health regulations specifically cover “unusual and unexpected” events, as well as those with serious public health impact and with significant risk of international spread, or that risk affecting trade or travel. But unfortunately, as with most international law, there’s no real enforcement mechanism. There is a reliance on broad cooperation across countries, with the understanding that sharing information on disease spread is in all nations’ best interests.I don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die? | Kiran SidhuRead moreThe US government has also put pressure on Russia for answers, withDonald Trumpsaying he would speak to Putin about the situation.The US state departmentalso formally requested further information under the international health regulations – the irony being that the US withdrew from the WHO in January 2026, but is now invoking the international framework it left behind.As a scientist watching this unfold, I’m reminded that while we can have research and expert conferences into better diagnostics, faster genomic sequencing, more effective vaccines and accessible treatments, none of these advances can compensate for a failure to share the information needed to identify a pathogen in the first place. Preparedness is a political challenge as well as a scientific one. And without transparency, it will be a case of one step forward, two steps back.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsInfectious diseasesOpinionWorld Health OrganizationHealthBubonic plagueRussiaMedical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through? | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh
Content: YemenExplainerWhy are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by RiyadhJason BurkeMon 12 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat happened over the weekend?On Saturday, a missile strike by the Houthis in Yemenhit Riyadh’s international airport, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. On Sunday, another attack ‌killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.CCTV footage showed people cowering at the moment of impact of Saturday’s attack.CCTV from inside Riyadh airport shows moment of deadly airstrikeFootage filmed in the aftermath of showed damage inside one of the terminal buildings at the airport, which is located about 22 miles north of the Saudi Arabian capital.Aftermath of strike on Riyadh’s international airportThe attacks by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, were the biggest escalation yet in their campaign ⁠against Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in recent weeks.View image in fullscreenSmoke rising from the site of the Saudi Aramco refinery south of Riyadh on 3 October after a suspect Houthi attack.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-3/ReutersThough the violence might appear at first sight to be restricted to the Arabian peninsula, itcould have global consequences, pushing up fuel prices and so international inflation.Why now?The Houthis’ timing is partly opportunistic but also rooted in the dynamics of the conflicts across the Gulf.The Houthis initially stayed on the sidelines of the conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran earlier this year. But last month, the Islamist militia movement seized control of key territory and gained virtual control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, which dominates the Red Sea, a critical shipping route for oil and gas exports from the region.View image in fullscreenA satellite view of Mayun island, also known as Perim island, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./APThe Yemeni government forces and local alliesbegan a major counteroffensivelast weekto drive backthe Houthisfrom the Bab al-Mandaband also hitother Houthi positions.Saudi Arabia is in the Houthis’ crosshairs because it supports Yemen’s UN-backed government and its forces. Their attacks on high-profile targets in the kingdom such as oil infrastructure and the capital’s airport – key symbols of its international integration and economic future – makes painfully obvious the costs of Riyadh’s strategic choices.Such attacks also benefit Iran, which has long supported the Houthis as part of its “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Islamist hardline movements that allows Tehran to project power and influence round the region.The new threat from the Houthis to the Red Sea and to Saudi Arabia highlights again the massive leverage Tehran and its allies can exert on global oil and gas supplies, countering recent US pressure in bold move on the conflict’s chessboard.How is this new territory for Saudi Arabia?The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia have been the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.They also marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. Businesses in Riyadh’s financial hub have told employees to work remotely, authorities in Riyadh have asked schools to switch to online classes this week, and top energy executives were ⁠dropped from the schedule of a high-profile conference this week in the capital.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from a video showing a fire at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Thursday 8 October.Photograph: APThough Saudi Arabia has intervened indirectly in conflicts around the Middle East and beyond for decades, violence has rarely struck the kingdom itself. In recent months, the country has found itself on a frontline, something its rulers have long sought to avoid.Why couldn’t Riyadh stop the missiles?Saudi Arabia has invested enormous sums in its military – the kingdom is the world’s eighth biggest spender on weapons – but Houthi attacks are very hard to stop.“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at Ottawa University.Other analysts point out that even the vaunted Israeli air defence systems failed to stop a ballistic missile narrowly missing Ben Gurion international airport last year.Reprisals against the Houthis and efforts to pre-emptively destroy the movement’s offensive capabilities are not easy either. The US bombardment in 2025 showed how hard it is to destroy the militia’s capabilities, which have been much enhanced over recent years, in part through Iranian advice and investment.What might happen next?The Houthis say their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – suggesting they are responding to ongoing Saudi strikes on the territory they control in Yemen – but show no sign of stopping their attacks.“Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” official statements carried by the Houthi-run al-Masirah television channel said.It seems unlikely Saudi Arabia will halt its counterstrikes, and equally unlikely the kingdom will be able to find a way to block all incoming Houthi missiles, though it may improve its intelligence gathering and early warning to allow better defence of specific high-value targets.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a Saudi airstrike on a factory in Houthi-controlled Sana’a on 9 October.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesNor is there any imminent prospect of an end to the hostilities between Iran and the US that are a major factor in the surge of the recent violence in Yemen. And though the Houthis are more a coalition of different factions than a coherent single movement, for the moment they appear unified behind hardline and ideologically committed leaders.Farea al-Muslimi, a specialist on Yemen and the Gulf at Chatham House in London, said the Houthis had been consistently underestimated over the years.“They have really upped their game and believe they can get something now which will reposition them within the region. They are very confident at the moment and feeling empowered …. But though they think they can control this [escalation], that may well be an illusion,” he said.Explore more on these topicsYemenSaudi ArabiaHouthisIranMiddle East and north AfricaexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Christian Horner: ‘Not all teams act that way. You don’t see the same brutality as when I left’ | Christian Horner | The Guardian
description: The 52-year-old talks to Donald McRae about the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse, questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacks
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: The 52-year-old talks to Donald McRae about the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse, questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacks
Content: Christian Horner says he is still in the dark about his Red Bull departure: ‘I wasn’t really given a reason.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChristian Horner says he is still in the dark about his Red Bull departure: ‘I wasn’t really given a reason.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianChristian HornerInterviewChristian Horner: ‘Not all teams act that way. You don’t see the same brutality as when I left’Donald McRaeThe 52-year-old reflects on the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse, questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacksMon 12 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristian Horner should be in steamy Singapore, preparing for another grand prix victory, but here he is, at home on an autumnal morning in genteel Highgate as his wife, Geri Halliwell-Horner, welcomes me with a cheerful hug. Horner smiles as the former Spice Girl produces an impressive imitation of my South African accent which echoes her old headteacher at Watford Girls.After the most controversial man in the recent history ofFormula Onesays hello, Halliwell-Horner and I discuss the fact that my two daughters also went to her school and that one of their history textbooks had her name printed on the inside page – while the ex-Ginger Spice talks about gritty old Watford, grammar school education and Nelson Mandela.I joke that it feels like I’m interviewing Halliwell-Horner instead of Horner. Everyone laughs but I will soon ask Horner about the impact on his marriage in 2024 when an investigation was carried out intoallegations he had sent “hundreds” of inappropriate texts and photographsto a female employee when Red Bull’s team principal. The woman was apparently“upset, angry, scared, intimidated and lonely”while the tabloids speculated that Halliwell-Horner was “furious”.Horner was exoneratedby two independent investigations but other hurtful circumstances then surrounded his sudden departure from Red Bull in July 2025. The team has struggled since then but, nine days ago, at the Bahrain Grand Prix,Max Verstappen wonRed Bull’s first race with an engine built entirely by the team.Verstappen then won againin Singapore this past Sunday. That feat of engineering had been conceived and instigated by Horner near the end of his remarkable 20 years at Red Bull.View image in fullscreenChristian Horner and Geri Halliwell-Horner after Red Bull won the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2024.Photograph: David Davies/PAWhen Halliwell-Horner disappears after a final hug, Horner is amiable yet careful. However, the 52-year-old admits his distress after he was forced out: “It felt particularly brutal and sad to finish in that manner. But I now have a reasonable relationship with Oliver Mintzlaff [the CEO of corporate projects at Red Bull]. He rang the other day and thanked me for all I’d done for the engine.”His dismissal, Horner reiterates, “was painful. Very painful. I didn’t really process it till a month later because, in the immediate aftermath, I focused on supporting my daughter [Olivia] through a hideous period.”Horner and his former partner, Beverley Allen, became parents to Olivia in 2013. After they separated, he and Allen remained on good terms and so grief, following her death from eye cancer, framed his demise at Red Bull. As he recalls that difficult period, he pays fleeting tribute to his arch-rival, Toto Wolff, the head of Mercedes,who has addressed his battle with depression.“Toto was very brave to talk openly about such a factor for people our age. I hadn’t experienced those issues but I had an appreciation during this period of how people could [suffer]. The identity of many middle-aged guys is through their work. Suddenly you have that stripped and taken from you. Who are you? What are you? What is your purpose? You either curl up into a ball or brush yourself down and get up.”Horner, who arrived in 2005 as the youngest team principal in F1 history, adds: “When I started at Red Bull, there were under 400 people. When I left, there was 2,200. I poured my heart and soul into that business and convinced people to leave other teams for Red Bull. I never had a big turnover in staff because there was tremendous loyalty over a long period. The startup engine business had been founded in 2021 and I was about to get it on the track when I left. I felt great sadness in not seeing that engine in a car.”Hebroke down briefly while telling staff of his fate. “It was very strange because that group became your extended family. So the tears on grown men’s faces was deeply moving.”View image in fullscreenChristian Horner on the grid at the Netherlands Grand Prix in 2023.Photograph: Tim Goode/PAIn his new book, which provides a thorough overview of his career, Horner describes the day he replaced Tony Purnell, his predecessor, in 2005: “Formula One is ruthless, I thought, watching from my car as Tony and Dave Pitchforth, their just-fired managing director, carried glum expressions and cardboard boxes stuffed with personal belongings … when I was eventually shown to my office, it resembled a crime scene. A barely drunk cup of coffee had been abandoned on the desk. Through the walls, I heard Tony’s PA sobbing.”Horner says now: “History repeats itself. Not all teams act in that way. A lot of teams haven’t delivered over the years but you don’t see the same brutality as when I left. We had pole position at the previous race.”Atlast year’s British Grand Prix, just before Horner’s sacking, Verstappen was leading when “the rain came”.Horner also mentions his “relief” at leaving. “The last two years had been pretty tough but it was a particularly sensitive time, with the bereavement of my daughter’s mum the previous week. I had an 11-year-old child grieving her mother. Nothing was more important than that.”There had been a power struggle at Red Bull followingthe death in 2022 of Dietrich Mateschitz, the company’s billionaire founder who always backed Horner. BothHelmut Marko, a key consultant, and Jos Verstappen, Max’s father, seemed keen to undermine Horner. “Helmut could be blunt and I was disappointed he’d stayed as a guest of our family two days before [Horner’s sacking] with no indication this was coming,” Horner reveals.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and Christian Horner in 2024.Photograph: Clive Rose/Getty ImagesWhat about Verstappen Sr? “There’s nothing to say.”Were the Verstappens partly responsible for Horner’s removal? “No, it was a Red Bull decision. After Dietrich died, things changed in the leadership.”Horner says the reasons for his sacking remain opaque, apart from a general discontent that the team no longer matched the domination it had enjoyed in two separate spells when Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen won multiple championships: “I think it was a feeling there was too much control in my hands. But I wasn’t really given a reason.”Did the 2024 allegations contribute to his dismissal? “I’d come through that, dismissed them. So this was more focused on performance and the future.”Was he worried his marriage might be in jeopardy after the texts and photographs were leaked? “My wife was a pillar of support throughout and I just had to believe in the process. I’ve said enough about it in the book and previously.”Yet the book does not outline the allegations against him or provide any details of his defence. “I’ve said everything I can say, and there are certain legal reasons [why] I’m not at liberty to go further.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHorner is more precise when asked if there is a chance he might never work in F1 again. “Absolutely. But if I don’t go back I had a hell of a run. I won one in every four races I competed in. I had 287 podiums out of 405 races.”He says: “Nobody could take away the 124 wins and 14 championships [six constructors’ and eight drivers’ titles]. But I felt particularly hurt and robbed I didn’t have the opportunity to see that [Red Bull-manufactured] Powertrains engine win.”Horner watched Verstappen’s victory the Sunday before last on television and “I felt very proud seeing what it meant to everybody and that they sent the Powertrains representative on to the podium. I had messages throughout the team and I texted Max after the race. He was very magnanimous and it was a landmark moment to see that engine win. It reinforced to me that, if you assemble the right people with the right culture and the necessary tools, anything is possible.”Yet he still believes the team has lost its mojo. “Red Bull has been the maverick team. It’s pushed the boundaries. Only Red Bull would do something crazy enough to build a new engine as a subsidiary of a fizzy drinks manufacturer. Its mantra was to be nonconformist, to be a disruptor. It’s a little different now.”View image in fullscreenLaurent Mekies, Christian Horner’s replacement at Red Bull.Photograph: Hollandse Hoogte/ShutterstockWho is in charge of Red Bull’s team – Laurent Mekies, his successor, or Max Verstappen? He laughs. “I’m not getting drawn into that. Ultimately Oliver Mintzlaff is the most senior guy and obviously Max is a massive asset. I employed Laurent but I can’t judge how he operates.”Horner argues that his comments last month about Ferrari being “a dream job” applied more to other people than himself. He would prefer to return with a team where he has a part-ownership stake. In regard to Ferrari and their currently beleaguered team principal, Horner suggests “Fred Vasseur is an experienced guy. He’s done a decent job. But I, more than anyone, know the pressures of running a competitive organisation.My comments got taken out of context.“Ferrari is the biggest brand in F1. It’s the most historic team. But I’ve accumulated some phenomenal capital behind me, to look at the next move I potentially make in the sport. That would be with ownership attached to it and Ferrari aren’t going to sell shares. So I’m happy to sit outside the sport and see what opportunities present themselves over the coming months or years. It’s not a prerequisite that I go back. I would only return for the right opportunity with like-minded people that want to win. I would never go back just to take part.”Horner says: “For the last 21 years I would have been sitting in Singapore right now. But it’s my daughter’s 13th birthday today and I’m taking her to see Hamilton at the theatre tonight.”What does he miss most about F1? “The people, the team, the competition. I still love the sport but I don’t miss the travel and politics.”Wolff said Horner had “broken too much glass” to return to F1. Horner grins: “He also said this [Red Bull] engine was going to be completely shit and a disaster. Toto’s got it quite easy at the moment. Zak Brown [the head of McLaren] is compromised because he’s using Toto’s engine so he can’t ruffle feathers. All sport needs rivalry, whether it’s Ferguson and Wenger, Mourinho and Guardiola. It percolates and polarises. I used that to galvanise good people to take on Mercedes.”View image in fullscreenChristian Horner on his great rivalry with Mercedes boss Toto Wolff: ‘All sport needs rivalry, whether it’s Ferguson and Wenger, Mourinho and Guardiola. It percolates and polarises.’Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesYet F1 takes its toll and Horner admits he has suffered panic attacks. “I didn’t know what it was. You suddenly feel dizzy and conscious of your breathing and you think there’s something strange going on. I put it down to having had too much coffee on an oppressive, muggy, thundery day. Then it happened again. I got checked out and there was nothing physically the matter. They said: ‘We think you have anxiety. Your breathing’s very shallow.’ It was my body telling me you’re pushing pretty hard here. I’m able to recognise the symptoms now and let it go, and breathe.”What might he be doing 10 years from now? “I’m looking forward to finding out. It could be at a racetrack, it could be sitting on a tractor.”He laughs again before showing his real conviction. “I know my strength is getting a group of people across different skill sets to work as a team. That’s possibly applicable to other things but, at the moment, the only thing that really motivates and excites me is Formula One.”Drive by Christian Horner is published by Bantam on 22 October.Available on pre-order from Guardian Bookshop. He will be sharing stories from the book ontour across the UK from 17-26 October.Explore more on these topicsChristian HornerFormula One 2026Formula OneRed BullMotor sportinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellion | Movies | The Guardian
description: Paul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nation
Author: Stuart Jeffries
Headline: Paul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nation
Content: You say you want a revolution … Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Betina La Plante/Focus Features/APView image in fullscreenYou say you want a revolution … Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Betina La Plante/Focus Features/APMoviesMort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellionPaul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nationStuart JeffriesMon 12 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British are perverse. We fetishise our failures, even if they are essentially tangential to a national narrative that should be about imperial conquest, slavery and being unremittingly unpleasant to foreigners. We tell and retell, for instance, the story of Captain Scott even though he died in Antarctica in 1912 after losing the race to reach the south pole first to the unacceptably Norwegian Roald Amundsen. Similarly, Christopher Nolan’s 2017 film Dunkirk typified the British tendency to snatch national glory from the jaws of defeat. And then there was the tragicomic disaster of the Charge of the Light Brigade during the 1853-56 Crimean war in which our boys raced to putatively glorious if stupid deaths. It’s as if, for us British, pointless sacrifice and embracing failure are what heroism means. And our cinema has colluded with this perversity.But there is an exception to this national veneration of failure. Britain has been reluctant to embrace its revolutionary defeats. There is, for instance, no film dealing with the Chartist movement’s 19th-century struggle for universal suffrage. Even more strikingly yet, it is only now, in 2026, that a film has been made about the calamitous 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, even though it is a pivotal event in British history. Paul Greengrass’sThe Uprising, starring Andrew Garfield as a – let’s just get this over with – revolting peasant, joins a mere handful of other movies, includingKevin Brownlow and Andrew Mollo’s 1975 Winstanley,Bill Douglas’s 1986 ComradesandMike Leigh’s 2018 Peterloo, that dare depict how radical collective action was crushed by a ruthless state.The Uprising review – Paul Greengrass turns revolutionary rage into a Robin Hood origin mythRead moreFor Stephanie Barczewski, author ofHeroic Failure and the British, our fetishisation of glorious disaster is a corollary of the 19th-century British private school ethos of stoic duty and crypto-S&M suffering culled from an ancient Roman exemplar. Revolutionary failure doesn’t fit this template; hence, one might suppose, its absence from our cinema.The Uprising, however, for all its flaws and missteps, is a bold attempt to correct a national wrong by depicting a collective uprising devoid of heroism. Greengrass tries to make sense of how a mass movement of riff-raff from the rough ends of Kent and Essex arose, and how its momentum was compromised of factionalism and conflicting aims. It shows how, ultimately, the revolutionary leaders were duped by the boy king Richard II, leaving the rebels winding up to be either slaughtered en masse in London’s Smithfield or skulking defeated back to their homes to work harder to pay the poll tax whose unfairness they had risen up against in the first place.It is an important – if belated, improbable and commercially dubious – addition to our national story.View image in fullscreenDepicting the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage … Cillian Murphy, right, and Martin Lucey in The Wind That Shakes the Barley.Photograph: Joss BarrattIn contrast, other countries have been more fortunate in their revolutionary heritage and as a result their national cinemas teem with examples of successful uprisings. From the advent of cinema, for instance, Americans have incessantly revelled in making movies about their war of independence – including silent features such as 1917’s The Spirit of 76 and DW Griffith’s America (1924), not to mention Bugs Bunny in Friz Freleng’s delightful period romp of a cartoon Bunker Hill Bunny (1950). The French have been making cinematic homages to their 1789 revolution going back the 1913 biopic Robespierre.In Russia, Grigori Aleksandrov and Sergei Eisenstein’s October, in 1928, typified how the Bolshevik revolution’s success against the odds made Russian spirit what it is. Movies such as Neil Jordan’s Liam Neeson-fronted biopic Michael Collins (1996) and The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006), set during the Irish war of independence and starring Cillian Murphy, depicted the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage – even if the latter had an English director in the shape of Ken Loach.But it isn’t just the deeply classist notion of what failures count as heroic that has made British cinema reluctant to embrace our failed revolutionary heritage. It is the result of how our culture has been reverse-colonised by Hollywood, with historical narratives only deemed filmable if they fit into American movie industry’s tropes. Whenever Hollywood deigns to make a movie about British history, it includes Downton-style upstairs-downstairs hokum, those crazy sexed-up murderous Tudors and, of course, that cod-historical franchise that never stops giving, Robin Hood.Equally, it is axiomatic in Hollywood that political struggles are always about one thing – a very American notion of freedom, individual freedom from presumed oppression. That’s why Mel Gibson’s 1995 Braveheart was possible: even though William Wallace’s struggles against the English ended in failure with his execution at Smithfield (not far from where Wat Tyler was murdered by Richard II’s lackeys), the biopic involved the classic Hollywood trope of the little guy fighting for freedom. Any other political goal (tax reform, wealth redistribution, solidarity, fraternity) scarcely makes a dent in the Hollywood narrative juggernaut.And that’s what makes Greengrass’s The Uprising problematic. Compromised by Hollywood values, it is conflicted about representing a failed political revolution as what it was – a collective struggle. It depicts the Peasants’ Revolt in the frame of one fictional man, Garfield’s Ploughman. Conceived by Greengrass as a representative everyman, Ploughman – with a disregard for historical truth that should make the film’s historical adviser Dan Jones wince – pops up Zelig-like to parlay with the king, catch the king’s mother’s eye, rally the rebels, scythe down the bad guys, as if he were a real-life historical figure. The collective struggle becomes individualised drama, betraying the positioning of the apostrophe – what happened in 1381 was the Peasants’ Revolt not the Peasant’s Revolt.View image in fullscreenCinema has been a failure at depicting the English civil war … Tim Roth and Dougray Scott in To Kill a KingWorse yet, the film includes a very silly coda in which, a year after the defeat of the revolt, Ploughman and a rump of rebels have retreated to the English greenwood to form an outlaw band of unmerry men. The corollary of this coda is to make the Peasants’ Revolt a kind of origin story for the legend of Robin Hood, even though that is nonsense: the folkloric rebel operated – if at all – about 200 years earlier. The whole idea may seem ridiculous, but the US distributors for The Uprising, Focus Features, leaned into this barmy interpretation bychanging the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood earlier this year, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”. Sensible Guardian readers will know of course that Robin Hood was a supporter of Richard I and foe of King John both of whom ruled England almost exactly two centuries earlier.Such absurdities are a great shame since Greengrass’s – worthwhile – intention was to make a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that resonates topically for our age. A collapse in trust of our rulers, a seemingly endless cost of living crisis, widening inequality, political discourse dominated by lies and nonsense: 2026 is more like 1381 than we realise.It’s worth pointing out that there has been one successful military revolution in British history, namely the English civil war. Cinema of course has been a failure at depicting it: there was Ken Hughes’s wildly inaccurate 1970 drama Cromwell starring Richard Harris and Alec Guinness and Mike Barker’s 2003 To Kill a King with Tim Roth and Dougray Scott. But our most enduring and successful revolution was scarcely cinematic: the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 in which the Catholic KingJames IIwas replaced by his Protestant daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William III of Orange was hailed by Bertrand Russell as “the most moderate and successful of all revolutions. Its aims were modest, but they were exactly achieved.” Yawn! Who wants to see that movie?View image in fullscreenIf Carlsberg did revolutionary failures … Winstanley.Photograph: Bfi/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockPerhaps the greatest film about British revolutionary failure was the aforementioned Winstanley, about a group of proto-communists called the Diggers who settled common land on St Georges’s Hill outside Weybridge, Surrey during the English civil war. They hoped to create a utopia devoid of private property and for a few weeks lived self-sufficiently until they were violently evicted by the local gentry. To clinch the point that the Diggers’ experiment was a failure, just go on to property website Rightmove. There you can find a “stunning and elegant” £25m mansion on Cavendish Road, St George’s Hill with “fairway views, seven individually themed bathrooms, two staff apartments, and a leisure complex” and 1.5 acres of carefully landscaped gardens. Not what their leader Gerrard Winstanley wanted at all. He wrote: “Was the Earth made to preserve a few covetous, proud men to live at ease, and for them to bag and barn up the treasures of the Earth from others, that these may beg or starve in a fruitful land; or was it made to preserve all her children?” Our radical history, so often absent from our national cinema, has been built over in a field in Surrey for real estate scarcely any of us can afford. A very British coup if ever there was one.Explore more on these topicsFilmPaul GreengrassBiopicsDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: If Russia had interfered with the Brexit vote, Nige would have been the first to know | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Burnham was lying, Farage told a press conference on Monday. This was clearly just another plot to undermine him
Author: John Crace
Headline: Burnham was lying, Farage told a press conference on Monday. This was clearly just another plot to undermine him
Content: Nigel Farage during a press conference in Hythe, Kent, on Monday.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage during a press conference in Hythe, Kent, on Monday.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAThe politics sketchBrexitIf Russia had interfered with the Brexit vote, Nige would have been the first to knowJohn CraceBurnham was lying, Farage told a press conference on Monday. This was clearly just another plot to undermine himMon 12 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.38 EDTShareLet’s face it. The very idea that Russia may have tried to interfere with theBrexitreferendum is clearly absurd. I mean, what could a hostile state hope to gain from sowing division between the UK and the EU? We all know that Vladimir Putin has nothing but the best interests of European democracies at heart. That’s why he invaded Ukraine. To help it become a bit more democratic. The sort of democracy which is so highly prized that 99% of its citizens vote for its leader. If only others could be more like Russia.If anything, Putin would have wanted the UK to remain within the EU and it was only his impartiality that prevented him from saying so. Besides which, why would the Russians want to get involved in anything so politically insignificant as the partial break-up of an organisation it considers an enemy. It just makes no sense. And it’s not as if Russia has any track record of clandestine foreign engagement. Next people will be suggesting Russia paid Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, at least £30,000 tomake helpful speeches in the European parliamentand recruit other MEPs.Andy Burnham sees it rather differently. Over the weekend he claimed that since he had become prime minister he had seen incontrovertible proof that the Russians had been involved in a misinformation campaign during the referendum. He didn’t say exactly what form the interference had taken. Merely that it was a reality. So it was no surprise that Nigel Farage was asked for his reaction during a Reform press conference in Kent on Monday morning.“The prime minister is a liar,” Nige snapped. “Yes, a liar.” Nige was beside himself with anger. He is getting more thin-skinned by the day. This was yet another myth fabricated by the Establishment. Another excuse to try to relitigate the result of the referendum. The whole thing was clearly a plot to undermine him. Everything that ever happens in the world somehow always becomes personal to Nige. His solipsism eclipses everything. We all only exist as satellites of his own imagination. When he dies, we will all die with him. If he hasn’t killed us first.It was like this. If Russia had tried to interfere with the referendum then he would have been the first to know about it. And frankly he had been deeply disappointed that no one had tried to buy him. Numerous punters had bought him for £80 a pop on Cameo. But despite having billions in petro-roubles, the Russians had blanked him.First the sound, then the fury. You can almost sense Nige’s desperation these days. It had all been going so well for so long. Reform had been 10 points clear in the polls for the best part of 18 months as Labour and the Tories flatlined. Nige was even being taken seriously as a possible next prime minister. Then along came the financial scandals and the election on the nod of Burnham and suddenly Farage found himself marginalised. His politics of grievance were no longer quite so attractive.Yet Nige can’t help himself. Logic would suggest that if the public mood was shifting more back to the centre ground of traditional two-party politics, then he would be better off heading in that direction himself. Instead, the Mr Nice Guy carapace – “I’m only saying what you’re all thinking” – is falling away. Nige is revealing himself to be a deeply unpleasant person all along. There is no longer the pretence of “let’s just have a pint and some bantz”. Everything has become actively nasty. Retreating to the safe ground of the 15% for whom nothing can ever be nasty enough. So much so that Nige is even back to sharing a platform with Zia Yusuf. A man who makes Honest Bob Jenrick look trustworthy. Almost cuddly.The Reform roadshow was in Kent to promote Nige and Zia’s war on immigrants. The UK had been invaded and everyone had to go. No exceptions for migrants with winning smiles or tragic backstories. There was no room for Afghan women and children.This was Toxicity Unfiltered. Prejudice 101. The Americans had removed their bombers from RAF Fairford because of the small boat crossings. He didn’t pause to wonder why the US president had kept some planes at other UK airbases. There would be tariffs on any countries who didn’t want their migrants back. Maybe even airstrikes. Asylum was just a scam, Zia insisted. He would starve the migrants in small boats. Refuse them medicines. Any civil servants who declined to activate the mass deportations would be lined up and shot in front of the white cliffs of Dover.Come the end we were treated to Nige’s stream of unconsciousness. Ukraine? Well, everyone had their limits and he was a bit fed up with Zelenskyy. You couldn’t go on supporting your allies indefinitely. And what had happened to the Sun? Not so long ago it would print any old bollox Nige told its reporters to write. Now they were daring to be nice to Kemi. It was an outrage. A stitch-up.Back in the Commons in the afternoon, you could almost feel the years peeling away in a return to the Brexit wars of a decade ago. And that’s without Burnham even suggesting the UK rejoins the EU. All he said was that he would try to reset the relationship in a way that worked for all parties and would grow the economy by £10bn a year. At all stages the British public would be boss. This was far too much for Kemi. Natch. She accused the prime minister of undermining the referendum result – for, er, speaking the truth – and that she would much rather the economy had zero growth than it came at the cost of closer ties with the EU. It was quite like old times. How I’ve missed them.Explore more on these topicsBrexitThe politics sketchBritish identity and societyReform UKNigel FarageAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Free ice-cream, glowing skin and camping wins: Filter UK writers reveal the unexpected perks of product testing | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Our testers reflect on a year of discoveries, from family game nights to fewer chores
Author: Lily Smith
Headline: Our testers reflect on a year of discoveries, from family game nights to fewer chores
Content: Making a meal of it: testing camping stoves turned one instant-noodles camper into a dab hand at outdoor cooking.Photograph: Sian Lewis/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMaking a meal of it: testing camping stoves turned one instant-noodles camper into a dab hand at outdoor cooking.Photograph: Sian Lewis/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleFree ice-cream, glowing skin and camping wins: Filter UK writers reveal the unexpected perks of product testingOur testers reflect on a year of discoveries, from family game nights to fewer choresDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereLily SmithMon 12 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s our birthday! So to celebrate turning two, we asked our contributors toreflect on their year of testing pretty much everything– from beauty products tovideo doorbells. It turns out they’ve had some unexpected wins along the way.Some managed to tick an extra thing off their to-do list. “After six months of testingIPL devices, epilators and then IPL devicesagain, I had no need to book in for my usual pre-beach wax this summer,” saysLise Smith.Rachel Ogdensaystesting toastershas meant knowing her smoke alarm “works just fine”.View image in fullscreenPressing matters: Caramel Quin gets a little help while testing irons.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianCaramel Quin’schildren, in turn, are grateful to have one fewer chore to do. “My teenagers got their clothes ironed while I wastesting irons. I’ve pressed thousands of items of school uniform over the years, but it’s iron your own clothes these days … except when mum’s testing!”Others learned an important lesson about value. “Testing so many products has cemented my belief that price isn’t always an indicator of quality,” saysSarah Matthews.Sabine Wiesel, meanwhile, was impressed by aBeauty of Joseon eye serumthat came in at just a fraction of the price of some competitors in her test of thebest eye creamsand left her with a “brighter and rejuvenated-looking eye area”.View image in fullscreenPitch perfect: testing camping gear at Holden Farm in Hampshire.Photograph: Matt Collins/The GuardianForMatt CollinsandSian Lewis,testing outdoor equipment has enhanced their camping experiences in unanticipated ways.Mattdiscovered a walking trail while trying outgear for camping with kids. “At lovelyHolden Farmin Hampshire, I discovered theSouth Downs Way. Glorious. This ancient route had my son and me wandering beneath veteran oaks and along spring meadows at sunrise.” AndSianupped her cooking skills while testing thebest camping stoves: “I’m usually an instant-noodles kind of person, but I’m now a dab hand at cooking on a dinky gas flame and have recently whipped up cornbread and egg muffin breakfast sarnies in the middle of the wild.”Meanwhile,Jane Hoskyn’sonce-white towel got a new lease of life after she purposely stained it to testeco-friendly laundry detergents. “It ended up a right old mess, so I had to dye it. It’s now a gorgeous deep forest green. Much prettier and more eye-catching than it was even before the stain test – it shows less dirt, too.”Video doorbellsunexpectedly helpedAndy Shawsleep more soundly. “If I wake up wondering whether one of my adult offspring has made it home from the pub, I only need to check the doorbell notifications on my phone. They’re so used to the surveillance that they wave at the camera when they come in.”View image in fullscreenGood sport: testing games led to a new family tradition.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianAnd finally, one of the biggest upsides seems to be an excuse to get loved ones together. “I spent a lot of time hosting ice-cream tasting sessions with my friends while trying to find thebest ice-cream makers. More quality time with friends and free ice-cream for them – I’d say that’s a win-win,” saysDanielle Amato. And forZoë Phillimore,trying out toys and games for our guide to the bestgifts for six-year-oldshas led to a new family tradition. “My husband, kids and I gather around the kitchen table and play board games together on a Saturday night. Hardly groundbreaking, but it’s easily my favourite time of the week.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterFamilyBeautyCamping holidaysHomesWalkingHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU | Brexit | The Guardian
description: PM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematic
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematic
Content: Andy Burnham gives an update in the House of Commons on Monday.Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham gives an update in the House of Commons on Monday.Photograph: House of Commons/PABrexitAndy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EUPM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematicPippa Crerar,Jennifer RankinandLisa O’CarrollMon 12 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s future place in Europe, saying the existing relationship is “not good enough” as he framed next month’s Brussels summit as a possible first step to EU membership.The prime minister said Britain must take a “clear-eyed rational look” at its long-term relationship with the bloc to boost economic growth and control immigration, which needed to go beyond Labour’s existing red lines.The next “reset” summit will take place on 20 November, ending months of uncertainty, with the two sides seeking to sign deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham hopes could provide a £10bn-a-year boost to the economy.One EU diplomat said a deal on the three “significant but modest” issues needed to be approved as a test of the UK’s good faith so both sides could get on with the “real reset” in the longer-term relationship.But the UK remains braced for a possible row over protectionist “Made in Europe” trade rules amid industry fears they could lock out UK manufacturers, prompting the prime minister to pledge he would raise concerns with his EU counterparts.Burnham was also forced to clarify that he did not think Russian interference in the 2016Brexitcampaign had affected the final result, after he raised questions about the legitimacy of the outcome in comments at the weekend.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch accused Burnham of being too loose with his language over remarks he made about Kremlin interference in Brexit.Photograph: House of Commons/PAIn a statement to MPs, the first since the party conference recess, an otherwise confident-sounding Burnham said it would be a “major dereliction of duty” for his government to turn away from exploring closer relations with the EU.“We should not turn our backs on this opportunity and I hope all sides of this house will get behind the government’s efforts to land a positive outcome,” he said.“I believe our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.“Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country.“Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.”View image in fullscreenNigel Farage speaks to reporters outside the Houses of Parliament in the days after the UK voted to leave the EU.Photograph: Matt Dunham/APBurnham denied he was reopening the Brexit debate, insisting he respected the referendum result, but added that he wanted to take a “pragmatic approach” to boost economic growth and improve cooperation on migration.He was forced on to the back foot over his remarks on a podcast on Sunday that Russia had interfered over Brexit, rejecting suggestions from Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, that he may have been loose with his language.“It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time,” he said.Burnham had said on Sunday it was clear thatRussia had interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendumafter he sought answers when he arrived in No 10. He did not disclose who gave him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or, crucially, whether any interference had affected the result.View image in fullscreenBurnham said he wanted to improve cooperation with the EU on migration.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyDowning Street said the prime minister “absolutely” accepted the Brexit referendum result and believed it to be legitimate, while the foreign minister, Stephen Doughty, said it was clear Russia had attempted to interfere but had failed.In his statement, Burnham told MPs they were right to raise the question of the “loss of immigration control” that came with Brexit, as Labour grapples with continuing public concern over the issue, and suggested Brussels recognised this.The UK is excluded from Eurodac, a database that holds biometric and ID data to identify asylum seekers and irregular migrants, and exited the Dublin regulation, a legal mechanism to return refugees to the European country through which they had first entered or transited.But while the prime minister told MPs a return to free movement was “not on the table” in his discussions with the EU, and said he would honour Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines, he was unable to rule it out for a post-election future.Sources on both sides believe they will be able to get other issues over the line at the summit next month, suggesting that a food and phytosanitary agreement would have been reached in July if the summit had gone ahead on its original date.View image in fullscreenBarley fields in Flamborough, East Yorkshire.Photograph: Rebecca Cole/The GuardianIssues still to be resolved include a transition period for grains grown in the UK using recently approved fungicides not yet licensed in the EU. This would allow farmers harvesting this year to sell stockpiles next year even with the different regulations.The thorniest issue remains the youth mobility programme, allowing EU and British citizens under 30 to live, work or study in each other’s countries for up to three years. The two sides are at odds over the overall numbers, as well as the tuition fees students would pay at British universities.The biggest current risk to the UK of not aligning more fully with the EU is being locked out of the new Made in Europe initiative – aimed primarily at imports from China in strategic sectors such as renewable energy, nuclear and electric cars – which will block British-made components being used in EU supply chains.EU sources have insisted there can be no agreement on the issue with the UK at the summit, because the bloc is yet to agree its own position on the proposals. EU lawmakers hope to agree a position on a key proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, in December.View image in fullscreenAn assembly line at the Volkswagen Sachsen GmbH plant, Europe’s largest and first all-electric vehicle manufacturing facility, in Zwickau, Germany.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBut Brussels is, at least, open to discussing the issue, and it may be part of the summit statement – a joint text agreed by both sides. The UK has the support of the Netherlands, Poland and Italy for inclusion in the scheme, but France in particular has posed a stumbling block.Burnham acknowledged that Made in Europe presented “risks” to British manufacturing, perhaps in an attempt to address some concerns inside government that Downing Street hasn’t been prioritising the issue.He said: “It is important that we get to an arrangement here that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we’re both trying to deal with the same issue, which is Chinese exports and the damaging effect that is having on our industry.”Explore more on these topicsBrexitAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionEuropeImmigration and asylumForeign policyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say
Author: Henry Dyer
Headline: Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say
Content: Chris Bruni-Lowe (left) and Nigel Farage at a Mayfair restaurant in London in May 2023.Photograph: MJ PicturesView image in fullscreenChris Bruni-Lowe (left) and Nigel Farage at a Mayfair restaurant in London in May 2023.Photograph: MJ PicturesNigel FarageRevealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firmExclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources sayHenry DyerandRowena MasonMon 12 Oct 2026 09.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA close adviser toNigel Faragehad an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal.Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there.The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate.As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under whichquotes were publishedby the Washington Post newspaper.As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties.Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative.The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling.In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton andReform UKor Farage.He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team.Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations.Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.”Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”.Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”.The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer.Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor.The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures.Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry hadcleared the officials of breaking the law. The matter remains under police investigation.Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman.Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”.He is considered to be part of Farage’s inner circle and was close enough to the Reform UK leader to have been present on a trip to party donor Christopher Harborne’s Thai wellness retreat at Christmas in 2022 to mark the crypto billionaire’s 60th birthday.View image in fullscreenLeft to right: George Cottrell’s then girlfriend Georgia Toffolo, Chris Bruni-Lowe, Cottrell, an unidentified man, Christopher Harborne and Nigel Farage pictured together in December 2022.Other guests photographed at the meeting include Farage’s unpaid aide and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.In May 2023, Van Scheltinga and Bruni-Lowe were photographed having drinks at a Mayfair restaurant with Farage, Cottrell and Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPictured around a restaurant table in May 2023 from left: Nigel Farage, Chris Bruni-Lowe, George Cottrell, Neil Gallacher of gambling group Mansion Group, Philip van Scheltinga, Richard Tice, and Cottrell’s then girlfriend Georgia Toffolo.Photograph: MJ PicturesRodrigues said: “The existence of personal or social meetings involving individuals associated with the company does not establish a corporate relationship between Redfield & Wilton Strategies and Reform UK.”While much of Redfield & Wilton’s published polling related to voter intentions in the UK and the US, sources said Bruni-Lowe had its staff develop a “dossier” on local authority performance between autumn 2024 and spring 2025.One source said he suggested the firm’s work could be sold to political parties, and that Bruni-Lowe appeared “obsessed” with the dossier. Research by employees included freedom of information requests to councils to find expenditure on translation services.Rodrigues said the FOI project was a “commercial research project” and translation services were just one of “several dozen categories” examined by the company in a project led by Van Scheltinga. He added that none of the research was supplied to Reform or Farage.The company’s other work, sources said, included polling in Montenegro, Hungary, Hong Kong and the Bahamas, as well as research about attitudes in the UK to gold and cryptocurrencies.Employees were not always told exactly how their work would be used. According to one former employee, they were told their work on a foreign election would be for the Telegraph, but the polling never appeared in the newspaper. Another said they believed their work on cryptocurrencies was for a client.Get in touchContact Henry Dyer about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Henry using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. Once you've set yourself up, to send a message to Henry  please click on the 'Change Recipient' button, then click on Journalists, then choose Henry Dyer.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailhenry.dyer@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreOne unusual piece of work by the company was an October 2021 submission to an inquiry into central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) carried out by the House of Lords economic affairs committee. The company cited polling it said “was self-funded internally by Redfield & Wilton Strategies Ltd for the purpose of this submission”.The submission said the scepticism of the British public over the UK government’s capacity for innovation meant “it is strategically important that alternatives to a CBDC from the private sector, including those that are already in use, are also given the opportunity to be developed further”.According to a person who worked at the company at the time of the submission, “all of the crypto stuff came down from Chris [Bruni-Lowe]”.One online profile for Rodrigues, a solicitor based in London, refers to him holding a directorship of an “innovative market research firm”. However, according to former employees, he had a limited role in the day-to-day running of Redfield & Wilton. One source said that at a rare in-person meeting Rodrigues was “paraded around on a laptop on a Zoom call”.Van Scheltinga was frequently quoted giving analysis of the company’s polling and wrote columns for the Times and Telegraph.Van Scheltinga was the listed contact for the company with the British Polling Council, the trade body for pollsters, but one industry source said he never attended BPC meetings. This led to demands from the BPC for a representative of the group to appear before them: that was ultimately Rodrigues, the nominal director, who maintained “total silence”, according to the industry source.Bruni-Lowe declined to comment. Van Scheltinga did not respond to requests for comment.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKOpinion pollsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian leader says he was surprised by Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement, posted as Russian drones hit Kyiv
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Ukrainian leader says he was surprised by Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement, posted as Russian drones hit Kyiv
Content: Cars burning after a Russian strike on a residential neighbourhood in Kharkiv on Sunday.Photograph: Andrii Marienko/APView image in fullscreenCars burning after a Russian strike on a residential neighbourhood in Kharkiv on Sunday.Photograph: Andrii Marienko/APUkraineZelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continueUkrainian leader says he was surprised by Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement, posted as Russian drones hit KyivAndrew Roth,Jennifer RankinandLuke HardingMon 12 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 06.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.”On Sunday, Trumpannounced an “energy ceasefire”between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones.Russia then launched a “targeted attack” on a Kharkiv power station hours later, as much of Kyiv was plunged into darkness. “It’s clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said.10:22Trump rewards Putin and betrays Ukraine with Russia diesel deal - The LatestRussia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said. “It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added.Zelenskyy also suggested that Ukraine’s recent counter-strikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex had reduced the number of bots posting messages in Europe and the US. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said.The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation.The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday, when Trump announced he waslifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post.View image in fullscreenRescuers work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine, on Monday. At least 12 people, including one child, were injured, according to the state emergency service.Photograph: Sergey Kozlov/EPAEarlier a furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraineneeded a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries.“We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.”Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision tolift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.“This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.”Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war.Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries.View image in fullscreenA rescuer takes shelter in an entrance of a Kharkiv apartment building amid the threat of another Russian drone strike on Monday.Photograph: Sofiia Gatilova/ReutersThe US president has blamed the high price of diesel on Ukraine’s attacks, rather than the global shock to energy markets from the US war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz.According to the Financial Times, the US ⁠has threatened ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons, paid for by its European allies. The White House has also said it could turn off intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halts its ‌long-range strikes on ​Russian oil refineries.The Kyiv Independent newspaper saidUkraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper.Ben Hodges, the former head of US forces in Europe, described the energy ceasefire “deal” as a fantasy and “a classic ‘Trumpian’ announcement of something not based on any facts.”“No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”.He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyRussiaEuropeDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: UK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incident
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: UK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incident
Content: A B‑1B Lancer bomber at RAF Fairford. A week after the incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers stationed at the base.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenA B‑1B Lancer bomber at RAF Fairford. A week after the incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers stationed at the base.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersUK security and counter-terrorismIran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says BurnhamUK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incidentDan SabbaghDefence and security editorMon 12 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month.The prime minister told MPs the UK would bring further sanctions against Tehran and the IRGC in the aftermath of an ambiguous episode that, despite over a fortnight of police investigation, has yet to lead to anybody being charged.After RAF Fairford incident, how big a threat to the UK is Iran?Read moreAddressing parliament on Monday about events at RAF Fairford, Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated inIran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards.”22:58Was Burnham right to talk about Russian interference in Brexit? | Politics WeeklyIn a statement to the House of Commons, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, told MPs that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had summoned the Iranian ambassador over the Fairford incident and that the government had imposed sanctions on two individuals accused of spying in Europe and the US.“He [Miliband] will condemn Iran’s continued attempts to undermine our safety.
