We are also sanctioning two individuals involved in conducting espionage and attacks on behalf of the government of Iran in Europe and the US, and we will not hesitate to take further action to restrict Iran’s capacity to threaten international security,” she said.Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found.However, the incident was followed by thewithdrawal of 12 B-1 bombersa week later, amid reports that the US was concerned about a possible drone attack on a base it had used to attack Iran during the Middle East war in the spring and summer.Burnham’s brief remarks were a step up from previous comments. The prime minister had said in the days after the incident that there were “strong indications” Iran had played a part – but now appeared confident enough to apportion responsibility.A joint statement from the UK, US and other European allies, released by the Foreign Office, added that the UK “has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors”.​However, despite his statement, it remains unclear what the authorities think happened at Fairford. Someexperts have speculated it was a “feint”to demonstrate that Iran could in theory attack a relatively open site.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish sources have repeatedly maintained that Iran lacks the capability to launch what would be a sophisticated drone attack, but the incident appears to have unnerved the US, which is worried about the security of its bases in Europe.The incident at Fairford comes after what the UK, in the joint statement, said was a recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and US interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).Though the US has detained and indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, whom it accuses of being behind the HAYI group, there is evidence to suggest that Iran-linked attacks have continued.A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb.Prosecutors told a magistrates court the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismIranGloucestershireUS militaryDefence policyMilitaryAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Coventry land long-awaited home win as Mfuni seals rout of Newcastle | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Jack Rudoni, Sidiki Cherif, Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni scored as Coventry beat Newcastle 4-1, their first home top-flight victory since 2001
Author: Peter Lansley
Headline: Jack Rudoni, Sidiki Cherif, Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni scored as Coventry beat Newcastle 4-1, their first home top-flight victory since 2001
Content: Stephen Mfuni reacts after scoring Coventry’s fourth goal against Newcastle.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenStephen Mfuni reacts after scoring Coventry’s fourth goal against Newcastle.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAPremier LeagueCoventry land long-awaited home win as Mfuni seals rout of NewcastlePeter Lansleyat the Coventry Building Society ArenaMon 12 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf ever validation is needed for attack being the best form of defence, Frank Lampard can call this game up on Wyscout. Coventry climbed out of the relegation zone to the heady heights of 14th place after their second successive win showcased the benefits of their manager’s willingness to balance risk with reward.Jack Rudoni’s early penalty underscored a sense of positivity that was enhanced by an even quicker goal at the start of the second half from Sidiki Cherif and not unduly dimmed by Sven Botman’s howitzer making it 2-1.Coventry City 4-1 Newcastle United: Premier League – liveRead moreLate goals from the substitutes Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni allowed promoted Coventry to pull away from a Newcastle side who, after a strong start to the season, also lost their last away game atLeeds by this scoreline.Newcastle could have gone fourth in thePremier Leaguewith victory but despite missing several chances they could not argue with the defeat. As their manager, Matthias Jaissle, said: “There were elements in both boxes where we need to step up and do better. Those fine margins can make all the difference.”Even when Botman had reduced the deficit with 20 minutes remaining and Newcastle threatened to take charge, Coventry left two or three players up on the halfway line. It could be perceived as a bold and brave move and Lampard, who wants supporters to be entertained throughout this first season back in the elite since 2000/01, deserves credit. On other days they might come unstuck but here it was a case of he who dares wins.Not that he was ready to take the plaudits. “It probably means I didn’t manage to scream well enough to tell one or two of them to get back,” the Coventry manager said. “But at times we do certainly leave one or two players up the pitch because I think it will occupy their defenders. And in this [kind of] game of transition, sometimes you can defend with eight players.”View image in fullscreenFrank Lampard is delighted by Coventry’s win.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersIt was 25 years since John Hartson had last scored a home Premier League goal for Coventry. So there was a momentous feel to the occasion when Rudoni stepped up to take his penalty in the sixth minute.After three weeks of international football had left Sky Blues fans longing for more following theirvictory at Nottingham Forest, the atmosphere went up another notch when Lukas Hornicek, hesitant when coming out to palm the ball away from Ephron Mason-Clark, brought Cherif down as they contested the loose ball.Coventry, for all their summer signings, feel very united after 18 successful months under Lampard, culminating in their Championship triumph. This sense of community was underlined as Rudoni lifted his shirt to show the message “Get well soon Nan” after scoring his penalty.Rudoni’s grandmother is in hospital after suffering a heart attack. “He’s such a great lad,” Lampard said. “I’ve been there for him. He’s so close with his family. So I’m pleased he could have that moment for them.”Newcastle had plenty of space and ball just about every time they attacked. But the risk-and-reward strategy meant Coventry were dangerous in the extreme on the transition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey had Bobby Thomas to thank for denying Newcastle twice shortly before the interval. Firstly the centre-back headed off the line after Jacob Murphy turned Harvey Barnes’s superb cross past Carl Rushworth.Then when Matias Fernandez-Pardo raced clear, rounded Rushworth and shot goalwards, Thomas had recovered sufficiently to clear. On his first Premier League start since signing from Fenerbahce for £21m in the summer, Cherif deputised for the suspended Taiwo Awoniyi.The 19-year-old forward is evidently not the finished product but he has raw attributes from which Coventry can build. When Malick Thiaw headed out a long throw-in, Cherif swivelled to strike a crisp drive that swished through four pairs of plum-coloured stockings and beyond Hornicek’s grasping fingers.View image in fullscreenSidiki Cherif doubles Coventry’s lead with a rocket.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersThen Cherif should have made the game safe. Botman miscued Brandon Thomas-Asante’s cross but unmarked from six yards out Cherif clunked his shot wide. That miss briefly appeared crucial as Botman was allowed to wander forwards unchallenged before belting a shot into the top corner of Rushworth’s goal.Simms made it 3-1 in the 81st minute, however, after the excellent Thomas-Asante nicked the ball on the edge of the area for the striker to shoot home. There was still time for Thomas-Asante to fire against a post before victory was emphatically sealed when Mfuni twinkle-toed his way into the penalty area to strike in left-footed.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueCoventry CityNewcastle Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34 | RJ Mitte | The Guardian
description: Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation
Author: Mollie Reilly
Headline: Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation
Content: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte, who has died aged 34.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBreaking Bad actor RJ Mitte, who has died aged 34.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianRJ MitteRJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representationMollie ReillyMon 12 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 21.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBreaking Badactor RJ Mitte died on Monday aged 34, his representatives confirmed.Mitte died in Brownsville,Texas. No cause of death was given.“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocateRJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”The Brownsville Police Department said no foul play was suspected and the investigation into his death was ongoing. Cameron County justice of the peace, Cyndi Hinojosa told the Associated Press that an autopsy would be performed.From the age of 15, Mitte played Walter White Jr, the son ofBryan Cranston’s high school chemistry teacher turned drug kingpin, on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, which isoftencitedas one of the best television programs of all time.Mitte had cerebral palsy, a condition he shared with hisBreaking Badcharacter.In 2015, hespoke to the Guardianabout being a disabled actor who plays disabled characters.“You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have.”Mitte’s costars paid tribute to him after news of his death broke.Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said in a statement: “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed.”Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr’s uncle Hank Schrader,wroteon social media: “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”In addition to Breaking Bad, Mitte had roles on several series, including Switched at Birth and The Guardians of Justice. Just days before his death, he waspromotinghis new movie, Talking to Strangers, billed as a “romantic tragedy”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier this month, Mitteappearedon the Joe Vulpis Podcast, speaking in depth about his time on Breaking Bad. He noted his character was based on a real-life friend of the show’s creator,Vince Gilligan.“It really felt real playing this character and getting into the groove with this character,” Mitte said.Offscreen, Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.Born in 1992, Mitte was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. In a2016 interviewwith the Guardian, he said he found out he was adopted when he was eight years old.“My step-brother told me. He’d overheard my mum and my stepdad at the time talking about it, and he threw it in my face. But I didn’t really care. It didn’t seem relevant, because I never once in my life felt unloved or like I was a burden.”Explore more on these topicsRJ MitteBreaking BadUS televisionTelevisionDisabilityDramaCelebritynewsShareReuse this content

title: English councils warn of ‘catastrophic’ Send debts forecast to hit £10bn by 2028 | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of support
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of support
Content: Applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) have risen sharply since the government announced its proposals to change the system.Photograph: Don Tonge/AlamyView image in fullscreenApplications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) have risen sharply since the government announced its proposals to change the system.Photograph: Don Tonge/AlamySpecial educational needsEnglish councils warn of ‘catastrophic’ Send debts forecast to hit £10bn by 2028Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of supportPatrick ButlerandRichard AdamsMon 12 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCouncils are warning of potentially “catastrophic” debts, which are forecast to reach a record £10bn over the next 18 months, as a result of rapid growth in demand for special educational needs and disability (Send) support in English schools.Although the government recently cleared more than £5bn in historic council Send debts, asurge in requestshas led to authorities predicting they will have re-accrued that debt figure by April, and doubled it by 2028.The recent acceleration in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs), which mandate support for conditions such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD, is thought to partly reflect a rush by parents and schools tosecure supportbefore the government’s changes to Send provision take effect.The prospect of council finances being overwhelmed by schools’ Send spending reflects similar concerns in the NHS and the benefit system over the strain the rising prevalence of mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions has put on public services.graphic of Send deficit forecastThe government-commissioned Fonagy report, published last week, found the increase in these conditions wasreal and a cause of distressto many who have them, but the resulting demand for supportwould be unsustainablewithout introducing new ways to manage the pressure on public services.The County Councils Network (CCN), which published the forecasts on Tuesday, said the overspending was not the fault of councils and called on ministers to guarantee future Send debts run up by local authorities, some of whom would be otherwise left effectively bankrupt as a result of meeting their legal duties.Linden Kemkaran, the CCN’s Send spokesperson, said: “These deficits have not accumulated because councils have chosen to spend recklessly: they are the result of having to meet rapidly growing statutory demand, which has only intensified this year, without funding keeping pace.“If councils are left carrying billions of pounds of Send debt, it will not just be a problem for local authorities. Taxpayers and local communities will ultimately bear the consequences as councils face impossible choices about how to protect frontline services while managing debts that have accrued through no fault of their own.She added: “As well as councils absorbing skyrocketing costs, children and young people will face increasingly long waits for support and educational outcomes will continue to flatline. New ministers now need to provide certainty that they will deliver the full package of reforms needed to ensure the system works much better for young people, schools and councils.”The government’s reforms aim to gradually replace the current system in England with amore inclusive approach of Send supportin mainstream schools that in principle obviates the need for an EHCP. However, parents appear to be rushing to secure formal support now to avoid any future uncertainty.Without a ministerial guarantee to wipe future overspending, councils say they are at risk of bankruptcy when those accumulated debts – currently kept off town hall balance sheets under a special “override” arrangement with the Treasury – go back on to the books in April 2028 when the override is due to expire.Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in OfstedRead moreMinisters have agreed to pay 90% of English top tier councils’ Send debts accumulated to March 2026, but it is unclear how far future Send debts will be covered. Ministers have previously said future debt support would be “appropriate and proportionate” but that it would “not be unlimited”.The CCN said anything less than a ministerial commitment to pay down 90% of future Send debt would be a “financial catastrophe” for councils – and some authorities would struggle with solvency even if they retained just 10% of their Send debts.Publicly available internal reports by local authorities show a number are predicting overspends of more than £100m in 2026-27 alone. Hampshire county council is forecasting a £200m deficit for this year. Others include Surrey, East Sussex, Kent, Worcestershire and Norfolk county councils.The EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools.In January, the number of young people with EHCPs reached 718,000, after a 12.5% increase over the past 12 months. This was the largest year on year increase since the plans were introduced in 2014. An additional 1.3 million young people haveidentified special needs, according toofficial data.Many councils are anticipating annual double digit increases over the next three years, with several now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.The Fonagy report said the growth in EHCPs had “substantially outpaced the capacity” of the education system to respond. Of the 105,300 statutory assessments carried out in 2024, 94% resulted in the award of an EHCP.Owen Mapley, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said: “The continued escalation of Send deficits exposes a serious failure to align statutory responsibilities with funding levels.Local governmentchief financial officers have been calling attention to this disconnect for years as it undermines proper financial management practice.”A government spokesperson said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain, and have always recognised that both deficits and EHCP applications will continue to rise before our reforms are fully rolled out.“On top of grants to pay off 90% of council deficits, we’re investing billions to make sure every community has easy, early access to specialists like speech and language therapists, and so councils can deliver their tailored local reform plans.“Fixing the Send system will take time and councils will need further support with deficits, so we will set out the details before March 2028.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchool fundingSchoolsPublic financeLocal governmentAutismDepartment for EducationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann Widdecombe | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs
Content: The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced an independent review of the protective security provided by the state.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced an independent review of the protective security provided by the state.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/ReutersUK security and counter-terrorismMahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann WiddecombeHome secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPsRajeev SyalHome affairs editorMon 12 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecurity arrangements for high-profile public figures including politicians and members of the royal family are to be urgently reviewed afterthe killing of Ann Widdecombe, the home secretary has said.Shabana Mahmood said former MPs, party leaders who are not MPs, peers, former members of devolved parliaments and party spokespeople will also be offered police support.The UK’s protective security system will be re-examined to combat the growing risks of terrorism, extremism and state threats, as well as harassment and intimidation, Mahmood said.The review will be carried out by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former UK national security adviser, who will look at whether current security arrangements ensure there is adequate protection for those most at risk.This includes high-profile individuals such as members of the royal family, government ministers, MPs, locally elected representatives and other prominent individuals in British politics. His review will not include an assessment of individual cases.Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokesperson, wasfound dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with Widdecombe’s murder. He is also accused of “online reconnaissance” of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage’s home in south London on 19 April 2025 and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed.Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says BurnhamRead moreAddressing the Commons, Mahmood said that, regardless of the outcome of the investigation into an attempted break-in at Farage’s home, it is “clear there is insufficient protection for those who serve”.“I can therefore announce today that I will expand, with immediate effect, police support to political figures who are not currently members of parliament,” she said. “This will include former members of parliament, peers and party spokespeople, giving them access to a named police officer, as well as help with wider security measures.Mahmood added: “Today I also announce an independent root-and-branch review of the protective security provided by the state to those in public life. We can defeat those who mean us harm, but we are strongest when we act together.“In a more dangerous world, we are faced by threats from without and within that target our democracy and our way of life. In response, we are adapting and strengthening our defences.“As ever, I commend the work of the police and our security services, who labour in silence to keep us safe. And I’m sure the whole house joins me in offering thanks to them for that vital life-saving work.”Lovegrove will look at how existing security is provided, whether funding and other measures are being used effectively and proportionately, and how decision-making can be more consistent in response to threat and risk.Robert Buckland is conducting a separate review into themurder of Sir David Amess MP, which will consider the security of MPs in their constituencies.In May’s local elections the Electoral Commission found that 55% of all candidates experienced some form of harassment and intimidation, as did the same proportion of candidates at the 2024 general election.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismShabana MahmoodAnn WiddecombePoliceCounter-terrorism policyCrimeHouse of CommonsnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history | The Archers | The Guardian
description: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures
Content: The Archers’ current recording studio at the BBC Mailbox in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Archers’ current recording studio at the BBC Mailbox in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe ArchersBBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year historyPlans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measuresMichael SavageMedia editorMon 12 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is set to stop recordingThe Archersin Birmingham for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after scrapping plans for a radio drama theatre that was to be the new home of the world’s longest-running soap opera.A pledge to move recordings to the so-called Tea Factory, the BBC’s new Birmingham hub in Digbeth, has become the latest victim of thecorporation’s £500m cuts plan.While the soap’s production team are still scheduled to make the move, theBBCis now looking to record it at an existing UK studio.It will also consider private studios in theWest Midlands, but BBC insiders are already concerned that ending its Birmingham-based recordings and separating the actors from the production crew will have an impact on the show.Production staff regularly engage with the actors at the last minute to tweak scripts and storylines, raising concerns that their being in different places will stifle creativity.“It is going to weaken the show,” said a source. “It will change the DNA of the show.”BBC axes long-running Radio 4 show You and Yours in push towards podcastsRead moreMoving the recording of The Archers from the BBC’s existingBirminghambase, The Mailbox, to the Tea Factory was due to take place in 2028.In an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth.“Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK.“To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings.“The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.”The show has been associated with Birmingham since it started in 1951. Sources said it remained part of the cultural fabric of the city, and the show employs local writers and freelancers.However, others said the show’s recording schedule meant actors were only in the studio for about eight days a month, while many of the cast live across the UK.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome now fear recordings will default to London and that the show’s staff will eventually follow. However, the BBC has been clear that production staff will move to the new Birmingham headquarters as planned.It is not clear whether Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, was aware of the plans. Boosting BBC production outside London has regularly been at the top of her agenda.It is a sign that even some of the BBC’s most revered titles are being affected by cuts, with more announcements expected in the coming days. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has already faced anger from staff who believe more of the corporation’s manager class should be targeted instead.BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cutsRead moreA BBC spokesperson said: “We recognise and value The Archers’ longstanding relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme’s future, and The Archers production team will remain in their current home in the Mailbox and move, as planned, to the Tea Factory in Digbeth in early 2028.“However, after careful consideration, as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, we are no longer building a new recording studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory.“We’re currently assessing the BBC’s existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands to find a more cost-effective solution.”Explore more on these topicsThe ArchersBirminghamRadio dramaWest MidlandsSoap operaRadioPublic service broadcastingnewsShareReuse this content

title: After two tragic incidents in months does safety at English zoos need a rethink? | Zoos | The Guardian
description: Even though a man was mauled to death by a tiger and three-year-old was attacked in crocodile enclosure, experts say public protection is robust
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Even though a man was mauled to death by a tiger and three-year-old was attacked in crocodile enclosure, experts say public protection is robust
Content: Crocodiles in an enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst zoo in Cambridgeshire.Photograph: Dorota "Dee" Trajdos/ReutersView image in fullscreenCrocodiles in an enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst zoo in Cambridgeshire.Photograph: Dorota "Dee" Trajdos/ReutersZoosAfter two tragic incidents in months does safety at English zoos need a rethink?Even though a man was mauled to death by a tiger and three-year-old was attacked in crocodile enclosure, experts say public protection is robustHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondent andGeorge Francis LeeMon 12 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a busy Saturday afternoon at a zoo in Yorkshire, visitors looked on in horror as a man climbed into a tiger habitat, minutes after posing for a photograph beside it.Eyewitnesses said he scaled a metre-high viewing barrier, before dropping into the enclosure below, overpowering a woman who tried to pull him back.The resident 30-stoneSiberian tiger, named Altai, was seen pawing at the man, who was dragged away, and laterdeclared dead at the scene.Yorkshire Wildlife Park remained closed on Monday, while a City ofDoncastercouncil spokesperson said the local authority had launched a health and safety investigation into the matter.View image in fullscreenYorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster.Photograph: Dave Higgens/PAIt marked the second serious incident at a UK zoo in just a few months. In June, athree-year-old boy was seriously injuredafter being attacked by one or more crocodiles when heended up in the enclosureat Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire.View image in fullscreenPolice on duty at Johnsons of Old Hurst after a man was arrested after a three-year-old boy ended up in a crocodile enclosure at the zoo in June.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PABut experts have said that recent events do not reflect on zoo practices, and may instead point to issues with human behaviour, or mental health or support services.“These were two really terrible events, but rather than being about zoos themselves, I wonder whether they could reflect wider issues in society,” said Amy Dickman, professor of wildlife conservation and the director of WildCRU at the University of Oxford.“Given how many millions of zoo visits there are in a year, these are vanishingly rare instances, although of course that doesn’t negate how deeply tragic they are when they occur,” Dickman, an expert in big cat conservation, added.“I would not conclude that there was a major issue with zoo safety – the harsh reality is that it is virtually impossible for zoos to stop people who are very determined to breach safety measures.”In the Cambridgeshire incident, the boy was allegedly thrown into the crocodile enclosure. Police arrested a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder at the time of the incident, and police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”.This week, a spokesperson for Cambridgeshire police said the investigation was still under way and the suspect had been bailed until 17 December.“Two incidents have happened in the last few months, which is obviously really upsetting and distressing for the sector, but they are actually very, very rare,” Jo Judge, the chief executive at British and Irish Association ofZoosand Aquariums (BIAZA), said.There are hundreds of zoos, aquariums and animal attractions in the UK, and about 32 million people visit BIAZA member zoos and aquariums across Britain and Ireland every year.“The industry has already put in place so many safety measures that it is not being seen as a rising problem or something that we’re not doing enough about. These are just very unusual and very rare incidences,” she added.“It is unbelievable that these two incidents have happened so closely together.”Dickman said that because animals kept in enclosures do not come into contact with humans as those in the wild may do, “for someone to walk into that environment is probably far more dangerous, ironically, than if you were out in the wild with animals that were used to navigating those spaces alongside people.”She said she had “never visited a zoo in the UK and thought ‘this is dangerous’,” adding there was “layer upon layer of protection against people interacting with dangerous animals” and that “you do have to do it very intentionally”.All zoos in the UK must be licensed and follow strict safety procedures to protect their animals and human staff and visitors, with guidelines in place for zoo enclosures, including for sizing and perimeter fences.“There is no accidental falling into a category 1A dangerous animal enclosure, it just doesn’t happen – it’s not designed that way,” said Campbell Murn, a lecturer in conservation science at University of Reading, who until recently sat on Defra’s Zoos expert committee.Category 1A refers to a high-risk species kept in zoos that is capable of causing a human fatality, and includes rhinos, elephants, great apes and big cats.“In terms of preventing intentional entry to enclosures, there’s locks, there’s barriers,” he added. “But short of putting an electric fence [up], which of course has its own health and safety considerations, the protocol remains patrolling staff keeping an eye out for unusual behaviour.“It’s simply not possible though, at an attraction like Yorkshire Wildlife Park that gets hundreds of thousands – if not over a million – visitors a year to keep an eye on everybody all the time.”He said safety had to be balanced against visitor experience, so zoo-goers don’t get “a sense of walking into an electrified fence fortress where they can’t do anything other than look through heavy steel bars”, and used the analogy of “a determined thief”.“If a determined thief wants to get in your house, they’re going to get in your house,” he said. “You can mitigate risk to a certain point but there’s sometimes no stopping events from happening, unfortunately.”Paul Rose, a senior lecturer in psychology (animal behaviour) at the University of Exeter, also said that “public behaviour can be unpredictable, as we all know”.“There will be mitigation in place, such as high fencing, standoff barriers, signage and explanation and a code of conduct for how to behave at the zoo (and for visitors to take responsibility for their actions),” he said. “Risk assessments will also be undertaken regularly.”Following Saturday’s incident, he said he imagined that “lessons will be learned regarding how zoos try to manage the behaviour of the public and how they instruct visitors to conduct themselves in and around enclosures”.“The majority of visitors behave in a way respectful of the animal and environment at the zoo, but there is always a risk of rogue or unusual behaviour, and this will continue to be risk assessed and part of zoo personnel training,” he added.Experts did say they had some concerns about the role the internet and social media may play in encouraging people to interact with wild animals.Judge said: “We do unfortunately see on social media quite often videos of people, mostly in other countries, entering the enclosures with some of these animals, and that is something that we do not support at all.”“They are dangerous wild animals and they should be respected as such,” she added, but said it wasn’t something UK zoos are “hugely concerned about” as they “will make it very, very clear that these are dangerous animals”.But Dickman said that online content was definitely of concern. “Though it may not have been a factor here, it is worrying how many videos exist online of people playing around with tigers and lions,” she added.“AI has made that even worse, and the illusion that people should have those interactions with wild, dangerous animals can be really damaging.”Explore more on these topicsZoosAnimalsSouth YorkshireDoncasterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Being Muslim After 9/11 review – other journalists wouldn’t dare to air this | Television | The Guardian
description: Mobeen Azhar isn’t afraid to tackle hard topics in a brilliant documentary about the rise of Islamophobia – even when it involves hearing criticism about his own decisions
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: Mobeen Azhar isn’t afraid to tackle hard topics in a brilliant documentary about the rise of Islamophobia – even when it involves hearing criticism about his own decisions
Content: A fascinating discussion … Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan in Being Muslim After 9/11.Photograph: BBC/ForestView image in fullscreenA fascinating discussion … Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan in Being Muslim After 9/11.Photograph: BBC/ForestTV reviewTelevisionReviewBeing Muslim After 9/11 review – other journalists wouldn’t dare to air thisMobeen Azhar isn’t afraid to tackle hard topics in a brilliant documentary about the rise of Islamophobia – even when it involves hearing criticism about his own decisionsJack SealeMon 12 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2024, the journalist Mobeen Azhar made a documentary calledSmall Town, Big Riotthat ought to have been highly influential, but, in our atomised modern media landscape, wasn’t. He deconstructed how anti-immigrant racists, radicalised by online propaganda, lies and hearsay, end up on the streets perpetrating shocking violence and rioting against a largely imaginary foe.Azhar’s new film tackles a wider, thornier problem and is less satisfying as a result. But in his willingness to debate hard topics – even if it means hearing difficult arguments, some of which are aimed at him personally – he is still provoking thoughts and airing views that better-known journalists would never go near.“There was a time, 25 years ago, when being British and Muslim was … OK, you know?” he says. “We were on the cover of magazines and getting elected to parliament. We even captained the England cricket team. And then this happened.” Cut to footage of the World Trade Center’s twin towers exploding on 11 September 2001.The world has not been the same since– and life for British Muslims certainly hasn’t.In the film, Azhar charts a quarter of a century of rising Islamophobia, his concern being how Muslims – and Muslim film-makers like him – have reacted. To do this, he teams up with an older documentarist, Masood Khan, who is the programme’s co-director and is often seen jammed into Azhar’s passenger seat wielding a handheld camera, to get those obligatory “musing while driving” shots. As the film develops, he becomes one of Azhar’s most important interlocutors, but he sticks to his main job as Azhar makes his first visit, to the Birmingham house of Salma Yaqoob.View image in fullscreen‘The fire is still the same’ … Salma Yaqoob and Azhar.Photograph: BBC/ForestYaqoob’s career in politics began when she was spat at in the street soon after 9/11, having previously been just “Salma, a mum at the school gate”. In 2003, she helped to organisethe biggest political demonstration in British history, against the forthcoming invasion of Iraq. “It was an amazing day,” she remembers. “Such a sea of humanity. And yeah, there was that hope.” Azhar comments that her weary countenance suggests the hope has now gone. “The fire is still the same,” Yaqoob says, although her eyes say different.While the consequence for Muslims in Iraq was that they were killed in large numbers, the less serious repercussions here were still deeply troubling. Azhar explains how radical Islamist agitators took advantage when their warnings about protests going unheeded were proved to be correct; they began preaching loudly against integration and in support of violent resistance. At the time, Azhar and Khan made films about the phenomenon; now, to their great credit, they are willing to listen to people who think that was a treacherous mistake.Alyas Karmani in Bradford and Farasat Latif in Luton are community leaders who have worked to deradicalise local Muslim men. Karmani is combative and Latif gentle, but both accuse Azhar of fanning the flames of Islamophobia by helping to boost an unrepresentative fringe. “The problem is the disproportionate publicity these people got,” Latif says. “They were given a platform on mainstream media because they fed into that narrative, post-9/11 and -7/7, that there was this huge Islamic threat.”View image in fullscreenAzhar with Ivan, a reformed former EDL organiser.Photograph: BBC/ForestThese meetings lead Azhar and Khan to debate their film-making careers. On the one hand, a journalist holds a mirror up to society and can’t be expected to ignore inconvenient truths; on the other, journalism is a series of choices about what to cover and what to ignore, and the choice of where to put one’s limited resources can have profound effects.Azhar goes to Lowestoft to meet Ivan, a reformed former organiser for the far-right English Defence League. He says the EDL used the 2007 Dispatches film Undercover Mosque and Stacey Dooley’s 2012 BBC documentary My Hometown Fanatics as recruitment videos and that he was radicalised by the media appearances of the much-quoted extremist preacher Anjem Choudary, nowserving a life sentencefor running a banned terrorist organisation.Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfoldRead moreAzhar and Khan’s fascinating discussion about that becomes, in the film’s closing scenes, laden with sad exhaustion. Azhar admits to feeling worn down by the events of 2017, when terror atrocities atWestminster Bridge,London Bridgeand theManchester Arenaprovoked a retaliatoryattack on a north London mosque. In 2026, as Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, agitates against Islam on the streets of London, Khan doesn’t go to cover it, to Azhar’s angry dismay. He’s had enough.Azhar keeps reporting on the ground, trying and failing to make sense of the chaos outside Yaxley-Lennon’s appearance at a cursed Oxford Union debate. Seeing that something has gone badly wrong is easy; pinpointing what could or should have been done to stop it is not. Life as a British Muslim, meanwhile, only gets harder.Being Muslim After 9/11 aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival | Wikipedia | The Guardian
description: Just 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Just 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?
Content: Fighting the good fight … Sandi Toksvig.Photograph: Nordin Catic/Getty Images For the Cambridge UnionView image in fullscreenFighting the good fight … Sandi Toksvig.Photograph: Nordin Catic/Getty Images For the Cambridge UnionPass notesWikipediaIs Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rivalJust 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?Mon 12 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Wikipedia.Age:25.Appearance:Patronising and deeply biased.Is this because you haven’t got your own page?Well, yes. But these aren’t my words. They’re the words ofSandi Toksvig.Butithas65marticles across more than300languages!It’s the largest knowledge resource ever assembled!That may be, but it isn’t very good at women.According toToksvig?Yes – and she’s very serious about it. As we speak, she is travelling the world trying to raise money to build something better.She is?Yes. Along with the University of Cambridge, she hopes that herMappa Mundiproject will be an “interactive digital atlas where we can find a home for the vast amount of knowledge that is currently sidelined or deleted”.And a lot of the sidelined or deleted knowledgeis about women?It is. She cites the case of Donna Strickland, a Canadian physicist who repeatedly had her draft biographiesrejected by Wikipedia, until she won a Nobel prize for her work.Awkward.But it goes broader. By the Wikimedia Foundation’sown estimate, only 19% of Wikipedia biographies concern women. Toksvig puts this down to the site being edited by “mostly white, middle-aged, European men who have both the time and the technology”,she told Cheltenham literature festivalthis weekend.I didn’t know that.Its content is weighted heavily towards wealthy countries. In 2013, for instance, the Oxford Internet Institute discovered that Wikipedia contained more coverage of Germany than ofAfrica and South America combined.Isn’t Wikipedia too leftwing anyway?Oh God, are you Elon Musk? This is a claim he has repeated for the last couple of years, to the extent of calling it “Wokepedia”.And what did he do about it?He started his own version –an AI-powered alternative called Grokipedia.And is it better?A paper published in November 2025discovered that Grokipedia articles are 13 times more likely to contain a source blacklisted by the English Wikipedia community.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat’s a blacklisted source?The paper pointed out that, at the time of its publication, Grokipedia included 42 citations forthe banned neo-Nazi website Stormfront.Yeesh. Bring on Mappa Mundi!Indeed, Toksvig’s version has better intentions. If nothing else, hopefully it will update Wikipedia’s list ofpeople who died on the toiletto include more women.Do say:“Wikipedia is systemically biased.”Don’t say:“At last, something Elon Musk andSandi Toksvigcan agree on.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsWikipediaPass notesWomenInternetSandi ToksvigfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nina review – a riveting series of horribly invasive auditions for The Seagull | Stage | The Guardian
description: Women up for a role as Chekhov’s aspiring actor navigate their meetings with a needling director in a tense show
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Women up for a role as Chekhov’s aspiring actor navigate their meetings with a needling director in a tense show
Content: ‘Tell me your trauma’ … Rowan Polonski as Goran and Samantha Begeman as Nina 02.Photograph: Ali WrightView image in fullscreen‘Tell me your trauma’ … Rowan Polonski as Goran and Samantha Begeman as Nina 02.Photograph: Ali WrightStageReviewNina review – a riveting series of horribly invasive auditions for The SeagullBattersea Arts Centre, LondonWomen up for a role as Chekhov’s aspiring actor navigate their meetings with a needling director in a tense showKate WyverMon 12 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmile. Introduce yourself. Say you’re such a big fan. Now do whatever he tells you. These are the unspoken rules the women follow as they take turns auditioning in Caroline Williams’ discomforting, rage-fuelled production about men and power and rotting winged roadkill.The women are auditioning for the role of Nina, the aspiring actor in Chekhov’s The Seagull, in an experimental production directed by sombrely pretentious wunderkind Goran (a brooding Rowan Polonski). Using live-feed cameras in his show, he is the type of director to dismiss the need for an intimacy coordinator while claiming credit for having one in the room.As the women file through, Goran’s requests to his Ninas (Maya Bartley O’Dea, Nina Bowers, Samantha Begeman and Gemma Barnett) become increasingly invasive. They slide from small, needling questions that might be deemed permissible from a truth-seeking visionary, to commands that are so terrible they could crack a person in two. Tell me your trauma, he demands. Show me what that looks like. The women are eager to please, eager to work, and Goran has the power to make them a star. Watching on, writer Tim (Joseph Payne) is a timid bystander, reading in for sour, lovesick Konstantin as Chekhov’s play slips in and out of both focus and reality.View image in fullscreenDiscomforting … Nina Bowers as Nina 03.Photograph: Ali WrightAs tension builds, our play, co-directed by Williams and Deborah Pearson, grows in scale and beauty too. Bowers’ exquisite, harrowing birth scene splits open the show’s depths of earned fury, while Begeman has a distressing masturbation scene. Projected loud and large across the stage, the latter is almost too hard to watch, but this show demands we bear witness.The final switch of power is an artistic act of wish fulfilment. It may be what we would dream of for these women but it rings hollow for the world the show has so carefully and grimly constructed. Williams and Pearson’s unflinching direction is most compelling in its bleak brutality. Why would any woman want to be an actor?At Battersea Arts Centre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageBattersea Arts CentreAnton ChekhovTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘When it went double platinum, Andy Burnham gave us the award’: how Courteeners made Not Nineteen Forever | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: ‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’
Content: ‘If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar in pubs for ever’ … Liam Fray of the Courteeners.Photograph: Edd Westmacott/Avalon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar in pubs for ever’ … Liam Fray of the Courteeners.Photograph: Edd Westmacott/Avalon/Getty ImagesHow we madeCulture‘When it went double platinum, Andy Burnham gave us the award’: how Courteeners made Not Nineteen Forever‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’Interviews byDave SimpsonMon 12 Oct 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiam Fray, songwriter/vocals, guitarI had the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever before the band existed. They were in a little red book of poems and scribbles that got me a place on the creative writing course at the University of Salford. Most of what became the songs for our first album, St Jude, were in that book. As well as uni, I was working in a shop and spending five nights a week at the Night & Day bar in Manchester, but in a nightclub I’d be the dude scribbling in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off.Not Nineteen Forever was probably inspired by a specific incident, although I can’t remember it exactly. The first line, “She had to peel me off the pavement”, could have happened on many a night out then. “Front-crawled the crowd down the stairs” is because the staircase at the 42nd Street club was so tight you’d have to literally front-crawl over people. The chorus: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together”, sounds like the sort of thing somebody might have said to me, but it could easily have been me giving myself a telling off after waking up with a fuzzy head.‘I’m not famous. But I can’t go to the chippy’: Courteeners’ Liam Fray on filling stadiums, defying extinction – and wearing M&S pantsRead moreI got the chords when I was trying to work out Someday by the Strokes but got the finger positions muddled up. I’d taken a bag of washing to my parents’ house and was working on it in my old bedroom when my dad poked his head in and said: “It sounds all right, that.” Not Nineteen Forever was one of the last songs I wrote before I convinced my three best mates to form the band. I told them: “If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar on my own in Manchester pubs for ever.”You never think a song’s going to resonate 20 years later, but it’s become easily Courteeners’ most popular song. Ironically, it initially charted at No 19, but years later when it went double platinum Andy Burnham – who comes to our gigs – presented us with the award in theBritons Protection pub. The song’s taken on a poignant dimension now. At gigs I see our original fans together with their kids – who are 17, 18, 19 – and they’re all singing: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together.”Stephen Street, producerCourteeners had just been signed by a major label who asked me if I could go to Manchester to meet them as they had expressed interest in working with me. I saw them play in one of the university halls and it was mind-blowing. They already had a devoted following who were singing along with the lyrics the way Smiths audiences used to. I’d produced the Smiths, so it was right up my avenue.In the mid-2000s there’d been a resurgence of indie guitar bands: Arctic Monkeys, Kaiser Chiefs and Kasabian. In a way Courteeners were the last hurrah of that kind of hugely popular guitar group. The next thing I knew we were all in Olympic studios in London recording the album. I was excited to work with them. Not Nineteen Forever was a ready-made anthem and stood out, but so did Cavorting or What Took You So Long?With a band like Courteeners, you want to capture their performance. Like the best bands, they were like a little gang: us against the world. So we recorded live, only using click tracks to set the tempos. Their arrangements were short and concise and didn’t need much editing. Liam and Conan [Daniel Moores]’s guitar parts were intrinsic to the sound – I lent Conan a nice old vintage Telecaster – and I found the emotion in Liam’s voice really attractive.When they’d started out in a garage, Liam had to shout to be heard over the guitar, but in the studio I vaguely remember telling him he didn’t need to. When I saw the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever written down it hit me how good they were. “Older woman and an ever so slightly younger man” always makes me laugh. He was 19. The “older woman” was probably 21 or something.When the album came out I was perplexed by the lukewarm reaction from elements of the press – probably because it was another four lads with guitars – but it’s a really strong collection that I think still stands up today. The reissue of St Jude went to No 1 15 years after it first came out. I’d never had that happen before in my career: I was quite emotional.God Bless the Band – the best of Courteeners is out now Ignition Music. A UK tour begins on 6 November at First Direct Bank Arena, Leeds.Explore more on these topicsCultureHow we madeCourteenersIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearance  | Amelia Earhart | The Guardian
description: Researchers will head to remote Pacific atoll, but sceptics say satellite images unlikely to be of her aircraft
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Researchers will head to remote Pacific atoll, but sceptics say satellite images unlikely to be of her aircraft
Content: Amelia Earhart on the wing of her Electra before she and her navigator vanished during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator.Photograph: Albert Bresnik/APView image in fullscreenAmelia Earhart on the wing of her Electra before she and her navigator vanished during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator.Photograph: Albert Bresnik/APAmelia EarhartIs it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearanceResearchers will head to remote Pacific atoll, but sceptics say satellite images unlikely to be of her aircraftOliver HolmesMon 12 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA team of US researchers is approaching a remote Pacific atoll where they suspect the famed aviatorAmelia Earhartcrash-landed in 1937, in the latest attempt to crack one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century.The 17-person expedition was inspired by satellite images taken over several years showing a submerged object in the uninhabited island’s sandy lagoon – evidence dismissed by other longtime Earhart sleuths who say it is probably a fallen tree.These researchers – led by archaeologists who raised funding from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University–hope it will instead be revealed as the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. Separate aerial footage of the area suggested the submerged object has a metallic glint, the team say.“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” said the expedition’s leader, Richard Pettigrew, before he set sail this month. “Confirming the plane wreckage there would be the smoking-gun proof.”Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator. By that point, Earhart, 39, was already a celebrity and aviation pioneer, having broken several records including being the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight​.Blogger discredits claim Amelia Earhart was taken prisoner by JapanRead moreLocating the wreck of the twin-engine plane would confirm a long-held – but unproven – hypothesis that Earhart and Noonan ditched at the atoll of Nikumaroro, part of the archipelago country of Kiribati and about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.View image in fullscreenA 2001 satellite images shows Nikumaroro, an uninhabited Pacific coral atoll in the Republic of Kiribati.Photograph: ReutersThey were en route to Howland Island, about 400 miles north of Nikumaroro, when their plane ran low on fuel and disappeared.After a six-day sea voyage from Tarawa, the capital of Kiribati, the research group is expected to arrive on the uninhabited atoll on Tuesday local time and will spend several days searching for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image.The expedition says it has been lying there for several years, and is even visible in aerial photography dating back to 1938.Pettigrew, who heads the Archaeological Legacy Institute, a nonprofit organisation, raised funds for the mission with Purdue University in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and which funded her ill-fated final flight on the modified plane she called her “flying laboratory”. The university runs an airport andopenedan Amelia Earhart Terminal last year.The expedition builds on an already large body of evidence pinpointing the atoll as the location where the aviators went down. Much of it was gathered duringdozens of visits between 1989 and 2019 by teams from the US explorers group Tigher (The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery).View image in fullscreenLocating the wreck of the twin-engine plane would confirm a long-held hypothesis that Earhart and Noonan ditched at the atoll.Photograph: APTighar’s co-founder – and perhaps Earhart’s most well-known explorer – Ric Gillespie, said the Taraia Object was likely a dead pandanus tree, which is ​native to the area, that washed into the ​lagoon.Gillespie, who is the author of One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy, said he and other teams had visited the exact site where the object was located in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors.“There’s nothing there, or we would have found it,” he said inan interviewthis year. “If they suddenly discover that Amelia Earhart’s wreckage is there, I’ll be very surprised, but I’d be the first one to congratulate them. But I don’t think they are going to find anything.”While Tighar agrees the Electra made an emergency landing on the atoll, they believe it was washed off a reef and now probably lies undiscovered and in pieces in deep water off the island’s western end.Tighar’sversionof the mystery was that Earhart, and possibly Noonan, were marooned on Nikumaroro but survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating small fish and turtles. This theory is based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and 1930s-era artefacts, such as a jar of what is believed to be cosmetics freckle cream.The pair’s disappearance led to a large US government search, including a flyover of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.The Purdue mission says the object may not have been found by previous expeditions as it could have been covered with sand.Explore more on these topicsAmelia EarhartPacific islandsArchaeologynewsShareReuse this content

title: I will have more police officers of colour in the UK capital – and the culture wars won’t stop me doing it  | Mark Rowley | The Guardian
description: In our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It’s not favouritism, it is fairness – it’s essential, says Metropolitan police commissioner Mark Rowley
Author: Mark Rowley
Headline: In our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It’s not favouritism, it is fairness – it’s essential, says Metropolitan police commissioner Mark Rowley
Content: Mark Rowley chats to police officers during a visit to Stratford, east London with the Community Outreach Team, 28 October 2022.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenMark Rowley chats to police officers during a visit to Stratford, east London with the Community Outreach Team, 28 October 2022.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionMetropolitan policeI will have more police officers of colour in the UK capital – and the culture wars won’t stop me doing itMark RowleyIn our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It is not favouritism, it is fairness – and it’s essentialMark Rowley is commissioner of the Metropolitan policeMet chief says ‘toxicity’ around DEI will not stop him recruiting more Black and Asian officersMon 12 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 04.17 EDTShareEffective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent that stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.Last Monday, we launched a major recruitment campaign. We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity.London is the world’s greatest and most diverse and globally connected city.Nine million people live here. Hundreds of languages are spoken. The scale and complexity of policing London today is unlike anything Sir Robert Peel imagined when founding the Metropolitan police. Yet, in 1829, he recognised that policing success in a democracy relies onpublic approval, respect and cooperation as much as on “impartial service to the law”.We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us, or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences.An inclusive workforce is not a public relations exercise. It makes us better at protecting victims, catching criminals and preventing crime.We cannot provide an equally good response to all victims if our understanding of some Londoners is weaker than others. That is obvious when it comes to issues such as language barriers or supporting deaf people, but it is just as important when culture, experience or background may make a victim less willing to talk about sexual abuse, domestic violence or other traumatic crimes.When victims speak to officers and staff who understand them, and therefore feel fairly and impartially treated, we solve more crime and prevent more harm. When victims feel understood, they are more likely to come forward. When communities trust the police, they are more likely to report crime, share intelligence and support investigations. That trust underpins our effectiveness and goes to the very heart of policing by consent.View image in fullscreenLondon Metropolitan police officers patrol outside the Houses of Parliament in January this year.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAWe cannot police London effectively without the trust and confidence of the communities we serve. By listening to people’s lived experiences and working in partnership with communities, we can build stronger relationships and greater legitimacy. This is particularly important when using police powers, includingstop and search, where fairness, empathy and accountability are essential to maintaining public confidence and keeping London safe.We need men and women who can carry out surveillance, work undercover and operate effectively across London. We need officers and staff who can build trust with victims of violence against women and girls, who can connect with London’s communities and who bring different experiences, perspectives and skills to complex policing challenges.These are not ideological arguments. They are practical policing realities. And yet, despite progress, we are still not attracting talent equally. Some worry they will not fit in. Others are discouraged by family or friends. We have a responsibility to challenge those perceptions and remove those barriers. That is what our recruitment campaign is designed to do.Last year we had the most representative intake of recruits in our history. More women joined. More Londoners from ethnic-minority backgrounds joined. That is welcome progress.We want the talent from every corner of London to join our courageous and resilient teams and to close the gap with communities we have previously drawn least from.Some will wrongly suggest that increasing representation means lowering standards. Nothing could be further from the truth. For generations, talented people from some communities have faced barriers that limited opportunities to join policing or build a career within it. Tackling those barriers is not favouritism. It is fairness. Our standards are unchanged and uncompromising. By reaching further into communities where we have historically been underrepresented, we are ensuring we attract the widest and strongest possible pool of talent, helping us build a Met that truly reflects and understands every corner of London.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe want to be an inclusive organisation in which everyone has an equal chance to thrive. Fairness, not favour, should be at the heart of opportunity.I also want to see more women and people from underrepresented backgrounds putting themselves forward for some of the most exciting roles in British policing.That means firearms teams, the flying squad, counter-terrorism, specialist operations, public protection and major investigations.Public debate about inclusion has become increasingly polarised in recent years. Too often there is an assumption that inclusion and impartiality or merit are competing objectives. They are not.As commissioner I know the Met’s success, in protecting communities and helping London thrive, requires inclusivity as well as impartiality. We will not be blown off course by the culture wars. This is not an ideological choice. It is, as Peel’s founding vision for “policing by consent” described, an operational necessity.Mark Rowley is commissioner of the Metropolitan policeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer | The Guardian
description: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future, says Labour life peer Richard Hermer
Author: Richard Hermer
Headline: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future, says Labour life peer Richard Hermer
Content: ‘Left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with profound consequences for economies, security and human happiness.’Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with profound consequences for economies, security and human happiness.’Photograph: ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrongRichard HermerLet’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the futureMon 12 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareIn my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late.Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of theHugging Face hackand theresignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic, that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate.Dystopian and dehumanising: that’s what it felt like when I was interviewed by an AI assistantRead moreAI has enormous potential benefits for us all. It will be the source of mind-blowing advances in science and medicine, and offers hope for empowerment of some of the world’s most dispossessed people. Yet the risks we are now facing are truly staggering. I would put them in two very broad categories. The first is existential risk: quite literally the possibility that AI could kill billions, either because it enables terrible people to do terrible things – such as design and deploy biological weapons – or because AI itself determines it is more efficient to dispense with humans.The second category is existential challenge – that, left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with utterly profound consequences for economies, national security and human happiness. As Bill Gatesrecently wrote, the AI era will herald “one of the most turbulent times in human history”, noting that it will either be the greatest equaliser ever invented or the worst source of injustice. He is right. On its current trajectory, it risks simultaneously revolutionising the meaning and availability of productive work, while placing unimaginable power in the hands of not only two states (the US and China) but also a small number of individuals who control the tech giants.Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreThe plain fact is that we really don’t know what the precise degree of risk is, or the full panorama of the challenge. Part of the problem is that AI is rapidly developing to a level that humans simply do not understand and will reach a point at which – even if they do – they will no longer have the means to control it. Recall that the 2008 financial crash was caused in part because no humans really understood the web of financial transactions that were leading inexorably to disaster. What we face today, though, is on a different scale in terms of the complexity of the systems and the human agency over them, as well as the level of devastation that might be wrought.The startling levels of risk we are discussing should be completely unacceptable to all of us. In today’s age it is unthinkable that the manufacturer of a toaster would be allowed to market a product with a 10% chance of electrocuting you. The case for slowing down frontier AI before we are clear that the risks can be managed is blindingly obvious.AI needs rigorous regulation now. There is more regulation governing the safety of your fridge than the work being undertaken by frontier AI labs that threaten to wipe out your family. It is ludicrous to suggest the industry can be left to regulate itself. The AI companies and the financial markets underpinning them are incentivised to develop new iterations as quickly as possible, all of this fuelled by the geopolitics of the race between China and the US for dominance. The sight of President Trump and Elon Musk on the White House Lawn brandishing a “voluntary code” provided little in the way of reassurance.It will be international law that matters. While the UK has shown sterling leadership (started by Rishi Sunak, embraced by Keir Starmer and now reflected in Andy Burnham’spromotion of Kanishka Narayan to cabinet), the scale of the challenge requires international cooperation to have any effect. Tragically, this moment of peril arises at the very time in which the international rules-based order is under strain as never before. We need to double down on our engagement with the US and China while simultaneously developing our work with coalitions of like-minded states, as well as the tech sector, to address the threats.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim | Devi SridharRead moreDemocracy demands that we have an urgent public debate about what lies on the horizon in order to retain agency over our own futures – rather than allow them to be determined by the tech sector. None of this needs be inevitable. There is still time for governments and individuals to shape AI, ensuring it serves the public good. Since the Industrial Revolution, modern political movements have been moulded by the dynamic between the “means of production” and the interests of the people. We need new governing theories of who should control AI, how it is regulated and most importantly who it serves.We need urgent public conversations about the values that should guide decision making. We must shape the benefits of technological advances for the benefit of the many, rather than abdicate our future to the few. Leave it much longer and AI itself may deprive us of that power.Richard Hermer is a Labour life peer. He is a former attorney general for England and Wales and former advocate general for Northern Ireland.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
