title: Reform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every day | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: On the Today programme, his comments were disconnected, cliche-riddled and unremittingly stupid. But to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense is exactly the point, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: On the Today programme, his comments were disconnected, cliche-riddled and unremittingly stupid. But to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense is exactly the point, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘I cannot let it slide. It would be an insult to words.’Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘I cannot let it slide. It would be an insult to words.’Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersOpinionReform UKReform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every dayZoe WilliamsOn the Today programme, his comments were disconnected, cliche-riddled and unremittingly stupid. But to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense is exactly the pointMon 12 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTShareHad Reform merely announced its intention to suspend the asylum system for an entire parliamentary term, I’d have just ignored it. Even to dignify its policy platform with a response is to enter its alternate universe, in which it’s preparing for government. I prefer, if only fractionally, this universe we’re in, where the party hangs by a thread on the results of a parliamentary inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from a disinterested well-wisher.Had Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, gone on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme merely promising a British version of ICE, I still would have ignored it, not due to complacency, more due to a bone-penetrating despair that anyone, even he, would look at the US’s shadow militia, performing staged acts of unfettered violence and inhumanity, and think: “That looks cool – I bet I could get some political capital out of that.”However, as Yusuf laid out his arguments, they were so dumb, so random, disconnected, hammy and cliche-riddled, just so unremittingly stupid, that it turned out to be impossible not to react. I cannot let his nonsense slide. It would be an insult to words.An elderly woman, he said, waited 23 hours for an ambulance and the coroner found this contributed to her death. A Welsh 15-year-old’s educational attainment is belowthe OECD average. Many young people have to live with their parents into their 30s and 40s because they can’t afford rent. How does any of this relate to asylum seekers? Are they displacing elderly people in ambulance-demand? It seems unlikely, although if they are an immediate fix would be to stop masked gangs surrounding their living quarters and scaring the hell out of them. Those are ethno-nationalist thugs, of course, and nothing to do with Reform.High private rents, meanwhile, are not driven by asylum seekers, who have no right to work even if they arrive through a formal route, and as for Welsh 15-year-olds … well, we have some data here. They’re underperforming compared with English 15-year-olds, who are above the OECD average, indeed, above every other European nation, except Estonia and Ireland. If migrants destroy educational standards, how is Ireland managing to thrive? Why, with its very low number of asylum seekers, is Slovenia full of 15-year-olds who (no offence) suck at reading?None of it makes sense because none of it was meant to. It’s bilge punctuated by soothing mantras (“Charity begins at home”, Yusuf repeated), aimed at the half-asleep mind dreaming of a whites-only yesteryear. It had that in common with a Trump rally, but lacked his pizzazz. Reform can’t even do neo-fascist mimicry right.A word entered my social-media lexicon recently, which I wish I’d never had cause to look up, because I wish it wasn’t so useful: “agnotology” is the deliberate creation of ignorance, confusion and doubt. You can do it with misinformation and fake news, or you can do it with half-truths pouring out of bot factories, then leave an entire body politic tearing chunks out of itself as it seeks to establish whether the discursive environment has been deliberately polluted, or whether people are just mean and wrong nowadays. But you can also do it by simply talking nonsense, which we’ve seen writ large in party conference season and its aftermath.“Let’s build an impenetrable and state-of-the-art defence dome for £10bn, and call it theBritannia Shield, even though that’s already the name of a Oxfordshire roofing company,” says the party thatspent vastly more than thattrying and failing to buildthe HS2 train line. “Let’s stop all refugees coming from everywhere, until the conditions for every single Briton at every conceivable stage of life have been improved,” from the party whose only discernible allegiance is to its billionaire donors.The policies don’t even matter. Florid, premeditated stupidity is an end in itself, to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense, chase down every citizen who woke up in a good mood, with a scintilla of confidence about the future, and kill their mojo. The only defence is to hold your line. Insist on the difference between truth and untruth; guard your precious mojo with everything you’ve got.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan. title: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: The latest attack by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia may prove to be more calamitous for the region than the world imagines, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: The latest attack by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia may prove to be more calamitous for the region than the world imagines, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: A Houthi soldier watching a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana’a, Yemen, 9 October 2026.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenA Houthi soldier watching a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana’a, Yemen, 9 October 2026.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAOpinionYemenThe Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrongNesrine MalikThe latest attack by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia may prove to be more calamitous for the region than the world imaginesMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTShareOn Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking anddeadly attackon Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response.Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such asSaudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge.The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just over a year ago, when Iranfired missilesat an airbase in Qatar that hosts American troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. But even then there was adegree of warningand coordination that signalled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later in 2025, with no similar warning or choreography,Israel struck Doha, targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation – that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US.Then came Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war onIran, which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants – an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace.The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks havedisrupted the integration of these countriesinto the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securingFormula One, golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk.The result is a fractious unravelling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shia homelands,took over the capital city, Sana’a. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered ahumanitarian catastrophe.The wardeescalated in 2022with a de facto but unformalised division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran.But the 2026 war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory in order to gain control of thenow crucial Bab al-Mandab straitin the Red Sea.Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed governmentbombing its own airportin Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the west. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit. A senior Houthi officialsaid that Saturday’s attacktook place “so that the world understands” that Yemeni civilian infrastructure has been, and is being, targeted by the Saudis, gesturing towards that sense that Riyadh treats Yemeni lives as cheap.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn three years, Israel’s war on Gaza hasn’t just changed the Middle East, it’s changed the world | Steve BloomfieldRead moreFrom another perspective, what we are witnessing in the region is another consequence of Hamas’s 7 October attacks on Israel, and what followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The final piece that was stabilising the region’s tense equilibriums fell away when Trump decided that the safety and security of the US’s Gulf allies was secondary to his Iran “excursion”, as he called it. The limits of relying on the US security umbrella became clear both to allies and enemies.Last month, the Trump administrationrefused to extendmilitary assistance to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis, after a meeting of US officials with the Houthis, who assured them that they would not attack US ships in the Red Sea, only Saudi vessels. What is upon Saudi Arabia now is a long, intractable war with a resourceful and impassioned antagonist, one willing to sustain a high degree of pain in ways that Riyadh can’t match without orienting itself entirely towards war.If the 2015 campaign is anything to go by, it will claim thousands of lives with only a remote possibility of a decisive outcome.And so Saudi, and the entire Gulf, are pulled further into the relentless storm. Trump cannot bring the Iran war to an end, Gaza remains an open wound, Israel continues tostrikeandoccupyparts of Lebanon. The Houthi resurgence represents a new reality in a region that is bewildered and losing lives and capital, stuck between old alliances that no longer work and new hostilities that are too calamitous to confront.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsYemenOpinionMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisSaudi ArabiaIranTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: I don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die? | Kiran Sidhu | The Guardian
description: The quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problem, says journalist and writer Kiran Sidhu
Author: Kiran Sidhu
Headline: The quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problem, says journalist and writer Kiran Sidhu
Content: ‘I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her, can I trust her to cherish it?’Photograph: mikroman6/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her, can I trust her to cherish it?’Photograph: mikroman6/Getty ImagesOpinionDeath and dyingI don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die?Kiran SidhuThe quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problemMon 12 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTShareAfriend of mine recently discussed his will with me. He talked about the importance of looking after his daughter financially when he’s gone. As a child-free woman, I confidently told him my money will go to organisations that have meant something to me: Macmillan Cancer Support and animal charities. It bemuses me how people think the absence of children is a problem when it comes to inheritance money; it’s always been obvious to me that I’d give my money to causes that touch my heart. But then my friend served something of a curveball. He asked me who will have my deceased mother’s ring?It made me think: where do theprecious artefacts from our lives gowhen we are no longer here? Whenever I’m away from home I look forward to being reunited with these things: the quirky vase that sits in the window of my study, and the owl candlestick, a birthday gift from my potter friend. These items carry parts of me – what will become of them? If you have children, the answer to this question is not presented to you as a puzzle; like a constellation of stars, the answer is perfectly aligned. If you don’t have children, the question can lead to existential angst.This problem has caused both consternation and fascination among my child-free friends. It is a conversation topic that is something of a black hole.I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her (she was one when my mother died and so doesn’t remember her), can I trust her to cherish it? If she was my own daughter, would it be different, would I still feel this angst? My friends and I have wrestled with this question.I’ve seen enoughepisodes of Antiques Roadshowto know that the world is full of people who cherish items that once belonged to relatives they have never met. If the ring went to my goddaughter, I’d be the last custodian who really knew what it meant to my mother. But a new relationship would be anchored with it: the one that I have with my goddaughter. Understanding this has made me realise that sentimentality can and does still get passed down.I realise my concerns about the passing on of my mother’s ring stems fromtrying to hold on to what is tangibly leftof her. Inadvertently, I have been willing time to stop. The philosopher Heraclitus said: “No man steps in the same river twice. For it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man.” Life moves forward and the lives of the first custodians of the things we hold dear, who have long passed, will become backstories.When I’m gone, I will no longer be the custodian of the ring – and its meaning will alter with its new owner. This is how life works; in the exchange of hands. One day I will have to let go of what can no longer belong to me. Acknowledging this has brought me some clarity and comfort.However, an unexpected conundrum has also popped up in my circle of child-free friends. My friend has two nieces and a nephew. The nieces don’t make an effort to be in her life and she plans to leave what she has to her nephew. She has been told this would cause strife among the siblings and her plan is “inconsiderate”. How much should we consider the feelings of others when it comes to writing our wills?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTop 10 novels about inheritanceRead moreThe contents of our wills are not just the last performance of our lives – but the lasting performance. Child-free people may be at liberty to choose the recipients of our possessions without being bound by expectation and tradition, but we’re more open to rigorous criticism because of that freedom. It’s not as formulaic as leaving it to the kids.The artist David Hockneydied without having had children, but will leave a bigger legacy to the world than most. I’m a writer; perhaps my words will touch 10 or a thousand people, certainly more than the number of children I could have had. I will be a benefactor to many, rather than a few, through my words and the money I will leave to charity.In the end, we all leave some form of a legacy whether we have children or not; traces of ourselves that whisper of our past existence. I’m not interested in any grandiose legacy when I’m gone, but I cannot deny, there’s something beautiful about leaving a token of ourselves in a world that we’ve left behind.Kiran Sidhu is a freelance journalist and writer. She is the author of I Can Hear the Cuckoo. She also wrote the Bafta award-winning documentary Heart Valley.Explore more on these topicsDeath and dyingOpinionWriting a willFamily financescommentShareReuse this content

title: Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Boaz Weinstein’s hedge fund is waging an aggressive campaign against the FTSE 250’s Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Boaz Weinstein’s hedge fund is waging an aggressive campaign against the FTSE 250’s Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust
Content: Assaults by Boaz Weinstein’s Saba Capital often look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors.Photograph: Richard Brian/ReutersView image in fullscreenAssaults by Boaz Weinstein’s Saba Capital often look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors.Photograph: Richard Brian/ReutersNils Pratley on financeFinancial sectorTime to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – againNils PratleyBoaz Weinstein’s hedge fund is waging an aggressive campaign against the FTSE 250’s Baillie Gifford US Growth TrustBusiness live – latest updatesMon 12 Oct 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTShareHere we go again: another episode inthe Saba saga, the story of a New York hedge fund causing havoc in the UK investment trust sector bytaking big stakes in fundsand then demanding change, often in only vague terms.The best that can be said about Saba Capital (and it’s not much) is that its belligerent boss, Boaz Weinstein, has disturbed the complacency that used to infect corners of the UK investment trust world, meaning companies that invest in other companies. It is now harder for a board to do nothing if the share price sits at a wide discount to the value of the underlying assets for long periods.Too often, though, Saba’s assaults look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors. The attack on Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, aFTSE250 constituent usually known by its USA ticker, is all three.Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business liveRead moreRegular shareholders in USA have roundly told Saba to get lost twice in the past 18 months but they will have to do so again if they value what they own, which they should. The US raider, sitting on a near-30% stake, wants to install three of its nominees on the board via a vote atnext week’s annual meeting.On a long view, USA’s performance has been excellent: an annualised return of 16.7% since launch in 2018, beating the S&P 500 over the period and within the top 10% of all UK investment companies. The only reason an opening, of a sort, has appeared for Saba is because the 16.7%-a-year returns haven’t happened in a straight line. The pop in AI valuations in late-2022 means USA’s five-year statistics are less impressive.But volatility is what investors accept when they buy into a strategy of backing high-growth US companies for the long-term. The portfolio is stuffed with stakes in big names in the AI world – Anthropic, Databricks, OpenAI, SpaceX and Stripe – that were acquired when the companies were smaller and sometimes still privately owned. A little bit of biodiversity in the UK investment landscape will be lost if USA falls under Saba’s control.What would a Saba-dominated board do? It’s hard to say definitively because this is all Saba says: “If our nominees are elected, we would urge them to offer all USA shareholders a 100% cash exit at or near NAV [net asset value] – providing a long-overdue liquidity event.”The absurdity of that proposal lies in the fact that the board of USA says it has already offered Saba what it supposedly wants – a chance to get out at a price nearly equivalent to the value of the assets. But the US hedge fund declined.The suspicion is that Saba’s nominees could try to appoint Saba itself as manager, or wrap USA into a Saba-managed vehicle. And, note, Saba’s main funds in the US now trade on far wider discounts to asset value than USA’s relatively modest 3%.Since Saba hasn’t spelled out much, all one can say is that its nominees cannot possibly be regarded as independent. One is a Saba employee; the other two are serial picks in Weinstein’s various campaigns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere is broker Investec’s assessment: “Saba offers no credible plan. Shareholders are being asked to give its nominees potential board control on the strength of a conditional, non-binding liquidity proposal, with no roadmap for the future manager, strategy or governance: vote first, then find out later what you’ve voted for.”The choice, then, is between a known strategy that has been successful, with a few bumps, or a mystery ride under Saba’s tame directors. The analysis should not be hard: shareholders should stick with the existing board. Independence matters.Here’s the tricky bit, however. Saba’s near-30% holding, plus 7.7% in the hands of assumed sympathiser Sessa Capital, means USA shareholders need to act. “Not voting is a vote for Saba,” says broker Panmure Liberum. “Support the board, or suffer the consequences,” warns Investec. Sound advice.The annual meeting is on 23 October but, for anybody holding via an investment platform, the effective voting deadline can be as soon as this Wednesday. Those platforms – looking at Hargreaves Lansdown, AJ Bell and Interactive Investor – should be warning clients of deadlines right now. Preferably in red for danger.Explore more on these topicsFinancial sectorNils Pratley on financeStock marketsInvestment fundsCorporate governanceHedge fundsFTSEInvestingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Narendra Modi’s gen Z crackdown: he cannot arrest his way out of a democratic crisis | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Young protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confront
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Young protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confront
Content: A protest march on 12 October 2026 in Delhi. ‘Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation.’Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/GettyView image in fullscreenA protest march on 12 October 2026 in Delhi. ‘Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation.’Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/GettyOpinionIndiaThe Guardian view on Narendra Modi’s gen Z crackdown: he cannot arrest his way out of a democratic crisisEditorialYoung protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confrontMon 12 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 20.56 EDTShareNarendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detainedjournalistsand shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, wasdetainedwith other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets wereroughedup by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday,thousandsmarched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although somecommissionershave raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP wonstate electionsin West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed votersexceededthe margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.View image in fullscreenNarendra Modi.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAMass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. TheCockroach movementwas born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakesimpossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.There is still reason for hope in India. TheIndian Expressnewspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011,corruption scandalsbecame evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Liberal Democrats: now is not the time to change leader | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Ed Davey’s critics want headlines, but their leader’s strategy wins seats. Undermining him could help the rightwing parties into power
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Ed Davey’s critics want headlines, but their leader’s strategy wins seats. Undermining him could help the rightwing parties into power
Content: ‘Sir Ed’s £17bn tax giveaway looks like a pre-emptive strike aimed at disillusioned Tory voters. His strategy has its detractors.’Photograph: Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreen‘Sir Ed’s £17bn tax giveaway looks like a pre-emptive strike aimed at disillusioned Tory voters. His strategy has its detractors.’Photograph: Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsOpinionLiberal DemocratsThe Guardian view on the Liberal Democrats: now is not the time to change leaderEditorialEd Davey’s critics want headlines, but their leader’s strategy wins seats. Undermining him could help the rightwing parties into powerMon 12 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTShareWill the first victim of the political conference season be theLiberal Democrats’ Sir Ed Davey? It might seem quixotic, given that he is the most successful liberalparliamentary leaderin a century. Yet a meeting of Lib Dem MPs on Tuesday night could see them collect the 18 signatures needed for a confidence vote. It’s hard to see what a putsch would achieve, apart from giving the party’s opponents a stick to beat it with. That may be the point:weakeningSir Ed in an internal war of attrition so that he walks away would be easier than removing him via a no-confidence vote passed by a majority of all Lib Dem MPs.“Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake,”saidNapoleon Bonaparte. With populistsslippingin the polls, Lib Dem plotters should remember this, especially as Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives are looking to advance at the Lib Dems’ expense. The Tory economic pitch is to end the 60% marginal tax rate on earnings between £100,000 and £125,000, and let couples pass on the family home plus another £1m tax-free. It’s a clear bid to win backaffluent southern votersin England’s “yellow wall”.In the face of such an offensive, Sir Ed’s£17bn tax giveawaylooks like a pre-emptive strike aimed at disillusioned Tory voters. His strategy has its detractors. Discontent has moved over the past year from private complaints to public criticism fromcouncil leaders, and frontbench resignations last week. At the heart of the row is how the Lib Dems turn their MPs into a more potent force. Sir Ed wants to expand from the party’s geographic base, mobilise tactical voters and firmly establish the Lib Dems in seats they can win as the best bet to stop a rightwing government headed by Reform UK.View image in fullscreenGail’s bakery.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHis opponents argue that parliamentary heft counts for little if voters barely notice it. Critics point topollingsaying that Lib Dems don’t “own” any one issue. It’s true that the Lib Dem leader has trained his fire on the Tories and Reform, not Labour. But that’s no bad thing. Sir Ed’s team pointedly argue that a more populist strategy would be as exhilarating as a plane in a nosedive. Just ask the Greens: no one knows if their pilot will be able to pull out before hitting the ground.Anupmarket Gail’s bakeryon the high street is the best predictor of a Lib Dem vote. It marks the party’s affluent electorate: Lib Dems hold five of Britain’s10 most prosperous seats, but just seven in the poorest half. For the Lib Dems, taking chunks out of Labour in their urban strongholds at the next election simply helps Reform by splitting the opposition. Sir Ed’s pro-Europeanism is a selling point. Although Mrs Badenoch denies it, the Tories and Reform could form a “marriage of convenience”coalitionto run the country after the next election. Sir Ed’s strategy may be low-key, but it is ruthlessly efficient: the party’s 3.7m votes won 11 seats in 2019, whereas 3.5m votes won 72 seats in 2024. The Lib Dems must help to keep the right out of Downing Street. Sir Ed’s critics risk handing the Tories and Reform the keys to No 10 by chasing headlines rather than seats.Explore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsOpinionEd DaveyLiberal Democrat conferenceReform UKLabourConservativesTax and spendingeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The surprising benefits of food rationing | Food | The Guardian
description: Letters: Among the hardships of the second world war, a restricted diet with little sugar did little harm, write Roger Wilkinson and Helen Keats; plus a letter from Jane Robbins
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Among the hardships of the second world war, a restricted diet with little sugar did little harm, write Roger Wilkinson and Helen Keats; plus a letter from Jane Robbins
Content: A shopkeeper in Britain cancels coupons in a household ration book in 1943.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA shopkeeper in Britain cancels coupons in a household ration book in 1943.Photograph: AlamyFoodLettersThe surprising benefits of food rationingAmong the hardships of the second world war, a restricted diet with little sugar did little harm, writeRoger WilkinsonandHelen Keats; plus a letter fromJane RobbinsMon 12 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTShareAn interesting juxtaposition: (While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution, 6 October); and (The generation raised on sugar rations – and what their health reveals 70 years later, 7 October). Shocking that the average family throws away 156 meals a year, but this knowledge allows us war babies, who still scrape our bowls clean and only throw away items where the mould is too developed to scrape off, to be very smug. And next we’re told that we will probably live longer as a result of our parsimonious cheeseparing. My cup of smugness overflows.Roger Wilkinson (born 1944)Leasgill, CumbriaMy 98-year-old aunt, who along with my mother and family lived in Rotterdam during the German occupation and “hunger winter”, is remarkably healthy. She lives independently, does her own shopping and cooking, and cycled to the local care home to “help out” until she was 80.She hasn’t eaten a potato since the liberation, because by then the Dutch were forced to eat raw potato skin (there was no fuel for cooking). She has left her body to medical science as they are interested in finding out how someone who now lives on peanut butter and chocolate has lived so long.Helen KeatsBrighstone, Isle of WightSo, join the club (The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread,6 October). I have had a freezer full of different salted, unsalted, European and American butters for cooking, baking or eating all my life (I am 78), and have been bringing butter back from Europe in my luggage since the 1970s.I always have an imported French or Irish salted butter on my counter for slathering on bread and pastry (yes, pastry gets extra butter); it sits next to the sea salt and is never refrigerated. I grew up in a house where margarine was forbidden, and where two types of butter – hard and soft – were both on the table every day. Butter is real food and a joy in life.Jane RobbinsSaunderstown, Rhode Island, USExplore more on these topicsFoodSecond world warSugarAgeingHealthlettersShareReuse this content

title: A new approach to tackle sexual abuse in schools | Child protection | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to an editorial on the extent of sexual abuse of pupils by their peers, a reader calls for more nuance and compassion. Plus a letter from Donna Hill
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to an editorial on the extent of sexual abuse of pupils by their peers, a reader calls for more nuance and compassion. Plus a letter from Donna Hill
Content: ‘Thirty per cent of all the children we care for in our sexual assault referral centre are harmed by other children.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Thirty per cent of all the children we care for in our sexual assault referral centre are harmed by other children.’Photograph: AlamyChild protectionLettersA new approach to tackle sexual abuse in schoolsResponding to an editorial on the extent of sexual abuse of pupils by their peers, a reader calls for more nuance and compassion. Plus a letter fromDonna HillMon 12 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTShareAs a paediatrician specialising in the care of children who have been sexually abused, I am well aware of sexual harm that occurs in school settings by peers (Editorial 5 October). This is just one aspect of the wider issue of children and young people who sexually harm other children and young people.Of all the children my organisation cares for, 30% are harmed by other children – data we shared with thechildren’s commissionerin their report in 2023 on the impact of pornography on harmful sexual behaviour on children.The solutions go way beyond the three tools described in your editorial (the promotion of sex and relationships education, online safety laws and improving criminal justice).Childrenneed to be raised in family units, however defined, and wider societies that are emotionally available to them (and be helped to achieve this). They need to be curious about their life and experiences, their voices valued, equality promoted and inequality called out across the genders in all settings. This needs a state that supports parents and carers from before birth; community role models of all genders, cultures and ethnicities; trusted adults in safe and available spaces; and education (not limited to school settings) that promotes empathy for others, critical thinking and takes a whole schools or systems approach to this.Recently, two of the young people I cared for who claimed that they were sexually harmed by other young people had their cases heard in court. In both, the outcome was not guilty. I am sure that the girls still believe their truth – that they were raped – and the boys still believe their truth, that the sex that occurred was voluntary.I doubt the criminal justice process and outcome has helped either the girls or the boys to begin to understand and empathise with the others’ “truth”. Instead, I suspect that the message received was that someone was “right” and someone was “wrong” – or worse, “lying”. Harmful sexual behaviour by children to other children deserves more thinking, nuance, compassion and care than that.Name and address suppliedThe Guardian is right to highlight that schools cannot tackle child sexual abuse alone. Children absorb messages about relationships and sex from far beyond the classroom. Social media, pornography, AI-generated content, peers and influencers are increasingly shaping children’s environments. Intervention after harm has occurred is essential, but it is not enough.Schoolshave a critical preventative role through high-quality, evidence-informed relationships, sex and health education.This starts well before adolescence. In primary school, children need to learn about boundaries, bodily autonomy, respect, empathy and how to recognise behaviour that makes them uncomfortable. These foundations can then develop into learning about consent, healthy relationships, coercion, pornography, online harms and sexual harassment in secondary school.Families, schools, technology companies, policymakers and wider society all have responsibilities. But giving children the knowledge, language and confidence to understand healthy relationships and challenge harmful behaviour is a fundamental safeguarding tool. Safeguarding cannot only begin when something has gone wrong. Prevention has to be part of the answer.Donna HillHead of Coram SCARFHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Remember the disabled adults who need social care | Social care | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to John Harris’s article on the need to consider disabled people of working age when reforming the care system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to John Harris’s article on the need to consider disabled people of working age when reforming the care system
Content: ‘Hundreds of thousands of disabled adults and children rely on support throughout their lives to participate in their communities.’ (Picture posed by model.)Photograph: Shotshop GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Hundreds of thousands of disabled adults and children rely on support throughout their lives to participate in their communities.’ (Picture posed by model.)Photograph: Shotshop GmbH/AlamySocial careLettersRemember the disabled adults who need social careReaders respond to John Harris’s article on the need to consider disabled people of working age when reforming the care systemMon 12 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTShareI found myself nodding in agreement at John Harris’s worries about his son’s future as he leaves full-time education to enter the world of adult social services (Social care for disabled adults is in as much crisis as support for elderly people – so why is the government silent about it?, 5 October). John’s concerns were shared by my wife and I as our disabled daughter moved from her specialist residential further-education setting 17 years ago.However, with her gutsy approach and strong financial support by way of 24-hour care from our local council, she is able to say, “I love my life”, and has expressed this in a little book, How I Flourished, published by Lewisham Adult Learning. This despite being quadriplegic, having no speech and being dependent on her personal assistants for all the necessaries of life.I could wax at length about her wheelchair dancing, the “proper job” she secured with a wonderful charity (the Deptford-based Entelechy Arts), her painting, thirst for maintaining social relationships involving long and tiring overseas travel, and so on. The blunt truth, however, is that we, as her parents, have always needed to be closely involved in managing her care and safety, and for taking up the opportunities to broaden her landscape. We are aware that she has had a much better deal than so many people in adult care institutions.Now we are at an age when the reality of our own mortality weighs heavily. Our daughter will have no close relatives or friends at hand when we depart this world. At that point, the good life that we have striven to provide for her will be cast to the winds of dire adult social care institutions.Chris BallBlackheath, LondonI was pleased that John Harris highlighted the crisis facing working-age disabled adults in the social care system. Too often, social care is presented primarily as a service for older people, obscuring the fact that hundreds of thousands of disabled adults and children rely on support throughout their lives to participate in their communities, sustain relationships, access education and employment, and live the life they want to live.The focus on older people also overlooks the diversity of support needs and variety of provision.Social careis not one thing. Support may come from home care workers, personal assistants (PAs), supported-living facilities, unpaid family carers and community organisations. For many disabled people, social care is not simply about receiving care, but about having choice and control over how support is organised and delivered.In my family, we have experience of employing PAs. They work directly with disabled people, providing support with daily life in a manner and at a time that suits their choices and lifestyle. This approach recognises social care as the means through which disabled people secure the rights, opportunities and independence that many others take for granted. While personal assistance is not the right option for everyone, it is an important part of the social care landscape that remains largely absent from public debate.As John Harris notes, disabled people’s organisations are calling for a national independent living service to sit at the heart of reform. This begins with recognising the diversity of people’s support needs and aspirations, and moving beyond seeing social care as a service for only one group, delivered in only one way. Without this broader perspective, reform will continue to fall short.Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of GlasgowThank goodness for John Harris drawing attention to the total absence of any discussion around younger adult social care. Our son is 35 and we too experienced good support in school, but a terrifying cliff edge after that.Our experience of 15 years of adult social care has included never-ending promises from social services amounting to nothing; the occasional motivated social worker who gets nowhere and the next time we call has left the service; our localLabourMP saying kind words but no action to follow; unqualified community health workers, with obscure job titles and only first names, who give up after a few months, and shortly afterwards our son is discharged.Despite having a lasting power of attorney, as parents we have been humoured, but ignored, as our anxious son declines treatment because he just wants everyone to leave him alone; apparently he has capacity even though he is in mental turmoil. Our son got steadily worse with crippling, overarching anxiety that was never treated effectively over several years, leading eventually to a psychotic episode. He was sectioned under the MentalHealthAct and, as legal requirements then kick in, he got to see a clinical psychiatrist for the first time. Only then was he prescribed medication and given a place in supported living.There he is fed and sheltered by a service with very limited resources, among other residents with such different mental health needs that he can have no connection with them. We had to initiate and organise six-monthly reviews with a GP ourselves, as well as a review after four years with a community health psychiatrist, otherwise the medical profession would have forgotten him and left him on powerful antipsychotic medication indefinitely.What happens when we can no longer advocate for him?Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Those other battles of Hastings | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Letters: In response to a report that rare footage of a 1966 re-enactment has been found, Sue Jenkins recalls her own that year. Plus a letter from Bryn Hughes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: In response to a report that rare footage of a 1966 re-enactment has been found, Sue Jenkins recalls her own that year. Plus a letter from Bryn Hughes
Content: A Battle of Hastings re-enactment takes place every year on the weekend nearest 14 October on the site of the battle.Photograph: Felix Clay/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Battle of Hastings re-enactment takes place every year on the weekend nearest 14 October on the site of the battle.Photograph: Felix Clay/The GuardianHeritageLettersThose other battles of HastingsIn response to a report that rare footage of a 1966 re-enactment has been found,Sue Jenkinsrecalls her own that year. Plus a letter fromBryn HughesMon 12 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTShareHaving read your article(‘A God-almighty punch-up’: rare footage shows Battle of Hastings (the 1966 one), 6 October),I would love to know if anyone else remembers the “battle” that took place at Hastings on 5 March 1966 between students from Leicester University and Leicester College of Art and Technology (later De Montfort University).We wore sacks painted with whitewash and made shields and helmets from cardboard; my diary entry (I was a second-year student at the university) gives a vivid picture of the day’s events, which ended with a dance on the pier. Apparently the BBC made a film – what happened to that, I wonder?Sue JenkinsThame, OxfordshireReading your report of the re-emergence of a film showing a historical re-enactment of 60 years ago evokes memories of how the Bayeux tapestry was used onadvertising hoardings60 years ago: “Battle of Hastings 1066, Bottle of Guinness 1966”.Bryn HughesWrexhamHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Matt Richardson dropped from GB cycling team amid claims of misconduct | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain team for next week’s track world championships in Shanghai amid allegations of misconduct
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain team for next week’s track world championships in Shanghai amid allegations of misconduct
Content: Matt Richardson switched allegiances from Australia to Britain after the Paris Olympics.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatt Richardson switched allegiances from Australia to Britain after the Paris Olympics.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesCyclingMatt Richardson dropped from GB cycling team amid claims of misconductRider was to take part in track world championshipsBritish Cycling confirms Richardson was withdrawnSean IngleMon 12 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain team for next week’s track world championships in Shanghai amid allegations of serious misconduct.The 27-year-old, who switched allegiances from Australia after the Paris 2024 Olympics, had been seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes, with chances in the team and individual sprints and the keirin. But after a Times story, which reported that there had been concerns about his behaviour from other riders, he is now in the process of leaving the team’s training base in China.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“BritishCyclingcan confirm that Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain cycling team squad for the upcoming 2026 track cycling world championships in Shanghai, China,” a statement said.The Times reported that when it had originally gone to British Cycling with its story it was told: “British Cycling takes any allegations of harassment, bullying or discrimination extremely seriously. Where concerns are raised, they are investigated thoroughly through our established procedures. Out of fairness to anyone involved in an investigation, we would not comment on any ongoing process.”British Cycling refused to go into further detail about the investigation when contacted by the Guardian. Richardson could not be reached for comment.Richardson, who was born in Maidstone before moving to Perth when he was nine, missed out on an England debut at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow this summer after he crashed in a keirin race shortly before he was due to fly to Scotland. However the cyclist, whose partner is his fellow British cyclist Emma Finucane, was expected to be a central figure for the British team in China and at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.When asked previously about his change in allegiances, Richardson said: “I grew up watching Chris Hoy race on the TV. Whenever I’ve raced in the UK, it felt as though I was racing in front of a home crowd. It made me think: ‘What would this feel like if I was racing for Great Britain?’ That’s something I want to find out. I want to chase that feeling.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saracens sack player who sparked Stokes captaincy crisis after latest incident | Saracens | The Guardian
description: Totoa Auvaa, the Saracens academy player who triggered the Ben Stokes captaincy crisis by throwing a punch at his England teammate Gus Atkinson, has left the club after another incident over the weekend
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Totoa Auvaa, the Saracens academy player who triggered the Ben Stokes captaincy crisis by throwing a punch at his England teammate Gus Atkinson, has left the club after another incident over the weekend
Content: Totoa Auvaa has been released by Saracens.Photograph: Ryan Hiscott/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTotoa Auvaa has been released by Saracens.Photograph: Ryan Hiscott/Getty ImagesSaracensSaracens sack player who sparked Stokes captaincy crisis after latest incidentPrem club release statement after releasing Totoa Auvaa‘His conduct falls short of the standards expected’Matt HughesMon 12 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaracens have sacked the rugby player who sparked English cricket’s captaincy crisis on a night out withBen Stokesand Gus Atkinson last summer following his involvement in another alcohol-related incident.In a statement released on Monday evening,Saracensconfirmed that Totoa Auvaa, a 21-year-old Samoan forward, has been dismissed following an internal investigation into an incident in St Albans last weekend.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Auvaa triggered the chain of events that resulted in Stokes resigning as England Test captainand retiring from international cricketby throwing a punch at Atkinson in a Chelsea nightclub in June, which led to both cricketers being stood down from the second Test match of England’s 2-1 series defeat against New Zealand.While both players returned for the third Test, Stokes’s unhappiness at the England and WalesCricketBoard’s (ECB) handling of the matter influenced his sudden retirement on the fourth day at Trent Bridge.Auvaa’s punch missed Atkinson and struck an ECB security guard, who required stitches but did not report the matter to the police, while Saracens also opted not to take disciplinary action,as revealed by the Guardian.Auvaa, who made his senior Saracens debut off the bench in thePrem RugbyCup victory over Northampton last month, was given a final warning following other alcohol-related incidents, however, and has now left the club.“Saracens can confirm that Totoa Auvaa, a member of the senior men’s academy, has left the club with immediate effect,” the club said. “Following an incident over the weekend, the club has determined that his conduct was inconsistent with the standards and values expected of all individuals representing Saracens, both on and off the field.“Saracens takes its responsibilities to its supporters, partners and the wider community seriously. The club remains committed to upholding the highest standards of behaviour, integrity and accountability across the organisation. The club will not be making any further comment on this matter.”Hertfordshire police also confirmed they were investigating an alleged assault in the early hours of Sunday morning in St Albans. “Police are investigating an altercation which occurred between 2.15am and 2.20am on Sunday [11 October] in St Peter’s Street, St Albans,” a statement read. “It is alleged a man aged in his 20s was approached by another man who then punched him to the face. Inquiries are ongoing at this time.”In a statement confirming that no action was being taken against Auvaa in June, Saracens criticised the ECB for failing to consult them before releasing a statement which referred to their employees being victims of “unprovoked attacks”.Saracens said the events were “regrettable” but that they were “supportive” of their player.The ECB was bemused that no action was taken against Auvaa, particularly given Stokes and Atkinson both missed a Test match despite being blameless.Explore more on these topicsSaracensRugby unionPrem RugbyBen StokesEngland cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Winning is not enough for Manchester City to move on from this crisis | Premier League | The Guardian
description: It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too
Content: Man City’s win over Liverpool came amid off-field problems.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMan City’s win over Liverpool came amid off-field problems.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonPremier LeagueWinning is not enough for Manchester City to move on from this crisisIt’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them tooSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 12 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe language of football is a fine and highly nuanced dialect. The majority of people involved in the game speak it with a high degree of sophistication. Minor deviations from the familiar, almost imperceptible to outsiders, can set off alarm bells: what’s really going on there? Why isn’t he happy? What’s she hinting at? But it’s an argot developed to talk about football, and when applied to other subjects, it can sound extremely jarring.Erling Haaland is one of the brighter, more engaging players. There’s an appealing quirkiness to him that suggests he has a higher-than-usual level of self-awareness. He doesn’t mind stepping outside the norms, being a bit different. But consider his assessment ofManchester City’s 3-0 winat Liverpool on Sunday.“It was tough,” he said. “It was hard but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone. [It’s] important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about, and the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That’s the only thing we can do.”Strip away the context and he could be talking about an injury crisis, or perhaps the resignation of a manager or a suspension to a key player. The tropes are familiar: it was hard but we stuck together and so we prevailed. “You want to win games, it’s as simple as that,” he went on. “Perform well, play good football and win games. This was a mental battle, [it’s] never easy coming back from internationals.”But of course this wasn’t really about coming back from internationals; that’s not what made this difficult for City. This was about the verdict of the independent panel looking into the charges brought against City, the fact that the club have been found guilty of thegreatest act of sustained cheatingin the history of English football. Nobody knows what’s coming next.The gravity of the situation still seems to have not dawned on many in football. City, as is their right, continue to maintain their innocence and have appealed. The propaganda battle goes on. But this is no longer about whether the financial regulations were fair. If City had objected to the regulations they had every opportunity to raise objections and vote against them. They did not. They agreed to the regulations, and while everybody else played to them, they did not.The excuse that they only spent what others did but that they operated under stricter controls because of a lack of historic success is not merely irrelevant but entirely bogus: in the nine years under investigation, City’s net spending on transfers, before taking into account wages, was over £1.2bn ($1.6bn), around 50% more than any otherPremier Leagueside. And for all their talk of being proud disruptors, of rebels taking on the “red cartel”, that spending transformed City into the most dominant side English football has ever known, with six league titles in seven years. They are, precisely, an argument for why spending controls are necessary.None of that, of course, is Haaland’s fault. He is a footballer offered a very competitive salary to play alongside very good players for a very good manager for a club for which his father played. This is another of football’s absurdities: it’s always the manager and players who end up becoming the faces of the institution, being quizzed about things that have very little to do with them as the executives and directors responsible lurk away from public scrutiny.“My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear,” Enzo Maresca said. “Guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy.”Which on the one hand is absurd: nobody knows whether the three points City claimed at Anfield will still be theirs by Christmas. Nobody knows what division they will be playing in next season. Nobody knows how bad the sanction could be. And this is not some unfortunate event that has befallen City; this is the direct consequence of the actions of their directors. But on the other, what else can players and managers do? How else can they respond to this situation other than by being professional and trying to win games, even if none of it ultimately means anything?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat this is emphatically not, though, is just another football crisis from which City can move on by winning football matches. This is a crisis unlike anything English football has ever known, and it is one with which football’s language is struggling to cope.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester CityLiverpoolUS sportsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Ronaldo’s Asian Champions League match delayed by missile alert in Riyadh | Asian Champions League | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Saudi-led military coalition said it intercepted a missile headed towards Riyadh before Cristiano Ronaldo scored in Al-Nassr’s 3-1 win against Neftchi Fergana
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo (right) scored Al-Nassr’s second goal in a match that was delayed by an hour.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo (right) scored Al-Nassr’s second goal in a match that was delayed by an hour.Photograph: ReutersAsian Champions LeagueRonaldo’s Asian Champions League match delayed by missile alert in RiyadhKick-off put back by an hour after attack interceptedPortuguese forward scores in Al-Nassr’s 3-1 victoryAFPMon 12 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr had theirAsian Champions Leaguematch delayed by an hour on Monday after the Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh.Saudi Arabia has recently come under a series of attacks from the Iran-backed group, with strikes on oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs – including a string of lethal hits on Riyadh’s international airport.Portugal suspend Cristiano Ronaldo after walking out on national teamRead moreThere was a sparse crowd in the stands of AlawwalPark for the game against Uzbekistan’sNeftchi Fergana, which was scheduled for kick-off at 9.15pm local time.The stadium announcer said the situation was safe, that the match would be played, and asked spectators to remain in their seats. However, the television channel broadcasting the match announced a one-hour delay.Shortly before the sound of explosions was reported in Riyadh. title: Six questions facing England as they target next year’s Women’s World Cup | England women's football team | The Guardian
description: Starting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the air
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Starting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the air
Content: Sarina Wiegman (left) is looking for a centre-back partner for Leah Williamson (centre). Erica Meg Parkinson (right), 18, has impressed.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSarina Wiegman (left) is looking for a centre-back partner for Leah Williamson (centre). Erica Meg Parkinson (right), 18, has impressed.Composite: Getty ImagesEngland women's football teamSix questions facing England as they target next year’s Women’s World CupStarting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the airTom GarryMon 12 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland have two jobs to do on Tuesday. The first, avoiding an almighty upset and progressing past Greece on aggregate in their Women’s World Cup playoff to reach a final tie, should be a formality for one of the world’s best-resourced teams. The second, honing their style to play like contenders for next summer’s World Cup in Brazil, is a far trickier but crucial challenge.Friday’s relatively uninspiring3-1 first-leg victory in Creteleft room for improvement and England had plenty to work on as they trained at St George’s Park on Monday under gloomy-looking clouds. More broadly, over the next eight months, there are six questions facing the European champions.Can England defend well enough to win a world title?England had 58 touches in Greece’s box and turned that into three goals, whereas Greece had two touches in England’s box but managed to score and hit the crossbar. Sarina Wiegman said she was not happy her team had conceded. Their defending inJune’s 4-0 defeat by Spainalso left much to be desired, and it feels as if England are not yet certain about who should partner the captain, Leah Williamson, at centre-back. Wiegman mentioned on Monday that stopping counterattacks was something they must fix – they also struggled defending quick breaks in April 2025when losing in Belgium. That year, they found a way to win the Euros but they must tighten up defensively if they want to win a first world title in the Maracanã in July.Why are the forwards not clicking?England were wasteful in the final third in Greece and not for the first time in recent months. In the World Cup qualifying group England were 1-0 and 2-0 winners over Iceland in games where they should have scored more. A ruthless Spain, the world’s No 1 side, secured 6-1 and 3-0 wins over Iceland. On Monday Wiegman was asked what one element of Friday’s performance she would most like to improve and replied: “The execution in the final third. We got in good positions but then it’s [about] staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time, and deciding what cross or cutback you’re going to choose.”View image in fullscreenEngland preparing for the second leg against Greece on Tuesday.Photograph: Jacob King/PAWho should start in attacking midfield?For the past year, it has repeatedly felt as if Wiegman does not know who should start as the No 10, with Jess Park, Lucia Kendall and Laura Blindkilde Brown given chances along with Lauren James. Dropping –and recalling– Ella Toone, plus the late addition of Grace Clinton to this squad, adds mystery. Erica Meg Parkinson’s debut on Friday adds another youngster into the mix, and Beth Mead can also play as a 10. Asked on Friday whether the No 10 position had the most question marks surrounding it, Wiegman said: “There’s a lot of competition on that position, where we have a lot of options, which also means, tactically, we can do different things. You can call it a ‘question mark’ – I call it many options.”What about the right wing?England’s left-wing starting position feels nailed on for Lauren Hemp, who has been in tremendous form for Manchester City. The right side, however, looks uncertain, not least because Chloe Kelly has been left out. James, England’s most technically gifted player, would be the first choice for many, but she can also play centrally, and the uncapped Freya Godfrey has impressed for London City Lionesses. On Friday, Blindkilde Brown started on the right before being replaced at half-time by Mead. Whoever starts, there are only a handful of matches before next summer to build fluidity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLaura Blindkilde Brown started at right wing in the first leg against Greece.Photograph: InTime Sports/APWhich youngsters should be given a chance?There have been growing calls for the 20-year-old Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter to be handed her debut and the 21-year-old Godfrey could be in line for her debut on Tuesday. If England held a greater first-leg advantage, England would surely be more likely to experiment in Leicester, although Wiegman confirmed she would make changes. Keira Walsh said of her Chelsea teammate Potter that it was “a really good thing that she’s finally being appreciated for how good she is”, and added: “Her intelligence gives me confidence, knowing that she’s perfectly capable of stopping the counter.” There has also been praise for Parkinson, with Esme Morgan, who has played against Parkinson in the NWSL, describing the 18-year-old as a “smart player, really tidy on the ball, with incredibly good movement”. It remains to be seen whether Wiegman will opt for youth or experience as the season progresses.Do England need clarity over Wiegman’s future?Off the pitch, the biggest unknown facing England is the future of Wiegman, whose contract runs until the end of the World Cup. There have been no reasons to suspect the squad are unsettled by the uncertainty, but the topic is likely to be mentioned in every England press conference until there is clarity. Walsh said on Monday: “Obviously I’d want her to stay. I think everyone in England would love her to stay. I really appreciate her as a manager but it’s her decision.” Wiegman did not wish to discuss the matter, saying: “We’re only focused on Greece and I don’t want to talk about me.”Explore more on these topicsEngland women's football teamWomen's World Cup 2027Women's World CupWomen's footballSarina WiegmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the open | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Long-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignore
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Long-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignore
Content: Fans of Rayo Vallecano throw paper planes in protest against their club’s chair, Raúl Martín Presa, during the match against Athletic Club, which was eventually abandoned.Photograph: Ángel Pérez Meca/AFP7/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFans of Rayo Vallecano throw paper planes in protest against their club’s chair, Raúl Martín Presa, during the match against Athletic Club, which was eventually abandoned.Photograph: Ángel Pérez Meca/AFP7/ShutterstockLa LigaGrounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the openLong-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignoreSid LoweMon 12 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt took 147 days for Rayo Vallecano to walk out for a competitive game on the Avenida de Albufera and 24 minutes and 56 seconds for them to walk off again. Half of those had been spent watching thousands of paper planes touch down on the turf, play suspended while a message was delivered, over and over, until it was impossible to avoid. Forced from their home, the team from thebarriohad been away for five months. On the bright Saturday afternoon that they came back, there were just 13 minutes of football, a fans’ protest instead forcing the abandonment of their match with Athletic Club, thelatest episode in a never-ending story.The last time there had been a league game here was a victory over Villarreal in May. A lot has happened since: little Rayo,RayoVallecano, hadplayed a European final, 11,000 fans heading to Leipzig where, as the banner perfectly put it, they knew no greater victory thanbeing with you in defeat. Iñigo Pérez, themanager who took them there, haddeparted. And Óscar Trejo, the man who gave up the armband over treatment of staff – the best thing he could do as captain was tostop being captain– had retired and been immortalised the way thebarriodoes best:in graffitifour storeys high. Then, in late July, the Madrid government suspended the agreement that allows them to use the ground in return for €81,784 (£69,094) a year.The cup, the coach and the captain were not coming back. As a new season began, nor were any of them. Rayo’s president, Raúl Martín Presa, said he was furious with the council, locking the gates to keep their technicians out and accusing them of condemning the club tosegunda. But when the report described the ground as unsafe and unhealthy, Rayo’s fans knew they were right: they had been saying so for years, relieved to be finally heard. The ground’s upkeep was the tenants’ responsibility but – like so much else – it had been abandoned, left to ruin. They were furious with the president they believe condemns them to a fate far worse that relegation, a man they could not despise more and whodespises them back, of whom they ask just one thing, as often as they can: for him to leave.View image in fullscreenTalk of the town: Raúl Martín Presa (centre) was all smiles despite the protests against him.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesThey are not alone. Last season players had complained about conditions, forced to train at Getafe andplay at Leganés; as the new season began they would have to do so again. After a long summer and threehomegames played 20km south, where 4,280, 4,529, and 3,742 came to see Alavés, Racing and Espanyol, respectively – collectively fewer than in a single afternoon in Vallecas – they were finally back. Leganés had been left three-quarters empty, boycotted by supporters, but in football terms it had been good to them, which sums Rayo up: all wrong but somehow all right. Last season’s victory over Atlético there was followed up by two wins and a draw this season. Yet this is home. Besides, down at Rayo, in the heart of the self-styled independent republic of Vallekas, the football is the least of it,striker Sergio Camello says; it’s about what they stand for. And this weekend they were going to make another stand.They could not have chosen a better opponent: Athletic’s fans are allies, supporters packed into the bars around the ground and theplazain front of the Mercado de Numancia alongside Rayo’s fans, singing in the sunshine. The protest had been planned from the start; what they probably did not plan for was the way it ended. On surfaces all around the stadium, green stickers proclaimed “SOS Rayo Vallecano”. Presa’s image appeared on walls and scarves with familiar Mickey Mouse ears. From bags they handed out little plastic balls in many colours. And from boxes they handed out flyers.View image in fullscreen‘It is the day to protest. It is the day to single out Presa.’ One of hundreds of protest flyers that eventually became a paper plane.Photograph: MARISCAL/EPAPrinted on grey A4, the sheets declared: “Today is a day to protest.” After “years of putting up with this”, they had reached a “point of no return”. And so, in the 13th minute, everyone was invited to chant “Presa, go now!” Then to turn the paper into a plane and fly it on to the field. On the back of the sheet were handy,Ikea-style instructionsfor those who did not know how to fold a paper plane.An Athletic corner arrived with perfect timing, setting it all up. The whistles started bang on the 13th minute and so did the planes, swooping in from all three stands. The referee, José María Sánchez Martínez, stopped the game and shrugged, which he did a lot. Small, multicoloured plastic balls came down too, bouncing and rolling across the pitch, while a banner unfurled in the main stand declared the ball in Presa’s court (which is precisely their problem).
