Content: Kanishka Narayan said the UK would ‘play its part’ in coordinating an international response to AI safety.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenKanishka Narayan said the UK would ‘play its part’ in coordinating an international response to AI safety.Photograph: James Manning/PAAI (artificial intelligence)Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says ministerKanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agentUK politics live – latest updatesDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 12 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAIbreach of Australia’s healthcare systemis likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister.Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity.In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when anOpenAIagent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK.“It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.”Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have.“The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said.Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.Narayan spoke before a parliamentary hearing on AI safety on Tuesdayinto the issue. Senior figures from OpenAI and Anthropic will be among those giving evidence to MPs on the business, innovation, science and trade committee. They will also be joined by the head of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Henry de Zoete.Narayan confirmed that the institute would gain access to advanced AI models before they were released, after the White House had reportedly placed restrictions on their availability.“I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generations of models, including [Google’s] Gemini … to identify risks early to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe,” he said.The minister added that leading AI companies must “listen” to warnings of safety risks posed by their technology – and not release models if they carried a serious threat.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers; investigate unexpected behaviours; and if you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” he said. “I want the labs to be honest.”Narayan said the UK would “play its part” in coordinating an international response to AI safety by making the technology a “central focus” of Britain’s G20 presidency next year.“We know that these challenges cannot be addressed by a single country alone, but by virtue of our capability, by virtue of the foundations of our trust, Britain will play its part,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Data and computer securityCybercrimeKanishka NarayanComputingOpenAIAnthropicnewsShareReuse this content

title: SAS personnel ‘refusing to answer’ questions about alleged extrajudicial killings in Afghanistan | Military | The Guardian
description: Judge leading inquiry says most operators using privilege against self-incrimination to refuse to provide information
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Judge leading inquiry says most operators using privilege against self-incrimination to refuse to provide information
Content: Ministers announced the inquiry after allegations 54 Afghans were killed in suspicious circumstances by an SAS unit in Helmand province between 2010 and 2011.Photograph: LA(Phot) Si Ethell/EPAView image in fullscreenMinisters announced the inquiry after allegations 54 Afghans were killed in suspicious circumstances by an SAS unit in Helmand province between 2010 and 2011.Photograph: LA(Phot) Si Ethell/EPAMilitarySAS personnel ‘refusing to answer’ questions about alleged extrajudicial killings in AfghanistanJudge leading UK inquiry says most operators using privilege against self-incrimination to refuse to provide informationUK politics live – latest updatesJamie GriersonandDan SabbaghMon 12 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost SAS personnel approached by an inquiry into alleged extrajudicial killings inAfghanistanhave refused to answer any questions, the judge leading the proceedings has said.Lord Justice Haddon-Cave is investigating allegations of more than 50 summary killings by UK special forces soldiers as well as claims of an alleged cover-up of illegal activity and inadequate investigations by the RoyalMilitaryPolice.In a public hearing, Haddon-Cave said a number of rule 9 requests – written notices asking for information – had been sent to SAS operators who were linked to the deliberate detention operations (DDOs) at the centre of allegations.“The inquiry has identified numerous SAS personnel from whom it wishes to hear direct evidence as to the DDOs in question and has issued rule 9 requests for information to each of them,” he said.“A high proportion have indicated their intention to rely on their privilege against self-incrimination and have refused to answer any questions asked by the inquiry.”View image in fullscreenLord Justice Haddon-Cave.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAMinistersannounced the statutory judge-led inquiryafter allegations that 54 Afghans were killed in suspicious circumstances by one SAS unit in Helmand province between 2010 and 2011, and accusations that these amounted to war crimes.A high court case brought by the law firm Leigh Day on behalf of one man, Saifullah, alleged that his father, two brothers and a cousin were killed during an SAS raid on a compound in southern Afghanistan in February 2011.The inquiry is tasked with determining whether investigations conducted by the Royal Military Police were carried out properly and effectively, and whether there is credible information that “numerous” extrajudicial killings were carried out by British armed forces between 2010 and 2013. The judge said the three-year period “sufficiently captures the allegations currently being made”.The inquiry will also seek to determine whether the circumstances of the alleged killings were covered up at any stage and what lessons could be learned.During Monday’s hearing, Haddon-Cave revealed the inquiry had obtained about 10,000 high-resolution photos, taken in the course of the DDOs, which do not appear to have formed part of Royal Military Police inquiries.He said the inquiry was seeking evidence from Afghan families whose loved ones died during the detention operations, adding that the inquiry had heard “extensive” witness evidence regarding concerns and complaints raised by both UK special forces personnel and other individuals about the manner in which the SAS were conducting detention operations in Afghanistan during the period in question.Last week, during a high court hearing, the Ministry of Defence identified material that suggested UK special forces personnel deployed on some operations being considered by the inquiry may have committed serious offences under the Armed Forces Act 2006.The open hearings will continue throughout October and November.Separately, ministers announced a package of amendments to the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, intended to raise the bar before former soldiers can be prosecuted in cases dating back to the Troubles between 1969 and 1998, in an attempt to meet concerns raised by veterans groups.In future, prosecutions will have to be approved by the attorney general, and any evidence has to be “new and compelling” as well as essential to the case before veterans are called to court. Legislation would also emphasise there is no equivalence between soldiers and terrorists.Explore more on these topicsMilitaryAfghanistanSouth and central AsiaCounter-terrorism policyForeign policyShareReuse this content

title: Celebrity Traitors’ Julie Hesmondhalgh: theatres should be 100% faithful to ‘local stories’ | Theatre | The Guardian
description: As she leaves the Traitors castle to star in The Pelicot Trial and receive a lifetime achievement award, the actor has highlighted a ‘loss of regional identity’ caused by funding pressures on UK theatres
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: As she leaves the Traitors castle to star in The Pelicot Trial and receive a lifetime achievement award, the actor has highlighted a ‘loss of regional identity’ caused by funding pressures on UK theatres
Content: ‘There’s room in my heart for the classics’ … Julie Hesmondhalgh on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertView image in fullscreen‘There’s room in my heart for the classics’ … Julie Hesmondhalgh on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertTheatreCelebrity Traitors’ Julie Hesmondhalgh: theatres should be 100% faithful to ‘local stories’As she leaves the Traitors castle to star in The Pelicot Trial and receive a lifetime achievement award, the actor has highlighted ‘a loss of regional identity’ caused by funding pressures on UK theatresChris WiegandStage editorMon 12 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been “a loss of regional identity” in the stories on stages around the UK due to the challenging circumstances facing theatres, according toJulie Hesmondhalgh.The actor, who last week was the fourth contestant to leave The Celebrity Traitors, observed that for financial reasons regional theatres are increasingly making co-productions with other venues. This can lead to a “generic” product, she said, rather than a show that specifically says something about the local area.Hesmondhalgh highlighted the phenomenal impact ofJames Graham’s Punch, a drama about restorative justice, which opened at Nottingham Playhouse in 2024 and was based on the true story of a one-punch death in the city. The play, which brought Hesmondhalghan Olivier awardfor her performance as the victim’s mother, went from Nottingham to the West End, a UK tour and Broadway. “New work is always so hard to sell but because it was such a local story, and by James Graham, it sold,” she said.Asked if programming had become risk-averse since Covid, Hesmondhalgh said: “It’s really hard for regional theatres. There’s room in my heart for musicals and Noël Coward. There’s a familiarity about the old classics that people love. But the world of co-pros is making things very difficult for people. In order to survive as a regional theatre now, you have to necessarily make so many co-productions with other regional theatres. There’s a definite loss of regional identity, locally made productions.”View image in fullscreenJulie Hesmondhalgh at home in Tameside, Greater Manchester, in 2020.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHesmondhalgh, who led a successful campaign to save Oldham Coliseum from closure, was earlier this year appointed as a guest curator for its reopening programme. The building is undergoing major refurbishment and redevelopment by the council. It will stage shows that have “a distinctive Oldham mark, a Coliseum mark” as well as work that will visit other venues. The actor stressed “the amount of fundraising we’re having to do to make some regionally specific work because we know we won’t be able to co-pro it”. The experience, she said, has given her “a new empathy for people trying to run regional theatres – it’s not easy”.When audiences watch shows with a genuine local resonance – productions “that are of and for them” – there is a visceral response, Hesmondhalgh added. She described witnessing such a response when she watched Beth Steel’s Till the Stars Come Down, the tale of a Mansfield community, when it ran atNottingham Playhouselast month. “It’s a real experience being an actor in a play in Oldham and Nottingham. Every time there’s the mention of a place [the audience] recognise, there’s a ripple of approval – it’s wonderful.”Next month Hesmondhalgh, 56, will receive the lifetime achievement prize at the inaugural Great British Theatres awards to mark the 50th anniversary ofTheatres Trust, the national advice and advocacy body for UK theatres. Its CEO, Joshua McTaggart, said the award “is to recognise someone who shares Theatres Trust’s belief that everyone should have access to theatre and live performance no matter where they live or what their background is. There is no one in the public eye who embodies this spirit more than Julie Hesmondhalgh. Julie has used her platform as one of the country’s most beloved actors to bang the drum for inclusive and equitable access to the performing arts and champion important community theatres.”Hesmondhalgh, who is from Accrington in Lancashire, had a recent TV hit withMr Bates vs the Post Officeand will soon star on stage in the Young Vic’s documentary theatre productionThe Pelicot Trialat County Hall in London. She joked that the award may be a tad premature – “I still think I’m 19!” – and said that she had been fortunate to appear in “a disproportionate number of plays and TV shows that have had something to say about the world, and that I’ve been so proud to be a part of”.She expressed faith, too, in Andy Burnham’s understanding of the arts. “He’s been to the theatre and seen me in stuff in Manchester and engaged with that. On a real level he knows that communities coming together – for a gig or a football match or a play – matters. I think he’s got a handle on that. I do have quite a lot of faith in him to deliver on that. For communities that are struggling, having a cultural policy and investment in culture is always a tool for regeneration.”Explore more on these topicsTheatreJulie HesmondhalghNottingham PlayhouseJames GrahamAwards and prizesThe TraitorsTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: One dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US | Georgia | The Guardian
description: Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop
Content: Visitors ride on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in April 2021.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreenVisitors ride on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in April 2021.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APGeorgiaOne dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in USSix Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft dropGuardian staff and agencyMon 12 Oct 2026 19.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags rollercoaster on Monday afternoon inGeorgia, according to police.The incident took place a Six Flags OverGeorgia, about 15 miles (25km) north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb county police department.Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. However, multiple outlets reported a person had fallen from the park’s Goliath rollercoaster, citingeyewitnessesand anonymouslocal officials.Six Flags permanently shuts down X2 rollercoaster after claims of brain injuriesRead moreTherollercoaster,which was introduced at the park in 2006, has a top speed of 70mph (110km/h) and a 175ft drop.A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.Late last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it wasretiringits famous X2 rollercoasteramid lawsuitsalleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recentlysettleda wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries werefiledlast week.Explore more on these topicsGeorgianewsShareReuse this content

title: Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’ | Paris | The Guardian
description: ‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: ‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames
Content: French firefighters at work after a fire ravaged the historic Marché des Enfants Rouges.Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPAView image in fullscreenFrench firefighters at work after a fire ravaged the historic Marché des Enfants Rouges.Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPAParisFire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flamesJon Henleyin ParisMon 12 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily.Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, ​said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.”The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red.The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor, Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground car park, a council daycare facility and community centre.View image in fullscreenThe Marché des Enfants Rouges in the Marais district in Paris drew thousands of locals and tourists daily.Photograph: Photononstop/AlamyA determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s.Rather than demolish the building, the city undertook a six-year, 13m-franc (about €3m, or £2.5m today) renovation project, restoring the market’s historic wood and ironwork frame and glass roof. Les Enfants Rouges reopened as a food court in 2000.While still hosting some traditional stalls including a greengrocer, butcher, cheesemonger and fishmonger, the 1,000 sq m market was mostly given over to more than a dozen stands offering French, Lebanese, Moroccan, Japanese and other street food at the counter or at casual chairs and tables.The current Time Out tourist guide describes Les Enfants Rouges as “the coolest market in Paris”, while the authoritative US website Food&Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year after other food courts in London, Bangkok, Lyon and Mexico City.Lt Col Pierre de Bouvier of the Paris fire service said much of the metal structure of the market had fallen in, and most of the stalls had gone up in flames. More than 150 firefighters and 50 fire trucks battled the blaze after being alerted at 4.15am, he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.Explore more on these topicsParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bolivia investigates ex-president Evo Morales over alleged ties to 2009 killings | Bolivia | The Guardian
description: Leftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two others
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two others
Content: Former Bolivian president Evo Morales last February.Photograph: Patricia Pinto/ReutersView image in fullscreenFormer Bolivian president Evo Morales last February.Photograph: Patricia Pinto/ReutersBoliviaBolivia investigates ex-president Evo Morales over alleged ties to 2009 killingsLeftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two othersAFPMon 12 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBolivia’s attorney general has announced an investigation into leftist former presidentEvo Morales, alleging his involvement in the murder and torture of European citizens in 2009.Seventeen years ago, police raided a hotel in the city of Santa Cruz, shooting dead Eduardo Rózsa Flores, a Bolivian-Croatian, Michael Dwyer, an Irishman, and Árpád Magyarosi, a Hungarian-Romanian.Bolivian-Croatian citizen Mario Tadic and Elöd Tóásó from Hungary survived and reported being tortured after their arrest.The Morales administration in power at the time claimed that Rózsa Flores was leading efforts to promote a separatist movement, with funding from the rightwing economic elite of Santa Cruz.Bolivia rocked by protests as US warns of ‘coup d’état’Read moreActing attorney general José Armando Urioste announced the preliminary investigation into Morales just one week into the job on Monday.In a letter to the supreme court, Urioste said authorities were gathering evidence againstMoralesand his former vice-president Álvaro García Linera “for the alleged commission of the crimes of murder, abuse, torture and unlawful detention”.The investigation comes after a complaint filed by rightwing lawmakers Tomasa Yarhui and Rodrigo Antonio.When the raid occurred, Morales told the press during an official visit to Venezuela that he had ordered the detention of the foreigners, whom he called “mercenaries”.Family members and victims brought the case before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which concluded in 2021 that the government had violated human rights.Neither of the accused has commented on the latest inquiry.Morales, the first-ever Indigenous person to lead Bolivia, is currently in hiding from two active arrest warrants against him. One relates to his alleged role in massive protests that paralysed the country for 53 days earlier this year. The other accuses him of trafficking a minor with whom he is said to have had a daughter. Morales denies the allegations.Explore more on these topicsBoliviaEvo MoralesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hackers force French supermarket fridges to heat up to 50C in ‘unprecedented’ cyber-attack | France | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affected
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affected
Content: The branches affected would have to ‘throw away all of the products’ that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché said.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe branches affected would have to ‘throw away all of the products’ that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché said.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceHackers force French supermarket fridges to heat up to 50C in ‘unprecedented’ cyber-attackHundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affectedReuters in ParisMon 12 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHackers have forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight, in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores across the country, with fires and food losses reported.The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday ⁠the large-scale attack was “affecting connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France”. Reported damage included “food losses and fires”, it added.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency ANSSI to investigate, ⁠a person in his office said.France “was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected”, while also investigating whether any other French ⁠firms were at risk, they said.Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarché, said about 150 of its stores had been ​hit, with fridges heated up to 50C for six hours. ‌It had thrown all the food away to avoid any health risks, a spokesperson said.Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Coopérative ‌U, said his supermarkets had also been hit by the attack. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X.Several other supermarket chains, including Carrefour, Monoprix and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment. According to BFM TV, France’s largest supermarket chain E Leclerc was also affected, with hackers “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. E Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment.The attack may not have been confined to France. The Dutch supermarket company ‌Ahold Delhaize said it was also dealing with a “security issue” in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them.Stores of its Albert Heijn chain, ​the largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands, which also has several stores in Belgium, remained open in both countries. But its online app and delivery system were down, while electronic price tags often displayed the wrong information.It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the ⁠problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize.Delhaize supermarkets, also part of Ahold Delhaize but operating ​in Belgium and Luxembourg, were ​also affected by the security issue, ​Belgian media reported.The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability ​in software supplied by ‌the Danish company Danfoss.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDanfoss ​said it was “aware ​of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”.The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by cyber-attacks by malicious actors.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from Russian “hybrid attacks”.Explore more on these topicsFranceCybercrimeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China
Content: Actor Omar Sy (second from right) and Stellantis’s Emanuele Cappellano (second from left) with other Stellantis executives and the Citroën 2CV electric concept car at the Paris motor show.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenActor Omar Sy (second from right) and Stellantis’s Emanuele Cappellano (second from left) with other Stellantis executives and the Citroën 2CV electric concept car at the Paris motor show.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersAutomotive industryStellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protectionBosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from ChinaJasper Jollyin ParisMon 12 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars.Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed“Made in Europe” legislation.The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries.EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a yearRead moreThe executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans.Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants.The EUconfirmed on Mondayit would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in alandmark four-year agreementmade in Beijing last week.The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise ofChinain key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals.Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details.If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included.Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans.“I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.”Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, includingFrance’s industry minister, had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit.Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits.“On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.”Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.”London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month saidthat decision was under review.Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.”He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules.“We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU.He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryStellantisRenaultEuropean UnionEuropeChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest | Roman Abramovich | The Guardian
description: Accountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assets
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Accountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assets
Content: Roman Abramovich has now been placed under sanctions by the UK and EU.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/UEFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRoman Abramovich has now been placed under sanctions by the UK and EU.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/UEFA/Getty ImagesRoman AbramovichRoman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggestAccountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assetsRob Daviesand Simon LockMon 12 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAides ofRoman Abramovich– including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets.New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents.The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate.Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine.But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers.The findings are based on theCyprus Confidential leak, more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC.View image in fullscreenEugene Tenenbaum with Roman Abramovich at a Chelsea FC match.Photograph: Matthew Ashton/Corbis/Getty ImagesThe digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union.From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion.This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier.Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that has elapsed.The disappearing $2bnA crown jewel in Russia’s rich seam of natural resources, Sibneft’s oilfields fell into Abramovich’s hands during the chaotic post-Soviet privatisation era.The famously shrewd entrepreneur obtained the business for roughly $250m, reportedly spending as little as $19m of his own money.By the time he sold the last of his shares to Gazprom in 2005, Abramovich had raised $16bn, money he ploughed into investments, mansions, superyachts and Chelsea FC.One Cyprus-based company, Kravin Investments, was among several early vehicles through which that cash flowed. Kravin received a $3bn windfall in May 2003, of which it retained about $2bn.The money sat in Kravin’s bank account or was loaned to other companies, accruing interest that was, in theory, taxable in Cyprus.But Abramovich’s aides soon began devising plans to “eliminate” a tax liability that one financial adviser warned could be “very large”, records suggest.View image in fullscreenDemetris Ioannides was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out Meritservus.Photograph: No CreditThe gatekeeper to Abramovich’s fortune was Demetris Ioannides, who was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out his own business Meritservus. That firm became Abramovich’s go-to financial advisory, serving him for nearly 20 years, before it wassanctioned by the UK in 2023, along with Ioannides, for its role helping Russian oligarch hide their wealth.“It will be necessary to change the [Kravin’s] financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004,” Ioannides wrote in an August 2005 email, citing discussions with Deloitte Cyprus partners and erstwhile colleagues Antonis Taliotis and Nicos Charalambous.The following month, in an email copying in staff at Meritservus and Abramovich’s investment vehicle, Millhouse, Taliotis appeared to agree.“Certain changes will have to be made to the accounts […]” he wrote.View image in fullscreenAn August 2005 email from Demetris Ioannides.Photograph: -Millhouse and Meritservus duly began producing paperwork showing that Kravin was simply holding and investing the Sibneft billions as a trustee for another business, the British Virgin Islands-based Kelvedon Worldwide.Documents detailing this supposed fact, including correspondence and trust agreements, were given dates between March and December 2003, despite being created at least two years later.The result was simple: although the billions had sat in Kravin’s accounts for years, it now appeared that the money had never really been Kravin’s at all. Deloitte Cyprus, apparently aware of the deception, duly signed off the accounts.History had effectively been rewritten, analysis of the documents suggests, disappearing $2bn from Kravin’s balance sheet – and with it any tax liability.Andrew Mitchell KC, a leading expert in financial crime and tax law, described the scheme as a “blatant move to protect from legitimate taxation assets which should otherwise have been subject to tax”. This, he claimed, would amount to “straightforward” tax evasion.Abramovich’s lawyers said: “Any suggestion that our client evaded tax, or sought to deceive the Cypriot authorities, is denied, and publication of the same would be defamatory of him. If an arrangement was proposed by professional advisers of Deloitte’s standing, it would have been entirely proper for companies linked to our client (in which he was not involved on a day-to-day basis) to rely on it.”The oligarch’s signatureIt was not the first time that Abramovich’s subordinates appear to have resorted to backdating to solve a money problem for their boss.In 2000, Tenenbaum and Ioannides, then still working for Deloitte Cyprus, met in London to discuss a delicate matter.Abramovich, it seemed, wanted to extract almost $100m from Cypriot companies that held stakes in Sibneft.According to Ioannides, it was essential that any transaction couldn’t reveal these Cyprus companies and that the money had to appear “earned”. The logic for these conditions was not explained.Deloitte Cyprus’s solution was a complicated but seemingly bogus arrangement, directly involving Abramovich, that appears to have relied on falsified, backdated consultancy agreements.These agreements appeared to show that Abramovich’s Sibneft-owning companies had paid an intermediary business $98m for “consultancy services”, namely advice on share purchases.That intermediary had then supposedly passed on 99.9% of the money to Abramovich, as “commission” for having acted as its “agent”.But the share purchases in question had already happened a year earlier, meaning the intermediary company had to be at least a year old too, if backdated deals involving it were to appear legitimate.Ioannides found a suitable Cypriot off-the-shelf company called PB Mediapower Enterprises.With Tenenbaum’s authorisation, directors of Deloitte Cyprus signed the backdated documents and incorporated their content into PB Mediapower’s annual accounts.Abramovich’s commission was then converted into promissory notes – effectively IOUs – which he cashed in over the following three years.View image in fullscreenAn application for repayment of a promissory note issued by PB Mediapower in 2000.Photograph: -The leaked files contain 50 such notes. Unlike much of the paper trail tracing the Abramovich fortune, which kept his name out of it, each of the applications for repayment of the notes bore his signature.Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum denied that they had participated in any improper backdating or falsification of documents. Both also stressed that they relied on specialist advice from professional advisers such as Deloitte Cyprus as well as Cypriot corporate advisers.The ghost houseOne of Abramovich’s most prestigious assets was the Fyning Hill estate in West Sussex, an imposing mansion set in 424 acres of South Downs countryside.The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly flew in for lunch here during his first UK state visit in 2003.Two years later, accounts show, the estate was listed among $650m of luxury assets – including a London penthouse, French chateau, helicopters, jets, yachts and a supercar – all held in a Cypriot company, Amiscan Investments.New Cypriot disclosure rules, introduced in 2003, meant that these would have to be included in Amiscan’s accounts.But by the time those accounts were filed, this vast billionaire’s toybox had vanished, thanks to Abramovich’s squad of financial fixers.In an October 2005 email, sent to Tenenbaum, Ioannides suggested it might be “more prudent not to disclose” them.View image in fullscreenAn October 2005 email from Demetris Ioannides to Eugene Tenenbaum.Photograph: -Files show that Abramovich aides, including Ioannides, worked together to backdate contractual agreements, giving the false impression that Amiscan’s assets had been shifted to its BVI shareholder, Kelvedon Worldwide, at the start of 2003.Deloitte Cyprus staff took part in discussions about this disappearing act, emails show.Yet the auditor signed off Amiscan’s accounts, now showing no trace of three properties and a fleet of luxury vehicles.Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum denied wrongdoing of any sort, including improper backdating, falsification, or any sort of tax evasion. They each also said that their clients could not recall the context or detail of documents more than 20 years old, which had not been provided to them by the Guardian.Both said their clients had relied on expert advice, including from Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus, also answering on behalf of Taliotis and Charalambous, said that it “acts in compliance with applicable laws”. It said the correspondence were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible, meaning it could not comment on whether the material was complete or accurate.View image in fullscreenA view of central Limassol in Cyprus, with the offices of MeritServus on the left of the picture.Photograph: Hernandez Jose Maria/AlamyA lawyer for Demetris Ioannides said he was unable to comment for personal reasons.Lawyers for Tenenbaum said that documents could sometimes be backdated for legitimate reasons, such as to show when a transaction became effective.Rachel Sexton, a forensic accountant experienced in fraud investigations, agreed that this was possible but added: “From the evidence I have seen, this does not appear to be the case.”She said backdating documents to create a false impression “could be considered to be fraudulent misrepresentation.”Two more accounting experts, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the files did not appear to show legitimate reasons for backdating.Mitchell raised concerns about Deloitte’s apparent role in the tactic.“What you take away from it is that there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law.”In one instance, backdating appears to have led to something else very serious: the misleading of a British court.View image in fullscreenAbramovich’s Sibneft deals made him Russia’s richest man.Photograph: Alexander Natruskin/ReutersThe whole truthIn 2008, Abramovich faced the prospect of a potentially costly lawsuit from Moscow businessman Chalva Tchigrinski, a former partner in their joint oil venture, Sibneft-Yugra.The partnership ended with Tchigrinski’s company, Sibir, ousted and left with nothing, leaving Abramovich free to sign the Sibneft deals that would make him Russia’s richest man.Tchigrinski’s lawyers claimed foul play.Abramovich, they claimed, had diluted his partner’s stake via a series of secret meetings that gave him full control and, as a result, the full financial benefit of the eventual sale to Gazprom.In a witness statement, Tenenbaum denied any knowledge of the project’s details before spring 2004, when Sibir’s made its complaints public.“I have searched my files, emails and documents from 2002 to 2004,” he told the court, “and I can confirm that I have in my possession no records or documents or other communications that relate to Sibneft-Yugra.”Files from theCyprus Confidentialleak appear to contradict this testimony.They show that Tenenbaum signed off on a string of agreements governing some of the very deals he claimed in court to know nothing about.They include the 2003 transfer of Sibneft-Yugra shares to an Abramovich-owned company called Ferenco Investment & Services, something Tenenbaum had told the court he knew nothing about.His testimony, according to the judgment, was “corroborated by” evidence submitted by Abramovich. The Guardian has not seen this evidence.What is more, documents submitted to the court in support of Abramovich’s case, which purported to justify Sibneft’s takeover of Sibir, appear to have been backdated.In other words, the documents – like Tenenbaum’s testimony – appear to have been false.Lawyers for Tenenbaum denied that his testimony misled the court, saying he had given evidence “honestly and in good faith” and denied “in the strongest terms” misleading the court. Lawyers for Abramovich denied that his corroboration of Tenenbaum’s testimony had misled the court.All in all, analysis of the Cyprus files suggest that more than 1,000 documents pertaining to the Abramovich empire were backdated.Often, it appears, this took place with the knowledge of those closest to the oligarch.Between them, that inner circle constructed a globe-spanning financial empire whose most important currency was, it seems, deceit.Get in touchContact us about this storyIf you have something to share about  this story, you can contact Rob using one of the following methods.Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.To send a message to Rob Davies please choose the ‘Business’ team.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailrob.davies@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsRoman AbramovichAccountancyFinancial sectorRussiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294
Content: The Road Haulage Association said that raising fuel duty amid high prices at the pumps would be a ‘hammer blow’ for many companies.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Road Haulage Association said that raising fuel duty amid high prices at the pumps would be a ‘hammer blow’ for many companies.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesPetrol pricesUK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures showCalls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294Jillian AmbroseMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 04.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMillions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise.The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs.The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption.The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number ofself-employed people working in trades.Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to aabove £2 a litre for the first timethis month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase –postponed from September– will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA).Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel.“Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.”Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group.The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC.“As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.”Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said.On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move whichinfuriatedthe Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy.The government was contact for comment.Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesMotoringFuel dutyTax and spendingTaxnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year | Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars | The Guardian
description: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose 350,000 vehicle-a-year quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose 350,000 vehicle-a-year quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%
Content: Any Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (known as PHEVs) imported above the new quota level will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAny Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (known as PHEVs) imported above the new quota level will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsEU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a yearBrussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%Business live – latest updatesVW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industryLisa O’CarrollMon 12 Oct 2026 07.23 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmarkfour-year agreement made in Beijing last week.The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under theWorld Trade Organizationsafeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spacesRead moreAny cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars inChinawill.China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the“Made in Europe” legislationwould do the same in public procurement.On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.Sources said there has been“a paradigm shift”withconcerns of deindustrialisationand job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.Explore more on these topicsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryInternational tradeEuropean UnionEuropeChinaWorld Trade OrganizationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph | Fontaines DC | The Guardian
description: This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generation
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generation
Content: ‘Indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey’ … Fontaines DC.Photograph: DOT/Ewen SpencerView image in fullscreen‘Indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey’ … Fontaines DC.Photograph: DOT/Ewen SpencerFontaines DCReviewFontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph(XL)This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generationLaura SnapesMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifteen centuries ago, the Byzantine archbishop Theophilus of Adana did first-hand business with the devil for his own superficial betterment. Today, we just blindly tick a little box marked “accept terms and conditions” or let high-street snake oil merchants inject poison into our faces. The Faustian pact has become as depressingly banal as it is endemic and destructive – and unlike Theophilus, we can’t rely on the Virgin Mary to save us now. In the midst of headlines about AI destroying humanity, the idea of listening to music submerged in precisely this shade of doom might sound like, well, hell. If anyone can thread that poisoned needle, it’sFontaines DC.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Dopamine ChamberWhen the Dublin band introduced their last album, 2024’sRomance, it came witha surprise new look. Their uncoordinated jeans and shirts had been replaced by neon hair, shiny trousers and bug-eyed sunglasses that split the difference between Korn and the Prodigy. As they faced up to having traded their anonymity to become arena fillers, it wasn’t hard to read this look as a sort of protective cosplay, a cybergoth Sasha Fierce for five fairly low-key Irish lads trying to make peace with leaving their roots behind. Newly melodic and lavishly produced, Romance made no bones about the band’s ambitions and became their first platinum-certified album.For their fifth LP, Fontaines’ wardrobes are more or less back to normal as the music reaches new heights, indicating a level of comfort and confidence that resounds through their most formidable, cohesive record. Frontman Grian Chatten has said he wanted to write about the context collapse of social media and the willing degradation of what it means to be human, living in a time when “the mask is wearing the face a little more”. For all that might sound ripped from the headlines, Dopamine Chamber embodies the idea with poetry and a frankly thrilling and terrifying aptitude for seduction. Chatten’s lyrics repeatedly question reality and the truth that animates desire while at the same time offering promises of salvation that may or may not be what they seem. Yet the band’s darkly alluring music, full of heady absolution, makes it impossible not to succumb.Fontaines DC: Marianne – videoLead singleMariannemakes that intention explicit. “I can help you disappear,” Chatten chants over spiralling strings – glinting wormholes amid the pearlescent cosmic gloom. It is a massive song, a beckoning void. There are few more cringeworthy musical tropes than when bands pre-emptively scale up for stadiums without having the substance to scaffold it – making a meal out of crumbs – but Fontaines pull off that kind of ecstatic overwhelm again and again on Dopamine Chamber.Ahead of the record, guitarist Conor Curley said he wanted to avoid sounds that immediately recalled historic bands. They don’t quite reinvent the wheel – Happy for You has the Cure’s unmistakably sour, lonely twang; Mimesis a roughshod New Order bassline; Demolition a sledgehammer grunge attack – yet they sound more like artefacts in the band’s gorgeous ruin of a soundworld than pastiche. Happy for You is full of beguiling flotsam, subtle echoes of pastoral guitar twang rippling like seaweed in the waves. You could spend a dozen listens focusing on the fine detail here – the agitatedTonguemixes Lankum’s dank chill with a taunting, pisky-like backing singer – but Dopamine Chamber gets its immediacy from Chatten’s scene-stealing vocal performances.He swerves between indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey and an insistent, addictive attack. One Man mixes both: “Do you have a genuine need to be desired / Call me up any time that you wanna fly yeah,” he incants against a wistful string crescendo, radiating both the possibility of redemption and the sense that accepting might mean grasping tight to Icarus’s feathers. At moments, Chatten’s voice hits on the level of pure sensation, feeling almost invasive in its capacity to worm its way into your veins: the way he exhales “I sweeeaaaaar” on Happy for You, or “surelyyou’ll wake up in yourself” on Mimesis.‘It’s impossible not to have contradictions in a contradictory world’: Catalan pop visionary Rosalía on critics, crisis and being ‘hot for God’Read morePlus if you’re going to invite Rosalía to be the first guest on any Fontaines record, you’d better be able to hold your own. Channelling Morricone grandeur and mid-century balladry, the absolutely astonishing duet Where Is Gone? is as spellbinding as Nick Cave and PJ Harvey’sHenry Leeand a peerless would-be Bond theme that’s too good for the ailing franchise. The pair swirl around one another, beautiful and deadly as thick smoke.When the band announced the album’s tracklist on Instagram, a weird number of fans were outraged at the Catalan singer’s presence, as if Fontaines had invited in some popsy rather than the best singer of her generation and an autodidact whose last record wasa concept album about ancient nuns. Clearly, some fans would like Fontaines DC to remain as pickled in aspic as the “beauty queens / Razor-faced / With private means” that Chatten disdains over the rising hiss of closer Intimate. His bitter broadside underscores that trying to cheat death means choosing spiritual death, the Faustian bargain of our times. By emphatically rejecting that fate, Fontaines have grown in dramatic, majestic fashion to become the best band of their generation – the kind that, to nick a phrase from another band, really might live for ever.Explore more on these topicsFontaines DCIndiePop and rockRosalíareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gabrielle Goliath: Elegy review – devastating lament is a furious, single-note call to action | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Too controversial for the Venice Biennale, this haunting video and audio work commemorates murders and genocides with an angry act of mourning
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Too controversial for the Venice Biennale, this haunting video and audio work commemorates murders and genocides with an angry act of mourning
Content: Gabrielle Goliath’s Elegy at Ibraaz in London.Photograph: Ollie HammickView image in fullscreenGabrielle Goliath’s Elegy at Ibraaz in London.Photograph: Ollie HammickArt and designReviewGabrielle Goliath: Elegy review – devastating lament is a furious, single-note call to actionIbraaz, LondonToo controversial for the Venice Biennale, this haunting video and audio work commemorates murders and genocides with an angry act of mourningEddy FrankelMon 12 Oct 2026 07.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sound of mourning spills out into the streets. A single, endless wailing note echoes out of the basement of Ibraaz, a relatively new cultural centre in London’s Fitzrovia. This is Gabrielle Goliath’s heart-wrenching Elegy, each of its three films featuring a woman singing just one note until their lungs falter and another woman steps up to fill in for her. Just as a note is about to die, it is sustained. It’s a haunting, shocking act of mourning for murder, injustice and genocide.And it almost never made it.A panel of five leading South African cultural voices picked Goliath’s work to represent their nation at this summer’s Venice Biennale. Goliath has been working on the project for a decade, collecting voices, collecting stories. This was a work about femicide and the murder of LGBTQ+ people in South Africa, but it had expanded. The latest iteration dealt withthe Ovaherero and Nama genocide in Namibia, and the death of a Palestinian poet in 2023. It was a step too far for Gayton McKenzie, South Africa’s sport, arts and culture minister.View image in fullscreenGabrielle Goliath, Elegy, at Ibraaz London.Photograph: Ollie HammickMcKenzie is the president of the far-right Patriotic Alliance party, and has been vocal in his support of Israel in recent years. He wrote a letter describing the work as “highly divisive”. He called for the work to be edited, for the offending passage about the Palestinian poet to be removed. Goliath refused, so McKenzie put a stop to the whole thing, cancelling her Venice pavilion.She fought it tooth and nail, taking her case to South Africa’s high court, but the case was dismissed. The South Africa pavilion at the biennale sat embarrassingly empty, a big, glaring visual metaphor for the global reach of the culture wars and a symbol of censorship in the face of violence.Goliath instead founda home for the work in a nearby church, which is where I first saw it. It was devastating then, an almost overwhelmingly emotional piece of art in a beautiful setting. Ibraaz lacks the ornate, quiet atmosphere of that Venetian church, but has made up for it with absolute sombre darkness. The space is pitch black save for the screens. One film is in commemoration of Ipeleng Christine Moholane, a woman who was strangled and left for dead in a field near Johannesburg in 2015. Another is in honour of two women who died at the hands of German colonial oppressors during the genocide in Namibia between 1904 and 1908. The third is for the poetHiba Abu Nadaand the thousands of Palestinians who have died in Gaza since 2023.This is not a soft, plaintive lament – the room is a discordant, uncomfortable place, filled with a wailing cacophony of clashing vibrato and just out of tune notes. It sounds angry, vicious, furious, because it is. It’s not just an act of commemoration, it’s a call to action, a demand for change and justice.While it’s incredibly emotional and deeply moving, the main feeling you get is frustration and hopelessness, not sadness. What makes Elegy so powerful is the endless proliferation of horrifying images we have to deal with on a daily basis. If you want to see images of death and genocide, you just have to look at social media or the news. We have more access to shocking, real imagery of awful current events than ever before. But Goliath has stripped the imagery away and left you with only the emotion, so just the anger and heartache remains.It’s an act of resistance against the image economy, against murder and femicide, against violence and genocide. It’s a feminist lament, a scream against it all.But it’s also a significant modern artwork, a symbol of our times, of our wars and cultural frictions, and its sound lingers in your ears long after you’ve walked away.Gabrielle Goliath: Elegyis at Ibraaz, London, from 8 October to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtPerformance artExhibitionsSouth AfricaAfricaVenice BiennalereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The missed opportunity of Jay-Z’s documentary series | Jay-Z | The Guardian
description: Jay-Z in 8, the rap mogul’s HBO docuseries, covers his life and career in effort to mend his image – with no pushback. Why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jay-Z in 8, the rap mogul’s HBO docuseries, covers his life and career in effort to mend his image – with no pushback. Why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion?
Content: Jay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.Photograph: MubiView image in fullscreenJay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.Photograph: MubiJay-ZThe missed opportunity of Jay-Z’s documentary seriesJay-Z in 8, the rap mogul’s HBO docuseries, covers his life and career in effort to mend his image – with no pushback. Why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion?Andre GeeMon 12 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the finale ofJay-Z’sJay-Z in 8, the recent eight-partHBOdocumentary series on his life and career, the billionaire rap mogul talked with record producer Rick Rubin about the song Family Feud from his4:44 album. He clarified one of its lyrics, “Al Sharpton in the mirror takin’ selfies / How is him or Pill Cosby ‘posed to help me?”, in which he chided Sharpton, the civil rights leader, and Cosby, the disgraced actor-comedian, forconstantlycriticizingrapmusic. He called Sharpton an “extortionist” who goes “from place to place” demanding: “You want our support … give us the money.” Listening to him chastise Sharpton, I pondered how he doesn’t see himself as a similar figure.Starting in 2019, Jay-Zpartneredwiththe NFL in 2019 as entertainment director, deciding the Super Bowl half-time performers and working with the league on other community endeavors.Colin Kaepernick, the former NFL quarterback, has recently alleged that the deal came after NFL owners decided they needed a “Black face” to help them quell outrage from Black people after Kaepernickwasblackballedby the league forkneelingduring the national anthems as a form of protest against police brutality. Jay-Z was lambasted for undercutting Kaepernick’s cause for personal gain, marring his reputation with many fans who came to view him as the same counterinsurgent figure he criticized in the documentary.Jay-Z in 8 review – the rapper’s interminable interview show should have been a podcastRead moreJay-Z in 8 is an effort that seeks to mend his public image; the series culls his 30-year oeuvre along with his life and times. In the sleek, black-and-white episodes, which were filmed at some point in 2024, Jay explicates his music history in interviews with Rubin, the 63-year-old Def Jam co-founder and producer. It’s a polished, low-frills watch. The two sit at a table in an empty room in the events center Palais Brongniart, France’s former stock exchange, while Rubin chooses songs from Jay-Z’s catalog and uses them as a springboard into broader topics such as his relationship with his parents, his creative process and wider cultural observations. The final instalment, which aired on 9 October, featuresJay-Zpontificating on racism and suggesting generational wealth as its remedy. Hearing him dismiss social justice movements by claiming “we never get together” to push for change, and discussing inequality through banal observations, indicates how little thought he has actually put into uprooting systemic oppression.Rubin offers no pushback. Throughout the series, his lack of deeper questioning fails to give the conversations the depth they require. Rubin comes across as an in-awe spectator tasked with polishing the Jay-Z mythos. It’s the opposite of what a conversation series needs. (A more incisive interviewer, for instance, would’ve asked Jay-Z, who, in referencing his marriage to Beyoncé, rapped, “What’s better than one billionaire? Two,” if redistributing $2bn would be even better for the community at large.) At one point in that episode, Jay-Z, the richest musician in the world, refers to the Black bourgeoisie as “they”. A poignant follow-up from Rubin could have been to ask what exactly Jay felt separated him from that group. Instead, as with most of the series, Rubin nodded approvingly. His sycophantic presence turns what could have been a quintessential music documentary into hagiography. And Jay-Z likely wanted it that way.Over the years, the 56-year-old Brooklyn native has rapped about several ugly truths in his life: shooting his brother, selling drugs to loved ones, cheating on his wife, feeding others’ substance abuse for profit. He touched on some of those topics in Jay-Z in 8, giving the documentary its best substance. There’s some cool trivia, too. He reveals that the second verse of 99 Problems is based on a true story, reflects on how his Uncle Butchie inspired him to grow locs, and says he is too self-conscious to be as vocally experimental as Beyoncé. But he also has limits.In 2005, he halted his The Black Book memoir with the writer dream hampton because the process, he said, was getting too personal. Later that year, hetoldRolling Stone: “I know that people really want to know about me and I thought it was OK, but as I got closer and closer I said, ‘What am I doing?’” Since then, he’s become more discerning about his access, rarely giving interviews. He doesn’t want to be prodded against his will, but he also won’t let public narratives go unchecked, offering public retorts to critics in feature verses andstadium performances. He compulsively seeks to control the story, almost always in forums that don’t allow for discussion or pushback.How Black banjo players are changing Americana musicRead moreAn eight-hour conversation series with Jay-Z needed someone with deep hip-hop knowledgeandan instinct for pointed questions (I wonder if there’s a profession from which they could’ve sought that person?) In episode three, Rubin plays the title track from 2017’s 4:44, a highly vulnerable song where he vents about being an immature, emotionally unavailable cheater. And while Jay-Z apologizes in the song for his conduct, he doesn’t necessarily promise to be a better husband. Seven years later, Rubin doesn’t push for advanced thoughts on life as a husband or father, instead offering a vague: “Do you feel like there’s been progress?”When Rubin asks him if the stakes of life are higher for him now or during his drug-dealing days, Jay chooses the latter. He says his mindset toward powerful industry figures threatening to punish him for not doing what they want is, “I don’t care what you do. It doesn’t matter to me.” But if he’s really “already home”, as he rapped on the 2009 track that boasted of career contentment, why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion? And more importantly, why isn’t he putting something on the line byjoiningartistsincludingMacklemoreto speak out against multiple genocides abroad and Donald Trump’s fascism? Someone who isn’t prone to just agreeing enthusiastically would’ve pulled at those threads.The crack era and the Black excellence ruse (in which Black capitalists claim the revolution will come by simply buying from Black-owned companies) have denied multiple generations of Black people liberation in disparate ways. Jay-Z is at the figurative scene of both crimes. He earned his legacy with brilliant music that chronicles the drug game with cinematic vigor and contextualizes his actions in a way that a socioeconomics professor could explain to his cohort. But he rarely broaches the tension of his third act as a billionaire music mogul in an “eat the rich” world. Here, Rubin never asked him to.​Jay-Z in 8 airs onHBOMax in the US and Mubi in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsJay-ZDocumentary filmsHBOBlack US cultureRapMusic documentaryRick RubinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Influencer Project review – ick-inducing thriller satirises social media content, and exploits it too | Movies | The Guardian
