description: When influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King visits Copenhagen all the trips to trendy shops and fancy restaurants soon take a turn for the worse
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: When influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King visits Copenhagen all the trips to trendy shops and fancy restaurants soon take a turn for the worse
Content: Moments of real fear … Chiara King as Chiara King.Photograph: Icon Film Distribution/PAView image in fullscreenMoments of real fear … Chiara King as Chiara King.Photograph: Icon Film Distribution/PAMoviesReviewThe Influencer Project review – ick-inducing thriller satirises social media content, and exploits it tooWhen influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King visits Copenhagen all the trips to trendy shops and fancy restaurants soon take a turn for the worseLeslie FelperinMon 12 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King stars as influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King, or some kind of parafictional version of herself, in this quease-inducing thriller exercise. The ick gets generated not necessarily by the eventual gore that erupts in the last reel, but by the tacky weirdness of the way the film apes the mannerisms of social media reels and streaming nonsense to both satirise the ugly side of the business but also exploit and profit off it at the same time. On one level, it’s an eerily clever exercise in bad faith, like a poor Michael Haneke film (think Funny Games) for gen-Z kicks; on another, maybe it’s just a crappy ripoff of online tropes that have been way overexposed already. Or both.Anyway, here’s what happens: influencer Chiara gets invited to visit Copenhagen by a tourist organisation, a deal set up by her avaricious manager Alice (Jazmine Summer). Of course, this means practically every moment of her time awake in the city will be filmed, both by Chiara herself on her trusty smartphone, or a camera crew led by director Mike (played by Mike Nybroe, who is also director of The Influencer Project, ha ha); Mike is supported by sound man Daniel (Daniel Parmo) and cameraman Victor (Luca Storm). The early sections turn in all the influence-slop you would expect, with shopping trips to trendy merch vendors such as Baum und Pferdgarten, and meals at fancy local restaurants, and then a livestreamed visit to a “haunted house,” which is the big thing on Instagram and TikTok these days.But the product placement is somewhat interrupted by moments of real fear (or “real fear”) when Chiara starts getting threatening direct messages (from someone calling themselves KingSlayer) who wants her to stop talking for reasons not clearly explained at first, otherwise he will kill and rape her, not necessarily in that order. This unsurprisingly creates a pall over Chiara’s trip, but if she just quits and goes home she’ll miss out on $100k in deals, so that’s not an option.So are we supposed to despise Chiara for her greed or applaud her girl-boss fortitude in not being intimidated by a stalker? And what to make of the film’s claims that this was partly inspired by real incidents of stalking? Nybroe and co work the debate into the endless stream of comments we see scrolling alongside Chiara’s livestream – a river of chat that doesn’t let up even when the credits start to roll, ersatz dialectics for an age of digital proliferation.The Influencer Project is in UK and Irish cinemas from 16 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsSocial mediaDenmarkDigital mediaEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocks | Movies | The Guardian
description: Debut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, Pumpkin
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Debut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, Pumpkin
Content: ‘Quite the showcase’ … Milly Shapiro in Hallowarrior.Photograph: Jessica Licata/PRView image in fullscreen‘Quite the showcase’ … Milly Shapiro in Hallowarrior.Photograph: Jessica Licata/PRMoviesReviewHallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocksDebut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, PumpkinCatherine BrayMon 12 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHome Alone meets Mad Max in this atmospheric seasonal chiller, named for Halloween and not a cheery greeting. A disease has wiped out most of humanity, leaving 16-year-old Pumpkin (Milly Shapiro) stranded alone in her rural family home in the middle of nowhere for the best part of four years. This classic American clapboard house has always been the perfect quaint yet unsettling place to celebrate Halloween, and she determines to uphold the family tradition and do just that, sending a radio broadcast to anyone listening to invite them to celebrate spooky season with her. Unfortunately, the message is picked up by some less than wholesome types, led by Thalia (Shannyn Sossamon), thus setting the stage for the proverbial to hit the fan.It’s the first major screen role for Shapiro since her memorable debut as the little sister inAri Aster’s Hereditary, and she is in almost every scene here, making for quite the showcase. It’s good casting: Pumpkin is an intriguing presence – at once young and old, presumably because she’s been fending for herself during such a key stage of her development. She’s not had any adult guidance since the age of 12 – arresting her development in some ways, while having to survive, be totally independent and grieve her entire family alone has simultaneously made her unusually tough in others.This turns out to be invaluable in a horror film; it gives the script plenty of room to have her make naive decisions which are wholly justified, as well as to prove surprisingly resilient in ways that the character’s backstory supports. This gives a plausible, grounded core to the story’s more outlandish trappings, and the splendid production design – ranging from cosy cottagecore Halloween to a timeless Bates motel aesthetic – makes for an appealing storyworld. Hallowarrior is the feature debut of Ben Sottak, an experienced short film-maker, and on this evidence he’s likely to be worth keeping an eye out for.Hallowarrior is on Shudder and AMC+ from 16 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Atlantic Requiem review – Önaç gives historical slavery documents howling raging life  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: From syncopated funk to the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant to bureaucratic recitative, the score to David Önaç new oratorio, premiered by the London Symphony Orchestra, is serious and beautiful
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: From syncopated funk to the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant to bureaucratic recitative, the score to David Önaç new oratorio, premiered by the London Symphony Orchestra, is serious and beautiful
Content: J'nai Bridges, Brittany Renee and Orson Van Gay II perform Atlantic Requiem at St Luke’s.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenJ'nai Bridges, Brittany Renee and Orson Van Gay II perform Atlantic Requiem at St Luke’s.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewAtlantic Requiem review – Önaç gives historical slavery documents howling raging lifeLSO St Luke’s, LondonFrom syncopated funk to the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant to bureaucratic recitative, the score to David Önaç new oratorio, premiered by the London Symphony Orchestra, is serious and beautifulAlexandra CoghlanMon 12 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do you put a value on a human life? If you’re an insurance underwriter that’s not a philosophical question, it’s a practical one. The answer, incidentally, as calculated by Lloyds of London in 1779 was £45: the figure placed on each enslaved person transported across the Atlantic alongside corn, fish and other cargo. Court transcripts from two decades later describe a woman quarantined for smallpox, subsequently bound, blindfolded and tossed overboard tied to a chair. The captain later expressed his regret for the loss of “so good a chair”.Archives can tell us what, but it takes art to give us the humanhowof the past. Enter composerDavid Önaç– commissioned to take the historical documents unearthed from the Lloyds archive and give them howling, raging life in his new Atlantic Requiem, premiered this weekend by the London Symphony Orchestra, an expanded BBC Singers, three soloists and (in a last-minute step-in) conductor Malcolm J Merriweather.Manchester-based composer creates requiem to honour enslaved AfricansRead moreThis is a big piece – in theme and scope. Önaç’s score is beautifully, seriously constructed, turning the pitches of the piano’s white and black keys into symbolic gestures of opposition, equality and – perhaps – reconciliation. It’s a microcosm of a work in which the syncopated funk and alternative scales of jazz and blues drift into the western classical architecture of the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant bleeds into the chattering banality of bureaucratic recitative, and soloists soar but also scream. The conversation is particularly effective in the convulsive dance of the finale – a chewily textural, highly rhythmic intervention after the rapt choral meditation of the Agnus Dei.Merriweather steered his forces safely through the choppy musical waters, though soloists Brittany Renee, the ever-expressive J’Nai Bridges and especially tenor Orson Van Gay II risked being overwhelmed from their position behind the orchestra. In many ways this pair of Sunday afternoon performances at LSO St Luke’s (too small for so large a project) felt like a workshop for a piece still under construction. Önaç packs a lot into a short span, at the expense of pacing that feels almost perfunctory. There’s a full-length work here dying to get out, and a major new composing talent who deserves the space to tell the stories that have been silenced for so long.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Symphony OrchestraSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Peasants by Maryam Aslany review – why an ancient way of life may hold the key to our future | History books | The Guardian
description: Modernity means cities – or so we’re told. This bold new study of those who make their living from the land argues otherwise
Author: Joe Moran
Headline: Modernity means cities – or so we’re told. This bold new study of those who make their living from the land argues otherwise
Content: Farmers planting rice in Thailand.Photograph: Karel Bittner/AlamyView image in fullscreenFarmers planting rice in Thailand.Photograph: Karel Bittner/AlamyBook of the dayHistory booksReviewPeasants by Maryam Aslany review – why an ancient way of life may hold the key to our futureModernity means cities – or so we’re told. This bold new study of those who make their living from the land argues otherwiseJoe MoranMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 03.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe word “peasant” has a negative edge: it has come to mean someone ignorant, unsophisticated, lowborn. Such an attitude, writes Maraym Aslany in this impressive piece of anthropology-cum-history, is “a residue of the massive psychodrama which made us who we are … we became modern by expelling the peasant parts of ourselves”. Her book weaves together a global history of peasants and an account of the four years she spent travelling in India, Cambodia, Peru and Ghana, living with and talking to peasant families.She aims to challenge the notion that the decline of the peasantry is the necessary condition for becoming “modern”. This notion arose in Britain, the first country to rid itself of its peasants when, with the enclosure acts, it turned its land from a common good into a financial asset. As this model of capitalist modernity began to take over the world, intellectuals of every stripe argued that peasants stood in the way of “progress”. Voltaire saw them as slow-witted people unable to understand their piteous state, stumbling blocks in the pursuit of enlightenment. Karl Marx believed that their “relentless property fanaticism” made them a reactionary element within capitalism.double quotation markThere are more ‘peasants’ today than at any time in historyYet, throughout history, peasant civilisations have thrived and endured. From 3000BC until industrial-era Britain, the common form of large-scale human society was the agrarian empire, sustained by the peasantry. The huge calorific surplus produced by such empires – rice in particular being a supremely efficient way of extracting calories from the earth – was spent on massive temples, sprawling cities and complex bureaucracies. For more than 2000 years, until the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, the Chinese empire was built on peasant farming, enabled by a vast irrigation system and run by a hands-on state staffed by the world’s most educated officials.The last century, though, has seen a long, undeclared war on the peasantry. In the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin’s policies of collectivisation killed millions of peasants. The US carpet-bombed the peasantry in Vietnam. The Maoism much nurtured on western university campuses in the 1960s and 1970s – with its belief that the peasant populations of newly decolonised countries were the best hope of fighting US imperialism – was too often turned on peasants themselves. Pol Pot’s murderous vision in Cambodia, that the country should be returned by force to its peasant essence, led to millions of deaths. More recently, peasants have been the main casualties of superpower-backed civil wars and conflicts over land and resources in Sudan, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.By the 1980s, many decolonised countries were in debt and needed bailing out by foreign capital. The price they paid was the introduction of market discipline into their agrarian economies. In much of contemporary global capitalism, western corporate power rests on peasant foundations. While producing valuable commodities – rice, sugar, cocoa – these peasants are excluded from the profits they generate. Now they have been left to deal with the climate emergency, and subsequent falling yields, on their own.In Maharashtra, in the heart of India, Aslany watches and listens to an eternal theme tune of the modern world: the double flash of machete on sugarcane, once to cut off the stalk, then to cut it in half. Maharashtra’s cotton farmers have been thrown into crisis by the droughts, alternating with catastrophic floods, produced by global heating. Amid such uncertainty, sugarcane is a good bet. Unlike cotton, though, sugarcane can’t be stored but must be crushed within hours of harvesting, and processors exploit this fact to pay farmers less. The women fear missing workdays so much that many have early hysterectomies.In Ghana, where the world’s chocolate industry has always relied on the work of peasants, Aslany finds the cocoa farmers struggling not just with climate change but with crop disease, chronic underinvestment and the poisoning of the land by galamsey – the local term for illegal, unregulated gold mining, the profits from which go to the chiefs and politicians. But peasants find a way of surviving. Peruviancocaleros– growers of coca leaf, much of it used to make cocaine – have learned to live with the drug cartels who offer them loans and administrative assistance. Abandoned by the state, they have created a competing moral system, informed by the demands of subsistence living and duty to family and community.This book has an ambitious range, often deviating into sweeping histories of the last few hundred years. Occasionally it comes unstuck. The economist Adam Smith did not believe that “the capitalist future would arrive only when peasants gave way to wealthy technocratic landlords”; he castigated landlords for collecting unearned income. The claim that William of Orange and his wife, Mary, took the English throne “without opposition or bloodshed” ignores the ensuing violence in Scotland and Ireland.Despite the odd misstep, a compelling argument develops, one that offers a useful counterpoint toPatrick Joyce’s excellent 2024 history, Remembering Peasants, which oddly Aslany cites only in one footnote. Joyce, focusing mainly on Ireland, Italy and Poland, sees the peasantry as “a vanished world”, already destroyed. Aslany reminds us that there are more peasants today than at any time in history.The west may have got rid of its peasantry but, 250 years after the Industrial Revolution, “most of the world has become modern without doing so”. Peasant households make up about 2 billion people, a quarter of the human race. Their way of life is far more resilient than factory work, and there is nothing backward about it. The 350m tonnes of sugarcane produced each year in India – the largest output of any country and a figure that has tripled since 1980 – all come from family farms. In the absence of universal industrialisation, which the Earth can ill afford, nothing sustains large populations as well as the land.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet most of the world’s leaders have come to believe what Aslany calls the “urban fairytale” – that people are moving inexorably to the cities and that the peasantry will soon, and should soon, no longer exist. This means that peasants lack the main thing they need: the long-term investment by states in soil, water and botanical stock that the agrarian empires once provided.What makes this tragic, as Aslany points out, is that, just when we need it most, peasants offer a model of sustainability and stewardship of the natural world. They serve as a buffer holding at bay a rapacious capitalism that has none of their respect for nature. One Cambodian peasant, farming in the floodplain of the country’s massive Tonle Sap lake, tells Aslany: “Rice is our companion. We say human beings have nineteen souls, and rice has the same number.”The peasant belief that the land is sacred is not some quaint relic, but a crucial way of ensuring that the pursuit of productivity doesn’t destroy the Earth. That much of the world’s cultivable land remains in the hands of peasants protects us against total corporate takeover and environmental breakdown. If we keep trying to enact the urban fairytale, it will destabilise food production, destroy the planet’s ecosystem and create an unprecedented wave of refugees. We must hope, for all our sakes, that peasants are not just part of our past, but part of our future.Peasants: Makers of the Modern World is published by Bloomsbury (£25). title: The Weight of Angels by John Boyne review – what if Oscar Wilde had lived? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The great Irish writer died, a broken man, at only 46. Imagining a second act for him is a great idea – but the results are sentimental and unconvincing
Author: Neil Bartlett
Headline: The great Irish writer died, a broken man, at only 46. Imagining a second act for him is a great idea – but the results are sentimental and unconvincing
Content: Oscar Wilde in 1882.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOscar Wilde in 1882.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesFictionReviewThe Weight of Angels by John Boyne review – what if Oscar Wilde had lived?The great Irish writer died, a broken man, at only 46. Imagining a second act for him is a great idea – but the results are sentimental and unconvincingNeil BartlettMon 12 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1895, four days after the opening of The Importance of Being Earnest, the Marquess of Queensberry left a card at Oscar Wilde’s club that publicly accused him of “posing as a somdomite”. Instead of instigating the libel case that led to his imprisonment and early death in a Paris hotel just five years later, what would have happened if Wilde had simply torn that card up? John Boyne’s new novel sets out to answer that intriguing question.For starters, Boyne contrives a fate for Wilde’s beloved Lord Alfred Douglas which entertainingly redistributes the details of the real Wilde’s life before, during and after his time in Reading jail. This sets up the novel’s cat-and-mouse game with the history it is reimagining. Wilde himself, conveniently released from marriage by the early death of his wife, is then free to live not as a tortured, scandal-haunted genius, but as a randy, wisecracking, party-going queen. The upside of this is that Oscar gets to swap bons mots with a crowded cast list of celebrities; the downside is that he shows little sign of the troubled and radical mind that produced the real Wilde’s late journalism and fiction, never mind the subversive linguistic pyrotechnics of The Importance.The storyline leaps elegantly across the years, and often drops the high-society comedy to show this alternative Wilde becoming embroiled in more than his fair share of melodrama. This allows for some highly effective tear-jerking, notably in the scene that re-imagines the departure of his beloved elder son for the Somme. Time jumps are delivered in the form of letters, newspaper articles and even scripts of hypothetical plays and films about Wilde; this genre-hopping keeps things lively, and allows Boyne some very effective shifts of tone, time and place.double quotation markBoyne doesn’t so much show his imaginary Wilde interacting with queer history as magically abolishing itThe real Wilde wrote no more plays after The Importance of Being Earnest; Boyne’s version lives to write nine more, plus a Hollywood screenplay. Sadly, of these we get to read not a single quotation. Curiously, Boyne goes out of his way to make these plays sound dull; he has his fictional alternative turn into a staunch aesthetic conservative, concerned only with success. We see his writing’s rewards (endless money, a knighthood) but are never made privy to its process or motives. In fact, we never see him functioning as a writer at all.With regard to Wilde’s queerness – the treatment of which Boyne clearly intends to be his novel’s main claim to seriousness – the narrative makes a point of having him collide with several of the most important early European theorists of what we now call gay liberation: George Cecil Ives, Magnus Hirschfeld, André Gide. However, it leaves Wilde untouched by their ideas, and keeps him well away from any experience of their respective gay subcultures in London, Berlin and Paris. Instead, Wilde stays in the closet and settles down in a Mayfair mansion with a conveniently doting schoolteacher. After a decade of monogamy, Oscar wrecks this happy home with the help of a hard-bodied student football player. As a direct outcome of this error, the deadly outcomes of gay shame and self-loathing invade the novel for the first time; Wilde promptly acquires a conscience, deciding that he really ought to use his status as a literary national treasure to do something to make the world a better place for homosexuals.From then on – around 1930 – Boyne doesn’t so much show his imaginary Wilde interacting with queer history as magically abolishing it. At yet another party, Winston Churchill is enlisted to promote gay rights in parliament; characters become helpfully psychic, imagining 1970s-style gay liberation marches, gay marriage and even some very specific post-Stonewall arguments about the respective merits of radical and assimilationist theories of gay freedom. Boyne’s Wilde clearly sides with the latter. Speaking in a voice that sometimes sounds suspiciously like Boyne’s own, Wilde gives a speech that not only allows him to publicly champion feminism and Irish independence, but also to single-handedly persuade an audience of MPs to vote for the complete and overnight decriminalisation of homosexuality. Luckily, all of this emotive nonsense happens just in time for the coronation of 1952, meaning that both Prince Philip and Elizabeth II get to congratulate Wilde on his efforts during their after party. Unsurprisingly, Wilde dies of happiness, and goes straight to heaven.Any historical fantasia worth its salt must play with its reader, continually asking them to assess whether the alternatives being imagined are credible or desirable. In this case, in a year that has seen attacks on queer and trans lives proliferate, Boyne’s decision to replace the real history of that community’s collective struggle with such a contrived and top-down miracle feels like a very odd fictional manoeuvre indeed. He has clearly done lots of research, but has chosen to put it at the service of creating a Wilde who is fatally less interesting and moving than the original. In this version of history, Ireland’s greatest lord of language is reduced to a sentimental, royalty-loving, champagne-quaffing showman. What a waste of a great idea.The Weight of Angels by John Boyne is published by Doubleday (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com.
