title: Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments! | Turbine Hall | The Guardian
description: The Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!
Content: ‘You have to surrender to it’ … Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installation at Tate Modern.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘You have to surrender to it’ … Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installation at Tate Modern.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTurbine HallReviewTarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments!Tate Modern, LondonThe Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!Jonathan JonesMon 12 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the floor of theTurbine Hall, there are wide water basins and huge flattish rough-hewn rocks you might see on moorland or in a desert. You can sit or stand or climb on them. But if you look up, you won’t be able to stop looking up – because it’s raining musical instruments. Immense elongated brass trumpets and giant glowing drums seem to float in the air, suspended from the girders of the former power station’s roof.If Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui had just left it at that, it would be an impressive, intriguing installation, but this isTate Modern, honey, and Atoui hasn’t been asked to occupy its grandest space with mere physical objects. Instead, his sculptural creations and found stuff resonate and echo with an ever-changing, invisible art of noises. An earth-shaking bass note throbs from a hanging trumpet – or is it from that translucent cone rising out of the ground like an ethereal minaret? Then a drumbeat booms through the space and a woman’s plangent, achingly lovely voice sings notes of infinite nostalgia and melancholy.Tarek Atoui admires his workIt’s entrancing. The music has you hooked. It is music, I think, though abstract, non-melodic, a rising and falling of sounds that lead you around and through the installation’s forest of solid things. But then – is music ever not sculptural? Listening to the scything percussive notes of Stravinsky certainly is; and the desire to crystallise sound waves into something visible has haunted everyone from the inventors of opera to designers of psychedelic lightshows.Yet Tarek Atoui still manages to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. He teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear, how the stones and water basins, pipes and strings have produced this sonic outpouring. The entire installation is an interconnected musical machine.It’s funny too. There’s a warm, generous if absurdist humour to it all. In the past, a crazy mechanical contraption like this would be called “Heath Robinsonish”, after the early 20th-century British cartoonist who came up with such things. A better comparison is Leonardo da Vinci, who invented wild musical instruments among his other real and impossible machines: organs worked by water, a string instrument shaped like a fantastic beast.Tarek Atoui at the Tate ModernAtoui, like Leonardo, seems to be looking for a lost harmony in the world, a secret note that pleased the Lord. Sadness hovers in the sounds that fill this vast grey space, as the bass notes pound harder, building up to an apocalyptic blast. What is being mourned and where is he taking us? You start to feel you are in a city of sounds and sights. The crowd of towering, floating pinnacles, the mysterious voice and crescendo of percussion, suggest an ancient, tumultuous labyrinth of a city. I thought of Lahore and Marrakesh, of a street-singer heard once in an Istanbul market. Yet this city is purer, less tangible. Its towers fly in the air.View image in fullscreenSonic king … Atoui at his Turbine Hall installation.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianUltimately, you can’t reduce this magical, elusive work of art to a fixed meaning. You have to surrender to it. The sound gathers you up in its ecstasy like a spiralling mystical dance. There is a strong similarity with Sufi drummers and dervishes who use music and motion to inculcate a liberating, trancelike calm. I certainly didn’t want to leave. The vibrations and complex visual composition keep your brain busy but you are also soothed and at peace.It also suggests the urban life all around this site, the exotic sounds of Bankside: the music of the city, gathered into Atoui’s collage of random noise. But reality slips and fades as you are shown a world beyond the physical. All these objects, from the cones to the stones to the electric guitar played live at the press view, are but as air. They fascinate the eye but the sound eventually dissolves the material world. The solid stuff Atoui begins with becomes as unreal as a reflection in a courtyard pool.Atoui has grabbed the opportunity to work in this vast space with both hands, creating something rich, ingenious, funny, sad, mystical. This is a Turbine Hall installation to lose yourself in for hours, dreaming and wondering. It’s the sonic answer to a sun indoors – and Atoui is a modern magus.Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installationis at Tate Modern, London, from 13 October until 11 April 2027Explore more on these topicsTurbine HallSound artTate ModernArtInstallationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Corruption has only got worse’: can a new version of Our Friends in the North still shock audiences 30 years on? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Peter Flannery’s 90s TV drama classic is getting a theatre reworking in Newcastle. The director and cast talk about doing justice to its themes of scandal and decay – and emulating its star-making actors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Peter Flannery’s 90s TV drama classic is getting a theatre reworking in Newcastle. The director and cast talk about doing justice to its themes of scandal and decay – and emulating its star-making actors
Content: Tyne after time … (From left) The stage cast of Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years: Ryan Nolan, Sam Neale, Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull.Photograph: Chris Bishop/PicturesbyBishView image in fullscreenTyne after time … (From left) The stage cast of Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years: Ryan Nolan, Sam Neale, Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull.Photograph: Chris Bishop/PicturesbyBishTheatre‘Corruption has only got worse’: can a new version of Our Friends in the North still shock audiences 30 years on?Peter Flannery’s 90s TV drama classic is getting a theatre reworking in Newcastle. The director and cast talk about doing justice to its themes of scandal and decay – and emulating its star-making actorsNeil ArmstrongMon 12 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a small room at the top of Newcastle upon Tyne’s Live theatre, four actors are bringing to life the principal characters from one of British television’s best-loved dramas. Sitting around a table strewn with coffee cups, water bottles and annotated scripts, Tosker and Geordie have been boozing in a nightclub and weighing up their chances of pulling. Mary and Nicky have been arguing about whether they have a future together.The scenes are from a new stage version ofOur Friends in the North, the landmark nine-episode series first broadcast in 1996 on BBC Two. Set against a backdrop of Labour politics and police corruption, it charted 30 years in the lives of four working-class geordies and made stars of Mark Strong, Daniel Craig, Gina McKee and Christopher Eccleston. It was a hit with critics and viewers, won awards and regularly makes “greatest ever” lists.Now it is back, after Live theatre’s artistic director Jack McNamara persuaded an initially reluctant Peter Flannery, the writer, to return to the characters he first created for a Royal Shakespeare Company play in 1982, before later rewriting and expanding the story for the screen.View image in fullscreenGeordie sure things … (From left) Christopher Eccleston, Gina McKee, Mark Strong and Daniel Craig in the 1996 TV series of Our Friends in the North.Photograph: BBC Photolibrary“In a way, the production came from a sense of frustration, of always having to think small and manageable in a historically underfunded region,” says McNamara. “We needed a bigger gesture. A wider story for a larger audience that had a familiar outline, but still something no one has seen on stage before. Put simply, I wanted to direct 12 actors on a big stage in a brand new work. The significance and agility of Our Friends offers a rare opportunity for that to happen.”Because of the scale of the show and its potential afterlife, it is a co-production between Live theatre, theTheatreRoyal in Newcastle upon Tyne and the theatre producers Eastlake Productions.Flannery has reworked two of the TV episodes, set in 1979 and 1984, into a two-act play. He has introduced a chorus and there are a couple of borrowings from other episodes for explanatory purposes. The stage design allows for it to be a fast-moving show.double quotation markI’m aware it is a bleak view of society, but the characters are survivorsPeter FlanneryOn TV, McKee was the only one of the four principal players who was from the region. For the play, four actors from the north-east have been cast. Ryan Nolan is the political idealist Nicky (Eccleston on TV). Sam Neale is the quietly driven Mary (McKee). Jack Robertson plays the would-be entrepreneurial Tosker (Strong). Scott Turnbull is the luckless Geordie (Craig).At the table read, a few days before rehearsals with the full cast begin, various scenes are stress-tested under the guidance of McNamara. There’s a long discussion about how best to make a particular joke land, and the two actors concerned try it in a number of different ways. In the script, one character is reprimanded for missing his son’s football final. “‘Football final’ is a bit of a cliche,” jokes Turnbull. “Maybe it should be a ‘bassoon recital’.” Everyone laughs.The actors want to know whether McNamara expects them to model their performances on their TV predecessors, but he is not interested in impersonations. The way to pay tribute to the originators of the roles, he says, is to do their own thing. There’s a sense of relief but the four are acutely aware that Our Friends in the North is a cherished TV show, and there is a weight of expectation.“I’m trying not to get into an anxiety spiral about it but it is there, looming,” says Neale, who recalls watching the show with her mum.“I do feel like there’s a lot of pressure,” says Turnbull. “This needs to be executed well.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen… Live theatre’s artistic director Jack McNamara.Photograph: Chris OrdMcNamara is well aware of the pressure the cast are feeling but he likes to keep things loose. “There is always an element of experimenting,” he says. “I don’t storyboard things down to a T. I like to have a little openness so that in rehearsals it feels like anything is possible.”Understandably, McNamara can’t help but imagine where things might go next. There are hopes the show will have a life beyond its short run in Newcastle but “it has to land here and have real resonance before it goes anywhere else”, McNamara says.Later, at the full-cast rehearsals, the energy level is palpably higher than at the table read. After a couple of hours, McNamara asks the performers to improvise various scenes. Improvisation is not a memory test, he reminds them, but a way of exploring intentionality. There are clear glimpses of what has the potential to be a powerful theatrical experience.“The show is about friendship and how it evolves and fractures. And there’s a lot about political optimism and political failure and how they sit alongside each other,” McNamara says.“The chances of real change through the Labour party is the central preoccupation of Our Friends in the North,” wrote the late campaigning journalist Paul Foot, but no one could consider the show – or the play – a paean of praise for politicians, especially their relationship with the police. In Our Friends – some of which was based on a scandal uncovered by Foot – decent Labour politicians are bested by cynical spivs and extremists. Honest police officers are outmanoeuvred, and perhaps outnumbered, by bent coppers. Lawmaking and law enforcement are rotten to the core.Although it was well researched and based on fact, Flannery says some viewers of the TV series thought the police corruption strand of the story had been exaggerated. “I don’t know that anybody’s going to be shocked now like they were 30 years ago,” he says. “That [corruption] has got worse. There have been serving officers prosecuted for rape and murder since then.”Of the political chicanery, Flannery says: “I can’t see what might have changed. The publicity around Neil Hamilton and Mohamed Al-Fayed and the ‘cash for questions’ affair must have made them change their tactics, but I think they’re still at it. There are so many paid lobbyists hanging around parliament now. What are they there for if not to suborn MPs and buy their votes and their support? It’s what’s ruined American politics and if we’re not careful it will ruin British politics as well.”As he approaches 75, Flannery says this will probably be the last thing he writes. “I’m acutely aware that I’m handing the audience a fairly bleak view of society,” he says. “However, the characters are vibrant and they’re all survivors, even Geordie, who seems to be kind of indomitable. No matter what bucket of shit gets poured over him he gets up and has another go. I want the audience to take hope from the characters.”Flannery insists he sees the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister as a positive thing. “I think the whole system is against him and he’ll find his road blocked at every turn. I’ve watched this rolling around again and again and there isn’t usually any real change. But, I’m an optimist. It is a triumph of hope over experience but until I’m proven wrong, I’ll hang on to that.”Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Yearsis at the Theatre Royal, Newcastle upon Tyne,15 to 24 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pine cones, glitter and a hip-hop head for sale: red-hot artists reveal their Frieze stunners | Frieze art fair | The Guardian
description: As the sprawling art jamboree hits London, eight of the most exciting exhibiting artists share what their work means to them – and who they hope will buy it
Author: Alex Needham
Headline: As the sprawling art jamboree hits London, eight of the most exciting exhibiting artists share what their work means to them – and who they hope will buy it
Content: ‘An enduring act of devotion’ … Louise Giovanelli at her studio in Manchester.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘An enduring act of devotion’ … Louise Giovanelli at her studio in Manchester.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianFrieze art fairPine cones, glitter and a hip-hop head for sale: red-hot artists reveal their Frieze stunnersAs the sprawling art jamboree hits London, eight of the most exciting exhibiting artists share what their work means to them – and who they hope will buy itInterviews byAlex NeedhamMon 12 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst held in 2003, theFrieze art fairis a giant art supermarket that descends on Regent’s Park, London, every October. Some detest it for its blatant commercialism, others relish it as the opportunity to see a mind-boggling amount of contemporary art in one enormous tent. Here, eight British-based artists of the moment talk through what they’re showing.Kira FreijeAge:41How would you describe what you do?I make sculpture. I work a lot with metal, fabrics, quite a collection of materials to make landscapes of figures that grow intuitively.What’s the highlight of your career so far?My exhibition at Hepworth Wakefield – getting major support in such an incredible institution.View image in fullscreen‘I call them gesture works’ … Kira Freije at her studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianName two favourite artists, one dead and one living.Dead:Marisa MerzorPaul Thek. Both had an attitude of freedom of making. Living: Liliane Lijn orDonna Huddleston, who I know quite well. I love them and I think they’re amazing.Tell me about the sculpture we’ve photographed you with.I call them gesture works. They’re wall-based, but they allude to a crowd. They’re cast in aluminium and bronze and one of them has a piece of fabric.Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years?Oh God, I can’t imagine. Hopefully still alive and excited with what I’m making.Mohammed Z RahmanAge:29How would you describe what you do?I’m a figurative painter, but I also work across sculpture and installation. I’m self-taught, so my work has been described as outsider art. I’ll make work drawn from nursery rhymes and ethnographic texts.What made you want to become an artist?My mum came to the UK in the 80s from rural Bangladesh and we lived in a series of dilapidated houses. She was a textile worker so she made curtains for the house. My sister would salvage wood and make furniture, so I was immersed in organic homemaking.View image in fullscreen‘Outsider art’ … Mohammed Z Rahman with his crate and fish pictures.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhat’s the highlight of your career so far?Going to the Venice Biennale earlier this year. In light of the death ofKoyo [Kouoh, who died while curating the show in which Rahman participated], the artists really came together.Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.Maybe it’s a cliche, but I really likeFrida Kahlo. I think she did what I’m trying to do in the sense of hitting a balance between social realism, being political, speaking to the current social conditions and introducing a world of fantasy and mythology and dreams. And I really like the work ofToyin Ojih Odutolawho had the Barbican Curve commission in London a few years ago. The storytelling and world building of that show was amazing. It’s a guiding star in terms of the direction I want to take my practice.Tell me about the sculpture we’ve photographed you with.At Frieze in 2023, I was amazed by all these beautiful wooden shipping crates that were coming in like a big parade. I thought: these would be so beautiful if they were painted. This was designed as a seat and storage for my gallery team – it’s like set design. The fish pictures are drawn from kheta stitching, a folk craft in rural Bangladesh.Jake GrewalAge:32How would you describe what you do?I make paintings and I draw, mostly in charcoal. I look at figures in the landscape at liminal times. The figures are anthropomorphic, but they also are genderless. So there’s this queer undertone.What’s the highlight of your career so far?The Studio Voltaire show inLondonincluded the biggest painting I’ve ever made.Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.I love Turner’s abstraction of the landscape, and his use of colour really inspired me when I was younger. His watercolours are so transcendent and he’s a master at capturing atmosphere. And I really loveNan Goldin. In a day when art is so capitalist and based on consumption, the artists who stand out are ones who are trying to bring about social change.View image in fullscreen‘There’s this queer undertone’ … Jake Grewal at his studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTell me about the picture we’ve photographed you with.It’s a large charcoal drawing of two figures following one another in a forest scene. The figures look quite adolescent, so it feels almost like an old film still. There’s something quite nostalgic about it.Who would you like to buy it?I would love someone who I really admire to buy it. I’m such a big fan ofAnohni, but I doubt she’s going to buy my drawing.Alvaro BarringtonAge:43Tell me about the painting we’ve photographed you with.It’s a head portrait. Portraiture has been such an incredible genre in painting, from the Mona Lisa to Girl with a Pearl Earring to Picasso’s The Weeping Woman. I’ve always wanted to deal with this genre in a way that felt unique to how I would understand it. I grew up in a very hip-hop culture and so I’ve been exploring how to make hip-hop versions of heads.What do you hope will happen when it gets sold at Frieze?Hopefully somebody would love to live with it. Because I think art should be lived with, whether that’s in a museum or someone’s house.Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.Tupac and Tupac. He’s the greatest artist in my lifetime. You’re born, there’s a trillion things to notice, and an artist is just someone who goes: “This thing has happened. This is how I feel about it. I’m going to make something that’s so convincing”, whether it’s a painting or a song or a dance performance or a lecture likeJoseph Beuysused to do. And then all of a sudden you go: “I get that. That makes sense to me.”View image in fullscreen‘You’re born first physically, but then you’re born culturally’ … Alvaro Barrington in the workshop at his studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhere do you think you’ll be in 20 years’ time?I have four chapters in my life. The first chapter is called Garvey: Birth. I think you’re born twice. You’re born first physically, but then you’re born culturally. And culture tells you how to understand yourself, who to love, who to hate. It’s the value of things. The second chapter is called Malcolm X: Innovation, someone who completely reinvented himself and chose his identity. And then the third chapter isAudre Lorde: Power– a poet and writer and also from Grenada, the island my mom is from. And then the last chapter is calledBiggie Smalls: Death.Louise GiovanelliAge:32How would you describe your work?I paint to capture the vibrating luminous residue of a glance turning a fleeting sensory encounter into an enduring act of devotion.What has been the highlight of your career so far?Probably a major show that began at the Hepworth Wakefield in 2024. It toured to Graz in Austria and then it went to Museum Villa Stuck in Munich, so that was a really nice year for me because I got to follow the works around Europe and see them in different institutional contexts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionName two favourite artists, one dead and one living.I like Rudolf Stingel. Every show that I’ve seen of his is completely different. He’s very willing to take risks. And for a historical one,Piero della Francesca. I just love those Italian fresco panel paintings. His depictions of women are just glorious.Tell me about the painting we’ve photographed you with.It’s the first time that I’ve fused two quite disparate series of mine. It’s a face projected on to this sparkly glitter curtain and the painting’s called Cathexis, which is from a Greek word which means to invest your energy into a specific thing. There have been so many examples throughout history where humans have invested in transient materials such as silk or flesh or marble, materialisations of desire, so that’s what I’m trying to do in this painting. It speaks to my interest in drapery and hair and in female beauty.What do you hope happens to this painting when it’s sold?Oh, that’s a hard question. Well, I put a lot of trust in my gallery with placing it with someone who has a knowledge of my work, supports my practice and would loan it to some museum shows maybe later down the line.Shaqúelle WhyteAge:26View image in fullscreen‘Rothko is my north star’ … Shaqúelle Whyte at his studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhat would you say the highlight of your career so far has been?My show at WolverhamptonArtGallery this year. I wanted to bring my work back to the city and to people who have varying understandings of art because of the degradation of the education system, and that was a privilege. To see them want to know more was highlight of my life. And I’ve got a solo show at South London Gallery coming up. I think I’m going to be the youngest person ever to do a solo show in that space. And that’s just like, Jesus Christ, how did we get here? I’m a kid from Wolves, you know what I mean? It’s all a bit mad.Tell me about the paintings you’re showing at Frieze.One’s called Gulliver’s Forrest and the other’s called Miss Mammy. They were made after the Wolverhampton show and before the beginnings of this new body of work. You’ve got periods of time where you can explore and mess around – that’s what it was.What do you hope happens to this painting when it’s sold?The most important thing is that the works are looked after and appreciated. So ultimately an institution [buying it] would be great but it needs to be somebody that will be responsible for it as my career grows, and not be flipping it.Who are your two favourite artists, one dead and one living?Rothko is my north star for what it means to make paintings. And alive, I think Ruprecht von Kaufmann is a phenomenal painter, and so isAndrew Cranston. I like bad-boy painters. In the pursuit of greatness you need to be reaching up to something.Is it true that Stormzy has been coming by your studio?Yeah, he came the other day. But ultimately, he’s just a guy who’s got interest in art and wants to see the work.Poppy JonesAge:41How would you describe your work?I work with a combination of painting, printmaking and photography, all at a very intimate scale. The canvases are cut from materials more common for clothing and sometimes out of my own clothing. There’s often like a conceptual play between the textile subject and the surface, so if it’s made from a suede jacket, the work will depict the suede jacket. I’m interested in the way things like eBay might be the record of our culture in the future and what’s happening to this digital archive. But I’m also really interested in creating atmosphere and the qualities of light and how objects can suddenly express an inner emotion.View image in fullscreen‘I feel like I let [my work] go on its own journey’ … Poppy Jones at Herald St Gallery, London.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhat’s been the highlight of your career so far?I saw a big Paul Nash retrospective 10 years ago at Tate Britain and became a massive fan. There’s a particular painting of his, Dead Spring, at Pallant House [in Chichester] which I used to look at on my way to or from work when I was teaching. They recently acquired work of mine and in the summer I went to see it and it’s hung opposite Dead Spring. My own work has become part of that conversation in the gallery.Can you name two favourite artists, one dead and one living?Eileen Agaras my dead artist. I like that she just did her own thing for her whole lifetime, and I like her approach to materials and to collage. Francis Offman is my favourite artist at the moment. He’s using digital technology to fabricate these large weavings but then painting on them. The colours are amazing.Tell me about the work you’re showing at Frieze.It’s called Statues Also Die (Man Ray). It’s based on a photographic image I took of a Man Ray monograph covered in pine cones and forest-like debris during a residency at a museum in very rural Denmark 10 years ago. The title references the 1950s film by Alain Resnais and Chris Marker [and Ghislain Cloquet] which explores the shifting power of images according to different contexts and that’s something I’m interested in doing in my own work.Who would you like to buy it, and who would you hate to buy it?I enjoy making the work, but I don’t get overly attached to it once it leaves the studio. I feel like I let it go on its own journey, which I leave to other people.Christina KimezeAge:40How would you describe your work?I came to the studio via a non-linear path. I studied science then had various jobs and set up a startup with my sister. Central to my practice is rejecting traditional materials and embracing imperfections. That’s informed by having to make art at home for a long time in cramped spaces.What has been the highlight of your career so far?My show at the South London Gallery was a turning point. The demographic wasn’t a sort of homogeneous room of art-world folk, politely nodding at the wall text. We had lots of local young people coming in, genuinely reacting to the energy of the work and the materials. It centred around this idea of roller-skating as a motif and some people turned up on their roller-skates.View image in fullscreen‘My work has always been informed by not having much time’ … Christina Kimeze at her studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianCan you tell me two artists you love, one living and one dead?Matisse had this ability to leave the rough in there as well as the polished, clean line.Chris Ofilihas parallels with Matisse, and there’s something I always try and take from both of those artists.Can you tell me about the picture that we’ve photographed you with?That picture is called Game On (Crane’s Cut) and it’s on suede mat board, which forces a battle between painting and drawing because I have to use oil sticks and pastels and stuff. It shows a woman shuffling cards and it’s about the seductive but scary ideas of chance. It’s using that as a motif to explore the luck of global migration and the lottery of birth. I’m Ugandan, and there’s this crane flying across the picture, referencing the national bird of Uganda, the crested crane.Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years?My work has always been informed by not having much time – I’m currently pregnant with my third child. Time is such a luxury, isn’t it? I hope I have that space to explore other media, to make sculpture, to make an installation.Frieze Londonruns from 14-18 OctoberThis article was amended on 12 October 2026 to correct the spellings of Louise Giovanelli’s painting Cathexis, those of Shaquélle Whyte, and Liliane Lijn’s name.Explore more on these topicsFrieze art fairArtPaintingSculptureInstallationLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Prem Sahib: Chamber review – master of unease twists the city into terror and pleasure | Art | The Guardian
description: There’s an atmosphere of sickly discomfort throughout this weird, intense mid-career survey for this brilliant artist
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: There’s an atmosphere of sickly discomfort throughout this weird, intense mid-career survey for this brilliant artist
Content: Risk and threat … Prem Sahib’s what you need to know to get rid of these blood sucking parasites (in the form of a whisper), 2023.Photograph: Ben Westoby/Prem Sahib/Phillida Reid, LondonView image in fullscreenRisk and threat … Prem Sahib’s what you need to know to get rid of these blood sucking parasites (in the form of a whisper), 2023.Photograph: Ben Westoby/Prem Sahib/Phillida Reid, LondonArtReviewPrem Sahib: Chamber review – master of unease twists the city into terror and pleasureDe La Warr Pavilion, BexhillThere’s an atmosphere of sickly discomfort throughout this weird, intense mid-career survey for this brilliant artistEddy FrankelMon 12 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrem Sahib turns the city inside out, twists it around and rips it apart. His show at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, a sort of mid-career survey for the 44-year-old English artist, is full of private spaces and urban nightmares that have been gutted and left on display. It’s minimal, claustrophobic, intense stuff.A sodium street lamp hangs upside down from the ceiling, casting its sickly pale orange glow across the gallery. You feel like you’ve stumbled into some urban back alley where physics has been flipped, it has all the threat of an underpass, but surreal and inverted. Nearby, three puffer jackets have been squeezed between sheets of glass – are these the blokes who were waiting for you in the underpass? Or are they three strangers who you’ve caught mid-embrace?That’s what Sahib does, over and over: he plays with the line between terror and pleasure, threat and intimacy, public and private.So much here is geared towards an atmosphere of discomfort. There’s a deep bass throb echoing out of one space, its tone eventually rising to an ear-piercing squeal, before settling back into a chest-rattling sub. A table has been made out of a grossly overgrown flea’s body, a street sign has been left blank but its light is still on. Two space heaters constantly flick on and ramp up the temperature. It is liminal, weird, uncomfortable.View image in fullscreenPlays with the line between terror and pleasure … an installation view from Chamber.Photograph: Rob HarrisQueerness is central to Sahib’s work. The double doors you pass as you walk in were taken from a Mile End leather bar that closed in 2022, the water fountain encased in resin is from Chariots sauna in Shoreditch which closed in 2016. Private spaces, places of intimate pleasure, that have been erased from the city.In one of his signature resin panels, clear droplets have accumulated on a sheet of black aluminium, like sweat gathering on a nightclub wall. You can almost smell it, almost feel hot, damp, writhing people coming together somewhere nearby. Hung up high, two acrylic discs nod to the visual results of rapid HIV tests. There’s intimacy here, but risk too.Risk, and threat: an obsidian mirror hangs cracked on the wall, burbling out discordant sounds, a slowed down recording of a homophobic rant sent to Sahib on a gay chat room.View image in fullscreenKnack for minimalist atmospherics … Prem Sahib's Horizon 1.3 2026.Photograph: Lewis Ronald/Prem Sahib/Phillida Reid, LondonIs this all about architecture, as the wall text here insists? I don’t know. Architecture is already about architecture – I don’t need art to make me think deep thoughts about buildings. This feels way more intimate than that description coldly implies. It’s about bodies being pressed together, sweat dripping down a wall, and feeling like it’s all about to be torn away from you.The whole way through, it’s as if Sahib is asking: what happens when the places that matter to me, where I express myself, are destroyed? What is left for me, for us? Who decides which spaces can survive, who decides what communities are worth preserving, who decides where bodies get to exist?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI don’t think it all works. The recording of Suella Braverman hatefully talking about the migrant crisis that you listen to while looking out at the sea is a bit on the nose, and the little dotty images of the horizon that line one wall don’t really add a huge amount.But for the most part, Sahib is brilliant, with an incredible knack for crushingly intense minimalist atmospherics. He’s been one of the most interesting artists working in this country for more than a decade now, and a big institutional show like this feels long overdue.Prem Sahib: Chamberis at De La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArtInstallationExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alex Gibney says Universal ‘wavered’ over releasing Elon Musk documentary | Movies | The Guardian
description: The revelation comes after the four-hour film’s Venice premiere drew a string of criticisms and insults from the founder of SpaceXAI
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The revelation comes after the four-hour film’s Venice premiere drew a string of criticisms and insults from the founder of SpaceXAI
Content: A douche? … Alex Gibney and Elon Musk.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenA douche? … Alex Gibney and Elon Musk.Photograph: APMoviesAlex Gibney says Universal ‘wavered’ over releasing Elon Musk documentaryThe revelation comes after the four-hour film’s Venice premiere drew a string of criticisms and insults from the founder of SpaceXAIAndrew PulverMon 12 Oct 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Gibney, director of the new four-hour documentary about Elon Musk, said that Universal, owners of the film’s international distribution rights “wavered” over releasing the film outside North America.Gibney was speaking to the New York Timesas the film opened in the US (where it is being released by the independent distributor Bleecker Street), and appeared to confirma story in the Hollywood Reporterthat Universal, which hadacquired the international rights to the film in 2023, had got cold feet. Asked by the New York Times, “Did Universal Pictures waver in setting up its international release plans?” Gibney replied: “Yes.”Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead moreA subsequent story in Variety suggested thatUniversal had been concerned about “legal threats from Musk”, but that the studio had “always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally”. Gibney was asked: “So it wasn’t about legal clearances?” The film-maker replied: “You can walk and chew gum at the same time.”However, it appears plans are back on track, as Gibney added: “We just had a meeting with [Universal], and we’re talking very concretely about a release plan.”Gibney also said his producer Jessie Deeter, who knew Musk from two previous films, had attempted on several occasions to ask Musk to be interviewed for the film. Musk’s response was topost “Gibney is a douche”on X, the social media platform owned by Musk-founded company SpaceXAI.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreIn the wake of the film’s premiere at the Venice film festival,Musk posted a string of criticisms of the film and insults aimed at Gibney, including calling the film a “hit piece that misses” and threatening legal action.Universal declined to comment further, pointing to its previous statement: “We’ve always been committed to releasing this film, and our plans haven’t changed.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAlex GibneyUniversal PicturesElon MuskDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Digger on course for $245m loss after box office collapse | Movies | The Guardian
description: Estimates suggest the eco satire starring Tom Cruise could join the list of top turkeys, including Cutthroat Island and The Marvels
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Estimates suggest the eco satire starring Tom Cruise could join the list of top turkeys, including Cutthroat Island and The Marvels
Content: Misunderstood? … Tom Cruise in Digger 2026.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenMisunderstood? … Tom Cruise in Digger 2026.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMoviesDigger on course for $245m loss after box office collapseEstimates suggest the eco satire starring Tom Cruise could join the list of top turkeys, including Cutthroat Island and The MarvelsAndrew PulverMon 12 Oct 2026 08.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDigger, the ambitious eco-fable starring Tom Cruise and directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, is heading for an even worse financial outcome thanpreviously thought, with reports suggesting it will lose around $245m (£185m), placing it among the biggest disasters in movie history.According to a report in Variety, Digger’s estimated second weekend revenue in North America of $3.2m is a 60% drop on its opening weekend figure of $8m, meaning its current domestic gross is $14.4m,for a global total of $35.3m, with a projected final box office total of around $50m worldwide.Though precise figures are not available, Variety estimates that Digger’s production costs are $160m-180m (well over the original budget of $125m), with another $100m spent on marketing the film. Another $15m was potentially on hand for awards-season marketing, but this is likely to be scaled back after the film’s failure. Given that cinemas keep around half the revenue of ticket sales, Variety estimates the film would need to make around $350m to cover costs. (A spokesperson for Digger’s producing studio Warner Bros, says that break-even point is $300m, suggesting a production spend of $150m.)A $245m loss would put Diggeron a par with such legendary turkeysas Cutthroat Island ($222m loss, adjusted for inflation), Mortal Engines ($224m adjusted) and The Marvels ($205-$250m adjusted).Reaction to the film has likely played a key role in its underperformance, with critical opinion radically divided. In the Guardian, chief film critic Peter Bradshaw called it “an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire”in a two-star review, while Guardian Australia’s deputy culture editor Sian Cain took the opposite position,describing it as “a masterpiece”. Warner Bros, whose last release this is before itstakeover by David Ellison’s Skydance, tried to play into the controversy with apost-release advertising campaign quoting its negative notices, but it seems to have had little effect.So far, 2026 has been a disappointing year for Warner Bros, as it prepares for new ownership, with poorly performing releases such as Supergirl and The Bride! and co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdydue to leaveahead of the takeover. This contrasts with a successful 2025, in which releases such as A Minecraft Movie, Sinners and F1 propelled it to the second most successful studio, behind Disney.Elsewhere, the Aaron Sorkin-directed The Social Reckoning also failed to live up to expectations on its first weekend,taking an estimated $5.5m at the North American box office and $9m globally. The sequel to The Social Network, which stars Jeremy Strong as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and Mikey Madison as whistleblower Frances Haugen, was comprehensively beaten by Jessica Chastain horror The Other Mommy,which led the North American box officewith an estimated $27.5m, part of a global take of $45.2m.Explore more on these topicsFilmDiggerTom CruiseAlejandro González IñárrituFilm criticismMarketing & PRFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: The Beach Boys’ Mike Love returns to the stage despite ‘facing serious health challenges’ | Beach Boys | The Guardian
description: The 85-year-old was helped on stage by actor John Stamos, who shared an emotional message about his ‘musical hero and mentor’
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: The 85-year-old was helped on stage by actor John Stamos, who shared an emotional message about his ‘musical hero and mentor’
Content: The Beach Boys’ Mike Love and John Stamos performing in 2025 in Chicago, Illinois.Photograph: Barry Brecheisen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Beach Boys’ Mike Love and John Stamos performing in 2025 in Chicago, Illinois.Photograph: Barry Brecheisen/Getty ImagesBeach BoysThe Beach Boys’ Mike Love returns to the stage despite ‘facing serious health challenges’The 85-year-old was helped on stage by actor John Stamos, who shared an emotional message about his ‘musical hero and mentor’Emma JoyceSun 11 Oct 2026 20.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 20.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter months of cancelled comeback tours, theBeach Boyshave played their first public show since July – with co-founder and frontman Mike Love joining the band on stage in Cincinnati, Ohio, despite “facing serious health challenges”.Love was helped on to the stage by his son Christian Love and the actor and band member John Stamos, who told the audience at PNC Pavilion on Saturday night that Love has “been going through some health issues … but he would not miss tonight”.“It’s what he loves the most,” Stamos said before the show. “He loves the audience, he loves the music. He knows how important it is to all of you. So we’re all here to support him and give him as much love as we can.”The 85-year-old musician – who was wearing a cap, hoodie and scarf – remained seated for the performance, with a microphone positioned on a stand before him. He sang back-up vocals and spoke to the audience to thank them for coming to the show.On Sunday night, Stamos shared an emotional messageon Instagramabout his “beloved friend, father figure, musical hero and mentor” as the band headed to Nashville, Tennessee, to play at the Ryman Auditorium with Love.“My beloved friend, father figure, musical hero and mentor, Mike Love, is facing serious health challenges,” said the post. “We hope he’ll be doing what he loves for years to come, but we don’t know what the future holds. We have tonight.”Stamos, who has played with the Beach Boys intermittently for 41 years, continued: “Mike is a fighter. Despite doctors, family and friends urging him to focus on his health, he insists on being on stage. He says he needs his band, the audience, his friends and drummer surrounding him to lift him up.”The Full House actor wrote that “the Mike Love we see tonight may not be exactly the Mike we’ve always known. But he’s still every bit the Mike we love”.In June, after performing in London’s Chelsea, Love sharedon Instagramthat he had been in recovery from bronchitis and later Covid.He wrote: “Losing my sister, Maureen, on the first anniversary of cousin Brian’s death, combined with my ongoing recovery from what started out as bronchitis, followed by Covid, has taken both an emotional and physical toll on me.“I feel stronger every day physically, but I am heartbroken emotionally. I couldn’t imagine being anywhere else than with our audience. For me, our audience is the medicine, and the music is the cure. Thank you all for your outpouring of love, well wishes, and healing prayers. I am deeply humbled and grateful.”The Beach Boys’ Endless Summer tour continues in the US until 13 November, when the band are set to play at the Hard Rock Hotel and Casino in Bristol, Virginia, followed by a make-up show on 8 May 2027 at River Cree Resort and Casino in Enoch, Alberta.Al Jardine, the only other surviving original member of the Beach Boys, is touring his own show Al Jardine and the Pet Sounds Band, with four more US dates listed on their website.Explore more on these topicsBeach BoysPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re in a brotherhood now’: the Bill Pickett rodeo – photo essay | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: For several years, Chloe Kerleroux has been photographing African American cowboy communities in the southern US. Her work has mainly focused on trail rides: large gatherings where horses, music, dancing, family and community life come together. This year, she explored rodeo culture including at the Bill Pickett invitational in Atlanta
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For several years, Chloe Kerleroux has been photographing African American cowboy communities in the southern US. Her work has mainly focused on trail rides: large gatherings where horses, music, dancing, family and community life come together. This year, she explored rodeo culture including at the Bill Pickett invitational in Atlanta
Content: Portrait of members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, many of whom are of Caribbean origin, after the competition at the Bill Pickett Invitational Rodeo in Conyers, Georgia, on 1 August 2026. Photograph: Chloe KerlerouxFor several years, Chloe Kerleroux has been photographing African American cowboy communities in the southern US. Her work has mainly focused on trail rides: large gatherings where horses, music, dancing, family and community life come together. This year, she explored rodeo culture including at the Bill Pickett invitational in AtlantaByChloe KerlerouxMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe image of the cowboy widely portrayed in westerns and popular culture has long been almost exclusively white. Yet Black cowboys hold an important place in the history of the American west. After the civil war and the abolition of slavery, many African Americans found work on ranches and on the great cattle drives westward. By the late 19th century, historians estimate about one in four cowboys were Black.Among the Black figures who shaped this history wasBill Pickett. Born in Texas in 1870, he became one of the most celebrated Black cowboys and rodeo performers of his time, known in particular for popularising bulldogging, which would eventually give rise to modern steer wrestling.View image in fullscreenAfter the national anthem, Josh, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted, rides around the arena to a pounding hip-hop track as his teammates cheer him on at the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo in Conyers, nearAtlanta, Georgia, on 2 August 2026View image in fullscreenMembers of the Outlaws Most Wanted joke and playfully challenge other riders, some of whom have travelled long distances to compete, backstage at the rodeoHis name was chosen by the promoter Lu Vason when he created the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. In 1977, Vason attended Cheyenne frontier days and was struck by the absence of Black cowboys in the arena. His research led him to the Black American West Museum in Denver, where he discovered the story of Pickett and the history of African Americans in the American west. In 1984, he created a rodeo designed to give Black cowboys and cowgirls a platform and bring greater visibility to this heritage.More than 40 years later, that mission remains at the heart of the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. Part sporting competition, part spectacle and part space for passing on history and culture, its 2026 tour crosses the US from February to October, with stops including Memphis, Atlanta, Oakland and Los Angeles.This year, I decided to join the tour in Atlanta.View image in fullscreenA family on horseback waits to enter the arena at therodeo, reflecting the intergenerational nature of a cowboy culture passed down through families. 1 August 2026While there, I met for the first time a contact I had been speaking with before my trip. He runs Diamondcut Ranch, where he works with and trains horses, and around which a wider community of riders has formed. It was there that I met the Outlaws Most Wanted, a team of “bronc riders” competing at the Bill Pickett.The organisers allowed me behind the barriers on the condition that I stayed with them. I found myself in the space just behind the arena, where the riders wait for their turn and prepare their equipment.Music is everywhere. The riders joke around, encourage one another and build each other up. The energy and adrenaline rise as their turn approaches, until each rider has to move away from that collective excitement and focus on the few seconds waiting for him in the arena.View image in fullscreenRachied Robins, AKA Django, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, who became my main contact and a key voice in telling the group’s story during the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. 1/08/2026One of them, Rachied Robins, AKA Django, describes the Outlaws Most Wanted as a group of Caribbean men, some of whom have come from difficult backgrounds, brought together by their love of horses. Some, he says, found “refuge in this horse world”. Over time, their bonds grew stronger: “We’re in a brotherhood now.”Django grew up in Kissimmee, Florida, surrounded by rodeo culture. He started out in bull riding before changing disciplines after a bull stomped on his face. He now competes in ranch bronc riding and laughingly describes himself as an “adrenaline junkie”.But behind the adrenaline, there is also fear. Before he gets on the horse, thoughts of the danger and all the “what ifs” run through his mind. Then he has to find a way to clear his head.View image in fullscreenThe Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team at the Bill Pickett rodeo“You just gotta clear your mind and leave it in God’s hands.”He has to trust his technique and make it through eight seconds. And even once the ride is over, the danger is not: Django tells me that getting off the horse can be one of the most dangerous moments.There is also a financial side to competing. Django tells me that the Bill Pickett is not among the rodeos offering the largest purses: at the April event he competed in, he says a rider could win up to about $1,500 (£1,135), compared with as much as $10,000 at some other rodeos. But money is only part of what is at stake.“It’s not just the money, but also your name, the respect, ranking.”What struck me most about the Bill Pickett, however, perhaps happens beyond the competition itself.View image in fullscreenRiders wait to enter the arena in a solemn moment, hats held over their hearts, as The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella at sunset before the start of the rodeoBefore the events begin, The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella. Hats are placed over hearts, the riders stand still, and silence falls across the stands and the arena. I remember getting goosebumps and tears in my eyes.Then, almost without transition, the atmosphere shifts completely and the adrenaline takes over.All the riders enter the arena to a powerful hip-hop track. The volume rises, the horses come in, and the crowd shouts, applauds and dances. Within moments, the atmosphere moves from solemn stillness to an almost explosive energy.That contrast captures much of what I felt at the Bill Pickett. History and memory are central to the event, but they are not frozen in the past. They coexist with hip-hop, fashion, competition and a deeply contemporary Black cowboy culture.View image in fullscreenAfter his ride, a cowboy walks along the edge of the arena as the crowd cheers him on at the Bill PickettThe audience is very much part of the spectacle. Western shirts, cowboy hats and boots fill the stands: people come to watch the rodeo, but also to gather, dance, show their style and celebrate a shared culture. Throughout the event, the announcers return again and again to the history of Black cowboys and the values the Bill Pickett seeks to pass on. That history is not confined to a few lines in a programme: it is an integral part of the event.When I ask Django what the Bill Pickett means to him, he tells me that it is about more than just rodeo: “Bill Pickett means a lot to me personally. Not just because it’s a rodeo, but because it’s a platform for us minorities to come together.”He talks about being able to show what they can do “as a group, as a unit”, but also about having a place where he can be himself and where he feels at home.The Outlaws Most Wanted do not compete only at Black rodeos. Django tells me they compete wherever they have the opportunity and rejects the idea that these events are a form of separation. For him, they are above all about making a heritage visible: “We just want to bring out our heritage and bring out our history and show that we are part of this history, and this is part of our history.”View image in fullscreenMembers of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arenaIt is also about passing something on. From trail rides to rodeos, horses create a space around which families, friendships and communities are formed. For some members of the Outlaws Most Wanted, this world has even become a refuge.When I ask Django what he hopes the young people in the stands take away from watching him ride, he does not talk about becoming a cowboy or winning competitions. Above all, he hopes to show them that another path is possible: “Do something safe, do something legal, get out the streets, keep your mind right, don’t be another statistic.”More than a century after Black cowboys helped shape the history of the American west while remaining largely absent from its popular image, the Bill Pickett offers a space where this heritage does not belong only to the past: it continues to be lived, passed on and reinvented.Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayBlack US cultureGeorgiaHorsesPhotographyAtlantafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: numb with grief, I sat in the dark, surrounded by strangers – and began to heal | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Life had come crashing to a halt when I lost my brother. But in the cinema I found comfort and a strange solidarity
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Life had come crashing to a halt when I lost my brother. But in the cinema I found comfort and a strange solidarity
Content: ‘I was reminded of the world beyond my bubble’ … Georgina Elliott at Genesis cinema, London.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I was reminded of the world beyond my bubble’ … Georgina Elliott at Genesis cinema, London.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: numb with grief, I sat in the dark, surrounded by strangers – and began to healLife had come crashing to a halt when I lost my brother. But in the cinema I found comfort and a strange solidarityGeorgina ElliottMon 12 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022, my younger brother drowned in an accident. His death reset life as I knew it. I had been offered my first proper job; I didn’t take it. I was planning to move out; I stayed at home. At this critical juncture, with my foot on the pedal, ready to enter adult life, everything exploded.At home, there were now three of us. We orbited separate corners of the house, each needing a different thing for comfort: for my mum, exercise; for my dad, music; for me, escape.It was a long, grey January, and I was stuck in the mud. My brain had puffed up like an airbag against the full force of grief; my head was fuzzy and foggy, my thoughts were sludge. I was so sensitive to light and sound that it felt as if a layer of my skin had been peeled off. Mostly, though, I just felt nothing.I was in limbo. In my early 20s, I couldn’t haunt the house indefinitely. At some point, I would need to rejoin the land of the living. But for now, stepping back on to the hamster wheel felt pointless.Getting out of the house, at least, I could manage. But where to go? I had seen a sign at my local cinema for an under-25s membership, which offered weekday tickets for £5.99. It would be a relief, I thought, to lose myself in a fantastical world for a few hours. So I pulled on my dad’s coat, made a flask of tea and took a blustery walk down the hill to Greenwich.View image in fullscreen‘Stepping back on to the hamster wheel felt pointless’ … Georgina Elliott at Genesis cinema, London.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianI peeled off my layers and sat down with four or five others for a screening ofCorsage, a feminist telling of the life of Sisi, the 19th-century Austrian empress, at 40. Vicky Krieps plays her as cheeky and conspiratorial – sticking her tongue out and her middle finger up, having affairs, playing tricks. Immersed in the ups and downs of her story, I felt dormant emotions rise to the surface. Her self-possession was emboldening. When the lights came up, I felt as though a valve had opened and some of the pressure had hissed out.Though it felt frivolous to escape to matinee screenings with retirees, I started to go to the cinema once a week. It was comforting to sit in silence with others. To be in the dark and let my face crumple and fold, and not worry about how it might be received. I was alone, but not really, feeling a kind of implicit solidarity from my fellow audience members. I read once that in a cinema,strangers’ hearts can start to beat in time. It was a better balm for grief than the more overt expressions of sympathy I had been receiving, like being asked how I was doing – it felt like loosening the muscles around an injury instead of pressing directly on the sore spot.For this reason, I found films about loss, such asOne Fine Morning, about a daughter coming to terms with her father’s degenerative illness, too hard-going, and instead watched life-affirming escapades: the swashbuckling adventures ofThe Count of Monte Cristo, the simple pleasures ofThe Taste of Things, the easy laughs ofPuss in Boots: The Last Wish.At some point, the cinema screenedHow to Blow Up a Pipelineand I thought about eco-anarchism for the first time since school. It set off a spark; the blurry edges of my brain came into sharper relief, and ideas for stories began to surface. Soon after, Aubrey Gordon’s documentaryYour Fat Friendgave me the idea for my first piece of journalism on atypical anorexia.January turned to February and then March, and I turned a corner. Watching all these funny, sad and silly films, I was reminded of the world beyond my bubble, and decided to rejoin it. Even now, on a bad day, I buy a ticket, sit in the dark, let my shoulders drop, breathe and reboot.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Is it true that … muscle turns into fat if you stop working out? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: If you take a break from the gym you may lose muscle and gain fat, but it isn’t as simple as one turning into the other
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: If you take a break from the gym you may lose muscle and gain fat, but it isn’t as simple as one turning into the other
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … muscle turns into fat if you stop working out?If you take a break from the gym you may lose muscle and gain fat, but it isn’t as simple as one turning into the otherKate LloydMon 12 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘This is not true,” says Prof Leigh Breen, a specialist in muscle physiology at the University of Leicester. But it’s a statement he hears a lot, particularly from people who have taken a long break from exercise. “They’ll often refer to the notion that their muscles have ‘softened’ or don’t feel as toned.”The reality is that there’s no biochemistry linking the two types of tissue. Muscle and fat are distinct. “There’s no known process in the human body that would support muscle turning into fat, or vice versa,” says Breen.double quotation markWhat we eat during an exercise break can also influence how much muscle and fat mass we gain or loseHe thinks the confusion comes from what happens when we stop exercising – particularly resistance training. We may begin to lose some of the muscle we built through training. And if we continue eating the same amount while exercising less, we may end up with an energy surplus, which can lead to an increase in body fat.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … sit-ups are the best exercise for abs?Read more“This combination of a reduction in muscle mass and potentially an increase in fat mass can give the impression that one is turning into the other,” he says. “Which isn’t the case.”If you take a couple of weeks off your usual training routine but remain relatively active, you’re likely to see fewer changes than if you are completely immobilised for an extended period because of an injury.What we eat during an exercise break can also influence how much muscle and fat mass we gain or lose. Breen recommends keeping protein intake high while slightly reducing calorie intake.Ultimately, our bodies are constantly changing, and small fluctuations in muscle and fat mass during breaks in our training are generally normal. “Slight fluctuations are generally nothing to worry about, as long as over the course of months and years consistent exercise and dietary habits have been maintained,” says Breen.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …Health & wellbeingFitnessHuman biologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Calum Franklin’s recipes for balti paratha pie with spicy green chutney | Indian food and drink | The Guardian
description: A pleasingly proper curry-filled pie with a zingy chutney to go with it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A pleasingly proper curry-filled pie with a zingy chutney to go with it
Content: Calum Franklin’s balti paratha pie with spicy green chutney.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.View image in fullscreenCalum Franklin’s balti paratha pie with spicy green chutney.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.Indian food and drinkCalum Franklin’s recipes for balti paratha pie with spicy green chutneyA pleasingly proper curry-filled pie with a zingy chutney to go with itCalum FranklinMon 12 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is one of my all-time favourite pies, pie born out of the Midlands. While studying at University College Birmingham, the now head of department at the college of food there, Lewis Walker, and I were in digs together and regularly ended up in very late-night balti houses after big nights out. These pies remind me of that really special time. It wasn’t much before my university days when balti cooking emerged in 1970s Birmingham, apparently created as a way to appease the British palate of the time. Its roots are in Pakistani-Kashmiri cooking and the base of the curry always has to contain tomatoes, onions, peppers and chillies, although variations can be built on those foundations. They’re a wonderful celebration of multicultural Britain.Balti pieEnjoyed on football terraces across the nation, thefirst balti pieis thought to have been served at Walsall football club in 1997, and they are now sold at more than 70 football grounds throughout the UK. There is a version of the balti pie that not many know (or have even considered) outside the UK, but it is the stuff of dreams: thebalti pie barm, or whole balti pie inside a soft bread roll. Don’t knock it until you’ve tried it. You will need a nonstick 12-hole muffin tray.Prep15 minChill15 minCook2 hrServes46 chicken thighs on the boneFine table salt1tsp medium curry powder1tsp garam masala½tsp ground turmeric½tsp chilli powder½tsp ground cumin½tsp ground cinnamon70g butter1 red onion, peeled and finely chopped1 green pepper, deseeded and cut into small cubes1 garlic clove, peeled and chopped2cm pieceginger, peeled and chopped400g tin chopped tomatoes1tsp tomato puree200ml chicken stock1 heapedtbsp cornflourZest and juice of 1 lime10g fresh coriander, roughly chopped16 frozen roti paratha1 egg yolk, strained and beaten with 1 tsp water, for egg washing1 pinch each nigella seeds and fennel seeds, for toppingHeat the oven to 210C (190C fan)//415F/gas 6½. Put the chicken thighs in a roasting tray, season with a pinch of salt, and roast for 25 minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool.Lower the oven to 205C (185C fan)//gas 6. Scatter all the ground spices over a sheet of foil, then put the foil in the oven and toast the spices for 10 minutes. Turn off the oven.Meanwhile, melt 50g of the butter in a wide-based pan. Add the red onion, green pepper, garlic and ginger, and cook on a low heat until softened.Add the toasted spices, cook for a minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, tomato puree and stock. Bring everything to a simmer on a medium heat, then reduce the sauce by half and turn off the heat.When cool enough to handle, strip the meat off the chicken bones and chop it into small nuggets.In a small bowl, mix a tablespoon of cold water into the cornflour to make a slurry, then stir that into the sauce. Stirring continuously, bring the sauce gently back to a simmer. Add the chopped chicken, mix well, then add the lime zest and juice. Taste to check the seasoning, and add a little salt, if need be. Fold through the chopped coriander, leave to cool to room temperature, then chill in the fridge.Use the rest of the butter to grease eight holes in the muffin tin. Take the paratha out of the freezer and, working swiftly, roll out eight of them to about 11cm. Line each greased hole in the muffin tin with a rolled-out paratha and fill three-quarters of the way with the balti mix. Lightly brush the exposed paratha with a little water, then use the remaining paratha to close the pies, gently crimping the edges together; don’t worry about being too neat – I like to give them a rustic look. Chill the pies in the fridge for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Using a sharp knife, cut a small hole in the top of each pie, lightly brush the tops with a thin coating of egg wash, then scatter with the nigella and fennel seeds. Bake for 30 minutes, then serve hot with the green chutney below for dippingSpicy green chutneyView image in fullscreenCalum Franklin’s spicy green chutney.A fresh yet heady dressing that is so easy to make. It complements the balti pies superbly.Prep15 minMakes150ml1 garlic clove, peeled2cm piece ginger, peeled1 green chilli½tsp cumin seeds, lightly toastedJuice of ½ lemon60g fresh coriander, leaves picked40g fresh mint, leaves picked1 pinch fine table saltIn a blender, blitz the garlic, ginger, chilli, cumin, lemon juice and four tablespoons of water, until smooth. Add the coriander and mint leaves and a pinch of salt, then blend again, until smooth. Store in an airtight container in the fridge, where the chutney will keep for up to a week.These recipes are edited extracts from The Modern Pie Maker: A Mouth-Watering Journey Around Britain in Eighty Recipes, by Calum Franklin, published by Bloomsbury at £26. title: Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri | Food | The Guardian
description: A spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauce
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauce
Content: Gurdeep Loyal’s Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenGurdeep Loyal’s Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.Quick and easyFoodGurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheriA spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauceGurdeep LoyalMon 12 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBiber salçasıis a Turkish paste made from concentrated cooked red peppers and salt. It comes in two varieties:acı(spicy) andtatlı(sweet). The hotter version adds a deep, umami heat to cumin-spiced lamb in this pasta recipe, which in Turkey is known asmarkana. Traditionally, markana is served with garlicky yoghurt and a generous drizzle of chilli butter enlivened with pul biber and sumac. With flavours this loud, it’s best to use a large pasta shape such as paccheri, because its cavernous middles can hold satisfying morsels of the filling.Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheriPrep10 minCook25 minServes41tbsp olive oil1 large red onion, peeled and dicedFine salt500g lamb mince2tsp cumin seeds, crushed6 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed4tbsp acı biber salçası(hot Turkish pepper paste)3tbsp tomato puree1tsp dried mintSugar400g paccheri200g natural yoghurtFinely grated zest and juice of 1 large unwaxed lemon50g unsalted butter1tsp pul biber or chilli flakes1tsp sumac15g fresh dill, leaves finely choppedPour the olive oil into a wide, deep frying pan, then add the onion and a quarter-teaspoon of salt, and saute for four minutes. Add the lamb mince, cumin and four of the crushed garlic cloves, and cook for six to seven minutes, until the meat is just beginning to brown.Add the hot pepper paste, tomato puree, dried mint, a teaspoon of fine salt and a generous pinch of sugar, and cook for two minutes. Pour in 250ml water, turn down the heat to medium-low and simmer gently for 10 minutes.Meanwhile, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions, then drain.In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the remaining two crushed garlic cloves and the lemon zest.Melt the butter in a small frying pan and cook for three to four minutes, until it just begins to tint brown. Stir in the pul biber and sumac, then take off the heat.Stir most of the lemon juice and most of the dill into the lamb sauce, then add the drained pasta and mix well to coat. Swirl over the garlic yoghurt, followed by the sumac butter, garnish with more dill and another squeeze of lemon, and serve straight from the pan.Flavour Heroes: 15 Modern Pantry Ingredients to Amplify Your Cooking, by Gurdeep Loyal, is published by Quadrille at £27.
