title: The pet I’ll never forget: Pumpkin, the rescue cat turned social media star | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Struggling to breathe, so big she could barely walk, Pumpkin practically begged for help when we met. Before long I was taking her home
Author: Faisa Mohamed
Headline: Struggling to breathe, so big she could barely walk, Pumpkin practically begged for help when we met. Before long I was taking her home
Content: ‘She’s lost almost 3lb since we’ve had her’ … Chris with Pumpkin.Photograph: Courtesy of Chris SeelbachView image in fullscreen‘She’s lost almost 3lb since we’ve had her’ … Chris with Pumpkin.Photograph: Courtesy of Chris SeelbachThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Pumpkin, the rescue cat turned social media starStruggling to breathe, so big she could barely walk, Pumpkin practically begged for help when we met. Before long I was taking her homeChris Seelbach, as told toFaisa MohamedMon 12 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePumpkin arrived at our animal shelter in March, after her owner passed away. As CEO and president of SPCA Cincinnati, I expect something heartbreaking when my team asks me to see an animal – perhaps they have been neglected or abused. Pumpkin was neither. She was dirty and had some fleas but that was not our concern. She was severely obese.View image in fullscreenPumpkin (left) with Dottie.Photograph: Courtesy of Chris SeelbachAt 25lb (11.3kg), Pumpkin could barely move. Her legs were bowed from the weight and she walked with a waddle. Examining her wasn’t easy. Her breathing became so laboured that she turned blue.Speaking to her late owner’s daughter, we were able to piece together that Pumpkin was around five and had likely gained weight after two litters and some well-meaning overfeeding.As a cat dad of three, if I fostered every animal that piqued my interest I would be out of a home. But Pumpkin had these massive, expressive eyes. She doesn’t miaow so everything is communicated through her alien-like gaze. As she lay on her back on the exam table, she was unable to lift her head. Still, she locked eyes with me as if to say: “Help!”My husband and I decided to bring Pumpkin home to meet our other cats. Jerry is an enormously loud black cat, Doe is sweet and shy, and Dottie is a hunter who gathers my socks in the night. They quickly realised Pumpkin was not threatening. She was far too slow to bother them, couldn’t jump on the counter to eat their food or climb the spiral stairs in our condo. She mostly sleeps on her cat bed, adjusting to her new diet.View image in fullscreen‘She mostly sleeps on her cat bed, adjusting to her new diet.’Photograph: Courtesy of Chris SeelbachWhen I first posted videos about Pumpkin online, I expected a handful of views. Instead, Pumpkin has captured millions. People stop me on the street to ask if I’m “Pumpkin’s dad”. Comments tell me they would “die for her” and they are “healed” by her videos.It’s always gratifying to help other people successfully foster and now I’ve experienced it myself. We have officially adopted her and decided to give her a very fitting sixth birthday party on Halloween.Pumpkin’s coat has grown glossier and she is more comfortable roaming around the house. She’s lost weight – almost 3lb since we’ve had her. She can now even climb on to our couch to lie with our other cats. I like to think her growth has come from a better diet and all the positive energy from her fans online. She’s certainly made our lives richer since she joined the family.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pet I'll never forgetCatsAnimalsPetsAnimal welfarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Father was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughter | Money | The Guardian
description: New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport
Content: Applying for a passport for a dual national has become more difficult under recent new rules.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenApplying for a passport for a dual national has become more difficult under recent new rules.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAConsumer championsMoneyFather was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughterNew post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passportAnna TimsMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport.I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport.I began her application for a British passport in February. I had to submit photos of my wife when pregnant, family photos from the birth to the present day, hospital records and official translations of French marriage and birth certificates.During an official interview I was asked about my job, commute and the layout of my house, but very little about my relationship with my daughter.I was then told that there was insufficient evidence to prove my paternity and was invited to consider a DNA test, which will cost £600 and take yet more time.We need to visit my elderly father who is unwell in the UK but cannot risk it in case our daughter is denied boarding.BN,FranceYour daughter is a victim of new rules that came into force in February and effectively deny entry to the UK to dual national Britons who do not have a British passport.Foreign nationals can enter freely on passports issued by their country of residence, but expats cannot unless they stump up £589 for a certificate of entitlement. The law has caused chaos, with children beingstranded abroadorarbitrarily denied a passportgranted to their siblings.Since the UK government is not accepting that your daughter is a UK national, you asked if she could travel on her French passport. No one could answer the question.As a result, you face Christmas apart from your parents. Home Office rules state that officials must consider a passport application on the“balance of probability”if an applicant refuses a DNA test. They must also explain why an application is refused. You have never been told why your copious proofs of paternity have been deemed inadequate.The Home Office will not comment on individual cases, but it did tell me that additional evidence, such as the layout of a home, may be requested to add “credible authenticity”.Soon afterwards, you were informed that the application had been accepted after all, despite no new paperwork having been sought since April. I can only assume that press scrutiny prompted the realisation that your domestic floorplan is credibly authentic.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsPassport OfficeBrexitfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake Iseo | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: Smaller and less visited than Como and Garda, Lake Iseo harbours a gorgeous car-free island ideal for easy-going cycling and sightseeing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Smaller and less visited than Como and Garda, Lake Iseo harbours a gorgeous car-free island ideal for easy-going cycling and sightseeing
Content: Monte Isola on Iseo Lake with Carzano village on shore.Photograph: Simone Polattini/AlamyView image in fullscreenMonte Isola on Iseo Lake with Carzano village on shore.Photograph: Simone Polattini/AlamyItaly holidaysA lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake IseoSmaller and less visited than Como and Garda, Lake Iseo harbours a gorgeous car-free island ideal for easy-going cycling and sightseeingSuzy PopeMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 03.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRust red and burnt sienna speckle the green mountain rising from Lake Iseo. Golden autumn sunlight shimmers on the water. Monte Isola, Italy’s largest lake island, is a peak of sheer cliffs and dense forest, dotted with old fishing hamlets and hillside villages, each as pretty as the terraced villas of Lake Como and Garda, but with far fewer visitors. I arrive at the small port town of Peschiera Maraglio – where striped wooden boats jut from the water like the gondolas of Venice – on a ferry from Sulzano, a five-minute hop across the water.“Only three people on the island are allowed to own a car: the priest, the doctor and the mayor,” says Chiara, my tour guide from Brescia. Residents can zip up and down the steep island roads on mopeds, and a small fleet of van-sized buses trundle around throughout the day, but nearly all cars are forbidden and visitors have to explore on foot or bike.Even bikes are banned from boats at the weekend. Not that it matters: the harbour front is lined with bike rentals (from €4 an hour for a standard bike). I’m normally a nervous cyclist, but car-free roads raise my confidence. Plus, most other visitors have the telltale front-wheel wobble of novice riders. This isn’t the place for Lycra and personal bests; the smooth-as-silk, quiet roads are for slow pedalling, and neck swivelling to take in another gorgeous view of Lake Iseo.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of Lake Iseo with Monte IsolaThe circular lakeside route winds past olive groves tumbling to the shore. I thought I’d need base layers and gloves this far into autumn, but I’m in shorts and a T-shirt and already working up a sweat in 24C sunshine. I pedal through the lakeside hamlet of Sensole in the island’s south-west and stop in Menzino, just along the shore. There’s a cafe-bar catering to cyclists, so I fuel up with an espressoconlake view.double quotation markThe south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyardsThe view from the western side of the island is somewhat marred by a huge concrete factory on the mainland, so I keep my head down on the pedal to Siviano, the island’s capital. The shambling streets are sleepy; the stacked skyline of orange, lemon and magnolia villas is punctuated by the looming facade of Santi Faustino e Giovita church and a medieval stone tower. Monte Isola has been inhabited since the Roman era. Venetian rule in the 15th and 16th centuries left the main towns resembling those on Garda and Como: hillside terraces of wooden-shuttered pastel villas. In the late 18th century, Monte Isola found its main industry: net making. AtRetificio La Rete Srl, a small shop and net factoryat Siviano’s port, fishing nets have been handwoven for centuries, along with nets for basketball hoops, football goals, shopping bags and hammocks.At the northern tip of the island, I get the best views of Lake Iseo’s craggiest mountains. The south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against gently undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyards. The north is where jagged peaks scrape the sky, plummeting to the emerald-green lake water. Just off the shore, a speck of an island (Isola di Loreto) is topped with a grand, castle-like building, which Chiara says is privately owned. A flotilla of kayakers from Marone make their way towards the private dock, slipping across the glass-still water.In Carzano, I pause to admire thepink-and-white facade of San Giovanni Battista church, before cycling along the more functional stretch of road along the eastern shore. The traffic-free spell is broken by an old Fiat Punto, apologetically crawling along the road. Maybe the driver is the doctor or priest.double quotation markThe steep trail to the top begins with the cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forestI complete my circle back in Peschiera Maraglio, where a late lunch of lake fish awaits atLa Foresta restaurant. To begin, pickled tench so vinegary it makes my mouth water and a chub carpaccio that tastes like fresh lake water; followed by the island staple of dried, saltedsardinason grilled polenta. “Sardinais not a sardine; it’s actually a type of shad fish,” Chiara explains. “In the middle ages, when Monte Isola had to pay tax to Venice, they didn’t understand how money worked, so they paid in saltedsardinasinstead.”View image in fullscreenFish drying in Peschiera Maraglio, Lago d’Iseo.Photograph: Matthias Scholz/AlamyAs the last ferries leave for the evening, it feels as if I have Peschiera Maraglio to myself. Accommodation is private holiday apartments or restaurants with rooms. AtDecio, a modern bistro dominates the ground floor, with a handful of sleek bedrooms above. The glass front shows off an uninterrupted lake view and the room is bathed in orange light at sunset. I spend the evening perched on a stool outsideL’Isola dei Sapori, a no-frills alfresco spot where sparkling franciacorta wine is perfectly chilled, and snacks of local salami, olives and fish dishes combine for a light dinner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMake tracks: 8 of the UK’s best walking and cycling trails on former railway linesRead moreThe next day, I forgo my bike and lace up my hiking boots. The steep trail to the top of the island begins with the enclosed cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forest. I pocket a particularly beefy conker, unable to resist the childhood urge for a blinder. My legs start to burn against the gradient – the trail is 450 metres of climbing. Rocks and twisting roots burst through the forest path and there’s a sheer drop to one side, but the glimpses of Lake Iseo between the trees are worth every wheeze.View image in fullscreenSantuario della Madonna della Ceriola chapel on the island of Monte Isola in Lake Iseo.Photograph: Image Professionals/AlamyAfter an hour, the trees thin out and I emerge atSantuario della Madonna della Ceriola. The striking white sanctuary was built in the 13th century, on the remains of a pagan temple and early Christian chapels. A vast golden altar and detailed frescoes adorn the interior, but it’s the panoramic view outside that really makes the hike worthwhile. The ferry to Sulzano is a toy boat, leaving a white tail of wake.From up high, I see that autumn colours are already creeping into the forest. I wipe the sweat from my eyes. This view is only going to get prettier as the season evolves, and the prize conkers are yet to fall.The trip was arranged byVisit Brescia.Bike rentalstartsat €4an hour.The ferryfrom Sulzano to MonteIsola is€2.60each way.Trainsrun from Brescia to Sulzanofrom€4.10. title: Did you solve it? The treacherous puzzle of the round table | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: The solutions to today’s puzzles
Author: Alex Bellos
Headline: The solutions to today’s puzzles
Content: King Arthur's round table on the wall in Winchester,Photograph: acceptfoto/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenKing Arthur's round table on the wall in Winchester,Photograph: acceptfoto/Getty Images/iStockphotoAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleMathematicsDid you solve it? The treacherous puzzle of the round tableThe solutions to today’s puzzlesAlex BellosMon 12 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier today I set you these six puzzles. Here they are again with solutions.The round tableThree people sit at a round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left.”1.What is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?2.What is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?Solution1.The oldest person must be lying, so the maximum is 2. Here is an example with 2 people telling the truth:30-40-20 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table)The answer istwo.2.The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the minimum is 1. Here is an example with 1 person telling the truth40-30-20The answer isone.Seven people sit at a different round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left, and I am younger than the person two places to my right”.3.At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?4.At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?Solution3.The two oldest people must be lying, so the answer cannot be six or seven.It turns out that the answer cannot be five either. If five were telling the truth, the third oldest would be one of them, and so the three oldest people would have to be arranged in one of the two cases below (suppose the ages are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70).* * * 60 * 50 70 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table)* * * 70 * 50 60But now there is nowhere for the next oldest (the 40-year-old) to sit and be telling the truth.It is, however, possible for four people to be telling the truth:10 20 40 70 30 50 60The answer isfour.4.The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the answer cannot be zero. If you order everyone in descending order of ages, no one is telling the truth apart from the youngest:70 60 50 40 30 20 10The answer isone.999 people sit at a third round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.Each of them says “I am younger than the person three places to my left, andolderthan the person three places to my right”.5.At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?6.At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?Solution5.We might think about this by colouring the seats gold, silver and bronze in a repeating pattern, like so (in the illustration there are only 21 people, but the idea works for 999 people as well).It can now be seen that each person makes a statement about people sitting on seats with the same colour as them; in particular, the closest people on either side with the same colour seat.Consider those 333 people sitting in gold. The youngest and oldest of these must be lying, so there cannot be 333 or 332 gold truthtellers. But, as the example below helps to illustrate, it is possible for every other gold person to be telling the truth, by seating them with age increasing as we move clockwise around the table. Applying the same reasoning to those seated on silver or bronze, we can have all but six people telling the truth.View image in fullscreenThe same idea with 999 people has 999-6=993 telling the truth.The answer is993.6.If the people are sat with age decreasing as we move clockwise around the table, then everybody is lying.The answer is0.Thanks to Daniel Griller for today’s puzzles. He is the author of the excellent puzzle booksElastic NumbersandA Ring of Cats and Dogs, and Other Curious Puzzles.I’ll be back in two weeks.I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one,email me.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleShareReuse this content

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone | iPhone | The Guardian
description: A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match
Content: This maxed out iPhone requires two hands to use.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThis maxed out iPhone requires two hands to use.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.iPhoneReviewiPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphoneA giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to matchSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s largest ProiPhonegets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera.The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of theregular 18 Proand, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of itsPro Max predecessors: take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support.View image in fullscreenAPopsocket on the back, or an official lanyard or wrist strap attached to a case, is almost a necessity for the 18 Pro Max.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianBut it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than itsnearest rival, 38g more thanits smaller siblingand heavier still thanfolding phones. It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap.The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro.SpecificationsScreen:6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)Processor:AppleA20 ProRAM:12GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:iOS 27Camera:48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facingConnectivity:5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)Dimensions:163.4 x 78 x 8.75mmWeight:249gBattery life for daysView image in fullscreenA full charge takes 70 minutes, hitting 80% in 32 minutes, but requires a 60W Power Delivery 3.1 USB-C adaptor with adjustable voltage supply (AVS) to reach its fastest speeds (not included).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro Max has the same new A20 Pro chipas the 18 Pro, which is one of the fastest chips you can get in a phone, plus a resigned cooling system that helps maintain peak performance during long gaming sessions.It has the longest battery of any iPhone, lasting almost three days of light usage between charges, actively using the screen for seven hours for apps, browsing, messaging and photos. That is about four hours longer than its predecessor and almost a day longer than the 18 Pro. Even with heavy use, the 18 Pro Max still managed to end the day with about 50% left in the tank, meaning most people will have to charge it only every second or third day.iOS 27View image in fullscreenThe black iPhone 18 Pro Max is the darkest and most inky black model yet with a colour-matched glass back, but it’s a bit of a fingerprint magnet.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro Max runs the same iOS 27 as smartphones from theiPhone 11onwards. The new software speeds up app launches and other parts of the system, refines the Liquid Glass redesignfrom last yearand revamps Apple’s AI tools.The new Siri AI chatbot is a significant step in the right direction, able to better understand you and perform tasks. It has its own app to review previous conversations and can see what is on your screen or through the camera. It can also suggest data from your various Apple apps, similar to Google’s proactive toolson the Pixels. But it relies on you using messages and mail, rather than third-party apps such as the WhatsApp or Gmail apps.SustainabilityThe battery will lastin excess of 1,000 full-charge cycleswith at least 80% of its original capacity, and it can bereplaced for £119. Out-of-warrantyscreen repairs cost £389. The specialists iFixit awarded thephone seven out of 10for repairability.It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.CameraView image in fullscreenThe new variable aperture can be left in automatic or manually adjusted along with a handful of other manual controls.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro Maxhas the same camera system as its smaller sibling, which includes an 18 megapixel centre stage selfie camera in the screen and three 48MP cameras on the back.The three rear cameras are some of the best on a phone, including a 4x/8x optical zoom and 0.5x ultra wide.The big addition for the 18 Pro Max is a variable aperture on the main camera, allowing it to open wider than other iPhones for better low light performance or to narrow to preserve depth of field. But it also allows additional creative photography possibilities, including shooting starbursts.The 18 Pro Max also has new AI-powered focus tracking, improved Photographic Styles for greater customisation, Apple’s new digital negative feature and automatic cinematic mode for video.PriceThe iPhone 18 Pro Max costs from£1,299(€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).For comparison, theiPhone 17costs£899, theiPhone Air£1,099and theiPhone 18 Pro£1,199; theGoogle Pixel 11 Procosts£1,279and theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultra£1,359.VerdictThe iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s biggest, longest-lasting and most expensive slab phone for 2026.It takes what is great about the regular 18 Pro and supersizes the screen and battery, giving it a run time of up to three days, which is a good half day more than its smaller sibling. That places it shoulder to shoulder with some of the longest-lasting phones available on any platform.But similar to superphones fromGoogleandSamsung, the 18 Pro Max is too big to use one-handed and tricky to pocket. It is also too heavy and made my hand hurt without using a Popsocket or a similar handle attached to it.Otherwise, it is a fairly iterative upgrade on the 17 Pro Max, with the same design and feel. The screen is still one of the very best on a phone, and the improved dynamic island is a useful upgrade. The A20 Pro chip is seriously quick, the cameras are some of the best you can get on a phone and the variable aperture on the main camera opens up some new creative opportunities, even if its impact on image quality is fairly minor.Pros:fabulous 6.9in screen, better dynamic island, very long battery life, great cameras with variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.Cons:very expensive, very heavy, hard to use one-handed, small upgrade on last year, AI tools still lag top competitors.View image in fullscreenThe iPhone 18 Pro Max is a towering monolith of a smartphone, particularly in the inky black colour.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsiPhoneAppleSmartphonesiOSMobile phonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We were not going to let this rapist destroy our lives’: how one couple came to terms with a devastating attack | Rape and sexual assault | The Guardian
description: After Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her. They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault. What did he get right – and wrong? And why did she want him to write about her ordeal?
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: After Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her. They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault. What did he get right – and wrong? And why did she want him to write about her ordeal?
Content: ‘She’s so incredibly brave. Her resilience is amazing’ … Thomas Trezise and his wife, Susan Brison, at home in Vermont, September 2026.Photograph: John Tully/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘She’s so incredibly brave. Her resilience is amazing’ … Thomas Trezise and his wife, Susan Brison, at home in Vermont, September 2026.Photograph: John Tully/The GuardianRape and sexual assaultInterview‘We were not going to let this rapist destroy our lives’: how one couple came to terms with a devastating attackAnna MooreAfter Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her. They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault. What did he get right – and wrong? And why did she want him to write about her ordeal?Mon 12 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a hot, still, silent noon, at a junction of dirt roads in ruralFrance, Thomas Trezise stood scanning the horizon, looking and listening for his wife. He tried to soothe a deep foreboding. Susan Brison had headed out for a morning walk two hours ago. How could she be gone so long?This was 4 July 1990, the start of what was meant to be a busy summer. Trezise and Brison were both assistant professors in the US – he in French at Princeton and Brison in philosophy at Dartmouth – and had just arrived at the remote farmhouse of Trezise’s French colleague. Life seemed packed with promise. “I’d found someone with whom I really wanted to spend my life and I just felt very, very lucky,” says Trezise. “Susan and I had fallen quickly and deeply in love – it was magical – and at that point, we were also trying to conceive a child. We loved being in France. I kind of felt I’d found my way. It was a good place … until it happened.”By 1pm, Trezise was still trying to push back a rising panic when, from the corner of his eye, he saw his colleague running towards him, yelling. “That’s the moment I remember,” says Trezise. “I just thought: ‘OK. I wasn’t wrong about something happening.’ It was terrifying.”An ambulance was at the gate, but Trezise could not recognise the figure inside. She was bandaged, bruised and bloodied, her cheeks hugely swollen, her eyes slits, an enormous bulge on her forehead. Seeing his reaction, Brison slowly lifted her oxygen mask and said in a hoarse voice: “I’ll be OK.”double quotation markI knew I needed to be there, I needed to listen, but – this is a masculine thing – I wanted to fix it and I knew I couldn’tOutside on the driveway, Trezise allowed himself one scream to the skies, fists clenched. Though it would be days before he would learn exactly what had happened, it was instantly clear to him that a man had done this to her. Back in the ambulance, en route to hospital in Grenoble, it took Trezise every ounce of will to contain his anger, fear and frenzied emotion, and to instead project calm. It was, he remembers, like “an actor taking the stage”. He became, or tried to become, “the strong, supportive spouse”.This is the starting point of Trezise’s memoir, Beginning Again, which gives a powerful account of the days, weeks and years ahead. It’s a voice we rarely hear, especially in such depth – a man’s experience of his wife’s rape and attempted murder.Trezise and Brison are in their seventies now, tenured professors, with an adult son. Within months of the assault, Brison had begun speaking publicly about sexual violence. Before long writing about it too. In 1993, her account was published in the New York Times and later, her book, Aftermath, was an exploration of finding sense and meaning when you have landed far beyond the moral universe. It was Brison who suggested that Trezise write about it too. “I knew he had it in him to write this book,” she says, “and I was always encouraging him.”For Trezise, there were many layers of difficulty in doing so. “One was this feeling of complicity,” says Trezise. “It’s impossible not to know that the vast majority of sex crimes are committed by men. A simple way of putting it is that, if I’d gone on that same walk that day, I would have been safe.” Entitlement was another barrier. “What voice do I say this in? I do not want to claim ‘victimhood’ when Susan’s victimisation was so much worse. But I did want to say that this has very dire effects and it’s not just my story, it’s the story of millions of people.” When men stay silent, sexual violence gets filed under ‘woman’s problems’, when of course, says Trezise, it’s “a problem for humanity”.During their first 11 days in hospital, Trezise slept beside his wife, with the help of sedatives prescribed to both of them. Brison could barely speak – she had been so badly strangled, she had a fractured trachea – and Trezise was her voice, her support, her advocate and also her guard, because Brison was terrified that her assailant might appear in the hospital. Trezise was on high alert too. They refused to be separated, even during treatments and examinations. His book describes helping with her first bath – just the two of them, locked in the bathroom, him washing her, then taking a shower himself, sticking his head out every 15 seconds to check she was still safe.The account of the attack itself is given by Brison, through the unedited deposition that she wrote with a detective in the hospital, a painstaking procedure that took eight hours to complete. It’s a horrifying, harrowing read that tells how Brison was grabbed from behind by the throat while walking, and taken to a muddy ravine. She was punched, assaulted, strangled, smashed by a rock; she came in and out of consciousness, and bargained and begged for her life. The ordeal only ended when she pretended to be dead.Brison had barely looked at the deposition since giving it – and had no intention of doing so until Trezise asked permission to include it in his book. “It was important, as wrenching as it is, for the readers to know exactly what she went through,” says Trezise. “If I had paraphrased it, I would have felt like I was appropriating her voice.” For Brison, reading it within her husband’s narrative gave her a different perspective. “I was very moved,” she says. “I had never stopped to think how he felt as I was giving it. It’s important for people to know the effect on him.” At one point in the deposition, Brison describes being in so much pain that she thinks it would be better to die – but then imagines her husband finding her body in a ravine and being “alone in the world”. This gives her the strength to carry on. “It left me speechless,” says Trezise. “Just like in the ambulance, when she said: ‘I’ll be OK.’ She didn’t say that for her own sake. She said that for my sake.”Still, through all this and back in the US, Trezise contained his emotions to be the “supportive spouse” he thought Brison needed. At Princeton, Brison at home on disability leave, doors and windows locked, it was Trezise who stepped back out into “normal life” – going to work, buying the groceries, performing all life’s admin. “The question for me was, ‘How can I help her? What should I do?’ – and those are the things I knew how to do,” he says. “The trouble is, I feel like at times, they were done to the exclusion of me being emotionally accessible, because that was more disorienting. I knew I needed to be there, that I needed to listen, but – this is a masculine thing too – I wanted to fix it and I knew I couldn’t. And that was a source of great frustration and, at times, anger and depression.”View image in fullscreen‘I knew, even during the hardest of times, he would stand by me’ … Brison and Trezise.Photograph: John Tully/The GuardianMany couples do not survive trauma like this and Brison can see why. “My trust in the world was so shattered, I didn’t feel viscerally that I could walk out the front door and not get killed or the ground would fall beneath me,” she says. “Tom was so strong, he was a rock. I know that’s what he thought I needed, but I needed to be accompanied. He hadn’t cried. He hadn’t shown that he was hurt. For a while, our ability to understand each other was shot.” Brison resented his ability to pick up his former life, and imagined him out there, doing fine. In truth, Trezise was barely coping. “It was hard to get through the day,” he says. “Before I taught my class, I lay on the floor of my study and just dreamed about being somewhere else. The most banal, everyday exchange like, ‘How was your summer?’ or ‘How are you doing?’, was so difficult to answer, and 99% of the time, I said nothing, which meant I was like a ghost.” Though he’d received a fellowship to write a book on Samuel Beckett, he’d lost all interest. (He never wrote it.) Having built a career around his love of France – the country and the language – Trezise had no wish to ever return and could hardly bear to hear French.Every aspect of their life and marriage had been profoundly changed. “It’s partly because the attack was of a sexual nature,” says Trezise. “We’d been trying to conceive a child before the attack, but physical intimacy – any intimacy, emotional, psychological – becomes really fraught. In one sense, you’re asking: ‘Am I entitled to feel attracted to Susan?’ ‘Am I entitled to cry?’ I didn’t feel entitled to my own feelings a lot of the time. It’s as though I couldn’t be myself. I had to walk on eggshells. Susan was angry – and I did not blame her in the least. But it can be hard to be in the presence of someone who’s angry, even if the person’s not angry at you.”What helped? For Brison, finding her own community, especially a survivors’ self-help group, was hugely important. Though there were no support groups for partners at that time, Trezise also began therapy. “It was absolutely essential,” he says. “It was a revelation to have one hour a week with someone who knew a great deal about trauma and whose job it was to listen so I didn’t feel like I was imposing.” He advises anyone in a similar position to seek support. “Just because you’re a carer doesn’t mean you don’t need care,” he says. “You need to find it, whether that’s family, friends, a group, a therapist. If you don’t have the support yourself, you’re not going to be a good care-giver.”double quotation markMy trust in the world was so shattered, I didn’t feel viscerally that I could walk out the front door and not get killedThough there is no linear path to recovery, Trezise found comfort in the passing of time. “Even when things seemed to be absolutely impossible, somehow we kept going the next minute or the next hour,” he says. “And I think the other side of it was that we were not going to let this rapist destroy our lives. As Susan put it in her book, we were not going to finish his job for him.” (The assailant, a local man, had been quickly identified and was later sentenced to 10 years for rape and attempted murder.)Perhaps most healing of all was the arrival of their son, Gabriel, four years after the assault almost to the day. “Having a child was terrifically important,” says Trezise. “It’s magical. Here comes this creature who’s absolutely unprecedented, he’s new, and guess what? It’s not a bad thing to be a boy. He knows nothing about this, and that was gratifying to me. Also, this is the start of a new story. It’s a story that’s going to be his but we can help him and he’s helping create a new story for us by showing, ‘Look, this chapter you’ve been going through, it’s not the only one you’re going to have in your book.’ It was a way for us to love each other too, through him.”The cover of Beginning Again depicts the Japanese art of kintsugi, where pottery is repaired with the breaks left visible, lined and lacquered in gold and silver. For Trezise, it seems apt. “Things got radically changed but they can be put back together in a very beautiful way,” he says. Decades on, there is still PTSD remaining for both of them. Brison will always turn around if she hears someone walking behind her, and, though they now live in a beautiful part of Vermont, she would never take a country walk alone. In Trezise’s case, he struggles to contain deep panic if he has arranged to meet his wife and she isn’t there. (She has learned to let him know when she’s running late.) And they both have a strong startle response. “He’s worse than I am!” says Brison. “When we’re in the house together and one of us is about to appear in the room, we whistle or say, ‘I’m coming!’”But, trite as it may sound, they are closer for having survived this. “I said it in the dedication in my book and it still brings tears to my eyes,” says Brison. “‘For Gabriel, who arrived, and Tom, who stayed.’ He stayed. It wasn’t easy, and lots of men don’t stay. I knew, even when we were having the hardest of times, that he would stand by me.“I always knew that he was a good human being,” she continues. “He has always been incredibly kind and generous and thoughtful. What has changed enormously is that he has become so much more aware of his feelings and able to articulate them. He has overcome decades of being socialised as a boy and man so that I don’t have to read his mind any more.”Trezise has learned more about Brison too. “The depth of her strength is just incredible,” he says. “She’s so incredibly brave. Her resilience is amazing. I already knew she was a wonderful person – she’s loving, she’s a terrific friend to her friends – but if one thing comes out of this, it’s that this is a person I can trust with everything. And I’m just so lucky.”Beginning Again by Thomas Trezise (University of California Press, £23) is published on 27 October. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations.In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsRape and sexual assaultFamilyFrancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive | Lebanon | The Guardian
description: Naffah Naffah makes the bells in the mountains near Beirut. His sons will take over the foundry when he retires
Author: William Christou
Headline: Naffah Naffah makes the bells in the mountains near Beirut. His sons will take over the foundry when he retires
Content: Naffah Naffah inspects the finish on an outer mould, ready for casting a bell. The family often relies on craftspeople to engrave the moulds with crosses or icons.Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNaffah Naffah inspects the finish on an outer mould, ready for casting a bell. The family often relies on craftspeople to engrave the moulds with crosses or icons.Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The GuardianLebanonLebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition aliveNaffah Naffah makes the bells in the mountains near Beirut. His sons will take over the foundry when he retiresWilliam Christouin Beit ChababMon 12 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe story of Lebanon’s last remaining church-bell maker begins with a rifle. In the 18th century, Youssef Gabriel, a local metalworker, was secretly making and equipping Arab revolutionaries with rifles to assist their revolt against the Ottoman empire, which controlledLebanonat the time.Then, one day, a Russian engineer came to the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab to make a church bell. Gabriel, intrigued, shadowed the man and picked up the process on sight.Or, another story goes, the Maronite patriarch at the time, frustrated by the Ottoman empire blocking the import of church bells to Mount Lebanon, tasked Gabriel with making a bell. After several attempts he succeeded and decided to give up making arms, converting his gunsmithery into Lebanon’s first church-bell foundry.Where the stories converge is that the village, impressed with Gabriel’s handywork, rechristened him Youssef Naffah –naffahmeaning useful or successful in Arabic.Three centuries later, the Naffah family is still making church bells in Beit Chabab. Once one of 10 bell foundries owned by the family, the workshop operated by the master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon. It is also the sole source of church bells for much of the Middle East and even Lebanese diaspora communities in Europe, Australia and the US.View image in fullscreenNaffah examines his workshop, which is tidied up at the end of each day.Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The GuardianNaffah, 57, said: “We have to pass it down to our kids, it’s been 300 years. I didn’t have any choice. My own father, he would come to the workshop when he could barely even walk.”The foundry sits under his home on the edge of a hill overlooking the red tiled roofs of Beit Chabab and the Lebanese coast that stretches beneath it. The picturesque town, in the Mount Lebanon range about a 30-minute drive from Beirut, offers an escape from the city’s chaos and a refuge from the violence of the country’s last two wars.The ceiling and walls of the foundry are blackened from decades of smoke that has belched from the furnace, and the floors are cluttered with bells in various stages of construction.Outside are mounds of white clay mixed with goat hair, each layer drying before the next is applied. The final product forms the interior mould that the molten metal is poured around. Inside the workshop, modern tools mix with the ancient, a hydraulic press sitting next to a well-worn anvil placed on top of a tree stump.View image in fullscreenYoussef Naffah looks for maker’s marks indicating who made each bell, when it was made and for which parish. One bell bears the inscription: ‘Suleiman Naffah and Sons’, his grandfather's name.Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The GuardianEach bell takes about two months to make. It takes about 40 days to make the interior mould and another month to create the outer mould, with crosses, decoration and the workshop’s signature imprinted on the white clay as it hardens.The third and final stage is the quickest: a foundry is heated using burning wood, and a mixture of copper and tin is placed inside to be melted down over 24 hours. When the metal is ready, it is poured over the bell mould, hardening within three minutes.The workshop produces about 25 bells a year, about 20 of which go to churches in Lebanon. The cost of the bell depends mostly on the size, with every 100kg (220lbs) costing $8,000 (£6,000). A medium-size bell that is ready in the foundry and weighs about a tonne costs about $80,000.“I hate giving the bells away, it always makes me upset, like I’m giving away a child,” said Naffah. He pointed to a mould being worked on, imprints of crosses on its clay interior. “Look at this bell, it’s the work of my two hands. I’ve poured my heart and soul into it.”View image in fullscreenSome bells await delivery while others await repair. Alongside them, moulds stand ready to cast new ones.Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The GuardianEach bell bears the names of those who worked on it. One bell ready to be installed has the name of Naffah, his son Charbel and the patron who commissioned it. Other bells in the shop for repairs – one from 1910, another from 1932 – bear the names of Naffah’s grandfathers.The family maps Lebanon by its churches, finding evidence of their ancestors up and down the small Mediterranean country. The earliest surviving bell that bears their name is in the town of Qalaat Sahyoun and was forged in 1725.The ringing of the bells is part of daily life in the villages that wind through Lebanon’s mountains and dot its sprawling coast; on a Sunday morning, the sound mingles with the chirping of the birds.View image in fullscreenAfter a day of deliveries outside the workshop, Naffah catches up with Youssef.Photograph: Gabriel Ferneini/The GuardianDuring the Hezbollah-Israel war in Lebanon, which reignited in March, the Christian villages of south Lebanon were cut off from the rest of the country. Israel’s ground invasion, which bulldozed dozens of villages in south Lebanon, mostly spared the Christian villages, but it left them isolated.The church was a crucial source of comfort for the besieged Christians. It organised the distribution and transfer of aid in and out of towns and across frontlines when necessary.Naffah, Charbel and his other son Youssef are determined to preserve this Lebanese tradition and their place within it. Charbel will succeed his father as the master of the family workshop, and Youssef helps when he is not busy with his studies at medical school.Youssef said if Charbel ever decided he no longer wanted to make bells, he would leave medical school and take his place as master of the foundry.“We have six churches in the village [Beit Chabab]. If all of the bells played at the same time, I could distinguish between each one from their sound alone,” he said, surveying the village from the edge of the foundry.“Traditions are important to us. We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”Explore more on these topicsLebanonChristianityHeritageMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content
