title: Bolivia investigates ex-president Evo Morales over alleged ties to 2009 killings | Bolivia | The Guardian
description: Leftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two others
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two others
Content: Former Bolivian president Evo Morales last February.Photograph: Patricia Pinto/ReutersView image in fullscreenFormer Bolivian president Evo Morales last February.Photograph: Patricia Pinto/ReutersBoliviaBolivia investigates ex-president Evo Morales over alleged ties to 2009 killingsLeftist former leader accused of involvement in shooting of three Europeans in Santa Cruz and torture of two othersAFPMon 12 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBolivia’s attorney general has announced an investigation into leftist former presidentEvo Morales, alleging his involvement in the murder and torture of European citizens in 2009.Seventeen years ago, police raided a hotel in the city of Santa Cruz, shooting dead Eduardo Rózsa Flores, a Bolivian-Croatian, Michael Dwyer, an Irishman, and Árpád Magyarosi, a Hungarian-Romanian.Bolivian-Croatian citizen Mario Tadic and Elöd Tóásó from Hungary survived and reported being tortured after their arrest.The Morales administration in power at the time claimed that Rózsa Flores was leading efforts to promote a separatist movement, with funding from the rightwing economic elite of Santa Cruz.Bolivia rocked by protests as US warns of ‘coup d’état’Read moreActing attorney general José Armando Urioste announced the preliminary investigation into Morales just one week into the job on Monday.In a letter to the supreme court, Urioste said authorities were gathering evidence againstMoralesand his former vice-president Álvaro García Linera “for the alleged commission of the crimes of murder, abuse, torture and unlawful detention”.The investigation comes after a complaint filed by rightwing lawmakers Tomasa Yarhui and Rodrigo Antonio.When the raid occurred, Morales told the press during an official visit to Venezuela that he had ordered the detention of the foreigners, whom he called “mercenaries”.Family members and victims brought the case before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which concluded in 2021 that the government had violated human rights.Neither of the accused has commented on the latest inquiry.Morales, the first-ever Indigenous person to lead Bolivia, is currently in hiding from two active arrest warrants against him. One relates to his alleged role in massive protests that paralysed the country for 53 days earlier this year. The other accuses him of trafficking a minor with whom he is said to have had a daughter. Morales denies the allegations.Explore more on these topicsBoliviaEvo MoralesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fugitive businessman taken into US custody in Venezuela bribery case | US crime | The Guardian
description: A businessman wanted in the US for allegedly bribing top Venezuelan officials has been taken into custody
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A businessman wanted in the US for allegedly bribing top Venezuelan officials has been taken into custody
Content: Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks as Vice-President JD Vance, right, listens behind him at news conference on the fraud taskforce in Washington, on 8 October.Photograph: Tom Brenner/APView image in fullscreenAttorney General Todd Blanche speaks as Vice-President JD Vance, right, listens behind him at news conference on the fraud taskforce in Washington, on 8 October.Photograph: Tom Brenner/APUS crimeFugitive businessman taken into US custody in Venezuela bribery caseA businessman wanted in the US for allegedly bribing top Venezuelan officials has been taken into custodyAssociated PressMon 12 Oct 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA businessman wanted for years in theUSfor allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts inVenezuelahas been taken into custody.Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted Venezuelan presidentNicolás Maduro. The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the state department had been offering a reward of up to $10m for information leading to his arrest.Pulido, 62, was taken into US custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agencies, American officials said on Sunday.It was unclear how Pulido ended up in US custody. He was scheduled to make his initial court appearance on Tuesday in Miami.“His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, wrote in a social media post Sunday.“No amount of time or distance will stop” the justice department “from working with our federal law enforcement and international partners to pursue these criminals and bring them to justice in an American courtroom,” he wrote.Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge that Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the US, sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro’s vice-president. She took over as Venezuela’s acting president following the US military’s ouster of Maduro in January.Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for more than $2bn in contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.Prior to these alleged offenses, Pulido had a prolific history of drug trafficking, including a 1997 conviction in Italy under the alias of German Enrique Rubio, the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Florida said in a statement.Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the US by Rodríguez in May. In September, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195m in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.Explore more on these topicsUS crimeVenezuelaUS politicsNicolás MaduroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece | Environment | The Guardian
description: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
Content: A warm day in Žabljak, Montenegro.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA warm day in Žabljak, Montenegro.Photograph: AlamyWeather trackerEnvironmentBalkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for GreeceClear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean SeaEurope live – latest updatesEd Walton and James Parrish for MetDeskMon 12 Oct 2026 06.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTemperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.In Kosanica,Montenegro, the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.Elsewhere inEurope, high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep acrossGreeceas a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.View image in fullscreenPeople cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersMeanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHeavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentWeather trackerMontenegroEuropeGreeceMexicoHurricanesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year | Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars | The Guardian
description: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose 350,000 vehicle-a-year quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose 350,000 vehicle-a-year quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%
Content: Any Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (known as PHEVs) imported above the new quota level will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAny Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (known as PHEVs) imported above the new quota level will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsEU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a yearBrussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%Business live – latest updatesVW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industryLisa O’CarrollMon 12 Oct 2026 07.23 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmarkfour-year agreement made in Beijing last week.The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under theWorld Trade Organizationsafeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spacesRead moreAny cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars inChinawill.China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the“Made in Europe” legislationwould do the same in public procurement.On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.Sources said there has been“a paradigm shift”withconcerns of deindustrialisationand job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.Explore more on these topicsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryInternational tradeEuropean UnionEuropeChinaWorld Trade OrganizationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Queensland prison where children self-harm to get transferred ‘more suitable’ than police watch houses: ombudsman | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Inmate advocacy group attacks watchdog’s ‘gutless retreat’ on Wacol youth remand centre
Author: Ben Smee
Headline: Inmate advocacy group attacks watchdog’s ‘gutless retreat’ on Wacol youth remand centre
Content: A toilet and shower in the admissions area of the Wacol youth remand centre, which was designed to be a police watch house.Photograph: Queensland ombudsmanView image in fullscreenA toilet and shower in the admissions area of the Wacol youth remand centre, which was designed to be a police watch house.Photograph: Queensland ombudsmanQueenslandQueensland prison where children self-harm to get transferred ‘more suitable’ than police watch houses: ombudsmanInmate advocacy group attacks watchdog’s ‘gutless retreat’ on Wacol youth remand centreFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBen SmeeQueensland state correspondentMon 12 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 21.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheQueenslandombudsman has backed away from calls to close a youth prison so “unsuitable” for children that some are self-harming in an attempt to get transferred, amid concerns that the Crisafulli government’s hardline bail laws could create a new crowding crisis in police watch houses.The ombudsman, Anthony Reilly, published an inspection report last week that raised serious new concerns about the suitability of the Wacol youth remand centre to hold children for extended periods, including the fact that young people were being held in conditions where there is “a lack of space, privacy and natural light”.The facility, near Brisbane, is often used to hold Indigenous children from north Queensland due to overcrowding at the Cleveland youth detention centre in Townsville.Queensland concedes law imposing mandatory jail on some offenders as young as 10 breaches human rightsRead moreThe report found that some children stayed for longer than a month and that some “complex and high risk” children were shifted back to the remand centre after being placed in a youth detention centre.Staff told inspectors that some children from north Queensland who had spent extended time at the centre “displayed negative behaviours and engaged in acts of self‑harm to influence and expedite their transfer to another centre”.The Wacol centre was designed as a police watch house but was converted under law to a youth detention centre.The operation of the Wacol centre has in some ways eased pressure on police watch houses, andthe practice of holding vulnerable children in crowded police cells– in some cases formore than 30 days– due to a lack of available places in youth detention. Data shows fewer children held in watch houses, and for shorter periods.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailCritics and children’s advocates say the government has simply shifted the problem to Wacol.Queensland is building a new youth detention centre at Woodford and Reilly had previously called for the Wacol facility – which he says is “austere and institutional” and unsuitable to hold children for long periods – to be closed when the new facility is opened.But the ombudsman has backed away from that recommendation in his latest report, over concerns that new state bail laws – dubbed “breach bail, go to jail” – could cause the population of young people in prison to explode, triggering a new crisis in watch houses.“In the year ahead, it may be the case that the impacts of the above reforms are such that the existing three youth detention centres and the new Woodford youth detention centre do not have sufficient capacity to accommodate the number of children that our criminal justice system requires to be detained,” Reilly said in his report.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As a consequence, it is possible that children will need to be detained in large numbers and for lengthy periods in watch-houses. In this scenario, it would be beneficial for the Wacol [centre] to continue to be available to accommodate children to minimise the number of children detained in watch‑houses, and the length of their stay.“While we do not consider the centre to be a suitable facility for the detention of children, we consider it to be more suitable than detention in police watch-houses.”Sisters Inside, an organisation that supports women and girls in custody, described the backdown as “a gutless retreat” that “allows the government’s determination to imprison more children to dictate what an independent watchdog is prepared to tolerate”.“The ombudsman has identified that Wacol is unsuitable for children, then backed away from demanding its closure because the government intends to lock up even more of them,” said Debbie Kilroy, Sisters Inside’s chief executive.“If a facility is unsuitable for children, it does not become suitable because the government creates something worse. Children’s safety cannot be negotiated down to accommodate a political agenda.”Kilroy said the findings demanded “a clear stand for children’s safety”.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandAustralian police and policingYouth justiceQueensland politicsYoung peopleIndigenous AustraliansIndigenous incarcerationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia may risk a diplomatic spat with the Trump administration if it limits the viewing of a US execution | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: A history of tech giant legal challenges and US politicians’ fierce criticism shows there’s no easy solution for the eSafety commissioner
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: A history of tech giant legal challenges and US politicians’ fierce criticism shows there’s no easy solution for the eSafety commissioner
Content: Australia's eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, has been labelled a ‘zealot for global takedowns’ by some Trump-aligned politicians.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralia's eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, has been labelled a ‘zealot for global takedowns’ by some Trump-aligned politicians.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralian politicsAnalysisAustralia may risk a diplomatic spat with the Trump administration if it limits the viewing of a US executionJosh TaylorA history of tech giant legal challenges and US political criticism shows there’s no easy solution for the eSafety commissionerGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastMon 12 Oct 2026 17.19 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTShareAustralia’s online safety regulator has a few levers to limit the public seeing the US’s planned live stream of an execution but history suggests it will lead to a very public fight.The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced last week the planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would be livestreamedwhen the military execution is carried out in early December.The Greens have called on the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, and the Albanese government to ensure that the event – if it goes ahead and is livestreamed – is not seen by Australians on TV or their devices.Australian Greens call for ‘barbaric’ US execution live stream to be blockedRead moreThe eSafety commissioner, under the Online Safety Act, has powers to order platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and X to block Australians from accessing posts that contain content deemed to be “refused classification” under Australian classification law.The classification of such extreme violent material is typically applied to content online of terror attacks, and other terror-related content, but it could be applied to clips of the video of the public execution after the fact.While some companies such as Meta will probably apply their own terms of service and prevent the distribution of the video, history suggests others will take a stand that the video should remain on their platforms.X has given no indication whether it will allow such videos but the platform owned by Elon Musk hasa long history of legal challengesagainst eSafety when it comes to this sort of content.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereIn 2024, X was successfulin allowing footage of the stabbing of a Sydney bishopin his church in 2024 to remain available to Australians –the platform even recruited the bishop, Mar Mari Emmanuel,to argue to the court to allow the footage to stay online.Most recently, Xwon an appealto the classifications review board to have the classification of the video of the assassination of rightwing influencer Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University downgraded from RC to R18+, after eSafety ordered the removal of clips of the assassination last year.It also won a similar case to reduce the rating of videos of the attack on Iryna Zarutska on a train in Charlotte, North Carolina, in August last year down to R18+.In laws passed by the former Coalition government in 2019 after the Christchurch terror attack, the eSafety commissioner also has powers to issue takedown notices to websites hosting footage that, among other things, depicts “actual violent crime such as murder, attempted murder, rape, torture”.These laws were developed with the view to block streaming of terror attacks but could have wider applications for state-sponsored violence such as executions.The eSafety commissioner last used these powers in 2022 to order websites to remove videos and related materials of theBuffalo, New York, terrorist attack in 2022. It can also declare an “online crisis event” and order internet service providers such as Telstra and Optus to block sites hosting the content, but this power has yet to be used.The ISPscomplied with eSafety’s requestto block sites hosting the Christchurch attack in 2019 before the parliament had passed the laws.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch a move – particularly if focused on large social media platforms, or potentially sites owned by the Trump administration – may lead to a domestic firestorm among conservative media as well as a potential diplomatic incident, and may not be the regulator’s preferred option – especially given it has not been used before.Last, there is the potential to seek penalties against platforms that fail to detect and remove violent material from their platform. The regulator is now testing this law out with messaging platform Telegram, which eSafety has alleged failed to remove some content that included executions conducted by terrorist groups.The eSafety commissioner is seeking fines of up to A$54.6m and the hearing for the case is set down for February next year.The other factor to consider is the laser-focus some in the US already have on Inman Grant. Her term is up in January next year, and Inman Grant has previously said she will not seek another term, but Trump-aligned politicians such as theRepublican congressman Jim Jordanhave labelled Inman Grant as a “zealot for global takedowns” and claimed she has threatened American speech on social media platforms.Inman Grant has rejected the claims and she declined an invitation to speak before a US congress hearing at the time.If Inman Grant bears the responsibility for decisions around whether Australians can see the livestreamed execution, it will likely provoke a new round of criticism.The regulator late on Monday said it did not have powers to proactively block the streaming in Australia, and said it would monitor and enforce existing standards that could obligate online platforms to block it themselves.The history of legal challenges and attention from the right of politics in the US suggests no easy solution in the eSafety toolkit – short of ministerial intervention.Josh Taylor is a technology reporter for Guardian AustraliaExplore more on these topicsAustralian politicsSocial mediaCapital punishmentanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU | Brexit | The Guardian
description: PM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematic
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematic
Content: Andy Burnham gives an update in the House of Commons on Monday.Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham gives an update in the House of Commons on Monday.Photograph: House of Commons/PABrexitAndy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EUPM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematicPippa Crerar,Jennifer RankinandLisa O’CarrollMon 12 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s future place in Europe, saying the existing relationship is “not good enough” as he framed next month’s Brussels summit as a possible first step to EU membership.The prime minister said Britain must take a “clear-eyed rational look” at its long-term relationship with the bloc to boost economic growth and control immigration, which needed to go beyond Labour’s existing red lines.The next “reset” summit will take place on 20 November, ending months of uncertainty, with the two sides seeking to sign deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham hopes could provide a £10bn-a-year boost to the economy.One EU diplomat said a deal on the three “significant but modest” issues needed to be approved as a test of the UK’s good faith so both sides could get on with the “real reset” in the longer-term relationship.But the UK remains braced for a possible row over protectionist “Made in Europe” trade rules amid industry fears they could lock out UK manufacturers, prompting the prime minister to pledge he would raise concerns with his EU counterparts.Burnham was also forced to clarify that he did not think Russian interference in the 2016Brexitcampaign had affected the final result, after he raised questions about the legitimacy of the outcome in comments at the weekend.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch accused Burnham of being too loose with his language over remarks he made about Kremlin interference in Brexit.Photograph: House of Commons/PAIn a statement to MPs, the first since the party conference recess, an otherwise confident-sounding Burnham said it would be a “major dereliction of duty” for his government to turn away from exploring closer relations with the EU.“We should not turn our backs on this opportunity and I hope all sides of this house will get behind the government’s efforts to land a positive outcome,” he said.“I believe our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.“Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country.“Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.”View image in fullscreenNigel Farage speaks to reporters outside the Houses of Parliament in the days after the UK voted to leave the EU.Photograph: Matt Dunham/APBurnham denied he was reopening the Brexit debate, insisting he respected the referendum result, but added that he wanted to take a “pragmatic approach” to boost economic growth and improve cooperation on migration.He was forced on to the back foot over his remarks on a podcast on Sunday that Russia had interfered over Brexit, rejecting suggestions from Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, that he may have been loose with his language.“It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time,” he said.Burnham had said on Sunday it was clear thatRussia had interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendumafter he sought answers when he arrived in No 10. He did not disclose who gave him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or, crucially, whether any interference had affected the result.View image in fullscreenBurnham said he wanted to improve cooperation with the EU on migration.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyDowning Street said the prime minister “absolutely” accepted the Brexit referendum result and believed it to be legitimate, while the foreign minister, Stephen Doughty, said it was clear Russia had attempted to interfere but had failed.In his statement, Burnham told MPs they were right to raise the question of the “loss of immigration control” that came with Brexit, as Labour grapples with continuing public concern over the issue, and suggested Brussels recognised this.The UK is excluded from Eurodac, a database that holds biometric and ID data to identify asylum seekers and irregular migrants, and exited the Dublin regulation, a legal mechanism to return refugees to the European country through which they had first entered or transited.But while the prime minister told MPs a return to free movement was “not on the table” in his discussions with the EU, and said he would honour Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines, he was unable to rule it out for a post-election future.Sources on both sides believe they will be able to get other issues over the line at the summit next month, suggesting that a food and phytosanitary agreement would have been reached in July if the summit had gone ahead on its original date.View image in fullscreenBarley fields in Flamborough, East Yorkshire.Photograph: Rebecca Cole/The GuardianIssues still to be resolved include a transition period for grains grown in the UK using recently approved fungicides not yet licensed in the EU. This would allow farmers harvesting this year to sell stockpiles next year even with the different regulations.The thorniest issue remains the youth mobility programme, allowing EU and British citizens under 30 to live, work or study in each other’s countries for up to three years. The two sides are at odds over the overall numbers, as well as the tuition fees students would pay at British universities.The biggest current risk to the UK of not aligning more fully with the EU is being locked out of the new Made in Europe initiative – aimed primarily at imports from China in strategic sectors such as renewable energy, nuclear and electric cars – which will block British-made components being used in EU supply chains.EU sources have insisted there can be no agreement on the issue with the UK at the summit, because the bloc is yet to agree its own position on the proposals. EU lawmakers hope to agree a position on a key proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, in December.View image in fullscreenAn assembly line at the Volkswagen Sachsen GmbH plant, Europe’s largest and first all-electric vehicle manufacturing facility, in Zwickau, Germany.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBut Brussels is, at least, open to discussing the issue, and it may be part of the summit statement – a joint text agreed by both sides. The UK has the support of the Netherlands, Poland and Italy for inclusion in the scheme, but France in particular has posed a stumbling block.Burnham acknowledged that Made in Europe presented “risks” to British manufacturing, perhaps in an attempt to address some concerns inside government that Downing Street hasn’t been prioritising the issue.He said: “It is important that we get to an arrangement here that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we’re both trying to deal with the same issue, which is Chinese exports and the damaging effect that is having on our industry.”Explore more on these topicsBrexitAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionEuropeImmigration and asylumForeign policyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Man rescued from cave on Sardinia after being trapped by rockslide for 26 hours | Italy | The Guardian
description: Luca Olmetto was trapped roughly 10 metres below ground in the Gorroppeddu cave in the Urzulei mountain range
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Luca Olmetto was trapped roughly 10 metres below ground in the Gorroppeddu cave in the Urzulei mountain range
Content: About 48 experts from Sardinia’s Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps and 30 firefighters, as well as civil protection staff, were involved in the rescue operation.Photograph: Corpo Nazionale Soccorso Alpino e Speleologico - CNSASView image in fullscreenAbout 48 experts from Sardinia’s Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps and 30 firefighters, as well as civil protection staff, were involved in the rescue operation.Photograph: Corpo Nazionale Soccorso Alpino e Speleologico - CNSASItalyMan rescued from cave on Sardinia after being trapped by rockslide for 26 hoursLuca Olmetto was trapped roughly 10 metres below ground in the Gorroppeddu cave in the Urzulei mountain rangeAngela Giuffridain RomeMon 12 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 31-year-old man has been pulled alive from a cave on the Italian island of Sardinia after being trapped roughly 10 metres below ground for 26 hours following a rockslide.In a huge and complex operation, rescuers worked non-stop after Luca Olmetto became trapped in the Gorroppeddu cave in the rugged Urzulei mountain range in central-eastern Sardinia on Sunday afternoon.He had been exploring the cave with his girlfriend, who was a few metres behind him and narrowly missed the collapse, which completely blocked the entrance to the cave. She managed to escape unharmed and immediately raised the alarm.Rescuers managed to reach Olmetto, who was conscious and responsive throughout the operation, by late Monday afternoon after manually removing rubble and earth blocking a narrow passage. They then proceeded with the delicate operation of removing the large amounts of debris that covered the caver before extracting him from the cavity. According to Rai News, Olmetto was brought to the surface just after 6pm CET and stabilised by medical staff before being airlifted to hospital.About 48 experts from Sardinia’s Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps and 30 firefighters, as well as civil protection staff, were involved in the rescue operation. A helicopter also provided materials and equipment needed to make the site secure.In a message posted on social media, the council of Codrongianos, the town in north-west Sardinia where Olmetto is from, wrote that the past 24 hours were filled with “great anxiety for the entire community”.“We are closely monitoring the situation and are hoping for good news soon,” the council said. “Our thoughts are with Luca and his family, and we extend our deepest gratitude to all the rescuers working tirelessly to bring him to safety. Hang in there, Luca – all of Codrongianos is with you.”The Gorroppeddu cave is a largely unexplored natural cavity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a similar incident in December 2024, another explorer, Ottavia Piana, 32, became trapped while exploring a cave in the Bueno Fonteno caves close to Bergamo in northern Italy. She remained underground at roughly 600 metres for 75 hours before being freed. Piana suffered injuries including fractured vertebrae, ribs and facial bones. Her high profile rescue involved 160 specialists.Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China
Content: Actor Omar Sy (second from right) and Stellantis’s Emanuele Cappellano (second from left) with other Stellantis executives and the Citroën 2CV electric concept car at the Paris motor show.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenActor Omar Sy (second from right) and Stellantis’s Emanuele Cappellano (second from left) with other Stellantis executives and the Citroën 2CV electric concept car at the Paris motor show.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersAutomotive industryStellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protectionBosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from ChinaJasper Jollyin ParisMon 12 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars.Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed“Made in Europe” legislation.The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries.EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a yearRead moreThe executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans.Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants.The EUconfirmed on Mondayit would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in alandmark four-year agreementmade in Beijing last week.The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise ofChinain key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals.Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details.If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included.Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans.“I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.”Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, includingFrance’s industry minister, had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit.Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits.“On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.”Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.”London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month saidthat decision was under review.Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.”He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules.“We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU.He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryStellantisRenaultEuropean UnionEuropeChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Hackers force French supermarket fridges to heat up to 50C in ‘unprecedented’ cyber-attack | France | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affected
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affected
Content: The branches affected would have to ‘throw away all of the products’ that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché said.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe branches affected would have to ‘throw away all of the products’ that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché said.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceHackers force French supermarket fridges to heat up to 50C in ‘unprecedented’ cyber-attackHundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affectedReuters in ParisMon 12 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHackers have forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight, in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores across the country, with fires and food losses reported.The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday ⁠the large-scale attack was “affecting connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France”. Reported damage included “food losses and fires”, it added.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency ANSSI to investigate, ⁠a person in his office said.France “was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected”, while also investigating whether any other French ⁠firms were at risk, they said.Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarché, said about 150 of its stores had been ​hit, with fridges heated up to 50C for six hours. ‌It had thrown all the food away to avoid any health risks, a spokesperson said.Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Coopérative ‌U, said his supermarkets had also been hit by the attack. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X.Several other supermarket chains, including Carrefour, Monoprix and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment. According to BFM TV, France’s largest supermarket chain E Leclerc was also affected, with hackers “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. E Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment.The attack may not have been confined to France. The Dutch supermarket company ‌Ahold Delhaize said it was also dealing with a “security issue” in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them.Stores of its Albert Heijn chain, ​the largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands, which also has several stores in Belgium, remained open in both countries. But its online app and delivery system were down, while electronic price tags often displayed the wrong information.It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the ⁠problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize.Delhaize supermarkets, also part of Ahold Delhaize but operating ​in Belgium and Luxembourg, were ​also affected by the security issue, ​Belgian media reported.The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability ​in software supplied by ‌the Danish company Danfoss.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDanfoss ​said it was “aware ​of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”.The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by cyber-attacks by malicious actors.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from Russian “hybrid attacks”.Explore more on these topicsFranceCybercrimeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences
Content: 0:44CCTV from inside Riyadh airport shows moment of deadly airstrike – videoSaudi ArabiaSaudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airportEnergy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defencesWhy are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?Patrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 12 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after afurther round of Houthi missile attackscaused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missileskilled 13 people on Saturdayand left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.View image in fullscreenBefore and after the strike as people queue up for flights at King Khalid international airport on Saturday.Photograph: Saudi Ministry of Media/ReutersThe country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, saidSaudi Arabiahad invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.”An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. TheHouthishave also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.A Houthi official on Monday warned the US it would receive a “painful response” if it entered the war inYemen, following Trump’s comments at the weekend that he was “going to look at” the possibility of joining Saudi strikes.“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview.He also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen.Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.View image in fullscreenA billboard displays an image of the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in Sana’a, Yemen on Sunday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAOn the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”.A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine MalikRead moreThe STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weakenDonald Trump.Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, includinghis call for the Ukrainian president to stand asideshowed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaHouthisVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineYemenMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary
Content: 1:55NAZA - official trailerNAZANAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s intervieweesIsraeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentaryLorenzo TondoMon 12 Oct 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentaryNAZAand prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini,the Israeli prime minister demandedthey “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where itwon the special jury prizeafter receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicatehow many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.View image in fullscreenNAZA’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival last month.Photograph: Capital Pictures/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor,threatening to strip them of their citizenshipand accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it ofspreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”View image in fullscreenGraffiti depicting Abraham and Szor, and the word ‘traitors’ in Hebrew, appeared on a wall in Ashdod, southern Israel, after NAZA was awarded the special jury prize at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersNAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sourcesfamiliar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.In recent days, the Israeli governmenthas promoted an online film projectthat mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival,have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuPalestinePress freedomHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme court | India | The Guardian
description: Thousands join rally to deliver petition calling for resignation of election commissioner
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Thousands join rally to deliver petition calling for resignation of election commissioner
Content: Rahul Gandhi, the leader of India’s opposition alliance (centre, making a peace sign), leading the march to the supreme court in Delhi.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenRahul Gandhi, the leader of India’s opposition alliance (centre, making a peace sign), leading the march to the supreme court in Delhi.Photograph: APIndiaIndian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme courtThousands join rally to deliver petition calling for resignation of election commissionerHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiMon 12 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 01.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDelhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.The leader of India’s opposition alliance,Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.View image in fullscreenSecurity personnel stand guard at barricades in Delhi to prevent thousands of protesters reaching the supreme court.Photograph: Manish Swarup/APKumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – beingdeleted from voter listssince last year.Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.India’s supreme court demands answers over changes to voter rollRead moreThe election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.View image in fullscreenSecurity personnel detain demonstrators during a protest demanding Kumar’s resignation on Sunday.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesIn a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “votechori”(cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people,led by the Cockroach Janta party(CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served forIndia, the youth won’t stop,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.View image in fullscreenThousands of people joined the march to the supreme court on Monday after a weekend of unrest.Photograph: Manish Swarup/APMahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the ​Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.Explore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaProtestRahul GandhiDelhiCivil liberties - internationalNarendra ModinewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan detains hundreds of politicians from Imran Khan’s PTI party | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: President Zardari suspends provincial government in escalation of tensions as Khan supporters march to Islamabad
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: President Zardari suspends provincial government in escalation of tensions as Khan supporters march to Islamabad
Content: Supporters of Pakistan’s PTI party take part in a protest march demanding Imran Khan's release from prison.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of Pakistan’s PTI party take part in a protest march demanding Imran Khan's release from prison.Photograph: ReutersPakistanPakistan detains hundreds of politicians from Imran Khan’s PTI partyPresident Zardari suspends provincial government in escalation of tensions as Khan supporters march to IslamabadReutersMon 12 Oct 2026 06.48 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 20.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePoliticians from ⁠the party of the former Pakistani ​prime ministerImran Khanhave been detained after the suspension of a provincial government now under emergency rule.Pakistan’s president declared a state of emergency and suspended the ⁠government in north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, led by Khan’s ally Sohail Afridi, on Sunday.Asif Ali Zardari’s federal government said the emergency rule was invoked after the provincial government failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province, which borders ⁠Afghanistan.Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party rejected that assertion, saying it was enforced to deter his supporters from marching to Islamabad, the capital, to pressure the ​government for his release.The imposition of emergency rule and suspension ‌of the provincial government have sharply escalated ‌confrontation between the 74-year-old former cricket star and the country’s powerful military.The emergency rule came a week ‌after Khan’ssupporters had rallied for days in the province, intending to march to Islamabad to demand his release and provide medical treatment.Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned fatherRead more“Yes, I can confirm that the chief minister and some of his cabinet members have been taken into preventive custody,” the government minister Talal Chaudhry told Reuters.If any were found to have cases to be tried against them, they would be charged and tried, he said, but the others would be released. He said the detentions occurred on Sunday at the provincial chief minister’s house in the ‌city of Peshawar in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.View image in fullscreenPolice guard a road in Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, after a state of emergency was declared.Photograph: ReutersWitnesses and officials said the chief minister’s house and other important facilities in the vicinity had been cordoned off with a heavy police presence, paramilitary forces and shipping containers.Shaukat ​Yousafzai, an aide of Khan, condemned the detentions and demanded the politicians’ release.Khan’s three sisters and hundreds of his supporters were also detained before the planned march.The party’s last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces, and Khan’s 2023 arrest prompted nationwide riots that led his supporters to attack military installations.Pakistan’s constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency.The minister of law, Azam Nazeer Tarar, ⁠said a provincial governor would take charge in the province after the president declared the ​state of emergency. The province has suffered an ​increasing number of militant attacks in recent ​months.The federal government and the military accuse Khan’s PTI of failing to curb the violence, a charge the party ​denies.Zardari’s administration and the PTI ‌held several rounds of ​talks since the call for the ​march was made last month.The government was ready to accept all of the PTI’s demands, including a go-ahead for the march, Tarar said, adding: “We asked for just one thing, that the party should publicly condemn the militancy and join our hands in the fight against militants.”They did not agree and that is why the talks broke down, he said.Explore more on these topicsPakistanImran KhanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: English councils warn of ‘catastrophic’ Send debts forecast to hit £10bn by 2028 | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of support
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of support
Content: Applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) have risen sharply since the government announced its proposals to change the system.Photograph: Don Tonge/AlamyView image in fullscreenApplications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) have risen sharply since the government announced its proposals to change the system.Photograph: Don Tonge/AlamySpecial educational needsEnglish councils warn of ‘catastrophic’ Send debts forecast to hit £10bn by 2028Surge in EHCP applications poses risk to public finances and may lead to deteriorating levels of supportPatrick ButlerandRichard AdamsMon 12 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCouncils are warning of potentially “catastrophic” debts, which are forecast to reach a record £10bn over the next 18 months, as a result of rapid growth in demand for special educational needs and disability (Send) support in English schools.Although the government recently cleared more than £5bn in historic council Send debts, asurge in requestshas led to authorities predicting they will have re-accrued that debt figure by April, and doubled it by 2028.The recent acceleration in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs), which mandate support for conditions such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD, is thought to partly reflect a rush by parents and schools tosecure supportbefore the government’s changes to Send provision take effect.The prospect of council finances being overwhelmed by schools’ Send spending reflects similar concerns in the NHS and the benefit system over the strain the rising prevalence of mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions has put on public services.graphic of Send deficit forecastThe government-commissioned Fonagy report, published last week, found the increase in these conditions wasreal and a cause of distressto many who have them, but the resulting demand for supportwould be unsustainablewithout introducing new ways to manage the pressure on public services.The County Councils Network (CCN), which published the forecasts on Tuesday, said the overspending was not the fault of councils and called on ministers to guarantee future Send debts run up by local authorities, some of whom would be otherwise left effectively bankrupt as a result of meeting their legal duties.Linden Kemkaran, the CCN’s Send spokesperson, said: “These deficits have not accumulated because councils have chosen to spend recklessly: they are the result of having to meet rapidly growing statutory demand, which has only intensified this year, without funding keeping pace.“If councils are left carrying billions of pounds of Send debt, it will not just be a problem for local authorities. Taxpayers and local communities will ultimately bear the consequences as councils face impossible choices about how to protect frontline services while managing debts that have accrued through no fault of their own.She added: “As well as councils absorbing skyrocketing costs, children and young people will face increasingly long waits for support and educational outcomes will continue to flatline. New ministers now need to provide certainty that they will deliver the full package of reforms needed to ensure the system works much better for young people, schools and councils.”The government’s reforms aim to gradually replace the current system in England with amore inclusive approach of Send supportin mainstream schools that in principle obviates the need for an EHCP. However, parents appear to be rushing to secure formal support now to avoid any future uncertainty.Without a ministerial guarantee to wipe future overspending, councils say they are at risk of bankruptcy when those accumulated debts – currently kept off town hall balance sheets under a special “override” arrangement with the Treasury – go back on to the books in April 2028 when the override is due to expire.Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in OfstedRead moreMinisters have agreed to pay 90% of English top tier councils’ Send debts accumulated to March 2026, but it is unclear how far future Send debts will be covered.
