Ministers have previously said future debt support would be “appropriate and proportionate” but that it would “not be unlimited”.The CCN said anything less than a ministerial commitment to pay down 90% of future Send debt would be a “financial catastrophe” for councils – and some authorities would struggle with solvency even if they retained just 10% of their Send debts.Publicly available internal reports by local authorities show a number are predicting overspends of more than £100m in 2026-27 alone. Hampshire county council is forecasting a £200m deficit for this year. Others include Surrey, East Sussex, Kent, Worcestershire and Norfolk county councils.The EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools.In January, the number of young people with EHCPs reached 718,000, after a 12.5% increase over the past 12 months. This was the largest year on year increase since the plans were introduced in 2014. An additional 1.3 million young people haveidentified special needs, according toofficial data.Many councils are anticipating annual double digit increases over the next three years, with several now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.The Fonagy report said the growth in EHCPs had “substantially outpaced the capacity” of the education system to respond. Of the 105,300 statutory assessments carried out in 2024, 94% resulted in the award of an EHCP.Owen Mapley, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said: “The continued escalation of Send deficits exposes a serious failure to align statutory responsibilities with funding levels.Local governmentchief financial officers have been calling attention to this disconnect for years as it undermines proper financial management practice.”A government spokesperson said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain, and have always recognised that both deficits and EHCP applications will continue to rise before our reforms are fully rolled out.“On top of grants to pay off 90% of council deficits, we’re investing billions to make sure every community has easy, early access to specialists like speech and language therapists, and so councils can deliver their tailored local reform plans.“Fixing the Send system will take time and councils will need further support with deficits, so we will set out the details before March 2028.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchool fundingSchoolsPublic financeLocal governmentAutismDepartment for EducationnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history | The Archers | The Guardian
description: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures
Content: The Archers’ current recording studio at the BBC Mailbox in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Archers’ current recording studio at the BBC Mailbox in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe ArchersBBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year historyPlans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measuresMichael SavageMedia editorMon 12 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is set to stop recordingThe Archersin Birmingham for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after scrapping plans for a radio drama theatre that was to be the new home of the world’s longest-running soap opera.A pledge to move recordings to the so-called Tea Factory, the BBC’s new Birmingham hub in Digbeth, has become the latest victim of thecorporation’s £500m cuts plan.While the soap’s production team are still scheduled to make the move, theBBCis now looking to record it at an existing UK studio.It will also consider private studios in theWest Midlands, but BBC insiders are already concerned that ending its Birmingham-based recordings and separating the actors from the production crew will have an impact on the show.Production staff regularly engage with the actors at the last minute to tweak scripts and storylines, raising concerns that their being in different places will stifle creativity.“It is going to weaken the show,” said a source. “It will change the DNA of the show.”BBC axes long-running Radio 4 show You and Yours in push towards podcastsRead moreMoving the recording of The Archers from the BBC’s existingBirminghambase, The Mailbox, to the Tea Factory was due to take place in 2028.In an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth.“Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK.“To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings.“The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.”The show has been associated with Birmingham since it started in 1951. Sources said it remained part of the cultural fabric of the city, and the show employs local writers and freelancers.However, others said the show’s recording schedule meant actors were only in the studio for about eight days a month, while many of the cast live across the UK.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome now fear recordings will default to London and that the show’s staff will eventually follow. However, the BBC has been clear that production staff will move to the new Birmingham headquarters as planned.It is not clear whether Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, was aware of the plans. Boosting BBC production outside London has regularly been at the top of her agenda.It is a sign that even some of the BBC’s most revered titles are being affected by cuts, with more announcements expected in the coming days. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has already faced anger from staff who believe more of the corporation’s manager class should be targeted instead.BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cutsRead moreA BBC spokesperson said: “We recognise and value The Archers’ longstanding relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme’s future, and The Archers production team will remain in their current home in the Mailbox and move, as planned, to the Tea Factory in Digbeth in early 2028.“However, after careful consideration, as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, we are no longer building a new recording studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory.“We’re currently assessing the BBC’s existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands to find a more cost-effective solution.”Explore more on these topicsThe ArchersBirminghamRadio dramaWest MidlandsSoap operaRadioPublic service broadcastingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann Widdecombe | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs
Content: The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced an independent review of the protective security provided by the state.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced an independent review of the protective security provided by the state.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/ReutersUK security and counter-terrorismMahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann WiddecombeHome secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPsRajeev SyalHome affairs editorMon 12 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecurity arrangements for high-profile public figures including politicians and members of the royal family are to be urgently reviewed afterthe killing of Ann Widdecombe, the home secretary has said.Shabana Mahmood said former MPs, party leaders who are not MPs, peers, former members of devolved parliaments and party spokespeople will also be offered police support.The UK’s protective security system will be re-examined to combat the growing risks of terrorism, extremism and state threats, as well as harassment and intimidation, Mahmood said.The review will be carried out by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former UK national security adviser, who will look at whether current security arrangements ensure there is adequate protection for those most at risk.This includes high-profile individuals such as members of the royal family, government ministers, MPs, locally elected representatives and other prominent individuals in British politics. His review will not include an assessment of individual cases.Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokesperson, wasfound dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with Widdecombe’s murder. He is also accused of “online reconnaissance” of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage’s home in south London on 19 April 2025 and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed.Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says BurnhamRead moreAddressing the Commons, Mahmood said that, regardless of the outcome of the investigation into an attempted break-in at Farage’s home, it is “clear there is insufficient protection for those who serve”.“I can therefore announce today that I will expand, with immediate effect, police support to political figures who are not currently members of parliament,” she said. “This will include former members of parliament, peers and party spokespeople, giving them access to a named police officer, as well as help with wider security measures.Mahmood added: “Today I also announce an independent root-and-branch review of the protective security provided by the state to those in public life. We can defeat those who mean us harm, but we are strongest when we act together.“In a more dangerous world, we are faced by threats from without and within that target our democracy and our way of life. In response, we are adapting and strengthening our defences.“As ever, I commend the work of the police and our security services, who labour in silence to keep us safe. And I’m sure the whole house joins me in offering thanks to them for that vital life-saving work.”Lovegrove will look at how existing security is provided, whether funding and other measures are being used effectively and proportionately, and how decision-making can be more consistent in response to threat and risk.Robert Buckland is conducting a separate review into themurder of Sir David Amess MP, which will consider the security of MPs in their constituencies.In May’s local elections the Electoral Commission found that 55% of all candidates experienced some form of harassment and intimidation, as did the same proportion of candidates at the 2024 general election.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismShabana MahmoodAnn WiddecombePoliceCounter-terrorism policyCrimeHouse of CommonsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham says ‘public will be the boss’ in any future decision about closer relationship with the EU – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: The prime minister tells MPs the next summit with the EU will be held on 20 November
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: The prime minister tells MPs the next summit with the EU will be held on 20 November
Content: 11.01 EDTBurnham says 'public will be the boss' in any future decisions about closer relationship with EUBurnhamconfirmed that he wanted to open a discussion about the UK’s future relationship with the EU.double quotation markIf we are serious, if we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.The status quo is not good enough for Britain.Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away.We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country.Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting.Share

title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: UK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incident
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: UK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incident
Content: A B‑1B Lancer bomber at RAF Fairford. A week after the incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers stationed at the base.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenA B‑1B Lancer bomber at RAF Fairford. A week after the incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers stationed at the base.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersUK security and counter-terrorismIran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says BurnhamUK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incidentDan SabbaghDefence and security editorMon 12 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month.The prime minister told MPs the UK would bring further sanctions against Tehran and the IRGC in the aftermath of an ambiguous episode that, despite over a fortnight of police investigation, has yet to lead to anybody being charged.After RAF Fairford incident, how big a threat to the UK is Iran?Read moreAddressing parliament on Monday about events at RAF Fairford, Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated inIran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards.”22:58Was Burnham right to talk about Russian interference in Brexit? | Politics WeeklyIn a statement to the House of Commons, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, told MPs that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had summoned the Iranian ambassador over the Fairford incident and that the government had imposed sanctions on two individuals accused of spying in Europe and the US.“He [Miliband] will condemn Iran’s continued attempts to undermine our safety. We are also sanctioning two individuals involved in conducting espionage and attacks on behalf of the government of Iran in Europe and the US, and we will not hesitate to take further action to restrict Iran’s capacity to threaten international security,” she said.Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found.However, the incident was followed by thewithdrawal of 12 B-1 bombersa week later, amid reports that the US was concerned about a possible drone attack on a base it had used to attack Iran during the Middle East war in the spring and summer.Burnham’s brief remarks were a step up from previous comments. The prime minister had said in the days after the incident that there were “strong indications” Iran had played a part – but now appeared confident enough to apportion responsibility.A joint statement from the UK, US and other European allies, released by the Foreign Office, added that the UK “has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors”.​However, despite his statement, it remains unclear what the authorities think happened at Fairford. Someexperts have speculated it was a “feint”to demonstrate that Iran could in theory attack a relatively open site.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish sources have repeatedly maintained that Iran lacks the capability to launch what would be a sophisticated drone attack, but the incident appears to have unnerved the US, which is worried about the security of its bases in Europe.The incident at Fairford comes after what the UK, in the joint statement, said was a recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and US interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).Though the US has detained and indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, whom it accuses of being behind the HAYI group, there is evidence to suggest that Iran-linked attacks have continued.A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb.Prosecutors told a magistrates court the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismIranGloucestershireUS militaryDefence policyMilitaryAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: One dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US | Georgia | The Guardian
description: Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop
Content: Visitors ride on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in April 2021.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreenVisitors ride on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in April 2021.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APGeorgiaOne dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in USSix Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft dropGuardian staff and agencyMon 12 Oct 2026 19.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags rollercoaster on Monday afternoon inGeorgia, according to police.The incident took place a Six Flags OverGeorgia, about 15 miles (25km) north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb county police department.Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. However, multiple outlets reported a person had fallen from the park’s Goliath rollercoaster, citingeyewitnessesand anonymouslocal officials.Six Flags permanently shuts down X2 rollercoaster after claims of brain injuriesRead moreTherollercoaster,which was introduced at the park in 2006, has a top speed of 70mph (110km/h) and a 175ft drop.A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.Late last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it wasretiringits famous X2 rollercoasteramid lawsuitsalleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recentlysettleda wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries werefiledlast week.Explore more on these topicsGeorgianewsShareReuse this content

title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34 | RJ Mitte | The Guardian
description: Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation
Author: Mollie Reilly
Headline: Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation
Content: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte, who has died aged 34.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBreaking Bad actor RJ Mitte, who has died aged 34.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianRJ MitteRJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representationMollie ReillyMon 12 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 21.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBreaking Badactor RJ Mitte died on Monday aged 34, his representatives confirmed.Mitte died in Brownsville,Texas. No cause of death was given.“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocateRJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”The Brownsville Police Department said no foul play was suspected and the investigation into his death was ongoing. Cameron County justice of the peace, Cyndi Hinojosa told the Associated Press that an autopsy would be performed.From the age of 15, Mitte played Walter White Jr, the son ofBryan Cranston’s high school chemistry teacher turned drug kingpin, on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, which isoftencitedas one of the best television programs of all time.Mitte had cerebral palsy, a condition he shared with hisBreaking Badcharacter.In 2015, hespoke to the Guardianabout being a disabled actor who plays disabled characters.“You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have.”Mitte’s costars paid tribute to him after news of his death broke.Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said in a statement: “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed.”Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr’s uncle Hank Schrader,wroteon social media: “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”In addition to Breaking Bad, Mitte had roles on several series, including Switched at Birth and The Guardians of Justice. Just days before his death, he waspromotinghis new movie, Talking to Strangers, billed as a “romantic tragedy”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier this month, Mitteappearedon the Joe Vulpis Podcast, speaking in depth about his time on Breaking Bad. He noted his character was based on a real-life friend of the show’s creator,Vince Gilligan.“It really felt real playing this character and getting into the groove with this character,” Mitte said.Offscreen, Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.Born in 1992, Mitte was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. In a2016 interviewwith the Guardian, he said he found out he was adopted when he was eight years old.“My step-brother told me. He’d overheard my mum and my stepdad at the time talking about it, and he threw it in my face. But I didn’t really care. It didn’t seem relevant, because I never once in my life felt unloved or like I was a burden.”Explore more on these topicsRJ MitteBreaking BadUS televisionTelevisionDisabilityDramaCelebritynewsShareReuse this content

title: Archbishop of US military condemns Pentagon plans to livestream execution | US military | The Guardian
description: Timothy Broglio says Catholics on army firing squad should ask to be excused since it clashes with church teachings
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Timothy Broglio says Catholics on army firing squad should ask to be excused since it clashes with church teachings
Content: Archbishop Timothy Broglio conducts an Easter Sunday mass in Washington DC on 12 April 2020.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenArchbishop Timothy Broglio conducts an Easter Sunday mass in Washington DC on 12 April 2020.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APUS militaryArchbishop of US military condemns Pentagon plans to livestream executionTimothy Broglio says Catholics on army firing squad should ask to be excused since it clashes with church teachingsGuardian staff and agencyMon 12 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe archbishop who oversees the spiritual care ofCatholicsserving in theUS militarycondemned the Pentagon’sproposedplansto livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan later this year.Archbishop Timothy Broglio also stipulated in a Monday statement that any Catholic soldier assigned to the US army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the live stream plans.‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnationRead moreHasan, an army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood inTexas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December.Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary,announced last weekthat Hasan’s execution would be public, and the Pentagon later confirmed it would be livestreamed.Broglio recalled that he presided over the funeral of Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack.The crime committed by Hasan “was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” Broglio asked.“TheUS militarygenerally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?”Explore more on these topicsUS militaryCatholicismReligionChristianityTexasFort Hood shootingsCapital punishmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Selma Blair arrested at JFK after she allegedly attacked flight attendants | Selma Blair | The Guardian
description: Several news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Several news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door
Content: Actor Selma Blair attends Variety’s 2026 Power of Women: Los Angeles event in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 September.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenActor Selma Blair attends Variety’s 2026 Power of Women: Los Angeles event in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 September.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersSelma BlairSelma Blair arrested at JFK after she allegedly attacked flight attendantsSeveral news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane doorMaya Yangin New YorkMon 12 Oct 2026 16.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actorSelma Blairwas arrested on Sunday at John F Kennedy (JFK) airport inNew Yorkon allegations that she attacked flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight, according to officials.Blair’s arrest happened at about 11pm, after Port Authority ofNew Yorkand New Jersey officials said they responded to a call “about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Air Lines flight 938 which was parked at the gate” at JFK after arriving from Los Angeles (LAX).Blair, 54, “was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation”, the port authority also said on Monday. “Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation.”The port authority said the FBI – which handles reports of crimes on airplanes – was investigating Sunday’s allegations against Blair.Asked to comment on Blair’s arrest, a Delta spokesperson said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”.The spokesperson added that Blair’s arrest did not affect the flight she and her fellow passengers were on – and that it still landed ahead of schedule at JFK.Several news outlets on Mondayreportedthat Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door.Statements released by officials did not immediately address those reported details.But an air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying “one flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks”.“I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which waspublishedby NBC Los Angeles.The flight controller replied that paramedics were approaching the gate – and that law enforcement was already there.The Guardian has reached out to Blair’s representatives for additional comment. Her publicisttoldthe Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.”Sunday marked at least the second time Blair was reported to be involved in such an incident. In 2016, shereportedlybegan screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico.Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”.“That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time.The actor has also made news headlines for a 2018multiple sclerosisdiagnosis. And in February 2024, sheapologizedfor an Islamophobic comment on social media.Blair’s starring film credits include Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy. She earned a best spoken world album for children nomination at the 2011 Grammy awards, for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition.Explore more on these topicsSelma BlairNew YorkUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Democrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’ | Ilhan Omar | The Guardian
description: Top House Democrats question the ‘corrupt weaponization’ of federal government against Trump’s adversaries
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Top House Democrats question the ‘corrupt weaponization’ of federal government against Trump’s adversaries
Content: Ilhan Omar speaks with members of the Congressional Progressive caucus, Maxwell Frost, Pramila Jayapal and Chuy Garcia, in Washington DC on 13 January.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreenIlhan Omar speaks with members of the Congressional Progressive caucus, Maxwell Frost, Pramila Jayapal and Chuy Garcia, in Washington DC on 13 January.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APIlhan OmarDemocrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’Top House Democrats question the ‘corrupt weaponization’ of federal government against Trump’s adversariesMaya YangMon 12 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlhan Omar’sDemocraticcolleagues have condemnedfederal agents’ searchof the Minnesota congresswoman’s home on Monday morning, describing it as “deeply disturbing” and emblematic of theTrump administration’s “corrupt weaponization” of the US government.HouseDemocratic leaders, including minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, party whip Katherine Clark and caucus chair Pete Aguilar, issued a joint statement excoriating the president for the search.“The Trump administration’s raid on congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against [the president’s] adversaries,” their statement said.Ilhan Omar says she will not be silenced after federal agents raid her homeRead more“For years,Donald Trumpand far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations. Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected member of Congress and her family.”The Democratic leaders vowed to “deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power” from the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, the latter of which oversees immigration enforcement.Citing unnamed sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News – which is typically friendly with the Trump administration –reportedthat the search on Omar’s home pertained to a criminal fraud investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Omar’s late father filled out that paperwork when Omar, a Somali-born, naturalized US citizen, was a child.California representative Ro Khanna also condemned Monday’s search,saying: “It is simply chilling that they are targeting political opponents this way, and it is disturbing that they are targeting Muslim Americans and a Muslim American legislator. Any decent American needs to stand up and speak out.”Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Khanna’s fellow Democrat and California representative,calledthe search “fascism in the extreme”.“This is an unadulterated abuse of power,” Kamlager-Dove said. “Trump is weaponizing the federal government to escalate his racist attacks against [representative] Omar, undermine her ahead of themidterms[on 3 November], and distract from his failures as president.”Pramila Jayapal, a Democratic House member from Washington state, similarlycalledthe search of Omar’s home a “disgusting abuse of power from an out of control president” facing widespread public disapproval fromhigh living costsamid the war in Iran that he helped start alongside Israel in February.“To use federal law enforcement resources to raid the home of a sitting Member of Congress weeks before an election is a dangerous sign of an authoritarian president who will stop at nothing to distract you from his deep unpopularity with the American people,” Jayapal added.Jayapal’s statement alluded to years of unsubstantiatedrumorsfrom Trumpand others about Omar and her family, including the accusation that her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother – and that the marriage was part of an effort to earn him immigration status. Omar has denied those rumors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHomeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar on Monday during a search.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APThe Illinois representative Delia C Ramirez called for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to be dismantled. Omar “has not backed down, so now they are using DHS and the federal government to target and persecute her”, Ramirezsaidin a post on X.“This is an absolute abuse of power and unacceptable. We must strip them of their weapons. We must dismantle DHS.”Similarly, Greg Casar, a Democratic representative from Texas,wrotethat the Trump administration is targeting Omar “because he thinks it’ll help his [Republican] party”during the midterms, when it isexpected to lose seatsin Congress.“Ilhan Omar stands up and won’t let Trump do whatever he wants to our country,” Casar said. “It’s up to us to do the same.”The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the US’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, also spoke out against the search of Omar’s home,saying: “We strongly condemn this unconscionable raid on her home for what it is: an obvious act of political persecution.”Criticizing the Trump administration’s handling of files pertaining to Jeffrey Epstein’s child sex-trafficking network as well as the president’spardonsfor those who attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, Cair said the justice department “could clearly [not] care less about fighting crime and is instead focused on conducting a witch hunt”.Explore more on these topicsIlhan OmarDemocratsUS politicsTrump administrationUS CongressDonald TrumpUS immigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises | Nobel economics prize | The Guardian
description: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies
Content: Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford are announced as the winners of the 2026 Nobel economics prize at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.Photograph: Tom Little/ReutersView image in fullscreenRobert E Hall and Michael Woodford are announced as the winners of the 2026 Nobel economics prize at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.Photograph: Tom Little/ReutersNobel economics prizeNobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crisesUS economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economiesBusiness live – latest updatesGraeme WeardenMon 12 Oct 2026 10.20 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo US economists have won the 2026Nobel economics prizefor their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised fordeveloping the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business liveRead more“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time.John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisisRead moreHall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions.Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP).Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now.This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said.Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows.Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”.And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an“unreliable boyfriend”for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWoodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news.The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour.“What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.”Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties.The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism.Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies.The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.Explore more on these topicsNobel economics prizeEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christian Horner: ‘Not all teams act that way. You don’t see the same brutality as when I left’ | Christian Horner | The Guardian
description: The 52-year-old talks to Donald McRae about the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse, questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacks
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: The 52-year-old talks to Donald McRae about the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse, questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacks
Content: Christian Horner says he is still in the dark about his Red Bull departure: ‘I wasn’t really given a reason.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChristian Horner says he is still in the dark about his Red Bull departure: ‘I wasn’t really given a reason.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianChristian HornerInterviewChristian Horner: ‘Not all teams act that way. You don’t see the same brutality as when I left’Donald McRaeThe 52-year-old reflects on the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse, questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacksMon 12 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristian Horner should be in steamy Singapore, preparing for another grand prix victory, but here he is, at home on an autumnal morning in genteel Highgate as his wife, Geri Halliwell-Horner, welcomes me with a cheerful hug. Horner smiles as the former Spice Girl produces an impressive imitation of my South African accent which echoes her old headteacher at Watford Girls.After the most controversial man in the recent history ofFormula Onesays hello, Halliwell-Horner and I discuss the fact that my two daughters also went to her school and that one of their history textbooks had her name printed on the inside page – while the ex-Ginger Spice talks about gritty old Watford, grammar school education and Nelson Mandela.I joke that it feels like I’m interviewing Halliwell-Horner instead of Horner. Everyone laughs but I will soon ask Horner about the impact on his marriage in 2024 when an investigation was carried out intoallegations he had sent “hundreds” of inappropriate texts and photographsto a female employee when Red Bull’s team principal. The woman was apparently“upset, angry, scared, intimidated and lonely”while the tabloids speculated that Halliwell-Horner was “furious”.Horner was exoneratedby two independent investigations but other hurtful circumstances then surrounded his sudden departure from Red Bull in July 2025. The team has struggled since then but, nine days ago, at the Bahrain Grand Prix,Max Verstappen wonRed Bull’s first race with an engine built entirely by the team.Verstappen then won againin Singapore this past Sunday. That feat of engineering had been conceived and instigated by Horner near the end of his remarkable 20 years at Red Bull.View image in fullscreenChristian Horner and Geri Halliwell-Horner after Red Bull won the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2024.Photograph: David Davies/PAWhen Halliwell-Horner disappears after a final hug, Horner is amiable yet careful. However, the 52-year-old admits his distress after he was forced out: “It felt particularly brutal and sad to finish in that manner. But I now have a reasonable relationship with Oliver Mintzlaff [the CEO of corporate projects at Red Bull]. He rang the other day and thanked me for all I’d done for the engine.”His dismissal, Horner reiterates, “was painful. Very painful. I didn’t really process it till a month later because, in the immediate aftermath, I focused on supporting my daughter [Olivia] through a hideous period.”Horner and his former partner, Beverley Allen, became parents to Olivia in 2013. After they separated, he and Allen remained on good terms and so grief, following her death from eye cancer, framed his demise at Red Bull. As he recalls that difficult period, he pays fleeting tribute to his arch-rival, Toto Wolff, the head of Mercedes,who has addressed his battle with depression.“Toto was very brave to talk openly about such a factor for people our age. I hadn’t experienced those issues but I had an appreciation during this period of how people could [suffer]. The identity of many middle-aged guys is through their work. Suddenly you have that stripped and taken from you. Who are you? What are you? What is your purpose? You either curl up into a ball or brush yourself down and get up.”Horner, who arrived in 2005 as the youngest team principal in F1 history, adds: “When I started at Red Bull, there were under 400 people. When I left, there was 2,200. I poured my heart and soul into that business and convinced people to leave other teams for Red Bull. I never had a big turnover in staff because there was tremendous loyalty over a long period. The startup engine business had been founded in 2021 and I was about to get it on the track when I left. I felt great sadness in not seeing that engine in a car.”Hebroke down briefly while telling staff of his fate. “It was very strange because that group became your extended family. So the tears on grown men’s faces was deeply moving.”View image in fullscreenChristian Horner on the grid at the Netherlands Grand Prix in 2023.Photograph: Tim Goode/PAIn his new book, which provides a thorough overview of his career, Horner describes the day he replaced Tony Purnell, his predecessor, in 2005: “Formula One is ruthless, I thought, watching from my car as Tony and Dave Pitchforth, their just-fired managing director, carried glum expressions and cardboard boxes stuffed with personal belongings … when I was eventually shown to my office, it resembled a crime scene. A barely drunk cup of coffee had been abandoned on the desk. Through the walls, I heard Tony’s PA sobbing.”Horner says now: “History repeats itself. Not all teams act in that way. A lot of teams haven’t delivered over the years but you don’t see the same brutality as when I left. We had pole position at the previous race.”Atlast year’s British Grand Prix, just before Horner’s sacking, Verstappen was leading when “the rain came”.Horner also mentions his “relief” at leaving. “The last two years had been pretty tough but it was a particularly sensitive time, with the bereavement of my daughter’s mum the previous week. I had an 11-year-old child grieving her mother. Nothing was more important than that.”There had been a power struggle at Red Bull followingthe death in 2022 of Dietrich Mateschitz, the company’s billionaire founder who always backed Horner. BothHelmut Marko, a key consultant, and Jos Verstappen, Max’s father, seemed keen to undermine Horner. “Helmut could be blunt and I was disappointed he’d stayed as a guest of our family two days before [Horner’s sacking] with no indication this was coming,” Horner reveals.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and Christian Horner in 2024.Photograph: Clive Rose/Getty ImagesWhat about Verstappen Sr? “There’s nothing to say.”Were the Verstappens partly responsible for Horner’s removal? “No, it was a Red Bull decision. After Dietrich died, things changed in the leadership.”Horner says the reasons for his sacking remain opaque, apart from a general discontent that the team no longer matched the domination it had enjoyed in two separate spells when Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen won multiple championships: “I think it was a feeling there was too much control in my hands. But I wasn’t really given a reason.”Did the 2024 allegations contribute to his dismissal? “I’d come through that, dismissed them. So this was more focused on performance and the future.”Was he worried his marriage might be in jeopardy after the texts and photographs were leaked? “My wife was a pillar of support throughout and I just had to believe in the process. I’ve said enough about it in the book and previously.”Yet the book does not outline the allegations against him or provide any details of his defence. “I’ve said everything I can say, and there are certain legal reasons [why] I’m not at liberty to go further.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHorner is more precise when asked if there is a chance he might never work in F1 again. “Absolutely. But if I don’t go back I had a hell of a run. I won one in every four races I competed in. I had 287 podiums out of 405 races.”He says: “Nobody could take away the 124 wins and 14 championships [six constructors’ and eight drivers’ titles]. But I felt particularly hurt and robbed I didn’t have the opportunity to see that [Red Bull-manufactured] Powertrains engine win.”Horner watched Verstappen’s victory the Sunday before last on television and “I felt very proud seeing what it meant to everybody and that they sent the Powertrains representative on to the podium. I had messages throughout the team and I texted Max after the race. He was very magnanimous and it was a landmark moment to see that engine win. It reinforced to me that, if you assemble the right people with the right culture and the necessary tools, anything is possible.”Yet he still believes the team has lost its mojo. “Red Bull has been the maverick team. It’s pushed the boundaries. Only Red Bull would do something crazy enough to build a new engine as a subsidiary of a fizzy drinks manufacturer. Its mantra was to be nonconformist, to be a disruptor. It’s a little different now.”View image in fullscreenLaurent Mekies, Christian Horner’s replacement at Red Bull.Photograph: Hollandse Hoogte/ShutterstockWho is in charge of Red Bull’s team – Laurent Mekies, his successor, or Max Verstappen? He laughs. “I’m not getting drawn into that. Ultimately Oliver Mintzlaff is the most senior guy and obviously Max is a massive asset. I employed Laurent but I can’t judge how he operates.”Horner argues that his comments last month about Ferrari being “a dream job” applied more to other people than himself. He would prefer to return with a team where he has a part-ownership stake. In regard to Ferrari and their currently beleaguered team principal, Horner suggests “Fred Vasseur is an experienced guy. He’s done a decent job. But I, more than anyone, know the pressures of running a competitive organisation.My comments got taken out of context.“Ferrari is the biggest brand in F1. It’s the most historic team. But I’ve accumulated some phenomenal capital behind me, to look at the next move I potentially make in the sport. That would be with ownership attached to it and Ferrari aren’t going to sell shares. So I’m happy to sit outside the sport and see what opportunities present themselves over the coming months or years. It’s not a prerequisite that I go back. I would only return for the right opportunity with like-minded people that want to win. I would never go back just to take part.”Horner says: “For the last 21 years I would have been sitting in Singapore right now. But it’s my daughter’s 13th birthday today and I’m taking her to see Hamilton at the theatre tonight.”What does he miss most about F1? “The people, the team, the competition. I still love the sport but I don’t miss the travel and politics.”Wolff said Horner had “broken too much glass” to return to F1. Horner grins: “He also said this [Red Bull] engine was going to be completely shit and a disaster. Toto’s got it quite easy at the moment. Zak Brown [the head of McLaren] is compromised because he’s using Toto’s engine so he can’t ruffle feathers. All sport needs rivalry, whether it’s Ferguson and Wenger, Mourinho and Guardiola. It percolates and polarises. I used that to galvanise good people to take on Mercedes.”View image in fullscreenChristian Horner on his great rivalry with Mercedes boss Toto Wolff: ‘All sport needs rivalry, whether it’s Ferguson and Wenger, Mourinho and Guardiola. It percolates and polarises.’Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesYet F1 takes its toll and Horner admits he has suffered panic attacks. “I didn’t know what it was. You suddenly feel dizzy and conscious of your breathing and you think there’s something strange going on. I put it down to having had too much coffee on an oppressive, muggy, thundery day. Then it happened again. I got checked out and there was nothing physically the matter. They said: ‘We think you have anxiety. Your breathing’s very shallow.’ It was my body telling me you’re pushing pretty hard here. I’m able to recognise the symptoms now and let it go, and breathe.”What might he be doing 10 years from now? “I’m looking forward to finding out. It could be at a racetrack, it could be sitting on a tractor.”He laughs again before showing his real conviction. “I know my strength is getting a group of people across different skill sets to work as a team. That’s possibly applicable to other things but, at the moment, the only thing that really motivates and excites me is Formula One.”Drive by Christian Horner is published by Bantam on 22 October.Available on pre-order from Guardian Bookshop. He will be sharing stories from the book ontour across the UK from 17-26 October.Explore more on these topicsChristian HornerFormula One 2026Formula OneRed BullMotor sportinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Deshaun Watson revival derailed, much to the joy of those with a functional memory | NFL | The Guardian
description: After three straight game-winning drives, Cleveland’s quarterback was sacked eight times in a dismal defeat that punctured the hype surrounding him
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: After three straight game-winning drives, Cleveland’s quarterback was sacked eight times in a dismal defeat that punctured the hype surrounding him
Content: Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson is sacked by Jets cornerback Jarvis Brownlee Jr during the second half of Sunday’s game in East Rutherford, New Jersey.Photograph: Adam Hunger/APView image in fullscreenBrowns quarterback Deshaun Watson is sacked by Jets cornerback Jarvis Brownlee Jr during the second half of Sunday’s game in East Rutherford, New Jersey.Photograph: Adam Hunger/APNFLThe Deshaun Watson revival derailed, much to the joy of those with a functional memoryAfter three straight game-winning drives, Cleveland’s quarterback was sacked eight times in a dismal defeat that punctured the hype surrounding himDave SchillingMon 12 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIguess the New York Jets didn’t get the memo. This was supposed to be a Deshaun Watson lovefest. A day where, much to the chagrin of those of us witha moral compass and a functional memory, football fans worldwide could declare Watson was “so back” and that the Browns were in some blinkered, alternate universe, a Super Bowl contender. No such luck, as the Browns looked like the Browns – reminding an otherwise jubilant city of Cleveland that they are trapped in the sports equivalent of the Backrooms.Limping along for 155 passing yards and one touchdown, Watson fell to Earth harder than David Bowie in a Nicolas Roeg film (yes, I just watched the Dennis Miller Monday Night Football documentary on HBO). He completed fewer than 50% of his passes and ended the day with a 69.6 passer rating. I should also probably mention he got sacked eight times. Yes, eight times.EIGHT TIMES. He only completed seven more passes than he received punishing hits behind the line of scrimmage. It was a performance NBC NFL writer Patrick Daugherty called “unspeakably bad.” Actually, I think the performance was very much speakable, as I’ve demonstrated here. Stick around for another 400 words.NFL roundup: Daniels’ overtime blunder costs Commanders as Giants salvage wild 27-27 tieRead moreThe thing that has defined Watson’s run as a potentially viableNFLquarterback has been his ability to march down the field and win a game in the dying embers of the contest. After three game-winning drives to start the season, it seemed like the Browns were poised to pull out another improbable victory from deep where the sun don’t shine, but no. Not today.On fourth and 11 – with less than a minute left in the fourth quarter, down by five –Watson dropped back, only for his pocket to evaporate faster than a spilled Dasani in the middle of the Mojave Desert. Ejected violently from the pocket, Watson begins to scramble. On fourth and 11, by the way. He’s unceremoniously tackled near the line of scrimmage, putting the game on ice.Starting off Sunday, these seemed like two teams going in the opposite direction, but the reality on the field was more like the Spider-Man pointing meme. Offensive ineptitude, with both the Jets and Browns recording fewer than 300 yards of total offense, giving away two fumbles, and failing to convert touchdowns twice in the red zone. The New York Post might havecalled this game “tense” and “gritty”, but I’m sure many viewers could think of more apropos adjectives to describe what they witnessed – a game that hinged on a botched snap sailing through the hands of Browns punter Corey Bojorquez. That wayward punt turned into a game-winning touchdown for Jets RB Braelon Allen.This loss, dropping Cleveland to 3-2 on the year, felt like a necessary corrective to the hyperbole andearly extension talksaround Watson’s early successes. American sports fans love a comeback story, but this one is mired inissues that are far more important than football. It certainly makes everyone’s life easier when he plays like this.MVP of the weekCam Little, K, Jacksonville Jaguars. Sure, there’s probably more splashy statistical performances from today. You could make a strong case for Drake Maye, whose 374 yards and four touchdowns gave the Patriots a resounding win over the Raiders. But I’m not going to do that, because we ride for placekickers when I’m around. In a bleak, dystopian ending that felt more like the final five minutes of Digger than a football game, the Eagles went up 17-16 with a mere eight seconds left in the contest. Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni, misplacing his copy of Football for Dummies, decided to have his kicker boot the ball in play rather than ice it with a touchback. A 53-yard return by Ameer Abdullah perfectly set up a gargantuan field goal to win the game for the Jags.View image in fullscreenJaguars kicker Cam Little celebrates after kicking the winning field goal against the Eagles in London on Sunday.Photograph: Ian Walton/AP“I didn’t make the right decision, and I lost us that game, and that’s what I said to our guys,” Siriannitold the mediaafter Christmas came early in London for Jacksonville. Now, a 57-yard field goal with nearly no time left on the clock isn’t exactly a gimme. One could maybe forgive Sirianni for thinking the chances of a field goal from distance to steal the game was unlikely. Except, the Jaguars’ kicker is Little – the man who holds the record for the longest made field goal in NFL history. A recordhe set almost a full year ago. The Eagles gave Little a dagger. He should be commended for knowing how to use it.Video of the weekThe Texans won their first game of the year, demolishing an equally troubled, still-winless Titans team 26-3. CJ Stroud dropped 261 yards, a passing touchdown, and a running touchdown on Tennessee, cementing a bounce-back moment that has the NFL buzzing about just how much money he’ll command on the free-agent market. More importantly, today’s result is coupled with news of Houston getting Stroud reinforcements. WR Marvin Harrison is on the way to the Texans from the Cardinals and Houston coach DeMeco Ryans was more than happy to officially drop the bomb in a brief post-game presser:Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueBrevity really is the soul of wit.Stat of the weekBefore their drubbing by the Patriots, the Raiders had scored at least 26 points in all four of their games this season. Here, they didn’t score more than a touchdown until the fourth quarter, managing a meager 17 points on the road at Gillette Stadium. Las Vegas had a chance to keep pace with the AFC West leading Chiefs during KC’s bye week, but Kirk Cousins was sacked three times and couldn’t convert scoring opportunities into touchdowns. Cousins was replaced by rookie Fernando Mendoza in garbage time, showing how thoroughly the Raiders were handled. They certainly didn’t benefit from giving up 165 rushing yards, spread across multiple New England players (including 25 yards on the ground for Maye). The Pats grabbed 8.1 yards per play, as efficient and deadly as it gets.Elsewhere around the leagueAfter a World Cup in North America, I hope everyone here has gotten used to the concept of a tie. The Giants and Commanders certainly have. In an example of hopeless, foggy-eyed game management, Washington blew a chance to win the game in overtime. A Cam Skattebo turnover handed the Commanders the ball with enough time for Jayden Daniels to march down to the New York 24-yard line. A luxurious 12 seconds remained on the clock. More than enough time to plunk in a field goal to win it. Except, the Commanders wandered around the line of scrimmage for exactly 12 seconds and never did snap the ball, let alone spike it to stop the clock to set up for a kick. Commanders coach Dan Quinn, like Sirianni in the Eagles-Jags game,took the blame for the mistake. For once, I’d like to see a coach just completely throw his players under the bus. “Hey man, I’m not playing. Don’t look at me.” Just for variety.Put the phone down. No need to call the authorities on your friends who are Steelers fans. After a game withvisible tension between Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthyon Thursday Night Football on 1 October, the ship was righted in Steel City, USA. Rodgers looked tidy and comfortable, connecting in the end zone with Pat Freiermuth twice to defeat the Colts 34-22.The Vikings are still undefeated, dropping the Saints to 1-4 on the year. The game was not as close as the 23-13 score, with Minnesota dominating every major team category. New Orleans finished with a paltry 142 total yards. Only 55 of those came on the ground. The Saints only recorded one offensive touchdown, with the other coming on a fumble recovery. The story was far different for the Vikes. Minnesota RB Aaron Jones gobbled up 113 yards and one touchdown in front of moribund Saints fans in the Superdome. Kyler Murray benefitted greatly from Justin Jefferson’s return to action, throwing for 229 yards and a touchdown. Can anyone beat this Vikings team? They’ve got a bye in week six, then the 2-3 Colts, back at US Bank Stadium. That doesn’t seem promising for Indy.View image in fullscreenVikings running back Aaron Jones Sr is congratulated by teammates after scoring a touchdown during Sunday’s 23-13 victory over the Saints in New Orleans.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APThe winless Dolphins almost pulled off a last-second miracle against the Bengals, getting within a touchdown with less than a minute left in the game. But kicker Riley Patterson missed the extra point before an onside kick attempt to recover possession was unsuccessful. Cincinnati took the win 31-24 off a splashy four-touchdown day for Joe Burrow. Can anyone lose to this Dolphins team? They’ve got a bye in week six, then the 2-3 Jets, on the road at MetLife Stadium. That doesn’t seem promising for viewers.The NFL’s oldest rivalry continued, with the Packers tossing the Bears in a meat freezer and locking the door. Green Bay danced away with the win in the teams’ 214th ever matchup (including playoffs), 31-7. Caleb Williams, perhaps the most hated man in Wisconsin after his ruthless comeback win against Green Bay in last year’s playoffs, remained out. In his stead, Tyson Bagent looked worse than anyone could have imagined, 12-of-21 for 87 yards and two interceptions before being benched for Case Keenum. At most, Bears coach Ben Johnson would say that Williams is “on track” to return, but with no definitive date set. NFL reporter Ian Rappaport did suggest that there’s a chance he can play in week six against the Atlanta Falcons. Perhaps the Chicago faithful shouldplace a call to Pope Leo to speed this thing along.As a Rams fan still smarting fromour disastrous Australian drubbing, the last thing I want to talk about is the 49ers looking like the class of the entire NFL. But San Francisco’s trip to Lumen Field to face Seattle might have been the most consequential matchup of week five. The NFC West has three legitimate Super Bowl contenders (and the Cardinals), and two of them faced off here on Sunday. Seattle and San Francisco traded punches all day, but the game came down to rare, crucial mistakes, as matchups between good teams often do.Sam Darnold threw two pivotal interceptions, RB George Holani fumbled right before halftime, leading to a touchdown that put the 49ers up by eight. Seattle exploded for a touchdown and two field goals in the third, tilting the scales back in their direction. But a seven-yard TD pass from Brock Purdy to Brandin Cooks flipped the script yet again. A successful two-point conversion gave the Niners a three-point lead. Seattle kicker Jason Myers tied it up with a little under seven minutes to play, but the Seahawks couldn’t get a stop to force overtime. A 44-yard Eddy Pineiro field goal gave the 49ers a slim advantage. Darnold linked with WR Cooper Kupp, who just nearly converted a fourth-and 10 at the 50, which would have given Seattle one last crack at the ballgame. But a controversial spot of the ball left Kupp short and handed San Francisco their fifth win of 2026. And they did it without ace receiver Deebo Samuel, who left the game in the third quarter with a hamstring injury. Niners fans hold their breath. And I put another pin in the voodoo doll.Explore more on these topicsNFLCleveland BrownsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ronaldo’s Asian Champions League match delayed by missile alert in Riyadh | Asian Champions League | The Guardian
description: The Saudi-led military coalition said it intercepted a missile headed towards Riyadh before Cristiano Ronaldo scored in Al-Nassr’s 3-1 win against Neftchi Fergana
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Saudi-led military coalition said it intercepted a missile headed towards Riyadh before Cristiano Ronaldo scored in Al-Nassr’s 3-1 win against Neftchi Fergana
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo (right) scored Al-Nassr’s second goal in a match that was delayed by an hour.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo (right) scored Al-Nassr’s second goal in a match that was delayed by an hour.Photograph: ReutersAsian Champions LeagueRonaldo’s Asian Champions League match delayed by missile alert in RiyadhKick-off put back by an hour after attack interceptedPortuguese forward scores in Al-Nassr’s 3-1 victoryAFPMon 12 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr had theirAsian Champions Leaguematch delayed by an hour on Monday after the Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh.Saudi Arabia has recently come under a series of attacks from the Iran-backed group, with strikes on oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs – including a string of lethal hits on Riyadh’s international airport.Portugal suspend Cristiano Ronaldo after walking out on national teamRead moreThere was a sparse crowd in the stands of AlawwalPark for the game against Uzbekistan’sNeftchi Fergana, which was scheduled for kick-off at 9.15pm local time.The stadium announcer said the situation was safe, that the match would be played, and asked spectators to remain in their seats. However, the television channel broadcasting the match announced a one-hour delay.Shortly before the sound of explosions was reported in Riyadh. At the same time, Riyadh residents received an alert on their phones stating: “The region is exposed to a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm and stay at home or in a safe place, away from windows and doors, and continue to follow civil defence instructions.”Subsequently the coalition announced the “interception and destruction” of a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis in a statement on X.This incident did not seem to affect Ronaldo, who scored the 981st goal of his career just before half-time, as the Saudi Arabian champions secured a 3-1 win.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 41-year-old wasprovisionally suspended by Portugalon Saturday after walking out on the national team during the international break.Explore more on these topicsAsian Champions LeagueCristiano RonaldoAl-NassrSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: 49ers’ Dre Greenlaw suspended after headbutt leaves opponent bleeding | San Francisco 49ers | The Guardian
description: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw was suspended for one game after headbutting Seattle’s Ernest Jones IV
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw was suspended for one game after headbutting Seattle’s Ernest Jones IV
Content: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw (57) leaves the field after being ejected on Sunday.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APView image in fullscreenSan Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw (57) leaves the field after being ejected on Sunday.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APSan Francisco 49ers49ers’ Dre Greenlaw suspended after headbutt leaves opponent bleedingErnest Jones IV was not wearing helmet during incidentLinebacker will miss game against CommandersAssociated PressMon 12 Oct 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSan Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw was suspended for one game afterheadbutting Seattle’s Ernest Jones IVin the wake of a late hit on the Seahawks sideline.TheNFLissued the suspension on Monday, saying the headbutt of a player without a helmet during Sunday’s 32-29 win against Seattle was “contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship.”Greenlaw will miss San Francisco’s game next Monday night against Washington, although he can appeal his punishment.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueSunday’s incident came when Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold scrambled and was hit late by Greenlaw after going out of bounds, leading to a personal foul in a game San Francisco went on to win 32-29.Several Seahawks defenders immediately confronted Greenlaw after the hit and the linebacker responded by headbutting Jones. Jones was bleeding after the hit and Greenlaw was ejected.“You’re going to get baited big time when, especially when you’re on their bench,” coach Kyle Shanahan said after the game. “They told me that he had butted a guy without a helmet. So if that’s exactly what happened, then yeah, we got to be a lot smarter than that. Can’t do that.”Greenlaw has a history of infractions, and has been ejected two other times in his career. He had a sideline altercation with Philadelphia’s head of security Dom DiSandro in 2023 and was also disqualified for a helmet-to-helmet hit on the Chargers’ Justin Herbert in 2022.Greenlaw was also suspended for one game last season when he played in Denver for berating an official after a win over the New York Giants.Greenlaw returned to San Francisco this season after playing for the Broncos in 2025. He has 37 tackles in five games.Explore more on these topicsSan Francisco 49ersNFLSeattle SeahawksUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Atlanta Dream scrambling to find WNBA finals venue amid scheduling conflicts | Atlanta Dream | The Guardian
description: The Dream are searching for a larger venue to host the WNBA finals after concerts and NBA games ruled out State Farm Arena in Atlanta
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Dream are searching for a larger venue to host the WNBA finals after concerts and NBA games ruled out State Farm Arena in Atlanta
Content: The Atlanta Dream’s Angel Reese and Rhyne Howard celebrate after defeating the New York Liberty in Game 3 of their WNBA semi-final series on Friday in Brooklyn.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APView image in fullscreenThe Atlanta Dream’s Angel Reese and Rhyne Howard celebrate after defeating the New York Liberty in Game 3 of their WNBA semi-final series on Friday in Brooklyn.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APAtlanta DreamAtlanta Dream scrambling to find WNBA finals venue amid scheduling conflictsState Farm Arena booked for all three home datesDream’s regular arena holds just 3,500 spectatorsAtlanta face Golden State in first finals since 2013Guardian sportSun 11 Oct 2026 23.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 00.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Atlanta Dream are still searching for a venue to host their WNBA finals games against theGolden State Valkyriesafter scheduling conflicts ruled out State Farm Arena in downtown Atlanta.The Dream are scheduled to host Games 3 and 4 of the best-of-seven series on 22 and 24 October, along with Game 6 on 29 October if necessary. But State Farm Arena, the 17,044-seat home of the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks, is unavailable on all three dates.‘I’m supposed to be here’: Angel Reese’s road from ridicule to the WNBA finalsRead moreThe arena is hosting a concert by singer Sombr on 22 October and Hawks regular-season games on 24 and 29 October.Atlanta’s regular home venue, Gateway Center Arena in College Park, Georgia, holds just 3,500 spectators for basketball. The Dream have been exploring larger alternatives, including the 13,000-seat Gas South Arena in Duluth and Georgia Tech’s 8,600-seat McCamish Pavilion, but have yet to secure an agreement, USA Today reported.Dream president and chief operating officer Morgan Shaw Parker said last week that the team were “finalizing details on their home venue and where we will be playing”. The team and theWNBAhad not announced a decision as of Sunday night.Atlanta played six of their 22 regular-season home games at State Farm Arena this season and hosted all three of their previous home playoff games there, averaging 9,695 fans.Quick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series.
