All times Eastern.Sat 17 OctGame 1: Atlanta at Golden State, 3.30pm (NBC)Mon 19 OctGame 2: Atlanta at Golden State, 3.30pm (USA)Thu 22 OctGame 3: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm (USA)Sat 24 OctGame 4: Golden State at Atlanta, 3.30pm (NBC)Mon 26 OctGame 5: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA)*Thu 29 OctGame 6: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm (USA)*Sat 31 OctGame 7: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA)**-if necessaryWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Dreamannounced last weekthat they will move to State Farm Arena full-time beginning in 2027 under a multi-year agreement. The move coincides with the WNBA’s expansion to a 50-game regular season, giving Atlanta 25 home dates.Golden State, meanwhile, will host Games 1 and 2, along with Games 5 and 7 if necessary, at the 18,064-seat Chase Center in San Francisco. The Valkyries have sold out every home game this season, becoming the first women’s professional sports teamto exceed $100m in annual revenue.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe WNBA has previously staged finals games at alternate venues because of scheduling conflicts. Atlanta hosted a game during the 2013 finals at what is now Gas South Arena, while the Washington Mystics played three games of the 2019 finals at their 4,200-seat home arena.The Dream are making their first finals appearance since 2013 aftersweeping the Mysticsin the first round andthe 2024 champion New York Libertyin the semi-finals.Atlanta have reached the finals three times previously, in 2010, 2011 and 2013, but have never won a game in the championship series.Explore more on these topicsAtlanta DreamWNBAGolden State ValkyriesBasketballAngel ReeseShareReuse this content

title: Coventry land long-awaited home win as Mfuni seals rout of Newcastle | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Jack Rudoni, Sidiki Cherif, Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni scored as Coventry beat Newcastle 4-1, their first home top-flight victory since 2001
Author: Peter Lansley
Headline: Jack Rudoni, Sidiki Cherif, Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni scored as Coventry beat Newcastle 4-1, their first home top-flight victory since 2001
Content: Stephen Mfuni reacts after scoring Coventry’s fourth goal against Newcastle.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenStephen Mfuni reacts after scoring Coventry’s fourth goal against Newcastle.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAPremier LeagueCoventry land long-awaited home win as Mfuni seals rout of NewcastlePeter Lansleyat the Coventry Building Society ArenaMon 12 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf ever validation is needed for attack being the best form of defence, Frank Lampard can call this game up on Wyscout. Coventry climbed out of the relegation zone to the heady heights of 14th place after their second successive win showcased the benefits of their manager’s willingness to balance risk with reward.Jack Rudoni’s early penalty underscored a sense of positivity that was enhanced by an even quicker goal at the start of the second half from Sidiki Cherif and not unduly dimmed by Sven Botman’s howitzer making it 2-1.Coventry City 4-1 Newcastle United: Premier League – liveRead moreLate goals from the substitutes Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni allowed promoted Coventry to pull away from a Newcastle side who, after a strong start to the season, also lost their last away game atLeeds by this scoreline.Newcastle could have gone fourth in thePremier Leaguewith victory but despite missing several chances they could not argue with the defeat. As their manager, Matthias Jaissle, said: “There were elements in both boxes where we need to step up and do better. Those fine margins can make all the difference.”Even when Botman had reduced the deficit with 20 minutes remaining and Newcastle threatened to take charge, Coventry left two or three players up on the halfway line. It could be perceived as a bold and brave move and Lampard, who wants supporters to be entertained throughout this first season back in the elite since 2000/01, deserves credit. On other days they might come unstuck but here it was a case of he who dares wins.Not that he was ready to take the plaudits. “It probably means I didn’t manage to scream well enough to tell one or two of them to get back,” the Coventry manager said. “But at times we do certainly leave one or two players up the pitch because I think it will occupy their defenders. And in this [kind of] game of transition, sometimes you can defend with eight players.”View image in fullscreenFrank Lampard is delighted by Coventry’s win.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersIt was 25 years since John Hartson had last scored a home Premier League goal for Coventry. So there was a momentous feel to the occasion when Rudoni stepped up to take his penalty in the sixth minute.After three weeks of international football had left Sky Blues fans longing for more following theirvictory at Nottingham Forest, the atmosphere went up another notch when Lukas Hornicek, hesitant when coming out to palm the ball away from Ephron Mason-Clark, brought Cherif down as they contested the loose ball.Coventry, for all their summer signings, feel very united after 18 successful months under Lampard, culminating in their Championship triumph. This sense of community was underlined as Rudoni lifted his shirt to show the message “Get well soon Nan” after scoring his penalty.Rudoni’s grandmother is in hospital after suffering a heart attack. “He’s such a great lad,” Lampard said. “I’ve been there for him. He’s so close with his family. So I’m pleased he could have that moment for them.”Newcastle had plenty of space and ball just about every time they attacked. But the risk-and-reward strategy meant Coventry were dangerous in the extreme on the transition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey had Bobby Thomas to thank for denying Newcastle twice shortly before the interval. Firstly the centre-back headed off the line after Jacob Murphy turned Harvey Barnes’s superb cross past Carl Rushworth.Then when Matias Fernandez-Pardo raced clear, rounded Rushworth and shot goalwards, Thomas had recovered sufficiently to clear. On his first Premier League start since signing from Fenerbahce for £21m in the summer, Cherif deputised for the suspended Taiwo Awoniyi.The 19-year-old forward is evidently not the finished product but he has raw attributes from which Coventry can build. When Malick Thiaw headed out a long throw-in, Cherif swivelled to strike a crisp drive that swished through four pairs of plum-coloured stockings and beyond Hornicek’s grasping fingers.View image in fullscreenSidiki Cherif doubles Coventry’s lead with a rocket.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersThen Cherif should have made the game safe. Botman miscued Brandon Thomas-Asante’s cross but unmarked from six yards out Cherif clunked his shot wide. That miss briefly appeared crucial as Botman was allowed to wander forwards unchallenged before belting a shot into the top corner of Rushworth’s goal.Simms made it 3-1 in the 81st minute, however, after the excellent Thomas-Asante nicked the ball on the edge of the area for the striker to shoot home. There was still time for Thomas-Asante to fire against a post before victory was emphatically sealed when Mfuni twinkle-toed his way into the penalty area to strike in left-footed.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueCoventry CityNewcastle Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Manchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the moment
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Manchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the moment
Content: Erling Haaland and Matheus Nunes, Florian Wirtz and Noni Madueke.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenErling Haaland and Matheus Nunes, Florian Wirtz and Noni Madueke.Composite: Getty ImagesTen talking points from the weekend footballPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionManchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the momentGuardian sportMon 12 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1City’s triumph leaves pressing questionsThe manner ofManchester City’s victory at Liverpoolwas an article of both vindication and vilification. Those gleefullywielding inflatable bananasin the Anfield away end could thumb their noses. Why not enjoy the dances of defiance until the music stops? The same went for City players, asked to perform under the darkest of clouds, able to focus, at last, on football, rather than legal argument and uncertain futures. Beyond City, the sight of a club found guilty of 100-plus charges laying waste to such rivals as Liverpoolwas deeply uncomfortable. The Premier League season and product are badly damaged until the matter is somehow resolved. What happened at Anfield should double the haste for a resolution. Chants of “cheat” whenever City players, the game already won, slipped the ball around, are bound to be repeated at other stadiums. Enzo Maresca has described his club’s plight as “noise” but his team’s victory did absolutely nothing to turn the volume down.John BrewinMatch report:Liverpool 0-3 Manchester CityView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca soaks up the acclaim of the travelling fans at the end of the match.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images2Iraola’s revolution yet to take offAndoni Iraola’s Liverpool reboot will require patience. They showed plenty of drive and determinationagainst Manchester City but also uneven edges, polish lacking. Iraola’s aim was to get his players in their opponents’ faces, deepening any doubts circulating in City’s players. Mission mostly accomplished during the first half. A flurry of chances at the beginning of the second half had City rocking only for Ryan Gravenberch’s dismissal to pull the rug. With Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo missing, Liverpool lacked the quality to cause the necessary damage. Lewis Koumas played well in the role of agitator as emergency centre-forward. Víctor Muñoz continues to be full of buzz but Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz, both players signed for £100m plus, are supposed to supply the cutting edge. Barcola has the mitigation of being a new arrival, while discussions about Wirtz border on football cliche. Once Gravenberch departed, and Trey Nyoni was required in midfield, the finger was always going to be pointed in the German’s direction.JB3Sage rides luck to get one over on GlasnerFor the second time this season, Pierre Sage watched his Crystal Palace side win a Premier League game despite not being at their best; the Frenchman was honest enough to admit they had been slightly fortunate againstNottingham Forest. But after overcoming Oliver Glasner on his return to Selhurst Park, Sage can look forward to a reunion of his own against Lyon in the Europa League on Thursday. He will know Palace must improve defensively. Axel Disasi will be available again after being suspended against Forest, although he will miss the trip to face Palace’s arch-rivals Brighton next weekend. “It’s not normal to concede as many chances as we conceded,” Sage said of the first 40 minutes against Forest, when Walter Benítez made a string of fine saves. “We need to be consistent but after the international break it’s a good result that can help us in our future games.”Ed AaronsMatch report:Crystal Palace 3-1 Nottingham Forest4Maitland-Niles makes a messAinsley Maitland-Niles has some apologising to do. The right-back made two errors that ultimately costEvertona first away victory in the league since February. The former Arsenal player contrived to botch what should have been an easy interception, gifting Sorba Thomas the chance to tee up Joe Gelhardt for Hull’s opener. With the visitors having turned the game around to lead, Maitland-Niles then got too cute defending against Elliot Stroud in the corner, allowing the Swede to find Mohamed Belloumi for the equaliser. With a squad short on attacking options, Everton cannot afford to score twice away from home and come away with only a point.Tom BassamMatch report:Hull City 2-2 EvertonView image in fullscreenAinsley Maitland-Niles (centre) did not have the best game for Everton.Photograph: Tony McArdle/Everton FC/Getty Images5Spurs’ slow progress is still progressWith Manchester United so sluggish and shapeless, they did not serve as much of a barometer of Tottenham’s progress under Roberto De Zerbi. Though if anyone can take positives fromSaturday’s clutter of a contest full of mistakes, it should be Spurs. “From a long time Tottenham played without this blood, this character, and I want it,” said De Zerbi. He has plenty to improve upon. Dominic Solanke wore the captain’s armband and got the late equaliser his team’s efforts with 10 men had threatened. If only Spurs’ finishing had not been so profligate in a first half when their energy made United fans mothballtheir jibes at Manchester Cityand resume worrying about the failings of Michael Carrick’s team. “Work together, stay together, have dinner together and get to know each other better,” is De Zerbi’s prescription for improvement. He continues to talk of a work in progress. Slow progress, slower than desirable, but Old Trafford offered hope.JBMatch report:Manchester United 1-1 Tottenham6Madueke shines as Arteta rolls diceA key topic of discussion for Arsenal fans before the Leeds match was who Mikel Arteta would pick on the left in the absence of the injured Christos Tzolis. Noni Madueke got the nod and the England winger, who was dropped from the latest Three Lions squad,proved a point. “He deserved the chance and he took it,” Arteta said of the wide man, who played out of position but whose pace was too explosive for Leeds’ James Justin and Jayden Bogle. Madueke’s deliveries were also consistently dangerous. He created the most chances in the game (three) and had the most touches in the box (eight). This was good news for a player who had looked to be receding from view at both club and international level. But it also cast a dim light on the range of attacking options available to Arteta after a summer in which Tzolis was the only addition to the forward line. Arsenal took a gamble on Madueke here and it worked out. How many more will they have to take over a long and arduous season?Paul MacInnesskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatch report:Arsenal 2-1 Leeds UnitedView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta ponders his attacking options, or possibly something else.Photograph: Vince Mignott/EPA7Swift starts prove a boon for BluesChelsea have scored during the first 10 minutes in five of their six games this season. Xabi Alonso says the fast starts are nothing to do with him but Morgan Rogers had a different view afterthe 5-1 win against Bournemouth. “I put it down to the manager’s team talks,” Rogers said. “He gets us firing, gets us going. We always want to start off on the front foot. It’s about starting well and getting the lead. A lot of games, especially at home, we have won after jumping on the back of early goals – it’s a good trait to have. We need to keep going.”Jacob SteinbergMatch report:Chelsea 5-1 Bournemouth8Aston Villa’s ground for concern?Home form has been a cornerstone of Unai Emery’s extraordinary success but a victory at Villa Park this seasonis proving elusive. It’s early days, of course, with Wednesday’s Champions League date at home to Fenerbahce offering another chance to get off the mark – but Emery recognises the value of a fortress. The stadium is different on the eye this season, the North Stand being rebuilt to take the ground’s capacity north of 50,000. Can a three-sided ground impact things? “I certainly hated it as a player,” said Brentford’s head coach, Keith Andrews, whose side remain unbeaten this campaign. “It just feels wrong, doesn’t it? When I was growing up as a kid, some Irish legends played here – Ray Houghton, Paul McGrath, Andy Townsend – so it’s always been a special place for me and you can feel the history of it. With a stand missing, it’s a bit different.”Ben FisherMatch report:Aston Villa 2-2 BrentfordView image in fullscreenKristoffer Ajer (third right) secures a point for Brentford late on at Villa Park.Photograph: Nick Potts/PA9Steely Tractor Boys show mettleSix games in Ipswich are well ahead of the run rate on points required for survival. Gary O’Neil, the modernPremier Leaguefirefighter, has brought a doggedness to the Tractor Boys that they lacked when Kieran McKenna took them into the Premier League two years ago. The new Ipswich manager has been ruthless too. The summer signing Kjell Scherpen was dropped for a known quantity in Christian Walton after the win at Palace and, while it did not secure a first clean sheet of the league campaign, the veteran keeper does look a more assured presence. The goals against column will concern O’Neil – only two sides in the division have conceded more – but his side’s stamina will be pleasing. Ipswich have now have scored winners after the 90-minute mark three times. It is not a sustainable strategy but it indicates a team with the stomach for a fight.TBMatch report:Ipswich Town 2-1 Fulham10Hamstrung Black Cats lacking threatSunderland’s supposed summer transfer market priority was the acquisition of a specialist right winger. Ultimately they failed to recruit one and it is arguably costing Régis Le Bris’s team dear. They started Saturday’sdeserved home defeatto an impressive Brighton with two natural right-backs on the pitch, the second, Thomas Meunier, operating in an advanced position. When Meunier, a far from shabby player, injured a hamstring, the industrious yet ineffective Nilson Angulo was shifted from his preferred left wing to the right. But a Sunderland XI lacking the hamstrung Brian Brobbey at centre-forward failed to threaten. Surely the moment has come for Le Bris to offer the talented but currently overlooked Chris Rigg or Chemsdine Talbi starting spots at Bournemouth next Sunday? Before that Sunderland travel to face Torreense in Portugal on Thursday. After collecting only four Premier League points this season, Le Bris is likely to rotate heavily for that Europa League engagement. With a Bournemouth trip followed swiftly by a game at Lech Poznan and a visit from Leeds, his task looks tricky.Louise TaylorMatch report:Sunderland 0-2 BrightonPosTeamPGDPts1Man City611182Arsenal65153Brighton613134Brentford66105Everton63106Chelsea62107Leeds6398Hull6299Liverpool60910Ipswich6-3911Newcastle50812Crystal Palace6-3713Man Utd60614Nottm Forest6-3515Aston Villa6-5516Sunderland6-6417AFC Bournemouth6-6318Tottenham Hotspur6-6319Coventry5-9320Fulham6-42Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen talking points from the weekend footballAston VillaBrentfordArsenalLeeds UnitedLiverpoolManchester CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Winning is not enough for Manchester City to move on from this crisis | Premier League | The Guardian
description: It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too
Content: Man City’s win over Liverpool came amid off-field problems.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMan City’s win over Liverpool came amid off-field problems.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonPremier LeagueWinning is not enough for Manchester City to move on from this crisisIt’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them tooSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 12 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe language of football is a fine and highly nuanced dialect. The majority of people involved in the game speak it with a high degree of sophistication. Minor deviations from the familiar, almost imperceptible to outsiders, can set off alarm bells: what’s really going on there? Why isn’t he happy? What’s she hinting at? But it’s an argot developed to talk about football, and when applied to other subjects, it can sound extremely jarring.Erling Haaland is one of the brighter, more engaging players. There’s an appealing quirkiness to him that suggests he has a higher-than-usual level of self-awareness. He doesn’t mind stepping outside the norms, being a bit different. But consider his assessment ofManchester City’s 3-0 winat Liverpool on Sunday.“It was tough,” he said. “It was hard but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone. [It’s] important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about, and the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That’s the only thing we can do.”Strip away the context and he could be talking about an injury crisis, or perhaps the resignation of a manager or a suspension to a key player. The tropes are familiar: it was hard but we stuck together and so we prevailed. “You want to win games, it’s as simple as that,” he went on. “Perform well, play good football and win games. This was a mental battle, [it’s] never easy coming back from internationals.”But of course this wasn’t really about coming back from internationals; that’s not what made this difficult for City. This was about the verdict of the independent panel looking into the charges brought against City, the fact that the club have been found guilty of thegreatest act of sustained cheatingin the history of English football. Nobody knows what’s coming next.The gravity of the situation still seems to have not dawned on many in football. City, as is their right, continue to maintain their innocence and have appealed. The propaganda battle goes on. But this is no longer about whether the financial regulations were fair. If City had objected to the regulations they had every opportunity to raise objections and vote against them. They did not. They agreed to the regulations, and while everybody else played to them, they did not.The excuse that they only spent what others did but that they operated under stricter controls because of a lack of historic success is not merely irrelevant but entirely bogus: in the nine years under investigation, City’s net spending on transfers, before taking into account wages, was over £1.2bn ($1.6bn), around 50% more than any otherPremier Leagueside. And for all their talk of being proud disruptors, of rebels taking on the “red cartel”, that spending transformed City into the most dominant side English football has ever known, with six league titles in seven years. They are, precisely, an argument for why spending controls are necessary.None of that, of course, is Haaland’s fault. He is a footballer offered a very competitive salary to play alongside very good players for a very good manager for a club for which his father played. This is another of football’s absurdities: it’s always the manager and players who end up becoming the faces of the institution, being quizzed about things that have very little to do with them as the executives and directors responsible lurk away from public scrutiny.“My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear,” Enzo Maresca said. “Guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy.”Which on the one hand is absurd: nobody knows whether the three points City claimed at Anfield will still be theirs by Christmas. Nobody knows what division they will be playing in next season. Nobody knows how bad the sanction could be. And this is not some unfortunate event that has befallen City; this is the direct consequence of the actions of their directors. But on the other, what else can players and managers do? How else can they respond to this situation other than by being professional and trying to win games, even if none of it ultimately means anything?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat this is emphatically not, though, is just another football crisis from which City can move on by winning football matches. This is a crisis unlike anything English football has ever known, and it is one with which football’s language is struggling to cope.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester CityLiverpoolUS sportsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Carrick promises Manchester United will ‘come out fighting’ after sticky start | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick admitted Manchester United must ‘accept reality’ of worst league start in 40 years but remained upbeat before Atlético Madrid test
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Michael Carrick admitted Manchester United must ‘accept reality’ of worst league start in 40 years but remained upbeat before Atlético Madrid test
Content: Michael Carrick takes training on Monday before Manchester United flew to Madrid.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick takes training on Monday before Manchester United flew to Madrid.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester UnitedCarrick promises Manchester United will ‘come out fighting’ after sticky startUnited have endured worst league start since 1986-87Trip to Atlético in Champions League awaits on TuesdaySid Lowein MadridMon 12 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have endured their worst league start in 40 years but Michael Carrick insists he is “loving it”. United arrived in Madrid without Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw, who both picked up knocks inthe draw against Tottenhamat the weekend, and with the coach admitting that his team are in “a spot”, but he vowed that they would “come out fighting”.Despite collecting just six points in the Premier League so far, Carrick claimed he did not feel under pressure and backed his captain, Bruno Fernandes, who he revealed was still “carrying something”, to rediscover his form. As he talked about building, there was a reminder too of the fact that Arsenal, the champions, finished “seventh or eighth” in Mikel Arteta’s first two seasons.Grounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the openRead more“To do something good, to do something great, you have got to be able to do something difficult,” said Carrick, whose side take on Atlético Madrid at the Metropolitano Stadium in the second round of games in theChampions Leagueleague phase on Tuesday.“We hoped for a lot more, we expected a lot more, and we are where we are,” Carrick added. “I was aware that, winning as many as we had [last season], it was going to get more challenging, stickier. I understand that when it is not going well there is a real clamour and a feeling that it’s a disaster, that it’s all wrong and that everything needs to be changed. I kind of get that, but that’s not our mindset and it’s certainly not mine. You have to deal with things and overcome them. That is what I did throughout my career. We have to accept reality but we are building and you can’t lose sight of the journey.”On the pressure he is under, Carrick said: “It depends on how you define ‘pressure’. There is our own expectation: we know what we want, what we are capable of and that comes from us. I don’t look outside. I don’t feel the pressure from that at all.“I’m pretty good at shutting off, to be honest; closing off and living a little bit in my bubble. And I think that’s what we do as a group. We look after each other, we all know what’s out there and it’s about managing it, controlling it and staying focused on what we can do. It is about us wanting to succeed, to win. That’s the drive. There is no negativity. It’s also fine lines sometimes. We are hugely confident and we have confidence in each other. I have the utmost confidence in the boys that we can win a lot of games.“[That’s] because I know them, I know how much they care, I know how strong the group is. And, anyway, you’ve got no choice: that’s why we’re here. We’re here to test ourselves and that’s the opportunity that’s in front of us. If you haven’t got that little bit in you where maybe it’s a little bit crazy times but you actually love the challenge and really want to dig deep to find the answers, then this is not the place for you.”View image in fullscreenMichael Carrick backed Bruno Fernandes to rediscover his form from last season.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPADespite the poor domestic start, which also included exiting the Carabao Cupagainst Brightonat Old Trafford, Carrick’s side did win their Champions League openerconvincingly against Sabahlast month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We need to do something about it now and accept the reality,” Carrick said. “I love this part of it: sometimes when it’s not quite going for you, you see who’s really there. You see within the group, the squad, the club, who’s really there and who wants to be there for the long term, [who] is really attached to it and [for whom it] really means something. The supporters are there: they know what they want, they’re desperate for it, and we’ve got to give them something. You have to embrace the challenge. I totally believe that we’ll work through it.”Asked if he believed that Fernandes could recover his form, Carrick said: “I think it’s pretty obvious to say that he can, yeah. I mean, he’s a top player, Bruno. Sometimes things don’t quite go for you, but he’s done some incredible things for this football club and he will do the same in the future, there’s no doubt about that. I’ve seen that a lot was made of [his fitness]. He was carrying something.“People don’t maybe realise it, but it happens a lot: players play with issues. I probably played 80% of the games with some sort of issue. It’s not ideal, but it’s manageable. Bruno was able to play the games; that’s the commitment he that he has. He’s pretty much over it. It’s not a major deal, he’s in good shape and he was really bright [in training] this morning, looking forward to the game.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickAtlético MadridChampions LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hincapié and Zubimendi out after warm-down injuries but Arsenal get Saliba boost | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi sustained ankle injuries owing to ‘two very unfortunate actions’ in Arsenal’s warm-down after beating Leeds but, in better news, William Saliba has resumed training on his own
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi sustained ankle injuries owing to ‘two very unfortunate actions’ in Arsenal’s warm-down after beating Leeds but, in better news, William Saliba has resumed training on his own
Content: Martín Zubimendi, Bruno Guimarães and Piero Hincapié watch from the sidelines during Arsenal’s 2-1 victory over Leeds.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenMartín Zubimendi, Bruno Guimarães and Piero Hincapié watch from the sidelines during Arsenal’s 2-1 victory over Leeds.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersArsenalHincapié and Zubimendi out after warm-down injuries but Arsenal get Saliba boostDefender and midfielder hurt after win against LeedsSaliba resumes training on his own after back injuryEd AaronsMon 12 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has admitted frustration after Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi sustained ankle injuries during the warm-down afterArsenal’s win against Leeds on Saturday.Both are due to have scans on Monday to determine the extent of the damage, although Arteta said they would miss the Champions League game at home to Lille on Tuesday and that Hincapié’s injury “looks a little bit more serious”.Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionRead more“We had a training session planned after the game for the players,” the manager said. “They didn’t have enough minutes to get everybody in the right rhythm and in two very unfortunate actions, we lost two players.”Arteta described it as “far from ideal” but dismissed suggestions he would change the post-match routine. “When they have to play, they have no rhythm, and when you ask them to play, they’re going to have no impact in the game,” he said. “That could happen at the Emirates; it never happened in the seven years I was here. It could happen the next day in the training session, and that has happened before, and hopefully it happens now and doesn’t happen again. What can you do? If I knew I had a crystal ball clear, I’d say: ‘Guys, go in the Jacuzzi, everybody, I’ll see you tomorrow.’”Hincapié and Zubimendi were expected to feature against Lille having not started in the Premier League this season. Arteta seemed disappointed with Illan Meslier and his staff after the reserve goalkeeper gave Hincapié a piggyback off the pitch rather than waiting for a stretcher.“That’s something else not to discuss here,” he said. “Today they’re going to have a further scan and probably tomorrow we’ll know more and then we’ll see how they’re going to go. Piero’s one looks a little bit more serious, I think, but we’ll have to wait and see.”There was better news for Arsenal as William Saliba has resumed training on his own as he recovers froma back injury sustained at the World Cup. Arteta would not be drawn on when the France defender could be back and is determined not to rush his recovery. “We’re still talking about weeks,” he said.Gabriel Magalhães is likely to be partnered by Ezri Konsa again against the Brazil defender’s former club on Tuesday. Gabriel insisted he would not hesitate to take another penalty in a shootout despite missing the crucial spot-kickin the Champions League final against Paris Saint-Germain. “I was sad, and I didn’t want to miss a penalty, but I have learned from this and if I have another opportunity, I will be ready to take it,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArteta has challenged Bukayo Saka to score more goals after the forward found the net five times in his past four England appearances and revealed that they had been working on rotating him into more central areas to finish moves.“He has been getting in great positions, getting shots, getting one-touch finishes and tap-ins,” he said. “That is the kind of unpredictability we have with that player, otherwise we know how the opponent is going to defend him. He is doing well. He could have had another four or five goals by now, easily. But if he continues like that, we know. When he talks about scoring a certain amount of goals, he … He needs to be thinking about scoring a certain amount of goals per game. If that shifts, that mentality, he will get into those positions and score more goals.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Football regulator to recommend cost controls in landmark report with 94% of clubs making loss | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Independent Football Regulator is to recommend clubs introduce greater cost controls in Tuesday’s long-awaited State of the Game report
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Independent Football Regulator is to recommend clubs introduce greater cost controls in Tuesday’s long-awaited State of the Game report
Content: Chelsea made a Premier League-record pre-tax loss of £262.4m for the year ending 30 June 2025.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenChelsea made a Premier League-record pre-tax loss of £262.4m for the year ending 30 June 2025.Photograph: Adam Davy/PASoccerFootball regulator to recommend cost controls in landmark report with 94% of clubs making lossReport published on Tuesday before consultation periodIt will have recommendations to improve sustainabilityExclusive byMatt HughesMon 12 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Independent Football Regulator (IFR) is to recommend clubs introduce greater cost controls in its long-awaited State of the Game report, to be published on Tuesday.The 250-page draft report, with a final version to follow in the spring after an eight-week public consultation beginning this week, will paint a damning picture of the financial state of English men’s football, including the stark finding that 94% of the top 116 clubs are loss-making.European FAs pushing for three-week international break to be abandonedRead moreThe report will include a series of recommendations for the regulator and clubs to improve sustainability, with theIFR chair, David Kogan, and chief executive, Richard Monks, to provide more details at a press ­conference in Manchester on Tuesday.That event is likely to be dominated by questions about whether the regulator could force the sale of Manchester City if the mass guilty verdicts of an independent commission are upheld on appeal.As administrators of an enhanced owners, directors and senior executives test the IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners and executives “where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals”.The State of the Game report sprung out of the Football Governance Act, which created the IFR, which has taken almost 18 months to produce the most detailed study ever of the football industry and its finances.EFL clubs have been waiting for the report in the hope that it will give them greater impetus as they continue to negotiate with the Premier League over a new financial ­settlement, although it may not ­necessarily do so given details that may emerge of extravagant and unsustainable spending by many lower-division clubs.The Premier League hasoffered a new dealto the EFL worth £180m a year over 10 years, a significant increase from the current £150m figure, but the EFL wants £207m a year and the option to renegotiate after five years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe EFL has also proposed the creation of a new so-called “lifeboat fund” for clubs in financial distress.The IFR has powers to impose a settlement on the leagues if they cannot agree themselves. Both sides are likely to seize on elements of the report to bolster their arguments.Explore more on these topicsFootballFinancesFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Grounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the open | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Long-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignore
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Long-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignore
Content: Fans of Rayo Vallecano throw paper planes in protest against their club’s chair, Raúl Martín Presa, during the match against Athletic Club, which was eventually abandoned.Photograph: Ángel Pérez Meca/AFP7/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFans of Rayo Vallecano throw paper planes in protest against their club’s chair, Raúl Martín Presa, during the match against Athletic Club, which was eventually abandoned.Photograph: Ángel Pérez Meca/AFP7/ShutterstockLa LigaGrounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the openLong-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignoreSid LoweMon 12 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt took 147 days for Rayo Vallecano to walk out for a competitive game on the Avenida de Albufera and 24 minutes and 56 seconds for them to walk off again. Half of those had been spent watching thousands of paper planes touch down on the turf, play suspended while a message was delivered, over and over, until it was impossible to avoid. Forced from their home, the team from thebarriohad been away for five months. On the bright Saturday afternoon that they came back, there were just 13 minutes of football, a fans’ protest instead forcing the abandonment of their match with Athletic Club, thelatest episode in a never-ending story.The last time there had been a league game here was a victory over Villarreal in May. A lot has happened since: little Rayo,RayoVallecano, hadplayed a European final, 11,000 fans heading to Leipzig where, as the banner perfectly put it, they knew no greater victory thanbeing with you in defeat. Iñigo Pérez, themanager who took them there, haddeparted. And Óscar Trejo, the man who gave up the armband over treatment of staff – the best thing he could do as captain was tostop being captain– had retired and been immortalised the way thebarriodoes best:in graffitifour storeys high. Then, in late July, the Madrid government suspended the agreement that allows them to use the ground in return for €81,784 (£69,094) a year.The cup, the coach and the captain were not coming back. As a new season began, nor were any of them. Rayo’s president, Raúl Martín Presa, said he was furious with the council, locking the gates to keep their technicians out and accusing them of condemning the club tosegunda. But when the report described the ground as unsafe and unhealthy, Rayo’s fans knew they were right: they had been saying so for years, relieved to be finally heard. The ground’s upkeep was the tenants’ responsibility but – like so much else – it had been abandoned, left to ruin. They were furious with the president they believe condemns them to a fate far worse that relegation, a man they could not despise more and whodespises them back, of whom they ask just one thing, as often as they can: for him to leave.View image in fullscreenTalk of the town: Raúl Martín Presa (centre) was all smiles despite the protests against him.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesThey are not alone. Last season players had complained about conditions, forced to train at Getafe andplay at Leganés; as the new season began they would have to do so again. After a long summer and threehomegames played 20km south, where 4,280, 4,529, and 3,742 came to see Alavés, Racing and Espanyol, respectively – collectively fewer than in a single afternoon in Vallecas – they were finally back. Leganés had been left three-quarters empty, boycotted by supporters, but in football terms it had been good to them, which sums Rayo up: all wrong but somehow all right. Last season’s victory over Atlético there was followed up by two wins and a draw this season. Yet this is home. Besides, down at Rayo, in the heart of the self-styled independent republic of Vallekas, the football is the least of it,striker Sergio Camello says; it’s about what they stand for. And this weekend they were going to make another stand.They could not have chosen a better opponent: Athletic’s fans are allies, supporters packed into the bars around the ground and theplazain front of the Mercado de Numancia alongside Rayo’s fans, singing in the sunshine. The protest had been planned from the start; what they probably did not plan for was the way it ended. On surfaces all around the stadium, green stickers proclaimed “SOS Rayo Vallecano”. Presa’s image appeared on walls and scarves with familiar Mickey Mouse ears. From bags they handed out little plastic balls in many colours. And from boxes they handed out flyers.View image in fullscreen‘It is the day to protest. It is the day to single out Presa.’ One of hundreds of protest flyers that eventually became a paper plane.Photograph: MARISCAL/EPAPrinted on grey A4, the sheets declared: “Today is a day to protest.” After “years of putting up with this”, they had reached a “point of no return”. And so, in the 13th minute, everyone was invited to chant “Presa, go now!” Then to turn the paper into a plane and fly it on to the field. On the back of the sheet were handy,Ikea-style instructionsfor those who did not know how to fold a paper plane.An Athletic corner arrived with perfect timing, setting it all up. The whistles started bang on the 13th minute and so did the planes, swooping in from all three stands. The referee, José María Sánchez Martínez, stopped the game and shrugged, which he did a lot. Small, multicoloured plastic balls came down too, bouncing and rolling across the pitch, while a banner unfurled in the main stand declared the ball in Presa’s court (which is precisely their problem). An announcement was made, a first warning, two more strikes and they were out. For now, they would play on but not until the pitch was clear.Ballboys dashed across, applauded all the way, to do what ballboys do:pick up the balls. Planes were pushed off the pitch. Players kicked about among themselves. And, after a pause of eight minutes and 43 seconds, Sánchez Martínez, satisfied now, sent them back over to take the corner, Pathé Ciss congratulating a ballboy on a job well done as he returned to his position. The corner came in, Yuri Berchiche volleyed just wide, shot flashing past the post, and then the planes came down again. Two touches, strike two. This time, the referee took them off. The stadium clock had rolled on but now it was reset as they headed down the tunnel to chants of “Presa, go now!”They had been out there 24 minutes and 56 seconds but it might as well have been half-time. In the shadows of the narrow corridor under the stand, conversations unfolded. In the sunshine, so did the tinfoil, supporters happily eating the sandwiches meant for the break. Half an hour after kick-off, there was an announcement: they would begin again in 20 minutes. And if more objects are thrown, the match would be abandoned. From the tunnel, Isi Palazón and Óscar Valentíncame out to speak to fans behind the goal. This wasbad: if it happens again, the game is over. This wasgood, a plan forming: if it happens again, the game is over. A clear protocol, postponement easily forced, a statement made more visible, more powerful than ever before.View image in fullscreenRayo supporters protest with a banner that reads ‘Presa, go now’.Photograph: Alvaro Medranda/Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesThirty-eight minutes and 16 seconds after kick-off, the players reappeared, Athletic first. Sánchez Martínez bounced the ball, said it is flat, swapped it over, and gave it to Emil Audero, whose goal-kick would be the new kick-off, 43 minutes since the first time. From behind him, someone started a countdown:five, four, three …As the ball flew into the air, so did more paper planes. Sánchez Martínez shrugged, looked at the end, a hint of defiance. Leaning against his post at the other end,Unai Simón watched it all happen.Sánchez Martínez called over the captains, then the coaches. A circle formed on the pitch: the referee, his assistant, two captains, two managers, a delegate, La Liga’s match director, the security adviser and a police officer. The Rayo coach, Beñat San José, translated for Edin Terzic, whispering in his ear. Terzic nodded. Álvaro García argued, but there was nothing he could do. The referee’s hands were tied, the police wanted to go, and at nine minutes to three, 49 minutes and 18 seconds after the game started, he signalled towards the tunnel. They had played 13 minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRayo’s players departed, Ivan Balliu first, to applause. The referee stood, hands on his hips, a disapproving parent who had sent the kids to their room. Athletic’s players went to their fans in the far corner, then back towards Rayo’s supporters, who chanted: “Athletic! Athletic!”Iñaki Williams andSimón werethe last off. They stopped for photos with the ballboys. Williams gave someone his shirt, Simón handed over his gloves. As they reached the tunnel, Williams signed someone’s shirt. As they disappeared, the stadium launched into the Vida Pirata, usually a victory song.View image in fullscreenAthletic players wait on the pitch (left) as the referee makes the decision to abandon the match (right).Photograph: Florencia Tan Jun/Getty ImagesThey may not have won, may never win, but many wonder what they had left to lose. They were not planning to get it postponed, an opportunity opening instead, but they might next time. Presa says he will never leave, even if they fall to the third tier, but what if they do it again and again? At what point does someone step in?The club attack the “ultras”– that old get-out clause – and call the rest of the ground “victims”, but that is not how the rest of the ground sees it, flying their paper planes and happily heading off into the afternoon. Even Athletic’s supporters, their big day out brought to an early end, were on side. They joined Rayo fans in the bars while down in the offices, there were negotiations over when to replay the game, probably behind closed doors: Athletic wanted to return the following morning but that was rejected and so at 4.23pm on Saturday their bus pulled out for Barajas, applauded up Payaso Fofo street and right on to Avenida Albufera, still none the wiser.Quick GuideLa Liga resultsShowMálaga 1-1 Espanyol, Rayo 0-0 Athletic (abandoned), Alavés 1-2 Atlético Madrid, Barcelona 3-0 Getafe, Real Madrid 1-0 Villarreal, Elche 0-0 Celta, Real Sociedad 3-2 Deportivo, Betis 5-2 Osasuna, Racing Santander 2-2 ValenciaMonday:Levante v Sevilla (8pm BST)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Rayo’s supporters’ association called this “the inevitable consequence of exhaustion, frustration and anger” after “15 years of abandonment of the facilities, chaotic management, a loss of identity and a continuous contempt for employees and fans, as well as the club and its values”. They called Presa “dictatorial”; the protest, by contrast, “peaceful and democratic, necessary”.“An unsustainable situation has reached its limit,” thecaptain Valentín posts. “This has got worse and worse bit by bit for too long without anyone doing anything to stop it getting this far. We have to listen to and understand the fans’ discontent. We need to find a way to bring everyone together for the common good and the good of Rayo Vallecano above all. That’s the only way we will ever live great moments together again.”PosTeamPGDPts1Barcelona827242Atletico Madrid810193Real Betis85194Real Madrid811185Sevilla71136Real Sociedad8-3137Alaves84118Deportivo A Coruna81109Celta Vigo82810Athletic Bilbao61811Villarreal80812Espanyol80813Rayo Vallecano7-5814Getafe8-6815Racing Santander8-10816Osasuna8-10817Elche8-6618Levante6-4519Valencia8-9520Malaga8-94Explore more on these topicsLa LigaRayo VallecanoEuropean club footballAthletic BilbaofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Daniel Maldini finds his feet at Cagliari after years in family’s Serie A shadow | Serie A | The Guardian
description: Son of Paolo and grandson of Cesare struggled to establish himself at Milan but Fabio Pisacane is beginning to unlock his potential in Sardinia
Author: Nicky Bandini
Headline: Son of Paolo and grandson of Cesare struggled to establish himself at Milan but Fabio Pisacane is beginning to unlock his potential in Sardinia
Content: Daniel Maldini’s critics label him as the ultimate nepo baby but he has shown his potential to the Cagliari faithful.Photograph: Gianluca Zuddas/LaPresse/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDaniel Maldini’s critics label him as the ultimate nepo baby but he has shown his potential to the Cagliari faithful.Photograph: Gianluca Zuddas/LaPresse/ShutterstockSerie ADaniel Maldini finds his feet at Cagliari after years in family’s Serie A shadowSon of Paolo and grandson of Cesare struggled to establish himself at Milan but Fabio Pisacane is beginning to unlock his potential in SardiniaNicky BandiniMon 12 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe abundance could not last for ever. Serie A’s first goalless draw of this season arrived in its 54th match, ironically between two of its more prolific teams. Perhaps things might have ended differently between Como and Roma if the division’s leading scorer, Donyell Malen, had not earned a red card at the start of the second half.A missed opportunity for both sides? Roma started brighter and hit the post through Lorenzo Pellegrini. Como dominated absolutely after the red card, with 80% of possession, but could not make pressure count.In the end, it was a result each team could live with. Returning from this season’s first international break, Como and Roma remain the most likely contenders to challenge Inter. But a couple of more surprising teams are making their presence felt near the top of the table. Lazio’s 3-1 win over Monza on Sunday kept them level with theNerazzurriin first place. An astonishing feat at a time when their fans won’t evencome to home games.And then there isCagliari. The Sardinians have finished in the upper half of Serie A only once in the last 30 years. Champions of Italy in 1970, they have scarcely made it into another title conversation since. But they began this season with four wins from five matches, their best start to a top-flight campaign for more than half a century.Should we have seen this coming? Cagliari ended last season strongly. The first signs of a project coming together under Fabio Pisacane, a popular former player who returned as assistant coach in 2022 and then worked with the academy for two years before leading the first team in 2025.An extraordinary individual, who earned the Guardian’s first-everPlayer of the Year award in 2016, Pisacane lived with Guillain-Barré syndrome as a teenager, becoming paralysed and spending 20 days in a coma, but recovered and ascended Italian football’s lower divisions to make his Serie A debut at 30. Along the way, he made headlines for reporting an attempt by a Ravenna director to bribe him to throw a match in the third tier. None of which necessarily meant he would succeed as a manager. Pisacane has shown himself to be a canny tacticianView image in fullscreenFabio Pisacane has risen from the ranks and shown himself to be an adept tactician.Photograph: Gianluca Zuddas/LaPresse/AP“I’ve worked with many great coaches in my career,” said the Cagliari midfielder Harry Winks in a recent interview. “Coach Pisacane is certainly at the very top level … Since I arrived here, he has already improved everyone, myself included. I really enjoy working with him; I think he can reach the very top of the sport.”OK, pause. Readers less acquainted with Cagliari’s story might need a moment to process that the person speaking is indeed Harry Winks, the former England international, previously of Tottenham and Leicester. Now 30 years old and enjoying his life and his football on the beautiful island of Sardinia.If I mention now that he has been playing with Yerry Mina at Cagliari, you might get the image of a team of Premier League castoffs, chucked together for one last sun-soaked hurrah. That would be the wrong impression. Most of Cagliari’s regulars are 25 and younger, including the pair who combined to carve open Juventus’s defence on Sunday night.View image in fullscreenBlast from the past: Yerry Mina and Harry Winks (not pictured) may be at Cagliari but the team is far from just a place for players to wind down their careers.Photograph: Gianluca Zuddas/LaPresse/ShutterstockThere was not much more than 15 minutes gone when Daniel Maldini cut in from the left. His initial shot from the corner of the box looked optimistic but it pinged back on to him from a defender and then to his teammate Paul Mendy, who held off a marker brilliantly and returned the ball to Maldini for a close-range finish. A fourth consecutive Serie A game with a goal for the forward, and an excellent way to celebrate his 25th birthday.To say that these have been a rollercoaster few weeks would be some understatement. Maldini had his driving licence confiscated last month after crashing his car and failing a breathalyser test in an incident that was reported to have left five people with minor injuries. Subsequent hospital tests for narcotics returned negative, and he was called up to the first Italy squad since Roberto Mancini’s reappointment as national team manager.Maldini’s individual performances for theAzzurriwere a mixed bag, but he lined up with his Cagliari teammate Alessandro Romano for the 3-1 home win over Turkey. It was the first time in more than half a century – since 1972 – that two of the club’s players have started a competitive game together for Italy.In both cases, the opportunity was well earned. Maldini, son of the great Milan defender Paolo, has often been dismissed by his critics as “un raccomandato” – someone who owes their opportunities to knowing the right people. Or, in his case, being part of the right family. Not just a nepo baby but a nepo grandbaby, whose grandfather Cesare won a European Cup with Milan and whose dad repeated that feat five times more. Those are big shoes to fill. Daniel, who grew up in Milan’s academy and made his senior debut for them as long ago as 2020, never cut it at San Siro and has bounced since then from Spezia to Empoli, Monza, Atalanta and Lazio without ever finding his stride.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideSerie A resultsShowGenoa 2-1 Fiorentina, Inter 3-0 Parma, Napoli 3-0 Frosinone, Como 0-0 Roma, Lazio 3-1 Monza, Lecce 1-2 Bologna, Sassuolo 1-1 Milan, Cagliari 1-1 JuventusMonday:Atalanta v Venezia (5.30pm BST), Torino v Udinese (7.45pm BST)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.But Pisacane has been adamant from the start about the player’s potential, highlighting the way he connects lines of midfield and attack. The manager has not been shy about addressing shortcomings, too, stressing that Maldini needs to be more consistent in his application.Plainly, he is not at the height of the previous two generations. Even the current scoring run has included a degree of fortune. Maldini’s goal against Udinese was facilitated by defending that Benny Hill could have considered a bit much. But there is a player in there, and Pisacane has been getting the best of him in a system that allows freedom to move between the wing and a more conventional No 10’s space.It is a similar story all throughout the team of individuals thriving in roles that suit them. Winks’s unshowy work in front of the defence allows the 20-year-old Romano, more freedom to get up and down the pitch. The 19-year-old Mendy is growing in confidence as a target man.And goalkeeper Elia Caprile has been magnificent. He helped Cagliari cling on to a point, after Juventus came to life in the second half. He had made saves from Edon Zhegrova already before Randal Kolo Muani equalised from Kerim Alajbegovic’s cross. Glanced across him at close range, there was little the keeper could have done on the goal. Moments later, Juventus hit the crossbar and Caprile held Nick Woltemade’s follow-up. There was then a brilliant stop from Muani’s point-blank volley, though the forward was in an offside position.View image in fullscreenElia Caprile is all smiles after winning player of the match for his efforts against Juventus.Photograph: Gianluca Zuddas/LaPresse/ShutterstockThe game ended 1-1, and Pisacane said Juventus deserved at least that much. He and Luciano Spalletti were both shown red cards after the final whistle for a post-game scuffle that was hard to parse. They clasped hands at first, but the Juventus manager was shouting angry words from the start and appeared to react to the way Pisacane put a hand on his elbow, though none of these gestures looked violent in any obvious way. Spalletti later said he had been praising Pisacane for his player’s cleverness at time-wasting. Pisacane, for his part, seemed bemused, overheard asking: “What did I do?”It all looked like a storm in a teacup. But we might answer Pisacane’s question another way. What he has done is take Cagliari to six wins and a draw from their last eight matches, dating to last season. Only Roma have picked up more points in that stretch.PosTeamPGDPts1Inter Milan610162Lazio67163Roma611144Cagliari63135AC Milan66126Juventus64117Como63118Napoli64109Frosinone621010Sassuolo60811Atalanta5-2612Lecce6-6613Bologna6-2514Udinese5-3415Torino5-3416Monza6-6417Genoa6-6418Parma6-6419Fiorentina6-7420Venezia5-90Explore more on these topicsSerie ACagliariEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Six questions facing England as they target next year’s Women’s World Cup | England women's football team | The Guardian
description: Starting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the air
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Starting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the air
Content: Sarina Wiegman (left) is looking for a centre-back partner for Leah Williamson (centre). Erica Meg Parkinson (right), 18, has impressed.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSarina Wiegman (left) is looking for a centre-back partner for Leah Williamson (centre). Erica Meg Parkinson (right), 18, has impressed.Composite: Getty ImagesEngland women's football teamSix questions facing England as they target next year’s Women’s World CupStarting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the airTom GarryMon 12 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland have two jobs to do on Tuesday. The first, avoiding an almighty upset and progressing past Greece on aggregate in their Women’s World Cup playoff to reach a final tie, should be a formality for one of the world’s best-resourced teams. The second, honing their style to play like contenders for next summer’s World Cup in Brazil, is a far trickier but crucial challenge.Friday’s relatively uninspiring3-1 first-leg victory in Creteleft room for improvement and England had plenty to work on as they trained at St George’s Park on Monday under gloomy-looking clouds. More broadly, over the next eight months, there are six questions facing the European champions.Can England defend well enough to win a world title?England had 58 touches in Greece’s box and turned that into three goals, whereas Greece had two touches in England’s box but managed to score and hit the crossbar. Sarina Wiegman said she was not happy her team had conceded. Their defending inJune’s 4-0 defeat by Spainalso left much to be desired, and it feels as if England are not yet certain about who should partner the captain, Leah Williamson, at centre-back. Wiegman mentioned on Monday that stopping counterattacks was something they must fix – they also struggled defending quick breaks in April 2025when losing in Belgium. That year, they found a way to win the Euros but they must tighten up defensively if they want to win a first world title in the Maracanã in July.Why are the forwards not clicking?England were wasteful in the final third in Greece and not for the first time in recent months. In the World Cup qualifying group England were 1-0 and 2-0 winners over Iceland in games where they should have scored more. A ruthless Spain, the world’s No 1 side, secured 6-1 and 3-0 wins over Iceland. On Monday Wiegman was asked what one element of Friday’s performance she would most like to improve and replied: “The execution in the final third. We got in good positions but then it’s [about] staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time, and deciding what cross or cutback you’re going to choose.”View image in fullscreenEngland preparing for the second leg against Greece on Tuesday.Photograph: Jacob King/PAWho should start in attacking midfield?For the past year, it has repeatedly felt as if Wiegman does not know who should start as the No 10, with Jess Park, Lucia Kendall and Laura Blindkilde Brown given chances along with Lauren James. Dropping –and recalling– Ella Toone, plus the late addition of Grace Clinton to this squad, adds mystery. Erica Meg Parkinson’s debut on Friday adds another youngster into the mix, and Beth Mead can also play as a 10. Asked on Friday whether the No 10 position had the most question marks surrounding it, Wiegman said: “There’s a lot of competition on that position, where we have a lot of options, which also means, tactically, we can do different things. You can call it a ‘question mark’ – I call it many options.”What about the right wing?England’s left-wing starting position feels nailed on for Lauren Hemp, who has been in tremendous form for Manchester City. The right side, however, looks uncertain, not least because Chloe Kelly has been left out. James, England’s most technically gifted player, would be the first choice for many, but she can also play centrally, and the uncapped Freya Godfrey has impressed for London City Lionesses. On Friday, Blindkilde Brown started on the right before being replaced at half-time by Mead. Whoever starts, there are only a handful of matches before next summer to build fluidity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLaura Blindkilde Brown started at right wing in the first leg against Greece.Photograph: InTime Sports/APWhich youngsters should be given a chance?There have been growing calls for the 20-year-old Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter to be handed her debut and the 21-year-old Godfrey could be in line for her debut on Tuesday. If England held a greater first-leg advantage, England would surely be more likely to experiment in Leicester, although Wiegman confirmed she would make changes. Keira Walsh said of her Chelsea teammate Potter that it was “a really good thing that she’s finally being appreciated for how good she is”, and added: “Her intelligence gives me confidence, knowing that she’s perfectly capable of stopping the counter.” There has also been praise for Parkinson, with Esme Morgan, who has played against Parkinson in the NWSL, describing the 18-year-old as a “smart player, really tidy on the ball, with incredibly good movement”. It remains to be seen whether Wiegman will opt for youth or experience as the season progresses.Do England need clarity over Wiegman’s future?Off the pitch, the biggest unknown facing England is the future of Wiegman, whose contract runs until the end of the World Cup. There have been no reasons to suspect the squad are unsettled by the uncertainty, but the topic is likely to be mentioned in every England press conference until there is clarity. Walsh said on Monday: “Obviously I’d want her to stay. I think everyone in England would love her to stay. I really appreciate her as a manager but it’s her decision.” Wiegman did not wish to discuss the matter, saying: “We’re only focused on Greece and I don’t want to talk about me.”Explore more on these topicsEngland women's football teamWomen's World Cup 2027Women's World CupWomen's footballSarina WiegmanfeaturesShareReuse this content
