A senior Houthi officialsaid that Saturday’s attacktook place “so that the world understands” that Yemeni civilian infrastructure has been, and is being, targeted by the Saudis, gesturing towards that sense that Riyadh treats Yemeni lives as cheap.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn three years, Israel’s war on Gaza hasn’t just changed the Middle East, it’s changed the world | Steve BloomfieldRead moreFrom another perspective, what we are witnessing in the region is another consequence of Hamas’s 7 October attacks on Israel, and what followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The final piece that was stabilising the region’s tense equilibriums fell away when Trump decided that the safety and security of the US’s Gulf allies was secondary to his Iran “excursion”, as he called it. The limits of relying on the US security umbrella became clear both to allies and enemies.Last month, the Trump administrationrefused to extendmilitary assistance to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis, after a meeting of US officials with the Houthis, who assured them that they would not attack US ships in the Red Sea, only Saudi vessels. What is upon Saudi Arabia now is a long, intractable war with a resourceful and impassioned antagonist, one willing to sustain a high degree of pain in ways that Riyadh can’t match without orienting itself entirely towards war.If the 2015 campaign is anything to go by, it will claim thousands of lives with only a remote possibility of a decisive outcome.And so Saudi, and the entire Gulf, are pulled further into the relentless storm. Trump cannot bring the Iran war to an end, Gaza remains an open wound, Israel continues tostrikeandoccupyparts of Lebanon. The Houthi resurgence represents a new reality in a region that is bewildered and losing lives and capital, stuck between old alliances that no longer work and new hostilities that are too calamitous to confront.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsYemenOpinionMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisSaudi ArabiaIranTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Strikes, teaching bans and slashed subjects: how Australian unis are an education in uncertainty and cost-cutting  | Saria Ratnam | The Guardian
description: The relationship between universities and their students and staff has reached an untenable level of conflict
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The relationship between universities and their students and staff has reached an untenable level of conflict
Content: ‘This week-long teaching ban, near the end of semester – which throws our final assessments and grades into uncertainty – is a serious disruption,’ writes Saria Ratnam.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘This week-long teaching ban, near the end of semester – which throws our final assessments and grades into uncertainty – is a serious disruption,’ writes Saria Ratnam.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianOpinionAustralian universitiesStrikes, teaching bans and slashed subjects: how Australian unis are an education in uncertainty and cost-cuttingSaria RatnamThe relationship between universities and their students and staff has reached an untenable level of conflictGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 12 Oct 2026 19.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 20.07 EDTShareThere’s an air of uncertainty around my university campus. This week, many of our lecturers and tutors at the University of Melbourneare taking part in a nationalstrike and week-long teaching ban; all but two of my classes have been cancelled. Posters announcing the industrial action are everywhere. Students are speculating about whether classes will resume by the end of semester or whether last Friday was, unexpectedly, our last day on campus for the year. We’re wondering whether our assessments will even be marked and what will happen to our marks and postgraduate plans as a result.Quite frankly, this sense of instability isn’t new to my university experience and it’s not just my university. In recent years, Australian tertiary education has been plagued by sharp and uneven fee hikes under the job-ready graduates scheme, controversy surrounding the management of pro-Palestine protests, difficulty regulating the use of AI and more.Regional universities struggle to enrol international students amid visa refusals and heated political rhetoricRead moreIt feels like, after years of dissatisfaction with universities’ handling of problems and the government’s treatment of the tertiary sector, staff have finally had enough. A week-long teaching ban, near the end of semester – which throws our final assessments and grades into uncertainty – is a serious disruption.It feels like a watershed moment forAustralian universities. The relationship between these establishments and their students and staff has reached an untenable level of conflict and it’s difficult to believe that things could go on like this for much longer.Course fees continue to rise exorbitantly, while the quality of education decreases and university staff are exposed to uncertain casual contracts, low wages and a lack of rights protection.I feel incredibly lucky to study my course at the university I’m attending; my tutors and lecturers are brilliant and dedicated, and the discussions I have in class with my fellow students are always thought-provoking.But at the same time, I’m frustrated by the $2,100 price tag on each of my subjects, while my contact hours are reduced to 2.5 hours a week for each one. More subjects are cut from my degree each year; none of the subjects I had hoped to study in my third year are running any more. And our assignments are becoming increasingly simple, designed to be AI-proof rather than to test our intellect or thinking skills.The treatment of the university’s staff is worsening the quality of our education even further. The Atlanticpreviously reportedon the correlation between the increasing casualisation of tertiary staff and grade inflation; as more and more university staff globally are hired on precarious casual contracts, where their employment depends on satisfaction surveys that students complete at the end of each semester, they feel an increasing amount of pressure to design easy assignments and hand out good grades so that students rate their subjects highly, bettering their chances at future employment.double quotation markMore subjects are cut from my degree each year; none of the subjects I had hoped to study in my third year are running any moreAlthough this is a global issue, the combination of issues plaguing the Australian university is unique and, in many ways, clearly attributable to our government and university executives.While Australian universities are subjecting staff to unreasonable working conditions while cutting students’ class options and contact hours, this has been enabled and exacerbated by years of federal policy missteps.Over the past decade or so, there’s been a lack of policy reform to protect staff from the casualisation of the tertiary workforce, alongside steep increases in student fees under the jobs-ready graduates scheme, leaving staff and students feeling abandoned.This will only worsen if an elected Coalition would implement its proposed cut to the international student intake, leaving asignificant gap in university revenue, likely exacerbating the subject and staff cuts and reduced quality of education that we’re already seeing.As more Australian universities use AI to mark students’ work, is it creating a ‘slop-cycle’?Read moreAll of this is taking place against the backdrop of a kind of worldwide tertiary ontological crisis. With the rise of AI, a drastically changing job market and grade inflation, it’s hard to know what the future of university looks like, or whether a university qualification will hold much real-world value in the future.More than ever, universities need to look at how they are treating their staff and students. It would be naive for our universities and government to continue assuming that students and staff will passively accept the ongoing deterioration of our studying and working conditions. If the Australian tertiary sector has any chance at surviving this era of instability, it needs to take a serious look at itself and make some drastic changes.The first steps would be for the government to scrap the job-ready graduates scheme and overhaul the laws governing tertiary employment. Additionally, universities must reinstate the staff, subjects, contact hours and assessments that they have cut.If our universities and governments are not careful, they will engineer the extinction of the tertiary system itself. When I left campus last week, I wasn’t sure whether I’d be returning before the end of the semester. I wonder if, one day, staff and students will walk out and not come back.Saria Ratnam is a bachelor of arts student, writer for Farrago Magazine and freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsAustralian universitiesOpinionAustralian educationHigher educationcommentShareReuse this content

title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer | The Guardian
description: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future, says Labour life peer Richard Hermer
Author: Richard Hermer
Headline: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future, says Labour life peer Richard Hermer
Content: ‘Left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with profound consequences for economies, security and human happiness.’Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with profound consequences for economies, security and human happiness.’Photograph: ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrongRichard HermerLet’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the futureMon 12 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareIn my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late.Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of theHugging Face hackand theresignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic, that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate.Dystopian and dehumanising: that’s what it felt like when I was interviewed by an AI assistantRead moreAI has enormous potential benefits for us all. It will be the source of mind-blowing advances in science and medicine, and offers hope for empowerment of some of the world’s most dispossessed people. Yet the risks we are now facing are truly staggering. I would put them in two very broad categories. The first is existential risk: quite literally the possibility that AI could kill billions, either because it enables terrible people to do terrible things – such as design and deploy biological weapons – or because AI itself determines it is more efficient to dispense with humans.The second category is existential challenge – that, left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with utterly profound consequences for economies, national security and human happiness. As Bill Gatesrecently wrote, the AI era will herald “one of the most turbulent times in human history”, noting that it will either be the greatest equaliser ever invented or the worst source of injustice. He is right. On its current trajectory, it risks simultaneously revolutionising the meaning and availability of productive work, while placing unimaginable power in the hands of not only two states (the US and China) but also a small number of individuals who control the tech giants.Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreThe plain fact is that we really don’t know what the precise degree of risk is, or the full panorama of the challenge. Part of the problem is that AI is rapidly developing to a level that humans simply do not understand and will reach a point at which – even if they do – they will no longer have the means to control it. Recall that the 2008 financial crash was caused in part because no humans really understood the web of financial transactions that were leading inexorably to disaster. What we face today, though, is on a different scale in terms of the complexity of the systems and the human agency over them, as well as the level of devastation that might be wrought.The startling levels of risk we are discussing should be completely unacceptable to all of us. In today’s age it is unthinkable that the manufacturer of a toaster would be allowed to market a product with a 10% chance of electrocuting you. The case for slowing down frontier AI before we are clear that the risks can be managed is blindingly obvious.AI needs rigorous regulation now. There is more regulation governing the safety of your fridge than the work being undertaken by frontier AI labs that threaten to wipe out your family. It is ludicrous to suggest the industry can be left to regulate itself. The AI companies and the financial markets underpinning them are incentivised to develop new iterations as quickly as possible, all of this fuelled by the geopolitics of the race between China and the US for dominance. The sight of President Trump and Elon Musk on the White House Lawn brandishing a “voluntary code” provided little in the way of reassurance.It will be international law that matters. While the UK has shown sterling leadership (started by Rishi Sunak, embraced by Keir Starmer and now reflected in Andy Burnham’spromotion of Kanishka Narayan to cabinet), the scale of the challenge requires international cooperation to have any effect. Tragically, this moment of peril arises at the very time in which the international rules-based order is under strain as never before. We need to double down on our engagement with the US and China while simultaneously developing our work with coalitions of like-minded states, as well as the tech sector, to address the threats.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim | Devi SridharRead moreDemocracy demands that we have an urgent public debate about what lies on the horizon in order to retain agency over our own futures – rather than allow them to be determined by the tech sector. None of this needs be inevitable. There is still time for governments and individuals to shape AI, ensuring it serves the public good. Since the Industrial Revolution, modern political movements have been moulded by the dynamic between the “means of production” and the interests of the people. We need new governing theories of who should control AI, how it is regulated and most importantly who it serves.We need urgent public conversations about the values that should guide decision making. We must shape the benefits of technological advances for the benefit of the many, rather than abdicate our future to the few. Leave it much longer and AI itself may deprive us of that power.Richard Hermer is a Labour life peer. He is a former attorney general for England and Wales and former advocate general for Northern Ireland.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionBill GatesComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: As a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Content: Lab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East in Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APView image in fullscreenLab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East in Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APOpinionInfectious diseasesAs a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victimDevi SridharRussia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheldMon 12 Oct 2026 10.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTShareInpandemic preparedness work, scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning.The World Health Organization(WHO), for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritise emerging disease threats and collect theevidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation.As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that thedeath of a single lab workerin Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwideevery month. But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened – and ongoing concern about biological weapons research.The 28-year-oldlab workerdied after developing severe pneumonia. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, established in 1934, which studies plague and other dangerous pathogens including anthrax and cholera, and is rumoured to be involved in biological weapons research. Prof Ashish Jha, who was the US White House Covid-19 response coordinator, and who co-chaired an Ebola commission with me,wrote on social media: “US intelligence assess that Russia’s scientists continue developing biological weapons capabilities. Those programmes operate in secret. Nobody outside inspects them and nobody inside has much incentive to admit when something goes wrong.”On top of that, initial local media coverage suggested that she had died from pneumonic plague after a lab accident, possibly a broken test tube. Pneumonic plague is caused by a bacterium (Yersinia pestis), and can spread through respiratory contact and isalways fatal if untreated. If antibiotics are given in the first 24 hours after symptoms, or even before onset of symptoms post-exposure, it is largely treatable. If she knew she had been exposed, why was treatment not given in time? (Pneumonic plague is a different disease to the more common bubonic plague, which transmits through flea bites.)Despite Russian health authorities denying that it was a case of plague and insisting it was pneumonia of unknown origin, they quickly placed about 200 contacts of the lab worker under quarantine. The authorities reported that no high-threat pathogens were detected and monitoring had ended. The WHOreleased a statementnoting a potential second linked case, but Russia denied this. The cause of death remains unconfirmed.The WHO has pushed the Russian government for more information – including confirmation of the diagnosis and details of the investigations, the reason why it put so many people in quarantine and more information on the second case – but it has not yet received this information.On the one hand, if this infection was spreading further, additional cases would have emerged by now. The lab worker died on 2 October, and the testing of contacts and release of those in quarantine indicates that any spread has been contained so far. However, given that theincubation periodcan be one to three days, continued monitoring is important.There are three hypothetical scenarios if we assume the illness was pneumonic plague. The first is that the lab worker was accidentally exposed to thebacterium while doing research, and either didn’t know, or didn’t tell anyone out of fear – and therefore didn’t ask for treatment immediately. So when she became sick, her window of treatment had been missed.Second, the lab worker was exposed to an antibiotic-resistant strain. This may sound like a conspiracy theory, but senior academics have raised concerns given thehistory of the Soviet biological weapons programmeand the potential for pathogens to be engineered for hostile purposes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYou have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi SridharRead moreThird,Dan Singer(the former White House director for countering biological threats) has suggested that this lab worker might have been given an outdated vaccine, which is only available in Russia as it is not approved by the WHO or most other countries. This is a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning a weakened version of the bacteria is given, but it doesn’t always provide protection and sometimes can cause disease.In short, we don’t know what happened because there is insufficient information from the Russian authorities. To understand what happened, investigators would need access to laboratory and clinical evidence, including genomic sequencing, pathogen identification and details of the worker’s research. Without this, we are left with speculationwhen only scientific certainty will do.As a member of the WHO, Russia has an international legal obligation to share information with the agency. The WHO’s health regulations specifically cover “unusual and unexpected” events, as well as those with serious public health impact and with significant risk of international spread, or that risk affecting trade or travel. But unfortunately, as with most international law, there’s no real enforcement mechanism. There is a reliance on broad cooperation across countries, with the understanding that sharing information on disease spread is in all nations’ best interests.I don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die? | Kiran SidhuRead moreThe US government has also put pressure on Russia for answers, withDonald Trumpsaying he would speak to Putin about the situation.The US state departmentalso formally requested further information under the international health regulations – the irony being that the US withdrew from the WHO in January 2026, but is now invoking the international framework it left behind.As a scientist watching this unfold, I’m reminded that while we can have research and expert conferences into better diagnostics, faster genomic sequencing, more effective vaccines and accessible treatments, none of these advances can compensate for a failure to share the information needed to identify a pathogen in the first place. Preparedness is a political challenge as well as a scientific one. And without transparency, it will be a case of one step forward, two steps back.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsInfectious diseasesOpinionWorld Health OrganizationHealthBubonic plagueRussiaMedical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: Dystopian and dehumanising: that’s what it felt like when I was interviewed by an AI assistant | Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen | The Guardian
description: Outsourcing the essential task of interviewing job applicants to a machine seems lazy at best, negligent at worst. I want better for all of us
Author: Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen
Headline: Outsourcing the essential task of interviewing job applicants to a machine seems lazy at best, negligent at worst. I want better for all of us
Content: Is the use of AI to interview job candidates a sign of the job losses to come?Photograph: AndreyPopov/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenIs the use of AI to interview job candidates a sign of the job losses to come?Photograph: AndreyPopov/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Dystopian and dehumanising: that’s what it felt like when I was interviewed by an AI assistantGiselle Au-Nhien NguyenOutsourcing the essential task of interviewing job applicants to a machine seems lazy at best, negligent at worst. I want better for all of usMon 12 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTShareOver the past 15 years of my working life, I’ve done a lot of interviews for a lot of different jobs and industries: call centre operator, social media manager, bookseller, copywriter, library worker. Recently, after completing my first year of a master’s degree in early childhood and primary teaching, I applied for a preschool education role and experienced a first: being interviewed by AI.I’d heard of this practice and was aware of its shortcomings, from howdemoralisingit is to therisk of discrimination.Yet I still wasn’t prepared for how dystopian and dehumanising it felt to be in the situation myself.The Guardian view on the changed world of job interviews: missing the human factor | EditorialRead moreI had applied for the role with great interest – it was at a sessional kindergarten managed by a not-for-profit. My initial excitement at being shortlisted soon faded as I realised I would be speaking with an “AI assistant”. Nevertheless, she persisted: I dressed as I would for any other job interview, shooed my cats out of the room, sat down at my laptop and clicked to enter the interview.A disembodied voice greeted me by name and the interview began. I found it disconcerting to see myself in the little video window with no one else visible, but I pushed through the discomfort to answer the questions. At one point the AI asked me a question that I needed time to consider. I’ve previously been told it’s acceptable to pause during job interviews to think through a particularly tricky question, so I did just that – and I was booted off the interview entirely. As I clicked the link once more to restart the interview, I could feel a guttural scream rising in my throat.At the end of the interview, the AI asked if I had any questions about the role. I did, but they were all answered with regurgitations from the job ad. For any clarification, the AI said, I would need to have a conversation with a manager. I stifled a laugh at the irony.Women and university graduates in Australia most at risk of losing jobs to AI, report findsRead moreThe AI thanked me for my time and said that my video would be reviewed by the company, which would be in touch. I closed the browser window and stared at my blank laptop screen and my own reflection. I had been alone the entire time, after all.In the following days, I could not stop thinking about this experience. I posted on early childhood forums asking if anyone had gone through the same thing. I was met with a ripple of shock from industry peers, including senior people, who couldn’t believe this was happening. I couldn’t either – it’s demeaning enough to put any job-seeker through AI interviews but the profession of caring for and educating children is surely one of the most human that still exists. Especially in light of the ongoing childcare crisis in Australia, outsourcing recruitment of this essential role to a machine seems lazy at best and negligent at worst.Still, I tried to bargain with myself: maybe the experience will be worth it. Surely this is only the first stage of the recruitment process and the next interview will be with a person? I really want to contribute positively to my community! This is the future, right?But that little voice in my head was only getting louder. I felt degraded: I’d put effort into my application and interview, so why shouldn’t I receive effort back? I noticed, too, that the organisation’s website had AI photos of “educators”. Was the interview a sign of labour erasure to come?I ultimately decided to withdraw my application and emailed the organisation to tell them precisely why. It has been over a month and I have received no response, no acknowledgment whatsoever. I still haven’t spoken to a single human being.I think of those sweet little children I could have taught, learning about the world, each other, themselves. They don’t know what an AI interview is yet but, if things continue this way, one day they will. I want better for them. I want better for all of us.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionChildcare AustraliaWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: I don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die? | Kiran Sidhu | The Guardian
description: The quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problem, says journalist and writer Kiran Sidhu
Author: Kiran Sidhu
Headline: The quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problem, says journalist and writer Kiran Sidhu
Content: ‘I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her, can I trust her to cherish it?’Photograph: mikroman6/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her, can I trust her to cherish it?’Photograph: mikroman6/Getty ImagesOpinionDeath and dyingI don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die?Kiran SidhuThe quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problemMon 12 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTShareAfriend of mine recently discussed his will with me. He talked about the importance of looking after his daughter financially when he’s gone. As a child-free woman, I confidently told him my money will go to organisations that have meant something to me: Macmillan Cancer Support and animal charities. It bemuses me how people think the absence of children is a problem when it comes to inheritance money; it’s always been obvious to me that I’d give my money to causes that touch my heart. But then my friend served something of a curveball. He asked me who will have my deceased mother’s ring?It made me think: where do theprecious artefacts from our lives gowhen we are no longer here? Whenever I’m away from home I look forward to being reunited with these things: the quirky vase that sits in the window of my study, and the owl candlestick, a birthday gift from my potter friend. These items carry parts of me – what will become of them? If you have children, the answer to this question is not presented to you as a puzzle; like a constellation of stars, the answer is perfectly aligned. If you don’t have children, the question can lead to existential angst.This problem has caused both consternation and fascination among my child-free friends. It is a conversation topic that is something of a black hole.I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her (she was one when my mother died and so doesn’t remember her), can I trust her to cherish it? If she was my own daughter, would it be different, would I still feel this angst? My friends and I have wrestled with this question.I’ve seen enoughepisodes of Antiques Roadshowto know that the world is full of people who cherish items that once belonged to relatives they have never met. If the ring went to my goddaughter, I’d be the last custodian who really knew what it meant to my mother. But a new relationship would be anchored with it: the one that I have with my goddaughter. Understanding this has made me realise that sentimentality can and does still get passed down.I realise my concerns about the passing on of my mother’s ring stems fromtrying to hold on to what is tangibly leftof her. Inadvertently, I have been willing time to stop. The philosopher Heraclitus said: “No man steps in the same river twice. For it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man.” Life moves forward and the lives of the first custodians of the things we hold dear, who have long passed, will become backstories.When I’m gone, I will no longer be the custodian of the ring – and its meaning will alter with its new owner. This is how life works; in the exchange of hands. One day I will have to let go of what can no longer belong to me. Acknowledging this has brought me some clarity and comfort.However, an unexpected conundrum has also popped up in my circle of child-free friends. My friend has two nieces and a nephew. The nieces don’t make an effort to be in her life and she plans to leave what she has to her nephew. She has been told this would cause strife among the siblings and her plan is “inconsiderate”. How much should we consider the feelings of others when it comes to writing our wills?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTop 10 novels about inheritanceRead moreThe contents of our wills are not just the last performance of our lives – but the lasting performance. Child-free people may be at liberty to choose the recipients of our possessions without being bound by expectation and tradition, but we’re more open to rigorous criticism because of that freedom. It’s not as formulaic as leaving it to the kids.The artist David Hockneydied without having had children, but will leave a bigger legacy to the world than most. I’m a writer; perhaps my words will touch 10 or a thousand people, certainly more than the number of children I could have had. I will be a benefactor to many, rather than a few, through my words and the money I will leave to charity.In the end, we all leave some form of a legacy whether we have children or not; traces of ourselves that whisper of our past existence. I’m not interested in any grandiose legacy when I’m gone, but I cannot deny, there’s something beautiful about leaving a token of ourselves in a world that we’ve left behind.Kiran Sidhu is a freelance journalist and writer. She is the author of I Can Hear the Cuckoo. She also wrote the Bafta award-winning documentary Heart Valley.Explore more on these topicsDeath and dyingOpinionWriting a willFamily financescommentShareReuse this content

title: I will have more police officers of colour in the UK capital – and the culture wars won’t stop me doing it  | Mark Rowley | The Guardian
description: In our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It’s not favouritism, it is fairness – it’s essential, says Metropolitan police commissioner Mark Rowley
Author: Mark Rowley
Headline: In our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It’s not favouritism, it is fairness – it’s essential, says Metropolitan police commissioner Mark Rowley
Content: Mark Rowley chats to police officers during a visit to Stratford, east London with the Community Outreach Team, 28 October 2022.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenMark Rowley chats to police officers during a visit to Stratford, east London with the Community Outreach Team, 28 October 2022.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionMetropolitan policeI will have more police officers of colour in the UK capital – and the culture wars won’t stop me doing itMark RowleyIn our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It is not favouritism, it is fairness – and it’s essentialMark Rowley is commissioner of the Metropolitan policeMet chief says ‘toxicity’ around DEI will not stop him recruiting more Black and Asian officersMon 12 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 04.17 EDTShareEffective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent that stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.Last Monday, we launched a major recruitment campaign. We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity.London is the world’s greatest and most diverse and globally connected city.Nine million people live here. Hundreds of languages are spoken. The scale and complexity of policing London today is unlike anything Sir Robert Peel imagined when founding the Metropolitan police. Yet, in 1829, he recognised that policing success in a democracy relies onpublic approval, respect and cooperation as much as on “impartial service to the law”.We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us, or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences.An inclusive workforce is not a public relations exercise. It makes us better at protecting victims, catching criminals and preventing crime.We cannot provide an equally good response to all victims if our understanding of some Londoners is weaker than others. That is obvious when it comes to issues such as language barriers or supporting deaf people, but it is just as important when culture, experience or background may make a victim less willing to talk about sexual abuse, domestic violence or other traumatic crimes.When victims speak to officers and staff who understand them, and therefore feel fairly and impartially treated, we solve more crime and prevent more harm. When victims feel understood, they are more likely to come forward. When communities trust the police, they are more likely to report crime, share intelligence and support investigations. That trust underpins our effectiveness and goes to the very heart of policing by consent.View image in fullscreenLondon Metropolitan police officers patrol outside the Houses of Parliament in January this year.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAWe cannot police London effectively without the trust and confidence of the communities we serve. By listening to people’s lived experiences and working in partnership with communities, we can build stronger relationships and greater legitimacy. This is particularly important when using police powers, includingstop and search, where fairness, empathy and accountability are essential to maintaining public confidence and keeping London safe.We need men and women who can carry out surveillance, work undercover and operate effectively across London. We need officers and staff who can build trust with victims of violence against women and girls, who can connect with London’s communities and who bring different experiences, perspectives and skills to complex policing challenges.These are not ideological arguments. They are practical policing realities. And yet, despite progress, we are still not attracting talent equally. Some worry they will not fit in. Others are discouraged by family or friends. We have a responsibility to challenge those perceptions and remove those barriers. That is what our recruitment campaign is designed to do.Last year we had the most representative intake of recruits in our history. More women joined. More Londoners from ethnic-minority backgrounds joined. That is welcome progress.We want the talent from every corner of London to join our courageous and resilient teams and to close the gap with communities we have previously drawn least from.Some will wrongly suggest that increasing representation means lowering standards. Nothing could be further from the truth. For generations, talented people from some communities have faced barriers that limited opportunities to join policing or build a career within it. Tackling those barriers is not favouritism. It is fairness. Our standards are unchanged and uncompromising. By reaching further into communities where we have historically been underrepresented, we are ensuring we attract the widest and strongest possible pool of talent, helping us build a Met that truly reflects and understands every corner of London.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe want to be an inclusive organisation in which everyone has an equal chance to thrive. Fairness, not favour, should be at the heart of opportunity.I also want to see more women and people from underrepresented backgrounds putting themselves forward for some of the most exciting roles in British policing.That means firearms teams, the flying squad, counter-terrorism, specialist operations, public protection and major investigations.Public debate about inclusion has become increasingly polarised in recent years. Too often there is an assumption that inclusion and impartiality or merit are competing objectives. They are not.As commissioner I know the Met’s success, in protecting communities and helping London thrive, requires inclusivity as well as impartiality. We will not be blown off course by the culture wars. This is not an ideological choice. It is, as Peel’s founding vision for “policing by consent” described, an operational necessity.Mark Rowley is commissioner of the Metropolitan policeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Narendra Modi’s gen Z crackdown: he cannot arrest his way out of a democratic crisis | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Young protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confront
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Young protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confront
Content: A protest march on 12 October 2026 in Delhi. ‘Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation.’Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/GettyView image in fullscreenA protest march on 12 October 2026 in Delhi. ‘Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation.’Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/GettyOpinionIndiaThe Guardian view on Narendra Modi’s gen Z crackdown: he cannot arrest his way out of a democratic crisisEditorialYoung protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confrontMon 12 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 20.56 EDTShareNarendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detainedjournalistsand shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, wasdetainedwith other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets wereroughedup by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday,thousandsmarched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although somecommissionershave raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP wonstate electionsin West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed votersexceededthe margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.View image in fullscreenNarendra Modi.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAMass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. TheCockroach movementwas born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakesimpossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.There is still reason for hope in India. TheIndian Expressnewspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011,corruption scandalsbecame evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments! | Turbine Hall | The Guardian
description: The Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!
Content: ‘You have to surrender to it’ … Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installation at Tate Modern.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘You have to surrender to it’ … Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installation at Tate Modern.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTurbine HallReviewTarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments!Tate Modern, LondonThe Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!Jonathan JonesMon 12 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the floor of theTurbine Hall, there are wide water basins and huge flattish rough-hewn rocks you might see on moorland or in a desert. You can sit or stand or climb on them. But if you look up, you won’t be able to stop looking up – because it’s raining musical instruments. Immense elongated brass trumpets and giant glowing drums seem to float in the air, suspended from the girders of the former power station’s roof.If Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui had just left it at that, it would be an impressive, intriguing installation, but this isTate Modern, honey, and Atoui hasn’t been asked to occupy its grandest space with mere physical objects. Instead, his sculptural creations and found stuff resonate and echo with an ever-changing, invisible art of noises. An earth-shaking bass note throbs from a hanging trumpet – or is it from that translucent cone rising out of the ground like an ethereal minaret? Then a drumbeat booms through the space and a woman’s plangent, achingly lovely voice sings notes of infinite nostalgia and melancholy.Tarek Atoui admires his workIt’s entrancing. The music has you hooked. It is music, I think, though abstract, non-melodic, a rising and falling of sounds that lead you around and through the installation’s forest of solid things. But then – is music ever not sculptural? Listening to the scything percussive notes of Stravinsky certainly is; and the desire to crystallise sound waves into something visible has haunted everyone from the inventors of opera to designers of psychedelic lightshows.Yet Tarek Atoui still manages to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. He teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear, how the stones and water basins, pipes and strings have produced this sonic outpouring. The entire installation is an interconnected musical machine.It’s funny too. There’s a warm, generous if absurdist humour to it all. In the past, a crazy mechanical contraption like this would be called “Heath Robinsonish”, after the early 20th-century British cartoonist who came up with such things. A better comparison is Leonardo da Vinci, who invented wild musical instruments among his other real and impossible machines: organs worked by water, a string instrument shaped like a fantastic beast.Tarek Atoui at the Tate ModernAtoui, like Leonardo, seems to be looking for a lost harmony in the world, a secret note that pleased the Lord. Sadness hovers in the sounds that fill this vast grey space, as the bass notes pound harder, building up to an apocalyptic blast. What is being mourned and where is he taking us? You start to feel you are in a city of sounds and sights. The crowd of towering, floating pinnacles, the mysterious voice and crescendo of percussion, suggest an ancient, tumultuous labyrinth of a city. I thought of Lahore and Marrakesh, of a street-singer heard once in an Istanbul market. Yet this city is purer, less tangible. Its towers fly in the air.View image in fullscreenSonic king … Atoui at his Turbine Hall installation.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianUltimately, you can’t reduce this magical, elusive work of art to a fixed meaning. You have to surrender to it. The sound gathers you up in its ecstasy like a spiralling mystical dance. There is a strong similarity with Sufi drummers and dervishes who use music and motion to inculcate a liberating, trancelike calm. I certainly didn’t want to leave. The vibrations and complex visual composition keep your brain busy but you are also soothed and at peace.It also suggests the urban life all around this site, the exotic sounds of Bankside: the music of the city, gathered into Atoui’s collage of random noise. But reality slips and fades as you are shown a world beyond the physical. All these objects, from the cones to the stones to the electric guitar played live at the press view, are but as air. They fascinate the eye but the sound eventually dissolves the material world. The solid stuff Atoui begins with becomes as unreal as a reflection in a courtyard pool.Atoui has grabbed the opportunity to work in this vast space with both hands, creating something rich, ingenious, funny, sad, mystical. This is a Turbine Hall installation to lose yourself in for hours, dreaming and wondering. It’s the sonic answer to a sun indoors – and Atoui is a modern magus.Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installationis at Tate Modern, London, from 13 October until 11 April 2027Explore more on these topicsTurbine HallSound artTate ModernArtInstallationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘When it went double platinum, Andy Burnham gave us the award’: how Courteeners made Not Nineteen Forever | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: ‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’
Content: ‘If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar in pubs for ever’ … Liam Fray of the Courteeners.Photograph: Edd Westmacott/Avalon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar in pubs for ever’ … Liam Fray of the Courteeners.Photograph: Edd Westmacott/Avalon/Getty ImagesHow we madeCulture‘When it went double platinum, Andy Burnham gave us the award’: how Courteeners made Not Nineteen Forever‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’Interviews byDave SimpsonMon 12 Oct 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiam Fray, songwriter/vocals, guitarI had the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever before the band existed. They were in a little red book of poems and scribbles that got me a place on the creative writing course at the University of Salford. Most of what became the songs for our first album, St Jude, were in that book. As well as uni, I was working in a shop and spending five nights a week at the Night & Day bar in Manchester, but in a nightclub I’d be the dude scribbling in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off.Not Nineteen Forever was probably inspired by a specific incident, although I can’t remember it exactly. The first line, “She had to peel me off the pavement”, could have happened on many a night out then. “Front-crawled the crowd down the stairs” is because the staircase at the 42nd Street club was so tight you’d have to literally front-crawl over people. The chorus: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together”, sounds like the sort of thing somebody might have said to me, but it could easily have been me giving myself a telling off after waking up with a fuzzy head.‘I’m not famous. But I can’t go to the chippy’: Courteeners’ Liam Fray on filling stadiums, defying extinction – and wearing M&S pantsRead moreI got the chords when I was trying to work out Someday by the Strokes but got the finger positions muddled up. I’d taken a bag of washing to my parents’ house and was working on it in my old bedroom when my dad poked his head in and said: “It sounds all right, that.” Not Nineteen Forever was one of the last songs I wrote before I convinced my three best mates to form the band. I told them: “If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar on my own in Manchester pubs for ever.”You never think a song’s going to resonate 20 years later, but it’s become easily Courteeners’ most popular song. Ironically, it initially charted at No 19, but years later when it went double platinum Andy Burnham – who comes to our gigs – presented us with the award in theBritons Protection pub. The song’s taken on a poignant dimension now. At gigs I see our original fans together with their kids – who are 17, 18, 19 – and they’re all singing: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together.”Stephen Street, producerCourteeners had just been signed by a major label who asked me if I could go to Manchester to meet them as they had expressed interest in working with me. I saw them play in one of the university halls and it was mind-blowing. They already had a devoted following who were singing along with the lyrics the way Smiths audiences used to. I’d produced the Smiths, so it was right up my avenue.In the mid-2000s there’d been a resurgence of indie guitar bands: Arctic Monkeys, Kaiser Chiefs and Kasabian. In a way Courteeners were the last hurrah of that kind of hugely popular guitar group. The next thing I knew we were all in Olympic studios in London recording the album. I was excited to work with them. Not Nineteen Forever was a ready-made anthem and stood out, but so did Cavorting or What Took You So Long?With a band like Courteeners, you want to capture their performance. Like the best bands, they were like a little gang: us against the world. So we recorded live, only using click tracks to set the tempos. Their arrangements were short and concise and didn’t need much editing. Liam and Conan [Daniel Moores]’s guitar parts were intrinsic to the sound – I lent Conan a nice old vintage Telecaster – and I found the emotion in Liam’s voice really attractive.When they’d started out in a garage, Liam had to shout to be heard over the guitar, but in the studio I vaguely remember telling him he didn’t need to. When I saw the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever written down it hit me how good they were. “Older woman and an ever so slightly younger man” always makes me laugh. He was 19. The “older woman” was probably 21 or something.When the album came out I was perplexed by the lukewarm reaction from elements of the press – probably because it was another four lads with guitars – but it’s a really strong collection that I think still stands up today. The reissue of St Jude went to No 1 15 years after it first came out. I’d never had that happen before in my career: I was quite emotional.God Bless the Band – the best of Courteeners is out now Ignition Music. A UK tour begins on 6 November at First Direct Bank Arena, Leeds.Explore more on these topicsCultureHow we madeCourteenersIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pine cones, glitter and a hip-hop head for sale: red-hot artists reveal their Frieze stunners | Frieze art fair | The Guardian
description: As the sprawling art jamboree hits London, eight of the most exciting exhibiting artists share what their work means to them – and who they hope will buy it
Author: Alex Needham
Headline: As the sprawling art jamboree hits London, eight of the most exciting exhibiting artists share what their work means to them – and who they hope will buy it
Content: ‘An enduring act of devotion’ … Louise Giovanelli at her studio in Manchester.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘An enduring act of devotion’ … Louise Giovanelli at her studio in Manchester.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianFrieze art fairPine cones, glitter and a hip-hop head for sale: red-hot artists reveal their Frieze stunnersAs the sprawling art jamboree hits London, eight of the most exciting exhibiting artists share what their work means to them – and who they hope will buy itInterviews byAlex NeedhamMon 12 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst held in 2003, theFrieze art fairis a giant art supermarket that descends on Regent’s Park, London, every October. Some detest it for its blatant commercialism, others relish it as the opportunity to see a mind-boggling amount of contemporary art in one enormous tent. Here, eight British-based artists of the moment talk through what they’re showing.Kira FreijeAge:41How would you describe what you do?I make sculpture. I work a lot with metal, fabrics, quite a collection of materials to make landscapes of figures that grow intuitively.What’s the highlight of your career so far?My exhibition at Hepworth Wakefield – getting major support in such an incredible institution.View image in fullscreen‘I call them gesture works’ … Kira Freije at her studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianName two favourite artists, one dead and one living.Dead:Marisa MerzorPaul Thek. Both had an attitude of freedom of making. Living: Liliane Lijn orDonna Huddleston, who I know quite well. I love them and I think they’re amazing.Tell me about the sculpture we’ve photographed you with.I call them gesture works. They’re wall-based, but they allude to a crowd. They’re cast in aluminium and bronze and one of them has a piece of fabric.Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years?Oh God, I can’t imagine. Hopefully still alive and excited with what I’m making.Mohammed Z RahmanAge:29How would you describe what you do?I’m a figurative painter, but I also work across sculpture and installation. I’m self-taught, so my work has been described as outsider art. I’ll make work drawn from nursery rhymes and ethnographic texts.What made you want to become an artist?My mum came to the UK in the 80s from rural Bangladesh and we lived in a series of dilapidated houses. She was a textile worker so she made curtains for the house. My sister would salvage wood and make furniture, so I was immersed in organic homemaking.View image in fullscreen‘Outsider art’ … Mohammed Z Rahman with his crate and fish pictures.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhat’s the highlight of your career so far?Going to the Venice Biennale earlier this year. In light of the death ofKoyo [Kouoh, who died while curating the show in which Rahman participated], the artists really came together.Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.Maybe it’s a cliche, but I really likeFrida Kahlo. I think she did what I’m trying to do in the sense of hitting a balance between social realism, being political, speaking to the current social conditions and introducing a world of fantasy and mythology and dreams. And I really like the work ofToyin Ojih Odutolawho had the Barbican Curve commission in London a few years ago. The storytelling and world building of that show was amazing. It’s a guiding star in terms of the direction I want to take my practice.Tell me about the sculpture we’ve photographed you with.At Frieze in 2023, I was amazed by all these beautiful wooden shipping crates that were coming in like a big parade. I thought: these would be so beautiful if they were painted. This was designed as a seat and storage for my gallery team – it’s like set design. The fish pictures are drawn from kheta stitching, a folk craft in rural Bangladesh.Jake GrewalAge:32How would you describe what you do?I make paintings and I draw, mostly in charcoal. I look at figures in the landscape at liminal times. The figures are anthropomorphic, but they also are genderless. So there’s this queer undertone.What’s the highlight of your career so far?The Studio Voltaire show inLondonincluded the biggest painting I’ve ever made.Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.I love Turner’s abstraction of the landscape, and his use of colour really inspired me when I was younger. His watercolours are so transcendent and he’s a master at capturing atmosphere. And I really loveNan Goldin. In a day when art is so capitalist and based on consumption, the artists who stand out are ones who are trying to bring about social change.View image in fullscreen‘There’s this queer undertone’ … Jake Grewal at his studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTell me about the picture we’ve photographed you with.It’s a large charcoal drawing of two figures following one another in a forest scene. The figures look quite adolescent, so it feels almost like an old film still. There’s something quite nostalgic about it.Who would you like to buy it?I would love someone who I really admire to buy it. I’m such a big fan ofAnohni, but I doubt she’s going to buy my drawing.Alvaro BarringtonAge:43Tell me about the painting we’ve photographed you with.It’s a head portrait. Portraiture has been such an incredible genre in painting, from the Mona Lisa to Girl with a Pearl Earring to Picasso’s The Weeping Woman. I’ve always wanted to deal with this genre in a way that felt unique to how I would understand it. I grew up in a very hip-hop culture and so I’ve been exploring how to make hip-hop versions of heads.What do you hope will happen when it gets sold at Frieze?Hopefully somebody would love to live with it. Because I think art should be lived with, whether that’s in a museum or someone’s house.Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.Tupac and Tupac. He’s the greatest artist in my lifetime. You’re born, there’s a trillion things to notice, and an artist is just someone who goes: “This thing has happened. This is how I feel about it. I’m going to make something that’s so convincing”, whether it’s a painting or a song or a dance performance or a lecture likeJoseph Beuysused to do. And then all of a sudden you go: “I get that. That makes sense to me.”View image in fullscreen‘You’re born first physically, but then you’re born culturally’ … Alvaro Barrington in the workshop at his studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhere do you think you’ll be in 20 years’ time?I have four chapters in my life. The first chapter is called Garvey: Birth. I think you’re born twice. You’re born first physically, but then you’re born culturally. And culture tells you how to understand yourself, who to love, who to hate. It’s the value of things. The second chapter is called Malcolm X: Innovation, someone who completely reinvented himself and chose his identity. And then the third chapter isAudre Lorde: Power– a poet and writer and also from Grenada, the island my mom is from. And then the last chapter is calledBiggie Smalls: Death.Louise GiovanelliAge:32How would you describe your work?I paint to capture the vibrating luminous residue of a glance turning a fleeting sensory encounter into an enduring act of devotion.What has been the highlight of your career so far?Probably a major show that began at the Hepworth Wakefield in 2024. It toured to Graz in Austria and then it went to Museum Villa Stuck in Munich, so that was a really nice year for me because I got to follow the works around Europe and see them in different institutional contexts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionName two favourite artists, one dead and one living.I like Rudolf Stingel. Every show that I’ve seen of his is completely different. He’s very willing to take risks. And for a historical one,Piero della Francesca. I just love those Italian fresco panel paintings. His depictions of women are just glorious.Tell me about the painting we’ve photographed you with.It’s the first time that I’ve fused two quite disparate series of mine. It’s a face projected on to this sparkly glitter curtain and the painting’s called Cathexis, which is from a Greek word which means to invest your energy into a specific thing. There have been so many examples throughout history where humans have invested in transient materials such as silk or flesh or marble, materialisations of desire, so that’s what I’m trying to do in this painting. It speaks to my interest in drapery and hair and in female beauty.What do you hope happens to this painting when it’s sold?Oh, that’s a hard question. Well, I put a lot of trust in my gallery with placing it with someone who has a knowledge of my work, supports my practice and would loan it to some museum shows maybe later down the line.Shaqúelle WhyteAge:26View image in fullscreen‘Rothko is my north star’ … Shaqúelle Whyte at his studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhat would you say the highlight of your career so far has been?My show at WolverhamptonArtGallery this year. I wanted to bring my work back to the city and to people who have varying understandings of art because of the degradation of the education system, and that was a privilege. To see them want to know more was highlight of my life. And I’ve got a solo show at South London Gallery coming up. I think I’m going to be the youngest person ever to do a solo show in that space. And that’s just like, Jesus Christ, how did we get here? I’m a kid from Wolves, you know what I mean? It’s all a bit mad.Tell me about the paintings you’re showing at Frieze.One’s called Gulliver’s Forrest and the other’s called Miss Mammy. They were made after the Wolverhampton show and before the beginnings of this new body of work. You’ve got periods of time where you can explore and mess around – that’s what it was.What do you hope happens to this painting when it’s sold?The most important thing is that the works are looked after and appreciated. So ultimately an institution [buying it] would be great but it needs to be somebody that will be responsible for it as my career grows, and not be flipping it.Who are your two favourite artists, one dead and one living?Rothko is my north star for what it means to make paintings. And alive, I think Ruprecht von Kaufmann is a phenomenal painter, and so isAndrew Cranston. I like bad-boy painters. In the pursuit of greatness you need to be reaching up to something.Is it true that Stormzy has been coming by your studio?Yeah, he came the other day. But ultimately, he’s just a guy who’s got interest in art and wants to see the work.Poppy JonesAge:41How would you describe your work?I work with a combination of painting, printmaking and photography, all at a very intimate scale. The canvases are cut from materials more common for clothing and sometimes out of my own clothing. There’s often like a conceptual play between the textile subject and the surface, so if it’s made from a suede jacket, the work will depict the suede jacket. I’m interested in the way things like eBay might be the record of our culture in the future and what’s happening to this digital archive. But I’m also really interested in creating atmosphere and the qualities of light and how objects can suddenly express an inner emotion.View image in fullscreen‘I feel like I let [my work] go on its own journey’ … Poppy Jones at Herald St Gallery, London.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWhat’s been the highlight of your career so far?I saw a big Paul Nash retrospective 10 years ago at Tate Britain and became a massive fan. There’s a particular painting of his, Dead Spring, at Pallant House [in Chichester] which I used to look at on my way to or from work when I was teaching. They recently acquired work of mine and in the summer I went to see it and it’s hung opposite Dead Spring. My own work has become part of that conversation in the gallery.Can you name two favourite artists, one dead and one living?Eileen Agaras my dead artist. I like that she just did her own thing for her whole lifetime, and I like her approach to materials and to collage. Francis Offman is my favourite artist at the moment. He’s using digital technology to fabricate these large weavings but then painting on them. The colours are amazing.Tell me about the work you’re showing at Frieze.It’s called Statues Also Die (Man Ray). It’s based on a photographic image I took of a Man Ray monograph covered in pine cones and forest-like debris during a residency at a museum in very rural Denmark 10 years ago. The title references the 1950s film by Alain Resnais and Chris Marker [and Ghislain Cloquet] which explores the shifting power of images according to different contexts and that’s something I’m interested in doing in my own work.Who would you like to buy it, and who would you hate to buy it?I enjoy making the work, but I don’t get overly attached to it once it leaves the studio. I feel like I let it go on its own journey, which I leave to other people.Christina KimezeAge:40How would you describe your work?I came to the studio via a non-linear path. I studied science then had various jobs and set up a startup with my sister. Central to my practice is rejecting traditional materials and embracing imperfections. That’s informed by having to make art at home for a long time in cramped spaces.What has been the highlight of your career so far?My show at the South London Gallery was a turning point. The demographic wasn’t a sort of homogeneous room of art-world folk, politely nodding at the wall text. We had lots of local young people coming in, genuinely reacting to the energy of the work and the materials. It centred around this idea of roller-skating as a motif and some people turned up on their roller-skates.View image in fullscreen‘My work has always been informed by not having much time’ … Christina Kimeze at her studio.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianCan you tell me two artists you love, one living and one dead?Matisse had this ability to leave the rough in there as well as the polished, clean line.Chris Ofilihas parallels with Matisse, and there’s something I always try and take from both of those artists.Can you tell me about the picture that we’ve photographed you with?That picture is called Game On (Crane’s Cut) and it’s on suede mat board, which forces a battle between painting and drawing because I have to use oil sticks and pastels and stuff. It shows a woman shuffling cards and it’s about the seductive but scary ideas of chance. It’s using that as a motif to explore the luck of global migration and the lottery of birth. I’m Ugandan, and there’s this crane flying across the picture, referencing the national bird of Uganda, the crested crane.Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years?My work has always been informed by not having much time – I’m currently pregnant with my third child. Time is such a luxury, isn’t it? I hope I have that space to explore other media, to make sculpture, to make an installation.Frieze Londonruns from 14-18 OctoberThis article was amended on 12 October 2026 to correct the spellings of Louise Giovanelli’s painting Cathexis, those of Shaquélle Whyte, and Liliane Lijn’s name.Explore more on these topicsFrieze art fairArtPaintingSculptureInstallationLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph | Fontaines DC | The Guardian
description: This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generation
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generation
Content: ‘Indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey’ … Fontaines DC.Photograph: DOT/Ewen SpencerView image in fullscreen‘Indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey’ … Fontaines DC.Photograph: DOT/Ewen SpencerFontaines DCReviewFontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph(XL)This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generationLaura SnapesMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifteen centuries ago, the Byzantine archbishop Theophilus of Adana did first-hand business with the devil for his own superficial betterment. Today, we just blindly tick a little box marked “accept terms and conditions” or let high-street snake oil merchants inject poison into our faces. The Faustian pact has become as depressingly banal as it is endemic and destructive – and unlike Theophilus, we can’t rely on the Virgin Mary to save us now. In the midst of headlines about AI destroying humanity, the idea of listening to music submerged in precisely this shade of doom might sound like, well, hell. If anyone can thread that poisoned needle, it’sFontaines DC.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Dopamine ChamberWhen the Dublin band introduced their last album, 2024’sRomance, it came witha surprise new look. Their uncoordinated jeans and shirts had been replaced by neon hair, shiny trousers and bug-eyed sunglasses that split the difference between Korn and the Prodigy. As they faced up to having traded their anonymity to become arena fillers, it wasn’t hard to read this look as a sort of protective cosplay, a cybergoth Sasha Fierce for five fairly low-key Irish lads trying to make peace with leaving their roots behind. Newly melodic and lavishly produced, Romance made no bones about the band’s ambitions and became their first platinum-certified album.For their fifth LP, Fontaines’ wardrobes are more or less back to normal as the music reaches new heights, indicating a level of comfort and confidence that resounds through their most formidable, cohesive record. Frontman Grian Chatten has said he wanted to write about the context collapse of social media and the willing degradation of what it means to be human, living in a time when “the mask is wearing the face a little more”. For all that might sound ripped from the headlines, Dopamine Chamber embodies the idea with poetry and a frankly thrilling and terrifying aptitude for seduction. Chatten’s lyrics repeatedly question reality and the truth that animates desire while at the same time offering promises of salvation that may or may not be what they seem. Yet the band’s darkly alluring music, full of heady absolution, makes it impossible not to succumb.Fontaines DC: Marianne – videoLead singleMariannemakes that intention explicit. “I can help you disappear,” Chatten chants over spiralling strings – glinting wormholes amid the pearlescent cosmic gloom. It is a massive song, a beckoning void.
