There are few more cringeworthy musical tropes than when bands pre-emptively scale up for stadiums without having the substance to scaffold it – making a meal out of crumbs – but Fontaines pull off that kind of ecstatic overwhelm again and again on Dopamine Chamber.Ahead of the record, guitarist Conor Curley said he wanted to avoid sounds that immediately recalled historic bands. They don’t quite reinvent the wheel – Happy for You has the Cure’s unmistakably sour, lonely twang; Mimesis a roughshod New Order bassline; Demolition a sledgehammer grunge attack – yet they sound more like artefacts in the band’s gorgeous ruin of a soundworld than pastiche. Happy for You is full of beguiling flotsam, subtle echoes of pastoral guitar twang rippling like seaweed in the waves. You could spend a dozen listens focusing on the fine detail here – the agitatedTonguemixes Lankum’s dank chill with a taunting, pisky-like backing singer – but Dopamine Chamber gets its immediacy from Chatten’s scene-stealing vocal performances.He swerves between indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey and an insistent, addictive attack. One Man mixes both: “Do you have a genuine need to be desired / Call me up any time that you wanna fly yeah,” he incants against a wistful string crescendo, radiating both the possibility of redemption and the sense that accepting might mean grasping tight to Icarus’s feathers. At moments, Chatten’s voice hits on the level of pure sensation, feeling almost invasive in its capacity to worm its way into your veins: the way he exhales “I sweeeaaaaar” on Happy for You, or “surelyyou’ll wake up in yourself” on Mimesis.‘It’s impossible not to have contradictions in a contradictory world’: Catalan pop visionary Rosalía on critics, crisis and being ‘hot for God’Read morePlus if you’re going to invite Rosalía to be the first guest on any Fontaines record, you’d better be able to hold your own. Channelling Morricone grandeur and mid-century balladry, the absolutely astonishing duet Where Is Gone? is as spellbinding as Nick Cave and PJ Harvey’sHenry Leeand a peerless would-be Bond theme that’s too good for the ailing franchise. The pair swirl around one another, beautiful and deadly as thick smoke.When the band announced the album’s tracklist on Instagram, a weird number of fans were outraged at the Catalan singer’s presence, as if Fontaines had invited in some popsy rather than the best singer of her generation and an autodidact whose last record wasa concept album about ancient nuns. Clearly, some fans would like Fontaines DC to remain as pickled in aspic as the “beauty queens / Razor-faced / With private means” that Chatten disdains over the rising hiss of closer Intimate. His bitter broadside underscores that trying to cheat death means choosing spiritual death, the Faustian bargain of our times. By emphatically rejecting that fate, Fontaines have grown in dramatic, majestic fashion to become the best band of their generation – the kind that, to nick a phrase from another band, really might live for ever.Explore more on these topicsFontaines DCIndiePop and rockRosalíareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellion | Movies | The Guardian
description: Paul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nation
Author: Stuart Jeffries
Headline: Paul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nation
Content: You say you want a revolution … Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Betina La Plante/Focus Features/APView image in fullscreenYou say you want a revolution … Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Betina La Plante/Focus Features/APMoviesMort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellionPaul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nationStuart JeffriesMon 12 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British are perverse. We fetishise our failures, even if they are essentially tangential to a national narrative that should be about imperial conquest, slavery and being unremittingly unpleasant to foreigners. We tell and retell, for instance, the story of Captain Scott even though he died in Antarctica in 1912 after losing the race to reach the south pole first to the unacceptably Norwegian Roald Amundsen. Similarly, Christopher Nolan’s 2017 film Dunkirk typified the British tendency to snatch national glory from the jaws of defeat. And then there was the tragicomic disaster of the Charge of the Light Brigade during the 1853-56 Crimean war in which our boys raced to putatively glorious if stupid deaths. It’s as if, for us British, pointless sacrifice and embracing failure are what heroism means. And our cinema has colluded with this perversity.But there is an exception to this national veneration of failure. Britain has been reluctant to embrace its revolutionary defeats. There is, for instance, no film dealing with the Chartist movement’s 19th-century struggle for universal suffrage. Even more strikingly yet, it is only now, in 2026, that a film has been made about the calamitous 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, even though it is a pivotal event in British history. Paul Greengrass’sThe Uprising, starring Andrew Garfield as a – let’s just get this over with – revolting peasant, joins a mere handful of other movies, includingKevin Brownlow and Andrew Mollo’s 1975 Winstanley,Bill Douglas’s 1986 ComradesandMike Leigh’s 2018 Peterloo, that dare depict how radical collective action was crushed by a ruthless state.The Uprising review – Paul Greengrass turns revolutionary rage into a Robin Hood origin mythRead moreFor Stephanie Barczewski, author ofHeroic Failure and the British, our fetishisation of glorious disaster is a corollary of the 19th-century British private school ethos of stoic duty and crypto-S&M suffering culled from an ancient Roman exemplar. Revolutionary failure doesn’t fit this template; hence, one might suppose, its absence from our cinema.The Uprising, however, for all its flaws and missteps, is a bold attempt to correct a national wrong by depicting a collective uprising devoid of heroism. Greengrass tries to make sense of how a mass movement of riff-raff from the rough ends of Kent and Essex arose, and how its momentum was compromised of factionalism and conflicting aims. It shows how, ultimately, the revolutionary leaders were duped by the boy king Richard II, leaving the rebels winding up to be either slaughtered en masse in London’s Smithfield or skulking defeated back to their homes to work harder to pay the poll tax whose unfairness they had risen up against in the first place.It is an important – if belated, improbable and commercially dubious – addition to our national story.View image in fullscreenDepicting the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage … Cillian Murphy, right, and Martin Lucey in The Wind That Shakes the Barley.Photograph: Joss BarrattIn contrast, other countries have been more fortunate in their revolutionary heritage and as a result their national cinemas teem with examples of successful uprisings. From the advent of cinema, for instance, Americans have incessantly revelled in making movies about their war of independence – including silent features such as 1917’s The Spirit of 76 and DW Griffith’s America (1924), not to mention Bugs Bunny in Friz Freleng’s delightful period romp of a cartoon Bunker Hill Bunny (1950). The French have been making cinematic homages to their 1789 revolution going back the 1913 biopic Robespierre.In Russia, Grigori Aleksandrov and Sergei Eisenstein’s October, in 1928, typified how the Bolshevik revolution’s success against the odds made Russian spirit what it is. Movies such as Neil Jordan’s Liam Neeson-fronted biopic Michael Collins (1996) and The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006), set during the Irish war of independence and starring Cillian Murphy, depicted the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage – even if the latter had an English director in the shape of Ken Loach.But it isn’t just the deeply classist notion of what failures count as heroic that has made British cinema reluctant to embrace our failed revolutionary heritage. It is the result of how our culture has been reverse-colonised by Hollywood, with historical narratives only deemed filmable if they fit into American movie industry’s tropes. Whenever Hollywood deigns to make a movie about British history, it includes Downton-style upstairs-downstairs hokum, those crazy sexed-up murderous Tudors and, of course, that cod-historical franchise that never stops giving, Robin Hood.Equally, it is axiomatic in Hollywood that political struggles are always about one thing – a very American notion of freedom, individual freedom from presumed oppression. That’s why Mel Gibson’s 1995 Braveheart was possible: even though William Wallace’s struggles against the English ended in failure with his execution at Smithfield (not far from where Wat Tyler was murdered by Richard II’s lackeys), the biopic involved the classic Hollywood trope of the little guy fighting for freedom. Any other political goal (tax reform, wealth redistribution, solidarity, fraternity) scarcely makes a dent in the Hollywood narrative juggernaut.And that’s what makes Greengrass’s The Uprising problematic. Compromised by Hollywood values, it is conflicted about representing a failed political revolution as what it was – a collective struggle. It depicts the Peasants’ Revolt in the frame of one fictional man, Garfield’s Ploughman. Conceived by Greengrass as a representative everyman, Ploughman – with a disregard for historical truth that should make the film’s historical adviser Dan Jones wince – pops up Zelig-like to parlay with the king, catch the king’s mother’s eye, rally the rebels, scythe down the bad guys, as if he were a real-life historical figure. The collective struggle becomes individualised drama, betraying the positioning of the apostrophe – what happened in 1381 was the Peasants’ Revolt not the Peasant’s Revolt.View image in fullscreenCinema has been a failure at depicting the English civil war … Tim Roth and Dougray Scott in To Kill a KingWorse yet, the film includes a very silly coda in which, a year after the defeat of the revolt, Ploughman and a rump of rebels have retreated to the English greenwood to form an outlaw band of unmerry men. The corollary of this coda is to make the Peasants’ Revolt a kind of origin story for the legend of Robin Hood, even though that is nonsense: the folkloric rebel operated – if at all – about 200 years earlier. The whole idea may seem ridiculous, but the US distributors for The Uprising, Focus Features, leaned into this barmy interpretation bychanging the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood earlier this year, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”. Sensible Guardian readers will know of course that Robin Hood was a supporter of Richard I and foe of King John both of whom ruled England almost exactly two centuries earlier.Such absurdities are a great shame since Greengrass’s – worthwhile – intention was to make a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that resonates topically for our age. A collapse in trust of our rulers, a seemingly endless cost of living crisis, widening inequality, political discourse dominated by lies and nonsense: 2026 is more like 1381 than we realise.It’s worth pointing out that there has been one successful military revolution in British history, namely the English civil war. Cinema of course has been a failure at depicting it: there was Ken Hughes’s wildly inaccurate 1970 drama Cromwell starring Richard Harris and Alec Guinness and Mike Barker’s 2003 To Kill a King with Tim Roth and Dougray Scott. But our most enduring and successful revolution was scarcely cinematic: the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 in which the Catholic KingJames IIwas replaced by his Protestant daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William III of Orange was hailed by Bertrand Russell as “the most moderate and successful of all revolutions. Its aims were modest, but they were exactly achieved.” Yawn! Who wants to see that movie?View image in fullscreenIf Carlsberg did revolutionary failures … Winstanley.Photograph: Bfi/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockPerhaps the greatest film about British revolutionary failure was the aforementioned Winstanley, about a group of proto-communists called the Diggers who settled common land on St Georges’s Hill outside Weybridge, Surrey during the English civil war. They hoped to create a utopia devoid of private property and for a few weeks lived self-sufficiently until they were violently evicted by the local gentry. To clinch the point that the Diggers’ experiment was a failure, just go on to property website Rightmove. There you can find a “stunning and elegant” £25m mansion on Cavendish Road, St George’s Hill with “fairway views, seven individually themed bathrooms, two staff apartments, and a leisure complex” and 1.5 acres of carefully landscaped gardens. Not what their leader Gerrard Winstanley wanted at all. He wrote: “Was the Earth made to preserve a few covetous, proud men to live at ease, and for them to bag and barn up the treasures of the Earth from others, that these may beg or starve in a fruitful land; or was it made to preserve all her children?” Our radical history, so often absent from our national cinema, has been built over in a field in Surrey for real estate scarcely any of us can afford. A very British coup if ever there was one.Explore more on these topicsFilmPaul GreengrassBiopicsDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gabrielle Goliath: Elegy review – devastating lament is a furious, single-note call to action | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Too controversial for the Venice Biennale, this haunting video and audio work commemorates murders and genocides with an angry act of mourning
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Too controversial for the Venice Biennale, this haunting video and audio work commemorates murders and genocides with an angry act of mourning
Content: Gabrielle Goliath’s Elegy at Ibraaz in London.Photograph: Ollie HammickView image in fullscreenGabrielle Goliath’s Elegy at Ibraaz in London.Photograph: Ollie HammickArt and designReviewGabrielle Goliath: Elegy review – devastating lament is a furious, single-note call to actionIbraaz, LondonToo controversial for the Venice Biennale, this haunting video and audio work commemorates murders and genocides with an angry act of mourningEddy FrankelMon 12 Oct 2026 07.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sound of mourning spills out into the streets. A single, endless wailing note echoes out of the basement of Ibraaz, a relatively new cultural centre in London’s Fitzrovia. This is Gabrielle Goliath’s heart-wrenching Elegy, each of its three films featuring a woman singing just one note until their lungs falter and another woman steps up to fill in for her. Just as a note is about to die, it is sustained. It’s a haunting, shocking act of mourning for murder, injustice and genocide.And it almost never made it.A panel of five leading South African cultural voices picked Goliath’s work to represent their nation at this summer’s Venice Biennale. Goliath has been working on the project for a decade, collecting voices, collecting stories. This was a work about femicide and the murder of LGBTQ+ people in South Africa, but it had expanded. The latest iteration dealt withthe Ovaherero and Nama genocide in Namibia, and the death of a Palestinian poet in 2023. It was a step too far for Gayton McKenzie, South Africa’s sport, arts and culture minister.View image in fullscreenGabrielle Goliath, Elegy, at Ibraaz London.Photograph: Ollie HammickMcKenzie is the president of the far-right Patriotic Alliance party, and has been vocal in his support of Israel in recent years. He wrote a letter describing the work as “highly divisive”. He called for the work to be edited, for the offending passage about the Palestinian poet to be removed. Goliath refused, so McKenzie put a stop to the whole thing, cancelling her Venice pavilion.She fought it tooth and nail, taking her case to South Africa’s high court, but the case was dismissed. The South Africa pavilion at the biennale sat embarrassingly empty, a big, glaring visual metaphor for the global reach of the culture wars and a symbol of censorship in the face of violence.Goliath instead founda home for the work in a nearby church, which is where I first saw it. It was devastating then, an almost overwhelmingly emotional piece of art in a beautiful setting. Ibraaz lacks the ornate, quiet atmosphere of that Venetian church, but has made up for it with absolute sombre darkness. The space is pitch black save for the screens. One film is in commemoration of Ipeleng Christine Moholane, a woman who was strangled and left for dead in a field near Johannesburg in 2015. Another is in honour of two women who died at the hands of German colonial oppressors during the genocide in Namibia between 1904 and 1908. The third is for the poetHiba Abu Nadaand the thousands of Palestinians who have died in Gaza since 2023.This is not a soft, plaintive lament – the room is a discordant, uncomfortable place, filled with a wailing cacophony of clashing vibrato and just out of tune notes. It sounds angry, vicious, furious, because it is. It’s not just an act of commemoration, it’s a call to action, a demand for change and justice.While it’s incredibly emotional and deeply moving, the main feeling you get is frustration and hopelessness, not sadness. What makes Elegy so powerful is the endless proliferation of horrifying images we have to deal with on a daily basis. If you want to see images of death and genocide, you just have to look at social media or the news. We have more access to shocking, real imagery of awful current events than ever before. But Goliath has stripped the imagery away and left you with only the emotion, so just the anger and heartache remains.It’s an act of resistance against the image economy, against murder and femicide, against violence and genocide. It’s a feminist lament, a scream against it all.But it’s also a significant modern artwork, a symbol of our times, of our wars and cultural frictions, and its sound lingers in your ears long after you’ve walked away.Gabrielle Goliath: Elegyis at Ibraaz, London, from 8 October to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtPerformance artExhibitionsSouth AfricaAfricaVenice BiennalereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Corruption has only got worse’: can a new version of Our Friends in the North still shock audiences 30 years on? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Peter Flannery’s 90s TV drama classic is getting a theatre reworking in Newcastle. The director and cast talk about doing justice to its themes of scandal and decay – and emulating its star-making actors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Peter Flannery’s 90s TV drama classic is getting a theatre reworking in Newcastle. The director and cast talk about doing justice to its themes of scandal and decay – and emulating its star-making actors
Content: Tyne after time … (From left) The stage cast of Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years: Ryan Nolan, Sam Neale, Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull.Photograph: Chris Bishop/PicturesbyBishView image in fullscreenTyne after time … (From left) The stage cast of Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years: Ryan Nolan, Sam Neale, Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull.Photograph: Chris Bishop/PicturesbyBishTheatre‘Corruption has only got worse’: can a new version of Our Friends in the North still shock audiences 30 years on?Peter Flannery’s 90s TV drama classic is getting a theatre reworking in Newcastle. The director and cast talk about doing justice to its themes of scandal and decay – and emulating its star-making actorsNeil ArmstrongMon 12 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a small room at the top of Newcastle upon Tyne’s Live theatre, four actors are bringing to life the principal characters from one of British television’s best-loved dramas. Sitting around a table strewn with coffee cups, water bottles and annotated scripts, Tosker and Geordie have been boozing in a nightclub and weighing up their chances of pulling. Mary and Nicky have been arguing about whether they have a future together.The scenes are from a new stage version ofOur Friends in the North, the landmark nine-episode series first broadcast in 1996 on BBC Two. Set against a backdrop of Labour politics and police corruption, it charted 30 years in the lives of four working-class geordies and made stars of Mark Strong, Daniel Craig, Gina McKee and Christopher Eccleston. It was a hit with critics and viewers, won awards and regularly makes “greatest ever” lists.Now it is back, after Live theatre’s artistic director Jack McNamara persuaded an initially reluctant Peter Flannery, the writer, to return to the characters he first created for a Royal Shakespeare Company play in 1982, before later rewriting and expanding the story for the screen.View image in fullscreenGeordie sure things … (From left) Christopher Eccleston, Gina McKee, Mark Strong and Daniel Craig in the 1996 TV series of Our Friends in the North.Photograph: BBC Photolibrary“In a way, the production came from a sense of frustration, of always having to think small and manageable in a historically underfunded region,” says McNamara. “We needed a bigger gesture. A wider story for a larger audience that had a familiar outline, but still something no one has seen on stage before. Put simply, I wanted to direct 12 actors on a big stage in a brand new work. The significance and agility of Our Friends offers a rare opportunity for that to happen.”Because of the scale of the show and its potential afterlife, it is a co-production between Live theatre, theTheatreRoyal in Newcastle upon Tyne and the theatre producers Eastlake Productions.Flannery has reworked two of the TV episodes, set in 1979 and 1984, into a two-act play. He has introduced a chorus and there are a couple of borrowings from other episodes for explanatory purposes. The stage design allows for it to be a fast-moving show.double quotation markI’m aware it is a bleak view of society, but the characters are survivorsPeter FlanneryOn TV, McKee was the only one of the four principal players who was from the region. For the play, four actors from the north-east have been cast. Ryan Nolan is the political idealist Nicky (Eccleston on TV). Sam Neale is the quietly driven Mary (McKee). Jack Robertson plays the would-be entrepreneurial Tosker (Strong). Scott Turnbull is the luckless Geordie (Craig).At the table read, a few days before rehearsals with the full cast begin, various scenes are stress-tested under the guidance of McNamara. There’s a long discussion about how best to make a particular joke land, and the two actors concerned try it in a number of different ways. In the script, one character is reprimanded for missing his son’s football final. “‘Football final’ is a bit of a cliche,” jokes Turnbull. “Maybe it should be a ‘bassoon recital’.” Everyone laughs.The actors want to know whether McNamara expects them to model their performances on their TV predecessors, but he is not interested in impersonations. The way to pay tribute to the originators of the roles, he says, is to do their own thing. There’s a sense of relief but the four are acutely aware that Our Friends in the North is a cherished TV show, and there is a weight of expectation.“I’m trying not to get into an anxiety spiral about it but it is there, looming,” says Neale, who recalls watching the show with her mum.“I do feel like there’s a lot of pressure,” says Turnbull. “This needs to be executed well.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen… Live theatre’s artistic director Jack McNamara.Photograph: Chris OrdMcNamara is well aware of the pressure the cast are feeling but he likes to keep things loose. “There is always an element of experimenting,” he says. “I don’t storyboard things down to a T. I like to have a little openness so that in rehearsals it feels like anything is possible.”Understandably, McNamara can’t help but imagine where things might go next. There are hopes the show will have a life beyond its short run in Newcastle but “it has to land here and have real resonance before it goes anywhere else”, McNamara says.Later, at the full-cast rehearsals, the energy level is palpably higher than at the table read. After a couple of hours, McNamara asks the performers to improvise various scenes. Improvisation is not a memory test, he reminds them, but a way of exploring intentionality. There are clear glimpses of what has the potential to be a powerful theatrical experience.“The show is about friendship and how it evolves and fractures. And there’s a lot about political optimism and political failure and how they sit alongside each other,” McNamara says.“The chances of real change through the Labour party is the central preoccupation of Our Friends in the North,” wrote the late campaigning journalist Paul Foot, but no one could consider the show – or the play – a paean of praise for politicians, especially their relationship with the police. In Our Friends – some of which was based on a scandal uncovered by Foot – decent Labour politicians are bested by cynical spivs and extremists. Honest police officers are outmanoeuvred, and perhaps outnumbered, by bent coppers. Lawmaking and law enforcement are rotten to the core.Although it was well researched and based on fact, Flannery says some viewers of the TV series thought the police corruption strand of the story had been exaggerated. “I don’t know that anybody’s going to be shocked now like they were 30 years ago,” he says. “That [corruption] has got worse. There have been serving officers prosecuted for rape and murder since then.”Of the political chicanery, Flannery says: “I can’t see what might have changed. The publicity around Neil Hamilton and Mohamed Al-Fayed and the ‘cash for questions’ affair must have made them change their tactics, but I think they’re still at it. There are so many paid lobbyists hanging around parliament now. What are they there for if not to suborn MPs and buy their votes and their support? It’s what’s ruined American politics and if we’re not careful it will ruin British politics as well.”As he approaches 75, Flannery says this will probably be the last thing he writes. “I’m acutely aware that I’m handing the audience a fairly bleak view of society,” he says. “However, the characters are vibrant and they’re all survivors, even Geordie, who seems to be kind of indomitable. No matter what bucket of shit gets poured over him he gets up and has another go. I want the audience to take hope from the characters.”Flannery insists he sees the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister as a positive thing. “I think the whole system is against him and he’ll find his road blocked at every turn. I’ve watched this rolling around again and again and there isn’t usually any real change. But, I’m an optimist. It is a triumph of hope over experience but until I’m proven wrong, I’ll hang on to that.”Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Yearsis at the Theatre Royal, Newcastle upon Tyne,15 to 24 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34 | RJ Mitte | The Guardian
description: Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation
Author: Mollie Reilly
Headline: Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representation
Content: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte, who has died aged 34.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBreaking Bad actor RJ Mitte, who has died aged 34.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianRJ MitteRJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad role, dies aged 34Mitte, who played Walter White Jr on acclaimed show, had cerebral palsy and advocated for disability representationMollie ReillyMon 12 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 21.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBreaking Badactor RJ Mitte died on Monday aged 34, his representatives confirmed.Mitte died in Brownsville,Texas. No cause of death was given.“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocateRJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”The Brownsville Police Department said no foul play was suspected and the investigation into his death was ongoing. Cameron County justice of the peace, Cyndi Hinojosa told the Associated Press that an autopsy would be performed.From the age of 15, Mitte played Walter White Jr, the son ofBryan Cranston’s high school chemistry teacher turned drug kingpin, on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, which isoftencitedas one of the best television programs of all time.Mitte had cerebral palsy, a condition he shared with hisBreaking Badcharacter.In 2015, hespoke to the Guardianabout being a disabled actor who plays disabled characters.“You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have.”Mitte’s costars paid tribute to him after news of his death broke.Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said in a statement: “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed.”Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr’s uncle Hank Schrader,wroteon social media: “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”In addition to Breaking Bad, Mitte had roles on several series, including Switched at Birth and The Guardians of Justice. Just days before his death, he waspromotinghis new movie, Talking to Strangers, billed as a “romantic tragedy”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier this month, Mitteappearedon the Joe Vulpis Podcast, speaking in depth about his time on Breaking Bad. He noted his character was based on a real-life friend of the show’s creator,Vince Gilligan.“It really felt real playing this character and getting into the groove with this character,” Mitte said.Offscreen, Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.Born in 1992, Mitte was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. In a2016 interviewwith the Guardian, he said he found out he was adopted when he was eight years old.“My step-brother told me. He’d overheard my mum and my stepdad at the time talking about it, and he threw it in my face. But I didn’t really care. It didn’t seem relevant, because I never once in my life felt unloved or like I was a burden.”Explore more on these topicsRJ MitteBreaking BadUS televisionTelevisionDisabilityDramaCelebritynewsShareReuse this content

title: Selma Blair arrested at JFK after she allegedly attacked flight attendants | Selma Blair | The Guardian
description: Several news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Several news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door
Content: Actor Selma Blair attends Variety’s 2026 Power of Women: Los Angeles event in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 September.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenActor Selma Blair attends Variety’s 2026 Power of Women: Los Angeles event in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 September.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersSelma BlairSelma Blair arrested at JFK after she allegedly attacked flight attendantsSeveral news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane doorMaya Yangin New YorkMon 12 Oct 2026 16.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actorSelma Blairwas arrested on Sunday at John F Kennedy (JFK) airport inNew Yorkon allegations that she attacked flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight, according to officials.Blair’s arrest happened at about 11pm, after Port Authority ofNew Yorkand New Jersey officials said they responded to a call “about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Air Lines flight 938 which was parked at the gate” at JFK after arriving from Los Angeles (LAX).Blair, 54, “was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation”, the port authority also said on Monday. “Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation.”The port authority said the FBI – which handles reports of crimes on airplanes – was investigating Sunday’s allegations against Blair.Asked to comment on Blair’s arrest, a Delta spokesperson said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”.The spokesperson added that Blair’s arrest did not affect the flight she and her fellow passengers were on – and that it still landed ahead of schedule at JFK.Several news outlets on Mondayreportedthat Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door.Statements released by officials did not immediately address those reported details.But an air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying “one flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks”.“I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which waspublishedby NBC Los Angeles.The flight controller replied that paramedics were approaching the gate – and that law enforcement was already there.The Guardian has reached out to Blair’s representatives for additional comment. Her publicisttoldthe Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.”Sunday marked at least the second time Blair was reported to be involved in such an incident. In 2016, shereportedlybegan screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico.Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”.“That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time.The actor has also made news headlines for a 2018multiple sclerosisdiagnosis. And in February 2024, sheapologizedfor an Islamophobic comment on social media.Blair’s starring film credits include Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy. She earned a best spoken world album for children nomination at the 2011 Grammy awards, for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition.Explore more on these topicsSelma BlairNew YorkUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history | The Archers | The Guardian
description: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures
Content: The Archers’ current recording studio at the BBC Mailbox in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Archers’ current recording studio at the BBC Mailbox in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe ArchersBBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year historyPlans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measuresMichael SavageMedia editorMon 12 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is set to stop recordingThe Archersin Birmingham for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after scrapping plans for a radio drama theatre that was to be the new home of the world’s longest-running soap opera.A pledge to move recordings to the so-called Tea Factory, the BBC’s new Birmingham hub in Digbeth, has become the latest victim of thecorporation’s £500m cuts plan.While the soap’s production team are still scheduled to make the move, theBBCis now looking to record it at an existing UK studio.It will also consider private studios in theWest Midlands, but BBC insiders are already concerned that ending its Birmingham-based recordings and separating the actors from the production crew will have an impact on the show.Production staff regularly engage with the actors at the last minute to tweak scripts and storylines, raising concerns that their being in different places will stifle creativity.“It is going to weaken the show,” said a source. “It will change the DNA of the show.”BBC axes long-running Radio 4 show You and Yours in push towards podcastsRead moreMoving the recording of The Archers from the BBC’s existingBirminghambase, The Mailbox, to the Tea Factory was due to take place in 2028.In an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth.“Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK.“To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings.“The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.”The show has been associated with Birmingham since it started in 1951. Sources said it remained part of the cultural fabric of the city, and the show employs local writers and freelancers.However, others said the show’s recording schedule meant actors were only in the studio for about eight days a month, while many of the cast live across the UK.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome now fear recordings will default to London and that the show’s staff will eventually follow. However, the BBC has been clear that production staff will move to the new Birmingham headquarters as planned.It is not clear whether Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, was aware of the plans. Boosting BBC production outside London has regularly been at the top of her agenda.It is a sign that even some of the BBC’s most revered titles are being affected by cuts, with more announcements expected in the coming days. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has already faced anger from staff who believe more of the corporation’s manager class should be targeted instead.BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cutsRead moreA BBC spokesperson said: “We recognise and value The Archers’ longstanding relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme’s future, and The Archers production team will remain in their current home in the Mailbox and move, as planned, to the Tea Factory in Digbeth in early 2028.“However, after careful consideration, as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, we are no longer building a new recording studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory.“We’re currently assessing the BBC’s existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands to find a more cost-effective solution.”Explore more on these topicsThe ArchersBirminghamRadio dramaWest MidlandsSoap operaRadioPublic service broadcastingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alex Gibney says Universal ‘wavered’ over releasing Elon Musk documentary | Movies | The Guardian
description: The revelation comes after the four-hour film’s Venice premiere drew a string of criticisms and insults from the founder of SpaceXAI
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The revelation comes after the four-hour film’s Venice premiere drew a string of criticisms and insults from the founder of SpaceXAI
Content: A douche? … Alex Gibney and Elon Musk.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenA douche? … Alex Gibney and Elon Musk.Photograph: APMoviesAlex Gibney says Universal ‘wavered’ over releasing Elon Musk documentaryThe revelation comes after the four-hour film’s Venice premiere drew a string of criticisms and insults from the founder of SpaceXAIAndrew PulverMon 12 Oct 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Gibney, director of the new four-hour documentary about Elon Musk, said that Universal, owners of the film’s international distribution rights “wavered” over releasing the film outside North America.Gibney was speaking to the New York Timesas the film opened in the US (where it is being released by the independent distributor Bleecker Street), and appeared to confirma story in the Hollywood Reporterthat Universal, which hadacquired the international rights to the film in 2023, had got cold feet. Asked by the New York Times, “Did Universal Pictures waver in setting up its international release plans?” Gibney replied: “Yes.”Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead moreA subsequent story in Variety suggested thatUniversal had been concerned about “legal threats from Musk”, but that the studio had “always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally”. Gibney was asked: “So it wasn’t about legal clearances?” The film-maker replied: “You can walk and chew gum at the same time.”However, it appears plans are back on track, as Gibney added: “We just had a meeting with [Universal], and we’re talking very concretely about a release plan.”Gibney also said his producer Jessie Deeter, who knew Musk from two previous films, had attempted on several occasions to ask Musk to be interviewed for the film. Musk’s response was topost “Gibney is a douche”on X, the social media platform owned by Musk-founded company SpaceXAI.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreIn the wake of the film’s premiere at the Venice film festival,Musk posted a string of criticisms of the film and insults aimed at Gibney, including calling the film a “hit piece that misses” and threatening legal action.Universal declined to comment further, pointing to its previous statement: “We’ve always been committed to releasing this film, and our plans haven’t changed.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAlex GibneyUniversal PicturesElon MuskDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Celebrity Traitors’ Julie Hesmondhalgh: theatres should be 100% faithful to ‘local stories’ | Theatre | The Guardian
description: As she leaves the Traitors castle to star in The Pelicot Trial and receive a lifetime achievement award, the actor has highlighted a ‘loss of regional identity’ caused by funding pressures on UK theatres
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: As she leaves the Traitors castle to star in The Pelicot Trial and receive a lifetime achievement award, the actor has highlighted a ‘loss of regional identity’ caused by funding pressures on UK theatres
Content: ‘There’s room in my heart for the classics’ … Julie Hesmondhalgh on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertView image in fullscreen‘There’s room in my heart for the classics’ … Julie Hesmondhalgh on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertTheatreCelebrity Traitors’ Julie Hesmondhalgh: theatres should be 100% faithful to ‘local stories’As she leaves the Traitors castle to star in The Pelicot Trial and receive a lifetime achievement award, the actor has highlighted ‘a loss of regional identity’ caused by funding pressures on UK theatresChris WiegandStage editorMon 12 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been “a loss of regional identity” in the stories on stages around the UK due to the challenging circumstances facing theatres, according toJulie Hesmondhalgh.The actor, who last week was the fourth contestant to leave The Celebrity Traitors, observed that for financial reasons regional theatres are increasingly making co-productions with other venues. This can lead to a “generic” product, she said, rather than a show that specifically says something about the local area.Hesmondhalgh highlighted the phenomenal impact ofJames Graham’s Punch, a drama about restorative justice, which opened at Nottingham Playhouse in 2024 and was based on the true story of a one-punch death in the city. The play, which brought Hesmondhalghan Olivier awardfor her performance as the victim’s mother, went from Nottingham to the West End, a UK tour and Broadway. “New work is always so hard to sell but because it was such a local story, and by James Graham, it sold,” she said.Asked if programming had become risk-averse since Covid, Hesmondhalgh said: “It’s really hard for regional theatres. There’s room in my heart for musicals and Noël Coward. There’s a familiarity about the old classics that people love. But the world of co-pros is making things very difficult for people. In order to survive as a regional theatre now, you have to necessarily make so many co-productions with other regional theatres. There’s a definite loss of regional identity, locally made productions.”View image in fullscreenJulie Hesmondhalgh at home in Tameside, Greater Manchester, in 2020.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHesmondhalgh, who led a successful campaign to save Oldham Coliseum from closure, was earlier this year appointed as a guest curator for its reopening programme. The building is undergoing major refurbishment and redevelopment by the council. It will stage shows that have “a distinctive Oldham mark, a Coliseum mark” as well as work that will visit other venues. The actor stressed “the amount of fundraising we’re having to do to make some regionally specific work because we know we won’t be able to co-pro it”. The experience, she said, has given her “a new empathy for people trying to run regional theatres – it’s not easy”.When audiences watch shows with a genuine local resonance – productions “that are of and for them” – there is a visceral response, Hesmondhalgh added. She described witnessing such a response when she watched Beth Steel’s Till the Stars Come Down, the tale of a Mansfield community, when it ran atNottingham Playhouselast month. “It’s a real experience being an actor in a play in Oldham and Nottingham. Every time there’s the mention of a place [the audience] recognise, there’s a ripple of approval – it’s wonderful.”Next month Hesmondhalgh, 56, will receive the lifetime achievement prize at the inaugural Great British Theatres awards to mark the 50th anniversary ofTheatres Trust, the national advice and advocacy body for UK theatres. Its CEO, Joshua McTaggart, said the award “is to recognise someone who shares Theatres Trust’s belief that everyone should have access to theatre and live performance no matter where they live or what their background is. There is no one in the public eye who embodies this spirit more than Julie Hesmondhalgh. Julie has used her platform as one of the country’s most beloved actors to bang the drum for inclusive and equitable access to the performing arts and champion important community theatres.”Hesmondhalgh, who is from Accrington in Lancashire, had a recent TV hit withMr Bates vs the Post Officeand will soon star on stage in the Young Vic’s documentary theatre productionThe Pelicot Trialat County Hall in London. She joked that the award may be a tad premature – “I still think I’m 19!” – and said that she had been fortunate to appear in “a disproportionate number of plays and TV shows that have had something to say about the world, and that I’ve been so proud to be a part of”.She expressed faith, too, in Andy Burnham’s understanding of the arts. “He’s been to the theatre and seen me in stuff in Manchester and engaged with that. On a real level he knows that communities coming together – for a gig or a football match or a play – matters. I think he’s got a handle on that. I do have quite a lot of faith in him to deliver on that. For communities that are struggling, having a cultural policy and investment in culture is always a tool for regeneration.”Explore more on these topicsTheatreJulie HesmondhalghNottingham PlayhouseJames GrahamAwards and prizesThe TraitorsTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary
Content: 1:55NAZA - official trailerNAZANAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s intervieweesIsraeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentaryLorenzo TondoMon 12 Oct 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentaryNAZAand prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini,the Israeli prime minister demandedthey “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where itwon the special jury prizeafter receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicatehow many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.View image in fullscreenNAZA’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival last month.Photograph: Capital Pictures/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor,threatening to strip them of their citizenshipand accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it ofspreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”View image in fullscreenGraffiti depicting Abraham and Szor, and the word ‘traitors’ in Hebrew, appeared on a wall in Ashdod, southern Israel, after NAZA was awarded the special jury prize at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersNAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sourcesfamiliar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.In recent days, the Israeli governmenthas promoted an online film projectthat mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival,have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuPalestinePress freedomHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re in a brotherhood now’: the Bill Pickett rodeo – photo essay | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: For several years, Chloe Kerleroux has been photographing African American cowboy communities in the southern US. Her work has mainly focused on trail rides: large gatherings where horses, music, dancing, family and community life come together. This year, she explored rodeo culture including at the Bill Pickett invitational in Atlanta
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For several years, Chloe Kerleroux has been photographing African American cowboy communities in the southern US. Her work has mainly focused on trail rides: large gatherings where horses, music, dancing, family and community life come together. This year, she explored rodeo culture including at the Bill Pickett invitational in Atlanta
Content: Portrait of members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, many of whom are of Caribbean origin, after the competition at the Bill Pickett Invitational Rodeo in Conyers, Georgia, on 1 August 2026. Photograph: Chloe KerlerouxFor several years, Chloe Kerleroux has been photographing African American cowboy communities in the southern US. Her work has mainly focused on trail rides: large gatherings where horses, music, dancing, family and community life come together. This year, she explored rodeo culture including at the Bill Pickett invitational in AtlantaByChloe KerlerouxMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe image of the cowboy widely portrayed in westerns and popular culture has long been almost exclusively white. Yet Black cowboys hold an important place in the history of the American west. After the civil war and the abolition of slavery, many African Americans found work on ranches and on the great cattle drives westward. By the late 19th century, historians estimate about one in four cowboys were Black.Among the Black figures who shaped this history wasBill Pickett. Born in Texas in 1870, he became one of the most celebrated Black cowboys and rodeo performers of his time, known in particular for popularising bulldogging, which would eventually give rise to modern steer wrestling.View image in fullscreenAfter the national anthem, Josh, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted, rides around the arena to a pounding hip-hop track as his teammates cheer him on at the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo in Conyers, nearAtlanta, Georgia, on 2 August 2026View image in fullscreenMembers of the Outlaws Most Wanted joke and playfully challenge other riders, some of whom have travelled long distances to compete, backstage at the rodeoHis name was chosen by the promoter Lu Vason when he created the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. In 1977, Vason attended Cheyenne frontier days and was struck by the absence of Black cowboys in the arena. His research led him to the Black American West Museum in Denver, where he discovered the story of Pickett and the history of African Americans in the American west. In 1984, he created a rodeo designed to give Black cowboys and cowgirls a platform and bring greater visibility to this heritage.More than 40 years later, that mission remains at the heart of the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. Part sporting competition, part spectacle and part space for passing on history and culture, its 2026 tour crosses the US from February to October, with stops including Memphis, Atlanta, Oakland and Los Angeles.This year, I decided to join the tour in Atlanta.View image in fullscreenA family on horseback waits to enter the arena at therodeo, reflecting the intergenerational nature of a cowboy culture passed down through families. 1 August 2026While there, I met for the first time a contact I had been speaking with before my trip. He runs Diamondcut Ranch, where he works with and trains horses, and around which a wider community of riders has formed. It was there that I met the Outlaws Most Wanted, a team of “bronc riders” competing at the Bill Pickett.The organisers allowed me behind the barriers on the condition that I stayed with them. I found myself in the space just behind the arena, where the riders wait for their turn and prepare their equipment.Music is everywhere. The riders joke around, encourage one another and build each other up. The energy and adrenaline rise as their turn approaches, until each rider has to move away from that collective excitement and focus on the few seconds waiting for him in the arena.View image in fullscreenRachied Robins, AKA Django, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, who became my main contact and a key voice in telling the group’s story during the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. 1/08/2026One of them, Rachied Robins, AKA Django, describes the Outlaws Most Wanted as a group of Caribbean men, some of whom have come from difficult backgrounds, brought together by their love of horses. Some, he says, found “refuge in this horse world”. Over time, their bonds grew stronger: “We’re in a brotherhood now.”Django grew up in Kissimmee, Florida, surrounded by rodeo culture. He started out in bull riding before changing disciplines after a bull stomped on his face. He now competes in ranch bronc riding and laughingly describes himself as an “adrenaline junkie”.But behind the adrenaline, there is also fear. Before he gets on the horse, thoughts of the danger and all the “what ifs” run through his mind. Then he has to find a way to clear his head.View image in fullscreenThe Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team at the Bill Pickett rodeo“You just gotta clear your mind and leave it in God’s hands.”He has to trust his technique and make it through eight seconds. And even once the ride is over, the danger is not: Django tells me that getting off the horse can be one of the most dangerous moments.There is also a financial side to competing. Django tells me that the Bill Pickett is not among the rodeos offering the largest purses: at the April event he competed in, he says a rider could win up to about $1,500 (£1,135), compared with as much as $10,000 at some other rodeos. But money is only part of what is at stake.“It’s not just the money, but also your name, the respect, ranking.”What struck me most about the Bill Pickett, however, perhaps happens beyond the competition itself.View image in fullscreenRiders wait to enter the arena in a solemn moment, hats held over their hearts, as The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella at sunset before the start of the rodeoBefore the events begin, The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella. Hats are placed over hearts, the riders stand still, and silence falls across the stands and the arena. I remember getting goosebumps and tears in my eyes.Then, almost without transition, the atmosphere shifts completely and the adrenaline takes over.All the riders enter the arena to a powerful hip-hop track. The volume rises, the horses come in, and the crowd shouts, applauds and dances. Within moments, the atmosphere moves from solemn stillness to an almost explosive energy.That contrast captures much of what I felt at the Bill Pickett. History and memory are central to the event, but they are not frozen in the past. They coexist with hip-hop, fashion, competition and a deeply contemporary Black cowboy culture.View image in fullscreenAfter his ride, a cowboy walks along the edge of the arena as the crowd cheers him on at the Bill PickettThe audience is very much part of the spectacle. Western shirts, cowboy hats and boots fill the stands: people come to watch the rodeo, but also to gather, dance, show their style and celebrate a shared culture. Throughout the event, the announcers return again and again to the history of Black cowboys and the values the Bill Pickett seeks to pass on. That history is not confined to a few lines in a programme: it is an integral part of the event.When I ask Django what the Bill Pickett means to him, he tells me that it is about more than just rodeo: “Bill Pickett means a lot to me personally. Not just because it’s a rodeo, but because it’s a platform for us minorities to come together.”He talks about being able to show what they can do “as a group, as a unit”, but also about having a place where he can be himself and where he feels at home.The Outlaws Most Wanted do not compete only at Black rodeos. Django tells me they compete wherever they have the opportunity and rejects the idea that these events are a form of separation. For him, they are above all about making a heritage visible: “We just want to bring out our heritage and bring out our history and show that we are part of this history, and this is part of our history.”View image in fullscreenMembers of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arenaIt is also about passing something on. From trail rides to rodeos, horses create a space around which families, friendships and communities are formed. For some members of the Outlaws Most Wanted, this world has even become a refuge.When I ask Django what he hopes the young people in the stands take away from watching him ride, he does not talk about becoming a cowboy or winning competitions. Above all, he hopes to show them that another path is possible: “Do something safe, do something legal, get out the streets, keep your mind right, don’t be another statistic.”More than a century after Black cowboys helped shape the history of the American west while remaining largely absent from its popular image, the Bill Pickett offers a space where this heritage does not belong only to the past: it continues to be lived, passed on and reinvented.Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayBlack US cultureGeorgiaHorsesPhotographyAtlantafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Being Muslim After 9/11 review – other journalists wouldn’t dare to air this | Television | The Guardian
description: Mobeen Azhar isn’t afraid to tackle hard topics in a brilliant documentary about the rise of Islamophobia – even when it involves hearing criticism about his own decisions
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: Mobeen Azhar isn’t afraid to tackle hard topics in a brilliant documentary about the rise of Islamophobia – even when it involves hearing criticism about his own decisions
Content: A fascinating discussion … Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan in Being Muslim After 9/11.Photograph: BBC/ForestView image in fullscreenA fascinating discussion … Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan in Being Muslim After 9/11.Photograph: BBC/ForestTV reviewTelevisionReviewBeing Muslim After 9/11 review – other journalists wouldn’t dare to air thisMobeen Azhar isn’t afraid to tackle hard topics in a brilliant documentary about the rise of Islamophobia – even when it involves hearing criticism about his own decisionsJack SealeMon 12 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2024, the journalist Mobeen Azhar made a documentary calledSmall Town, Big Riotthat ought to have been highly influential, but, in our atomised modern media landscape, wasn’t. He deconstructed how anti-immigrant racists, radicalised by online propaganda, lies and hearsay, end up on the streets perpetrating shocking violence and rioting against a largely imaginary foe.Azhar’s new film tackles a wider, thornier problem and is less satisfying as a result. But in his willingness to debate hard topics – even if it means hearing difficult arguments, some of which are aimed at him personally – he is still provoking thoughts and airing views that better-known journalists would never go near.“There was a time, 25 years ago, when being British and Muslim was … OK, you know?” he says. “We were on the cover of magazines and getting elected to parliament. We even captained the England cricket team. And then this happened.” Cut to footage of the World Trade Center’s twin towers exploding on 11 September 2001.The world has not been the same since– and life for British Muslims certainly hasn’t.In the film, Azhar charts a quarter of a century of rising Islamophobia, his concern being how Muslims – and Muslim film-makers like him – have reacted. To do this, he teams up with an older documentarist, Masood Khan, who is the programme’s co-director and is often seen jammed into Azhar’s passenger seat wielding a handheld camera, to get those obligatory “musing while driving” shots. As the film develops, he becomes one of Azhar’s most important interlocutors, but he sticks to his main job as Azhar makes his first visit, to the Birmingham house of Salma Yaqoob.View image in fullscreen‘The fire is still the same’ … Salma Yaqoob and Azhar.Photograph: BBC/ForestYaqoob’s career in politics began when she was spat at in the street soon after 9/11, having previously been just “Salma, a mum at the school gate”. In 2003, she helped to organisethe biggest political demonstration in British history, against the forthcoming invasion of Iraq. “It was an amazing day,” she remembers. “Such a sea of humanity. And yeah, there was that hope.” Azhar comments that her weary countenance suggests the hope has now gone. “The fire is still the same,” Yaqoob says, although her eyes say different.While the consequence for Muslims in Iraq was that they were killed in large numbers, the less serious repercussions here were still deeply troubling. Azhar explains how radical Islamist agitators took advantage when their warnings about protests going unheeded were proved to be correct; they began preaching loudly against integration and in support of violent resistance. At the time, Azhar and Khan made films about the phenomenon; now, to their great credit, they are willing to listen to people who think that was a treacherous mistake.Alyas Karmani in Bradford and Farasat Latif in Luton are community leaders who have worked to deradicalise local Muslim men. Karmani is combative and Latif gentle, but both accuse Azhar of fanning the flames of Islamophobia by helping to boost an unrepresentative fringe. “The problem is the disproportionate publicity these people got,” Latif says. “They were given a platform on mainstream media because they fed into that narrative, post-9/11 and -7/7, that there was this huge Islamic threat.”View image in fullscreenAzhar with Ivan, a reformed former EDL organiser.Photograph: BBC/ForestThese meetings lead Azhar and Khan to debate their film-making careers. On the one hand, a journalist holds a mirror up to society and can’t be expected to ignore inconvenient truths; on the other, journalism is a series of choices about what to cover and what to ignore, and the choice of where to put one’s limited resources can have profound effects.Azhar goes to Lowestoft to meet Ivan, a reformed former organiser for the far-right English Defence League. He says the EDL used the 2007 Dispatches film Undercover Mosque and Stacey Dooley’s 2012 BBC documentary My Hometown Fanatics as recruitment videos and that he was radicalised by the media appearances of the much-quoted extremist preacher Anjem Choudary, nowserving a life sentencefor running a banned terrorist organisation.Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfoldRead moreAzhar and Khan’s fascinating discussion about that becomes, in the film’s closing scenes, laden with sad exhaustion. Azhar admits to feeling worn down by the events of 2017, when terror atrocities atWestminster Bridge,London Bridgeand theManchester Arenaprovoked a retaliatoryattack on a north London mosque. In 2026, as Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, agitates against Islam on the streets of London, Khan doesn’t go to cover it, to Azhar’s angry dismay. He’s had enough.Azhar keeps reporting on the ground, trying and failing to make sense of the chaos outside Yaxley-Lennon’s appearance at a cursed Oxford Union debate. Seeing that something has gone badly wrong is easy; pinpointing what could or should have been done to stop it is not. Life as a British Muslim, meanwhile, only gets harder.Being Muslim After 9/11 aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kerry Washington takes A-listers back to the streets they grew up on: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Scandal star talks to Ben Affleck about his childhood in Massachusetts. Plus, the Eras strand returns with the story of 90s pop phenomenon the Spice Girls
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The Scandal star talks to Ben Affleck about his childhood in Massachusetts. Plus, the Eras strand returns with the story of 90s pop phenomenon the Spice Girls
Content: Celebrity chat … Kerry Washington hosts Street You Grew Up On.Photograph: Jim Ruymen/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCelebrity chat … Kerry Washington hosts Street You Grew Up On.Photograph: Jim Ruymen/UPI/ShutterstockBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioKerry Washington takes A-listers back to the streets they grew up on: best podcasts of the weekThe Scandal star talks to Ben Affleck about his childhood in Massachusetts. Plus, the Eras strand returns with the story of 90s pop phenomenon the Spice GirlsHannah J Davies,Alexi DugginsandHollie RichardsonMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekStreet You Grew Up OnScandal star Kerry Washington’s web series is now a podcast, with big-name guests talking about the places they were raised. Cambridge, Massachusetts local Ben Affleck is the first to have a frank conversation on his parents’ divorce, and the things he didn’t tell his mum – such as being mugged at knifepoint at 14. “I loved hearing everything he shared,” says Washington. “Even though he tried to interview me at times.”Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyDeep SecretsAfter becoming a father, comedian Hunter Hill decided to make a parenting podcast. Until, that is, an attempt to research his dad threw him down a rabbit hole that made him question everything he knew about his family – including whether his goat-farming grandad was really a secret CIA operative. It’s a wild, detail-packed listen told in highly hooky fashion.Alexi DugginsWidely available, episodes weeklyEras: Spice GirlsView image in fullscreenWannabes … the story of Britain’s most successful girl group is told in Eras: Spice Girls.Photograph: Photoshot/Getty ImagesRosie Ramsey draws on the BBC’s massive music archive to tell the story of Britain’s biggest girl group (pictured above right). It’s a lively celebration of girl power, stuffed with trivia (the idea for personas was inspired by the TV series Friends) and insight from the likes of music manager Chris Herbert and Little Mix’s Jade Thirlwall.HJDBBC Sounds, episodes weekly13 Minutes: Trouble With HubbleThis compelling space podcast, hosted by Sky at Night presenter Maggie Aderin, looks at the world’s most famous telescope. Interviews with the key personnel lend drama to the post-launch discovery that its primary mirror’s curvature was off by the equivalent of around one-fiftieth of the width of a human hair – rendering it useless. The only option? Dispatching astronauts on a zero-gravity repair mission.ADBBC Sounds, episodes weeklyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFame Under FireAnoushka Mutanda-Dougherty will be at Southwark crown court daily to report on Russell Brand’s trial, in which he denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault.
