title: Treasure Island review – this TV stinker does its best to ruin a literary classic | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Did Robert Louis Stevenson’s timeless swashbuckling tale need the addition of a superpower? Is it better for reducing its young hero to an afterthought? Nope
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Did Robert Louis Stevenson’s timeless swashbuckling tale need the addition of a superpower? Is it better for reducing its young hero to an afterthought? Nope
Content: Tom Sweet as Jim Hawkins, David Oyelowo as Long John Silver and Hayley Atwell as Bess in Treasure Island.Photograph: Paramount Plus (UK)View image in fullscreenTom Sweet as Jim Hawkins, David Oyelowo as Long John Silver and Hayley Atwell as Bess in Treasure Island.Photograph: Paramount Plus (UK)TV reviewTelevision & radioReviewTreasure Island review – this TV stinker does its best to ruin a literary classicDid Robert Louis Stevenson’s timeless swashbuckling tale need the addition of a superpower? Is it better for reducing its young hero to an afterthought? NopeSarah DempsterMon 12 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 06.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlever groans, a pipe judders andthunk:another unsolicited adaptation of a beloved literary classic is deposited on our screens. This particular emission is a six-part take on Treasure Island, Robert Louis Stevenson’s timeless tale of swashbuckling adventure, high-seas treachery and thick eyebrowed youths in tiny britches wrestling with double-edged superpowers. The 19th-century novel has of course long captured the public imagination, its themes of … hang on.Superpowers? Aye, that there be. An’ plenty more bilge besides. For this US-UK co-production be what lubbers refer to as a “reimagining”. Which essentially means much effort has been made to “jazz up” – or, if you will, “ruin” – the source material.And so, for better or significantly worse, the Jim Hawkins (Tom Sweet) of this new Treasure Island, titivated by writer Robert Murphy, has been given a photographic and possibly quasi-mystical memory; a preternatural talent for recollection that is demonstrated in scenes of much whooshing excitement. Here we find the youngster scowling at various documents while the soundtrack whispers mysteriously and the camera zooms slowly in then quickly out of his face, like a bee too embarrassed to ask for directions to the toilet. Not that any of this makes him interesting, mind.Indeed, Jim’s main contribution to the first couple of episodes is to stand with his mouth open as “feisty” mum Bess (Hayley Atwell) snogs pirates, bribes pirates and burns maps belonging to pirates while bellowing things such as:“I am but a poor widow”. Poor Jim Hawkins; one of literature’s most spirited young heroes has been reduced here to a gulping afterthought, his buccaneering twinkle eclipsed by mummy’s smudged eyeliner.To darkest Devon, then, where a storm brings with it further indignities in the form of the plot.Innkeeper Bess Hawkins ’as lost her ’usband and ’er aitches in “the siege of Gibraltar” and now must eke a livin’ from ’er dull son’s ability to speed-memorise passages chosen at random from the King James Bible for the entertainment of ’er soused clientele.But avast, who be the stranger who just staggered in from the sea? And what is the strange an’ hauntin’ cacophony that emanates from his beard?Could it be … anaccentof some sort? It’s certainly possible! “I hem por iiin coin but riiiich in dreeeeeam,” gargles Billy Bones (Tomer “The Boys” Capone) as Bess paws his incomprehensible chest. “An udder quart o’ yor Jamaicanrempor favorrrr …?”From which benighted pocket of the continent could such a tortuous tumult originate? Frangland? Spitaly? Eeet ez a mysteree!View image in fullscreenSeadog … Billy Bones played by Tomer Capone.Photograph: Treasure Island Series 1/Paramount Plus (UK)Enter terrifying “sea bastard” Long John Silver, who has understandably taken exception not just to Bones’ Vowels de Confusión but also to the fact that his former shipmate has nabbed their dead captain’s treasure map. The nerve! Silver wants said map back and is not best pleased to learn that it now exists solely in Jim’s noggin, the latter having committed its squiggles to memory prior to Bess torching the thing in a fit of widowy pique.Silver is played by David Oyelowo, who appears to be acting in another adaptation altogether. An adaptation that doesn’t expect him to endure lines such as “we’re sailin’ to freedom!” while balancing a CGI parrot on his shoulder. He is mesmerising and his explosive charisma reduces everyone in the blast zone to a smoking hillock of tricorn. But, alas, not even Oyelowo can lift the plot, which drags its wooden leg towards the Caribbean and limply waggles its rubber cutlass at the ensuing guff storm. Further pointless reimaginings include slow-motion spy battles, additional swirly “magic memory” scenes and family altercations more befitting a teatime soap than a big swanky thing on Paramount+ (“It’s hard doing this all by myself!”)At one point, a grizzled seadog wobbles to his feet and, apropos not much, barks; “This place stinks!” An observation to which one feels compelled to reply: that it does, matey. That it does.Treasure Island is on Paramount+ nowThis article was amended on 12 October 2026. An earlier version said that Treasure Island was published in the 18th century. It was published as a book in the 19th century (1883), but is set in the 18th century.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: how did 9/11 affect the experience of being Muslim in Britain? | Television | The Guardian
description: Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan look at life after the terror attacks. Plus: investigating Roman Abramovich. Here’s what to watch tonight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan look at life after the terror attacks. Plus: investigating Roman Abramovich. Here’s what to watch tonight
Content: ‘There was a time, 25 years ago, when being a British Muslim was OK’ … Azhar (left) and Khan.Photograph: BBC/ForestView image in fullscreen‘There was a time, 25 years ago, when being a British Muslim was OK’ … Azhar (left) and Khan.Photograph: BBC/ForestTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: how did 9/11 affect the experience of being Muslim in Britain?Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan look at life after the terror attacks. Plus: investigating Roman Abramovich. Here’s what to watch tonightMon 12 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeing Muslim After 9/119pm, BBC Two“There was a time, 25 years ago, when being a British Muslim was OK,” says journalist Mobeen Azhar. “We were on the cover of magazines, getting elected to parliament and even captained the England cricket team.” Then 9/11 happened. He and his film-making partner, Masood Khan, have made this documentary to explore how the terror attacks affected the Muslim community – including their own experiences – and why they still reverberate today.Hollie RichardsonPanorama: Roman Abramovich – How He Hid His Fortune8pm, BBC OneNew evidence from a data leak sees Panorama sift through hundreds of documents that may have been falsified to conceal the vast wealth of the ex-Chelsea owner and oligarch. Will it manage to set the news agenda like theaccusations levelled against Man City’s ownersdid? Abramovich disputes the allegations and denies any wrongdoing.Alexi DugginsJamie’s 20 Minute Meals8pm, Channel 4The chef continues his real-time cookery class with a steak night dinner, complete with a shallot and brandy sauce and a serving of garlicky gnocchi chips. Then he puts together a crispy trout with green veggies and a tomato and tarragon salsa. Both are ready in 20 minutes.HRClickbait Clinic With Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneIs there truth behind influencers’ claims that testosterone levels are at a historic low? T-maxxing is the next social media “wellness trend” investigated by Dooley. She meets men who believe that artificially increasing their levels will boost bone density, sex drive and muscle mass, before putting questions to the experts.HRPierre9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenMichael (Ezrae Maye) films PC Tanner (Tom Rhys Harries) with Jason Granger (Jack Bandeira) in Pierre.Photograph: Olly Courtney/Channel 4“I just don’t want to be the one to tell the aunt that her nephew wasn’t the boy she thought he was.” Charismatic duty solicitor Pierre (David Harewood) looks into the murder of his teen client Michael – and questions if he was wrong to believe he wanted to turn away from crime. It only makes him want to dig deeper for answers …HRMichael Palin in the Philippines9pm, Channel 5Palin spends his third and final week on the southern island of Mindanao: a no-travel zone and the home of disgraced former president Rodrigo Duterte. In the city of Davao, the Monty Python star meets the DJ behind Budots, the perky song and twerking-like dance craze, improbably inspired by Duterte’s death squads who hunted for drug dealers.Priya ElanFilmKilling Anna (Sam Benstead, 2026), 11.05pm, Channel 4“I weaponise myself, my trauma.” Annsar Shahhoud, a Syria-born researcher in genocide studies at the University of Amsterdam, is the focus of this remarkable documentary. After being sent videos of massacres by the Assad regime, she set up a fake Facebook account (under the name of Anna Sh), befriended Syrian officials and militia, and got them to admit their role in the mass murders of civilians in Damascus. The toll on Shahhoud is clear, but so is her will to bring the truth to light.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Weight of Angels by John Boyne review – what if Oscar Wilde had lived? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The great Irish writer died, a broken man, at only 46. Imagining a second act for him is a great idea – but the results are sentimental and unconvincing
Author: Neil Bartlett
Headline: The great Irish writer died, a broken man, at only 46. Imagining a second act for him is a great idea – but the results are sentimental and unconvincing
Content: Oscar Wilde in 1882.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOscar Wilde in 1882.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesFictionReviewThe Weight of Angels by John Boyne review – what if Oscar Wilde had lived?The great Irish writer died, a broken man, at only 46. Imagining a second act for him is a great idea – but the results are sentimental and unconvincingNeil BartlettMon 12 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1895, four days after the opening of The Importance of Being Earnest, the Marquess of Queensberry left a card at Oscar Wilde’s club that publicly accused him of “posing as a somdomite”. Instead of instigating the libel case that led to his imprisonment and early death in a Paris hotel just five years later, what would have happened if Wilde had simply torn that card up? John Boyne’s new novel sets out to answer that intriguing question.For starters, Boyne contrives a fate for Wilde’s beloved Lord Alfred Douglas which entertainingly redistributes the details of the real Wilde’s life before, during and after his time in Reading jail. This sets up the novel’s cat-and-mouse game with the history it is reimagining. Wilde himself, conveniently released from marriage by the early death of his wife, is then free to live not as a tortured, scandal-haunted genius, but as a randy, wisecracking, party-going queen. The upside of this is that Oscar gets to swap bons mots with a crowded cast list of celebrities; the downside is that he shows little sign of the troubled and radical mind that produced the real Wilde’s late journalism and fiction, never mind the subversive linguistic pyrotechnics of The Importance.The storyline leaps elegantly across the years, and often drops the high-society comedy to show this alternative Wilde becoming embroiled in more than his fair share of melodrama. This allows for some highly effective tear-jerking, notably in the scene that re-imagines the departure of his beloved elder son for the Somme. Time jumps are delivered in the form of letters, newspaper articles and even scripts of hypothetical plays and films about Wilde; this genre-hopping keeps things lively, and allows Boyne some very effective shifts of tone, time and place.double quotation markBoyne doesn’t so much show his imaginary Wilde interacting with queer history as magically abolishing itThe real Wilde wrote no more plays after The Importance of Being Earnest; Boyne’s version lives to write nine more, plus a Hollywood screenplay. Sadly, of these we get to read not a single quotation. Curiously, Boyne goes out of his way to make these plays sound dull; he has his fictional alternative turn into a staunch aesthetic conservative, concerned only with success. We see his writing’s rewards (endless money, a knighthood) but are never made privy to its process or motives. In fact, we never see him functioning as a writer at all.With regard to Wilde’s queerness – the treatment of which Boyne clearly intends to be his novel’s main claim to seriousness – the narrative makes a point of having him collide with several of the most important early European theorists of what we now call gay liberation: George Cecil Ives, Magnus Hirschfeld, André Gide. However, it leaves Wilde untouched by their ideas, and keeps him well away from any experience of their respective gay subcultures in London, Berlin and Paris. Instead, Wilde stays in the closet and settles down in a Mayfair mansion with a conveniently doting schoolteacher. After a decade of monogamy, Oscar wrecks this happy home with the help of a hard-bodied student football player. As a direct outcome of this error, the deadly outcomes of gay shame and self-loathing invade the novel for the first time; Wilde promptly acquires a conscience, deciding that he really ought to use his status as a literary national treasure to do something to make the world a better place for homosexuals.From then on – around 1930 – Boyne doesn’t so much show his imaginary Wilde interacting with queer history as magically abolishing it. At yet another party, Winston Churchill is enlisted to promote gay rights in parliament; characters become helpfully psychic, imagining 1970s-style gay liberation marches, gay marriage and even some very specific post-Stonewall arguments about the respective merits of radical and assimilationist theories of gay freedom. Boyne’s Wilde clearly sides with the latter. Speaking in a voice that sometimes sounds suspiciously like Boyne’s own, Wilde gives a speech that not only allows him to publicly champion feminism and Irish independence, but also to single-handedly persuade an audience of MPs to vote for the complete and overnight decriminalisation of homosexuality. Luckily, all of this emotive nonsense happens just in time for the coronation of 1952, meaning that both Prince Philip and Elizabeth II get to congratulate Wilde on his efforts during their after party. Unsurprisingly, Wilde dies of happiness, and goes straight to heaven.Any historical fantasia worth its salt must play with its reader, continually asking them to assess whether the alternatives being imagined are credible or desirable. In this case, in a year that has seen attacks on queer and trans lives proliferate, Boyne’s decision to replace the real history of that community’s collective struggle with such a contrived and top-down miracle feels like a very odd fictional manoeuvre indeed. He has clearly done lots of research, but has chosen to put it at the service of creating a Wilde who is fatally less interesting and moving than the original. In this version of history, Ireland’s greatest lord of language is reduced to a sentimental, royalty-loving, champagne-quaffing showman. What a waste of a great idea.The Weight of Angels by John Boyne is published by Doubleday (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionOscar WildeLGBTQ+ rightsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A rare indulgence’: why Black Swan is my feelgood movie | Black Swan | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers explaining their go-to comfort films is a tribute to Darren Aronofsky’s dark and unusually satisfying ballet nightmare
Author: Charles Carrall
Headline: The latest in our series of writers explaining their go-to comfort films is a tribute to Darren Aronofsky’s dark and unusually satisfying ballet nightmare
Content: Natalie Portman in Black Swan.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyView image in fullscreenNatalie Portman in Black Swan.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyMy feelgood movieBlack Swan‘A rare indulgence’: why Black Swan is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers explaining their go-to comfort films is a tribute to Darren Aronofsky’s dark and unusually satisfying ballet nightmareCharles CarrallMon 12 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn early 2011, sometime after the film was released on home video, I sat down with mum to watch what she had heard was a “new ballet movie” byDarren Aronofsky. I was 12 years old, spending school nights training to be a professional dancer. Without any warmup, knowing very little of the ballet and pointe work that earnedNatalie Portmanher best actress Oscar, we pressed play onBlack Swan.Well beforeBrendan Fraser’s time on the couchand the many houseguests ofMother!, Aronofsky increased the wattage with a companion piece to follow his heavy-hitter, The Wrestler. Watching Nina Sayers’ (Portman) intense physical trials and her stilted sexual awakening, with my mum beside me, I was understandably disturbed. At this point in my adolescence, I thought Jumanjiwas a scary movie. Like the film’s injured bird, I was being introduced to a darkness I didn’t understand. And somehow I couldn’t get enough. Why did it feel so good?‘Exceptionally crafted’: why Little Shop of Horrors is my feelgood movieRead moreIn the years since, I have returned toBlack Swanin search of that same dread and delight. With each viewing, my affection for it deepens. The pale pinks and gentle powdery blues, Nina’s cosy wrap sweaters and leotards, even Barbara Hershey’s smothering presence, all of it has become an unexpected comfort.Almost hermetically sealed within a world of its own, Black Swan is strangely soothing. It’s a retreat into the insular private life of an artist committed to just one thing. For Nina, there is only space for ballet, and for the duration of the film, I too am consumed. It’s an obsessive story told in tight closeups and staged in cramped spaces. From the subway to her apartment, where she lives with her mother, Erica (Hershey), Nina spends her time fenced-in. Even in the outside world – a sunshine-less New York City – she walks the street under scaffolding; her only sky, the ceiling of the Lincoln Center.Having served plenty of time in the company’s corps de ballet, Nina’s dedication has gone mostly unnoticed – as her mother reminds her each night, brushing her hair and tucking her into bed (Nina’s infantine bedroom is perhaps the scariest part of Black Swan). When artistic director Thomas (Vincent Cassel) announces that prima ballerina Beth – a scene-stealingWinona Rydercast brilliantly as a mean drunk over the hill – will be stepping down, Nina is hellbent on taking her place. Like All About Eve and Showgirls, it’s out with the old and in with the new. The company will begin its season with Thomas’s version of Swan Lake. His plans are simple: “Strip it down, make it visceral and real.”This is easier said than done for Nina, who finds herself cast as Swan Queen after a stolen kiss with Thomas in his office. Much to his surprise, she bites him on the lip – an uncharacteristically brazen move from the virgin ballerina seemingly unfit to play the titular role. In rehearsals, Nina demonstrates her rigor with every arabesque, virtuosic as the White Swan. Her Black Swan, however, lacks edge, something friendly rival Lily – played by a bacchanalMila Kunis– makes up for in spades.‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movieRead moreWith Lily as her liberated double, the sexually repressed Nina invites darkness into her life, hoping that it will bring her closer to the vamp Thomas has asked her to become. At times she is seduced by menacing flashes of herself in others; on the street, in the studio, looming over her in the bathtub. In the subway window, I see a wicked smile momentarily cross her reflected face and wonder if I am also seeing things. Loosening my grip on the barre, it feels good to give in to an ambiguous and unstable nightmare. I revel in every rewatch because Black Swan still feels dangerous.Portman’s commitment to the role, and the pleasure of watching her, is a reminder of ballet’s enigma: a delicateness that is contingent on the endurance of extreme physical pain. It’s not simply that ballet is formally brutal, but that watching it is also a kind of brutality. Black Swan knows this to be true. With its exquisite horrors, the film is a rare indulgence, much like a trip to the ballet but at a fraction of the cost.When at last Nina is transformed into the Black Swan, she falls to her death on stage. Diving on to a hidden mattress behind the set. Still catching her breath, she can barely speak, “I felt it, perfect.” Nina is finally pleased with herself. “It was perfect,” she concludes of her swan song. With every rewatch, still somehow keeping me on my toes, I find myself agreeing with her.Black Swan is available to rent digitally in the US and on Disney+ in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsBlack SwanMy feelgood movieDarren AronofskyNatalie PortmanMila KunisThrillersBalletDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Fidai Film review – Palestinian collage film transforms suppressed footage into works of art | Movies | The Guardian
description: Using archive material of destroyed houses, terrorised children and dead bodies, Kamal Aljafari adds humanity to the reels by overlaying poems by Palestinian authors
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Using archive material of destroyed houses, terrorised children and dead bodies, Kamal Aljafari adds humanity to the reels by overlaying poems by Palestinian authors
Content: ‘Brings liberation, if only momentarily’ … A Fidai Film.Photograph: Courtesy of True StoryView image in fullscreen‘Brings liberation, if only momentarily’ … A Fidai Film.Photograph: Courtesy of True StoryMoviesReviewA Fidai Film review – Palestinian collage film transforms suppressed footage into works of artUsing archive material of destroyed houses, terrorised children and dead bodies, Kamal Aljafari adds humanity to the reels by overlaying poems by Palestinian authorsPhuong LeMon 12 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Arabic, “fidai” means someone willing to sacrifice themselves for the greater good. Borrowing this word, which is at times used in a military context, for his collage film, Palestinian film-maker Kamal Aljafari stages a potent uprising of images against the tide of propaganda and historical erasure. Much of the film draws on archive materials once housed in thePalestineResearch Centre in Beirut. In 1982, during the Lebanese civil war, Israeli forces raided the centre and seized the archive. Most of these documents on Palestinian history – books, newspapers, audiovisual artefacts – are believed to still be in the hands of the Israeli army.Obtained through clandestine means, the footage that resurfaces in Aljafari’s film bears the physical traces of political suppression. The images are scratched, grainy and pixelated, yet through the power of montage they evoke startling visual parallels that point to the relentless violence endured by Palestinians through the decades. Black-and-white film taken during the British mandate show soldiers patrolling the streets and inflicting violence upon the Indigenous population; similar acts then committed by Israeli forces. In place of a chronological order, the editing builds a sense of continuity through recurring images. Time and time again, we see torn-down houses, terrorised children and the bodies of Palestinians murdered by occupation forces.More than simply a work of compilation, the film also performs its own historical intervention. Many of the reels are imprinted with pejorative captions added by Israeli authorities, which Aljafari covers in streaks of red paint. In their place are excerpts from poems by Palestinian authors such as Ghassan Kanafani, whose words return a sense of humanity to these past images. Through these strategies of reclamation, Aljafari’s film brings liberation, if only momentarily, to a captive archive.A Fidai Film is on True Story from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPalestineLebanonIsraelMiddle East and north AfricareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Deadline review – shocking threat sends tremors through authoritarian school | Movies | The Guardian
description: Set in a dystopian private academy rife with surveillance and cut-throat competition, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama cements his status as an important film-maker
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Set in a dystopian private academy rife with surveillance and cut-throat competition, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama cements his status as an important film-maker
Content: Heavy secrets … a still from Deadline.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenHeavy secrets … a still from Deadline.Photograph: PRMoviesReviewDeadline review – shocking threat sends tremors through authoritarian schoolSet in a dystopian private academy rife with surveillance and cut-throat competition, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama cements his status as an important film-makerPhuong LeMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilmed inTaiwanand set entirely inside a prestigious high school, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama frames educational systems not merely as a preparation for the real world but as a microcosm of society at large. At this elite private institute, pupils studiously march in lines like obedient soldiers, their purple uniforms the only pop of colour in a grey building of glass and steel. The school’s operations have a touch of dystopian sci-fi: students check in with AI recognition panels, which also display their class standing and disciplinary scores. In this sterile environment where human worth is measured by standardised metrics, the breathing room for individuality is nil.This panopticon atmosphere of surveillance and cut-throat competition is punctured by a shocking incident: an anonymous student drops a flurry of leaflets announcing their intent to take their own life on the day of the final exam, unless the school changes its authoritarian ways. The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.Though grappling with heavy subjects such as self-harm, bullying and drug use, Chow treats these youthful foibles as evidence of a systemic malaise rather than individual failings. A staunch anti-authoritarian message is smuggled in the conventions of a whodunnit thriller; it parallels Chow’s previous films, including the2021 documentary Revolution of Our Times, about the2019-2020 Hong Kong protests. Like the rebellion in Deadline, that movement also began on campuses and was led by students. That both titles are banned in Hong Kong only underscores the urgency and importance of Chow’s film-making.Deadline is in UK cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsTaiwanAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Influencer Project review – ick-inducing thriller satirises social media content, and exploits it too | Movies | The Guardian
description: When influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King visits Copenhagen all the trips to trendy shops and fancy restaurants soon take a turn for the worse
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: When influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King visits Copenhagen all the trips to trendy shops and fancy restaurants soon take a turn for the worse
Content: Moments of real fear … Chiara King as Chiara King.Photograph: Icon Film Distribution/PAView image in fullscreenMoments of real fear … Chiara King as Chiara King.Photograph: Icon Film Distribution/PAMoviesReviewThe Influencer Project review – ick-inducing thriller satirises social media content, and exploits it tooWhen influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King visits Copenhagen all the trips to trendy shops and fancy restaurants soon take a turn for the worseLeslie FelperinMon 12 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King stars as influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King, or some kind of parafictional version of herself, in this quease-inducing thriller exercise. The ick gets generated not necessarily by the eventual gore that erupts in the last reel, but by the tacky weirdness of the way the film apes the mannerisms of social media reels and streaming nonsense to both satirise the ugly side of the business but also exploit and profit off it at the same time. On one level, it’s an eerily clever exercise in bad faith, like a poor Michael Haneke film (think Funny Games) for gen-Z kicks; on another, maybe it’s just a crappy ripoff of online tropes that have been way overexposed already. Or both.Anyway, here’s what happens: influencer Chiara gets invited to visit Copenhagen by a tourist organisation, a deal set up by her avaricious manager Alice (Jazmine Summer). Of course, this means practically every moment of her time awake in the city will be filmed, both by Chiara herself on her trusty smartphone, or a camera crew led by director Mike (played by Mike Nybroe, who is also director of The Influencer Project, ha ha); Mike is supported by sound man Daniel (Daniel Parmo) and cameraman Victor (Luca Storm). The early sections turn in all the influence-slop you would expect, with shopping trips to trendy merch vendors such as Baum und Pferdgarten, and meals at fancy local restaurants, and then a livestreamed visit to a “haunted house,” which is the big thing on Instagram and TikTok these days.But the product placement is somewhat interrupted by moments of real fear (or “real fear”) when Chiara starts getting threatening direct messages (from someone calling themselves KingSlayer) who wants her to stop talking for reasons not clearly explained at first, otherwise he will kill and rape her, not necessarily in that order. This unsurprisingly creates a pall over Chiara’s trip, but if she just quits and goes home she’ll miss out on $100k in deals, so that’s not an option.So are we supposed to despise Chiara for her greed or applaud her girl-boss fortitude in not being intimidated by a stalker? And what to make of the film’s claims that this was partly inspired by real incidents of stalking? Nybroe and co work the debate into the endless stream of comments we see scrolling alongside Chiara’s livestream – a river of chat that doesn’t let up even when the credits start to roll, ersatz dialectics for an age of digital proliferation.The Influencer Project is in UK and Irish cinemas from 16 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsSocial mediaDenmarkDigital mediaEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocks | Movies | The Guardian
description: Debut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, Pumpkin
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Debut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, Pumpkin
Content: ‘Quite the showcase’ … Milly Shapiro in Hallowarrior.Photograph: Jessica Licata/PRView image in fullscreen‘Quite the showcase’ … Milly Shapiro in Hallowarrior.Photograph: Jessica Licata/PRMoviesReviewHallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocksDebut feature from Ben Sottak provides outlandish Halloween-based scares, with Milly Shapiro superb as the naive yet resilient home-defender, PumpkinCatherine BrayMon 12 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHome Alone meets Mad Max in this atmospheric seasonal chiller, named for Halloween and not a cheery greeting. A disease has wiped out most of humanity, leaving 16-year-old Pumpkin (Milly Shapiro) stranded alone in her rural family home in the middle of nowhere for the best part of four years. This classic American clapboard house has always been the perfect quaint yet unsettling place to celebrate Halloween, and she determines to uphold the family tradition and do just that, sending a radio broadcast to anyone listening to invite them to celebrate spooky season with her. Unfortunately, the message is picked up by some less than wholesome types, led by Thalia (Shannyn Sossamon), thus setting the stage for the proverbial to hit the fan.It’s the first major screen role for Shapiro since her memorable debut as the little sister inAri Aster’s Hereditary, and she is in almost every scene here, making for quite the showcase. It’s good casting: Pumpkin is an intriguing presence – at once young and old, presumably because she’s been fending for herself during such a key stage of her development. She’s not had any adult guidance since the age of 12 – arresting her development in some ways, while having to survive, be totally independent and grieve her entire family alone has simultaneously made her unusually tough in others.This turns out to be invaluable in a horror film; it gives the script plenty of room to have her make naive decisions which are wholly justified, as well as to prove surprisingly resilient in ways that the character’s backstory supports. This gives a plausible, grounded core to the story’s more outlandish trappings, and the splendid production design – ranging from cosy cottagecore Halloween to a timeless Bates motel aesthetic – makes for an appealing storyworld. Hallowarrior is the feature debut of Ben Sottak, an experienced short film-maker, and on this evidence he’s likely to be worth keeping an eye out for.Hallowarrior is on Shudder and AMC+ from 16 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sindhu Vee: Swanky review – from the perils of parenting to the glories of self-pleasure | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The standup’s new tour covers cross-cultural identity, Hollywood mix-ups and exactly how honest to be about your children’s arts and crafts output
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The standup’s new tour covers cross-cultural identity, Hollywood mix-ups and exactly how honest to be about your children’s arts and crafts output
Content: Diverting digressions … Sindu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettView image in fullscreenDiverting digressions … Sindu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettComedyReviewSindhu Vee: Swanky review – from the perils of parenting to the glories of self-pleasureReading Town HallThe standup’s new tour covers cross-cultural identity, Hollywood mix-ups and exactly how honest to be about your children’s arts and crafts outputBrian LoganMon 12 Oct 2026 05.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 05.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow British isSindhu Vee? And how Indian? That’s what her new standup show Swanky addresses in a wonderfully self-possessed opening that sees her give account of herself to an old duffer at a party. It’s a subject well suited to Vee’s beady and sceptical style, as she drops a tart gag about India-Pakistan relations, or later interrogates the assumptions of a micro-aggressing mum at the school gate. One might wish the whole show were themed around this topic, but its larger part majors in the relatable if not always revelatory subject of parenting. And that’s before we even mention her tacked-on final section, on another matter entirely.The parenting material dominates the show, and ranges from the generic to the specific. Specifically, Vee has a big age gap between her first two kids and her third, and many of the jokes are about how differently Child 3 has been raised – cue sardonic eye-rolling at the helicopter parenting of others, and of her own younger self. Sometimes this shades into over-familiarity (teens and their mobile phones), or cynicism, or both – as in the routine about the rubbishness of her kid’s arts and craft output.View image in fullscreenThe ring of hard-won truth … Sindhu VeePhotograph: Paul GilbeyBut at its best, Vee’s over-it mum shtick (“if they ‘air’ you, gaslight them!”) has the ring of hard-won truth – such as the parental Zoom call into which she must, subliminally and strategically, interpolate life advice to a daughter who would never otherwise listen to it.Sindhu Vee: ‘Makeup, music to feel reckless, two pieces of milk chocolate – and then I go on’Read moreSuch is the thrust of Swanky’s central section, and it is always diverting, with frequent lively digressions – including a droll one about the uniquely British deployment of the word “kindly”. Vee has an acute eye for this stuff, and I perked up when she belatedly returns to the cross-cultural theme. That feels like the show’s natural ending point, but she ekes out one anecdote too many, about a misunderstanding on a Hollywood film set, then appends a whole new section: a hymn to the glories of female masturbation no less. There is no denying it hits the audience’s G-spot, that one – even if it seems to come from another show entirely.Touring until 17 AprilExplore more on these topicsComedySindhu VeereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nina review – a riveting series of horribly invasive auditions for The Seagull | Stage | The Guardian
description: Women up for a role as Chekhov’s aspiring actor navigate their meetings with a needling director in a tense show
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Women up for a role as Chekhov’s aspiring actor navigate their meetings with a needling director in a tense show
Content: ‘Tell me your trauma’ … Rowan Polonski as Goran and Samantha Begeman as Nina 02.Photograph: Ali WrightView image in fullscreen‘Tell me your trauma’ … Rowan Polonski as Goran and Samantha Begeman as Nina 02.Photograph: Ali WrightStageReviewNina review – a riveting series of horribly invasive auditions for The SeagullBattersea Arts Centre, LondonWomen up for a role as Chekhov’s aspiring actor navigate their meetings with a needling director in a tense showKate WyverMon 12 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmile. Introduce yourself. Say you’re such a big fan. Now do whatever he tells you. These are the unspoken rules the women follow as they take turns auditioning in Caroline Williams’ discomforting, rage-fuelled production about men and power and rotting winged roadkill.The women are auditioning for the role of Nina, the aspiring actor in Chekhov’s The Seagull, in an experimental production directed by sombrely pretentious wunderkind Goran (a brooding Rowan Polonski). Using live-feed cameras in his show, he is the type of director to dismiss the need for an intimacy coordinator while claiming credit for having one in the room.As the women file through, Goran’s requests to his Ninas (Maya Bartley O’Dea, Nina Bowers, Samantha Begeman and Gemma Barnett) become increasingly invasive. They slide from small, needling questions that might be deemed permissible from a truth-seeking visionary, to commands that are so terrible they could crack a person in two. Tell me your trauma, he demands. Show me what that looks like. The women are eager to please, eager to work, and Goran has the power to make them a star. Watching on, writer Tim (Joseph Payne) is a timid bystander, reading in for sour, lovesick Konstantin as Chekhov’s play slips in and out of both focus and reality.View image in fullscreenDiscomforting … Nina Bowers as Nina 03.Photograph: Ali WrightAs tension builds, our play, co-directed by Williams and Deborah Pearson, grows in scale and beauty too. Bowers’ exquisite, harrowing birth scene splits open the show’s depths of earned fury, while Begeman has a distressing masturbation scene. Projected loud and large across the stage, the latter is almost too hard to watch, but this show demands we bear witness.The final switch of power is an artistic act of wish fulfilment. It may be what we would dream of for these women but it rings hollow for the world the show has so carefully and grimly constructed. Williams and Pearson’s unflinching direction is most compelling in its bleak brutality. Why would any woman want to be an actor?At Battersea Arts Centre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageBattersea Arts CentreAnton ChekhovTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The missed opportunity of Jay-Z’s documentary series | Jay-Z | The Guardian
description: Jay-Z in 8, the rap mogul’s HBO docuseries, covers his life and career in effort to mend his image – with no pushback. Why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jay-Z in 8, the rap mogul’s HBO docuseries, covers his life and career in effort to mend his image – with no pushback. Why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion?
Content: Jay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.Photograph: MubiView image in fullscreenJay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.Photograph: MubiJay-ZThe missed opportunity of Jay-Z’s documentary seriesJay-Z in 8, the rap mogul’s HBO docuseries, covers his life and career in effort to mend his image – with no pushback. Why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion?Andre GeeMon 12 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the finale ofJay-Z’sJay-Z in 8, the recent eight-partHBOdocumentary series on his life and career, the billionaire rap mogul talked with record producer Rick Rubin about the song Family Feud from his4:44 album. He clarified one of its lyrics, “Al Sharpton in the mirror takin’ selfies / How is him or Pill Cosby ‘posed to help me?”, in which he chided Sharpton, the civil rights leader, and Cosby, the disgraced actor-comedian, forconstantlycriticizingrapmusic. He called Sharpton an “extortionist” who goes “from place to place” demanding: “You want our support … give us the money.” Listening to him chastise Sharpton, I pondered how he doesn’t see himself as a similar figure.Starting in 2019, Jay-Zpartneredwiththe NFL in 2019 as entertainment director, deciding the Super Bowl half-time performers and working with the league on other community endeavors.Colin Kaepernick, the former NFL quarterback, has recently alleged that the deal came after NFL owners decided they needed a “Black face” to help them quell outrage from Black people after Kaepernickwasblackballedby the league forkneelingduring the national anthems as a form of protest against police brutality. Jay-Z was lambasted for undercutting Kaepernick’s cause for personal gain, marring his reputation with many fans who came to view him as the same counterinsurgent figure he criticized in the documentary.Jay-Z in 8 review – the rapper’s interminable interview show should have been a podcastRead moreJay-Z in 8 is an effort that seeks to mend his public image; the series culls his 30-year oeuvre along with his life and times. In the sleek, black-and-white episodes, which were filmed at some point in 2024, Jay explicates his music history in interviews with Rubin, the 63-year-old Def Jam co-founder and producer. It’s a polished, low-frills watch. The two sit at a table in an empty room in the events center Palais Brongniart, France’s former stock exchange, while Rubin chooses songs from Jay-Z’s catalog and uses them as a springboard into broader topics such as his relationship with his parents, his creative process and wider cultural observations. The final instalment, which aired on 9 October, featuresJay-Zpontificating on racism and suggesting generational wealth as its remedy. Hearing him dismiss social justice movements by claiming “we never get together” to push for change, and discussing inequality through banal observations, indicates how little thought he has actually put into uprooting systemic oppression.Rubin offers no pushback. Throughout the series, his lack of deeper questioning fails to give the conversations the depth they require. Rubin comes across as an in-awe spectator tasked with polishing the Jay-Z mythos. It’s the opposite of what a conversation series needs. (A more incisive interviewer, for instance, would’ve asked Jay-Z, who, in referencing his marriage to Beyoncé, rapped, “What’s better than one billionaire? Two,” if redistributing $2bn would be even better for the community at large.) At one point in that episode, Jay-Z, the richest musician in the world, refers to the Black bourgeoisie as “they”. A poignant follow-up from Rubin could have been to ask what exactly Jay felt separated him from that group. Instead, as with most of the series, Rubin nodded approvingly. His sycophantic presence turns what could have been a quintessential music documentary into hagiography. And Jay-Z likely wanted it that way.Over the years, the 56-year-old Brooklyn native has rapped about several ugly truths in his life: shooting his brother, selling drugs to loved ones, cheating on his wife, feeding others’ substance abuse for profit. He touched on some of those topics in Jay-Z in 8, giving the documentary its best substance. There’s some cool trivia, too. He reveals that the second verse of 99 Problems is based on a true story, reflects on how his Uncle Butchie inspired him to grow locs, and says he is too self-conscious to be as vocally experimental as Beyoncé. But he also has limits.In 2005, he halted his The Black Book memoir with the writer dream hampton because the process, he said, was getting too personal. Later that year, hetoldRolling Stone: “I know that people really want to know about me and I thought it was OK, but as I got closer and closer I said, ‘What am I doing?’” Since then, he’s become more discerning about his access, rarely giving interviews. He doesn’t want to be prodded against his will, but he also won’t let public narratives go unchecked, offering public retorts to critics in feature verses andstadium performances. He compulsively seeks to control the story, almost always in forums that don’t allow for discussion or pushback.How Black banjo players are changing Americana musicRead moreAn eight-hour conversation series with Jay-Z needed someone with deep hip-hop knowledgeandan instinct for pointed questions (I wonder if there’s a profession from which they could’ve sought that person?) In episode three, Rubin plays the title track from 2017’s 4:44, a highly vulnerable song where he vents about being an immature, emotionally unavailable cheater. And while Jay-Z apologizes in the song for his conduct, he doesn’t necessarily promise to be a better husband. Seven years later, Rubin doesn’t push for advanced thoughts on life as a husband or father, instead offering a vague: “Do you feel like there’s been progress?”When Rubin asks him if the stakes of life are higher for him now or during his drug-dealing days, Jay chooses the latter. He says his mindset toward powerful industry figures threatening to punish him for not doing what they want is, “I don’t care what you do. It doesn’t matter to me.” But if he’s really “already home”, as he rapped on the 2009 track that boasted of career contentment, why is he so fixated on the court of public opinion? And more importantly, why isn’t he putting something on the line byjoiningartistsincludingMacklemoreto speak out against multiple genocides abroad and Donald Trump’s fascism? Someone who isn’t prone to just agreeing enthusiastically would’ve pulled at those threads.The crack era and the Black excellence ruse (in which Black capitalists claim the revolution will come by simply buying from Black-owned companies) have denied multiple generations of Black people liberation in disparate ways. Jay-Z is at the figurative scene of both crimes. He earned his legacy with brilliant music that chronicles the drug game with cinematic vigor and contextualizes his actions in a way that a socioeconomics professor could explain to his cohort. But he rarely broaches the tension of his third act as a billionaire music mogul in an “eat the rich” world. Here, Rubin never asked him to.​Jay-Z in 8 airs onHBOMax in the US and Mubi in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsJay-ZDocumentary filmsHBOBlack US cultureRapMusic documentaryRick RubinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Atlantic Requiem review – Önaç gives historical slavery documents howling raging life  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: From syncopated funk to the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant to bureaucratic recitative, the score to David Önaç new oratorio, premiered by the London Symphony Orchestra, is serious and beautiful
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: From syncopated funk to the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant to bureaucratic recitative, the score to David Önaç new oratorio, premiered by the London Symphony Orchestra, is serious and beautiful
Content: J'nai Bridges, Brittany Renee and Orson Van Gay II perform Atlantic Requiem at St Luke’s.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenJ'nai Bridges, Brittany Renee and Orson Van Gay II perform Atlantic Requiem at St Luke’s.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewAtlantic Requiem review – Önaç gives historical slavery documents howling raging lifeLSO St Luke’s, LondonFrom syncopated funk to the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant to bureaucratic recitative, the score to David Önaç new oratorio, premiered by the London Symphony Orchestra, is serious and beautifulAlexandra CoghlanMon 12 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do you put a value on a human life? If you’re an insurance underwriter that’s not a philosophical question, it’s a practical one. The answer, incidentally, as calculated by Lloyds of London in 1779 was £45: the figure placed on each enslaved person transported across the Atlantic alongside corn, fish and other cargo. Court transcripts from two decades later describe a woman quarantined for smallpox, subsequently bound, blindfolded and tossed overboard tied to a chair. The captain later expressed his regret for the loss of “so good a chair”.Archives can tell us what, but it takes art to give us the humanhowof the past. Enter composerDavid Önaç– commissioned to take the historical documents unearthed from the Lloyds archive and give them howling, raging life in his new Atlantic Requiem, premiered this weekend by the London Symphony Orchestra, an expanded BBC Singers, three soloists and (in a last-minute step-in) conductor Malcolm J Merriweather.Manchester-based composer creates requiem to honour enslaved AfricansRead moreThis is a big piece – in theme and scope. Önaç’s score is beautifully, seriously constructed, turning the pitches of the piano’s white and black keys into symbolic gestures of opposition, equality and – perhaps – reconciliation. It’s a microcosm of a work in which the syncopated funk and alternative scales of jazz and blues drift into the western classical architecture of the Latin requiem mass, Gregorian chant bleeds into the chattering banality of bureaucratic recitative, and soloists soar but also scream. The conversation is particularly effective in the convulsive dance of the finale – a chewily textural, highly rhythmic intervention after the rapt choral meditation of the Agnus Dei.Merriweather steered his forces safely through the choppy musical waters, though soloists Brittany Renee, the ever-expressive J’Nai Bridges and especially tenor Orson Van Gay II risked being overwhelmed from their position behind the orchestra. In many ways this pair of Sunday afternoon performances at LSO St Luke’s (too small for so large a project) felt like a workshop for a piece still under construction. Önaç packs a lot into a short span, at the expense of pacing that feels almost perfunctory. There’s a full-length work here dying to get out, and a major new composing talent who deserves the space to tell the stories that have been silenced for so long.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Symphony OrchestraSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Girl from Arles review – Bizet’s music for forgotten rustic tragedy has punch and poetry | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Bizet’s incidental music for Daudet’s 1872 play The Girl from Arles was given its first UK complete performance by Sir Mark Elder, the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment and strong soloists in Jeremy Sams’ staging
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Bizet’s incidental music for Daudet’s 1872 play The Girl from Arles was given its first UK complete performance by Sir Mark Elder, the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment and strong soloists in Jeremy Sams’ staging
Content: Passionate but pragmatic … Helena Lymbery as Rose with Mercedes Assad in The Girl from Arles.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenPassionate but pragmatic … Helena Lymbery as Rose with Mercedes Assad in The Girl from Arles.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewThe Girl from Arles review – Bizet’s music for forgotten rustic tragedy has punch and poetryQueen Elizabeth Hall, LondonBizet’s incidental music for Daudet’s 1872 play The Girl from Arles was given its first UK complete performance by Sir Mark Elder, the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment and strong soloists in Jeremy Sams’ stagingErica JealMon 12 Oct 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The prettiest music in the world” was how the playwright Alphonse Daudet described the incidental music Bizet composed for his 1872 play The Girl from Arles – which is a bit like describing Carmen, the opera Bizet would compose less than three years later, as a charming little love story.Daudet’s play initially flopped but was saved by the music Bizet wrote for it, which comprises 27 separate numbers ranging from string whispers a few bars long to full-blown orchestral entr’actes and celebratory choruses. Two orchestral Suites from L’Arlésienne have long been familiar in the concert hall. But, after more than 150 years, this was the first chance for UK audiences to hear the complete incidental music in its proper context. Presented by theOrchestra of the Age of Enlightenmentand conducted by Mark Elder, there was a danger this play with music could turn into music with a play – but in fact the two elements complemented each other at equal strength.View image in fullscreen‘Pretty is only the half of it’ … Mark Elder conducting the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment at Queen Elizabeth Hall.Photograph: Mark AllanIn this earthy, ultimately tragic story set in rural Provence, the girl of the title, like Godot, remains unseen – she’s over in town, where people are no better than they should be. But her betrayal of the farm boy Frédéri, played here with wide-eyed openness by Kerill Kelly, and his inability to give up his infatuation, wreaks havoc. There are few surprises – given that we are pointedly told in Act 1 how high the farm’s hayloft is, there can be only one ending for despairing Frédéri. Yet Daudet’s characters are not drawn from stock: in particular, Frédéri’s mother Rose is passionate but pragmatic in a way that came across here every moment Helena Lymbery was on stage. In Alex Doidge-Green’s designs, the playing area was flanked on either side by the shepherd’s grubby caravan and a neat laundry hanger, and by the orchestra and chorus at the back. Directing, Jeremy Sams set the action in the north of England not so long ago, with the text in his own pleasingly to-the-point translation.As for the music, written for a small, cello-heavy orchestra coloured with saxophone and harmonium, pretty is only half of it. This is music that smells of lavender and pine trees, yes, but also of farm animals in the sun. With the chorus contributing snappily, the OAE and Elder brought out its rustic flavour punchily while never losing sight of its elegance.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicGeorges BizetMark ElderOrchestra of the Age of EnlightenmentreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Prem Sahib: Chamber review – master of unease twists the city into terror and pleasure | Art | The Guardian
description: There’s an atmosphere of sickly discomfort throughout this weird, intense mid-career survey for this brilliant artist
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: There’s an atmosphere of sickly discomfort throughout this weird, intense mid-career survey for this brilliant artist
Content: Risk and threat … Prem Sahib’s what you need to know to get rid of these blood sucking parasites (in the form of a whisper), 2023.Photograph: Ben Westoby/Prem Sahib/Phillida Reid, LondonView image in fullscreenRisk and threat … Prem Sahib’s what you need to know to get rid of these blood sucking parasites (in the form of a whisper), 2023.Photograph: Ben Westoby/Prem Sahib/Phillida Reid, LondonArtReviewPrem Sahib: Chamber review – master of unease twists the city into terror and pleasureDe La Warr Pavilion, BexhillThere’s an atmosphere of sickly discomfort throughout this weird, intense mid-career survey for this brilliant artistEddy FrankelMon 12 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrem Sahib turns the city inside out, twists it around and rips it apart. His show at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, a sort of mid-career survey for the 44-year-old English artist, is full of private spaces and urban nightmares that have been gutted and left on display. It’s minimal, claustrophobic, intense stuff.A sodium street lamp hangs upside down from the ceiling, casting its sickly pale orange glow across the gallery. You feel like you’ve stumbled into some urban back alley where physics has been flipped, it has all the threat of an underpass, but surreal and inverted. Nearby, three puffer jackets have been squeezed between sheets of glass – are these the blokes who were waiting for you in the underpass? Or are they three strangers who you’ve caught mid-embrace?That’s what Sahib does, over and over: he plays with the line between terror and pleasure, threat and intimacy, public and private.So much here is geared towards an atmosphere of discomfort. There’s a deep bass throb echoing out of one space, its tone eventually rising to an ear-piercing squeal, before settling back into a chest-rattling sub. A table has been made out of a grossly overgrown flea’s body, a street sign has been left blank but its light is still on. Two space heaters constantly flick on and ramp up the temperature. It is liminal, weird, uncomfortable.View image in fullscreenPlays with the line between terror and pleasure … an installation view from Chamber.Photograph: Rob HarrisQueerness is central to Sahib’s work. The double doors you pass as you walk in were taken from a Mile End leather bar that closed in 2022, the water fountain encased in resin is from Chariots sauna in Shoreditch which closed in 2016. Private spaces, places of intimate pleasure, that have been erased from the city.In one of his signature resin panels, clear droplets have accumulated on a sheet of black aluminium, like sweat gathering on a nightclub wall. You can almost smell it, almost feel hot, damp, writhing people coming together somewhere nearby. Hung up high, two acrylic discs nod to the visual results of rapid HIV tests. There’s intimacy here, but risk too.Risk, and threat: an obsidian mirror hangs cracked on the wall, burbling out discordant sounds, a slowed down recording of a homophobic rant sent to Sahib on a gay chat room.View image in fullscreenKnack for minimalist atmospherics … Prem Sahib's Horizon 1.3 2026.Photograph: Lewis Ronald/Prem Sahib/Phillida Reid, LondonIs this all about architecture, as the wall text here insists? I don’t know. Architecture is already about architecture – I don’t need art to make me think deep thoughts about buildings. This feels way more intimate than that description coldly implies. It’s about bodies being pressed together, sweat dripping down a wall, and feeling like it’s all about to be torn away from you.The whole way through, it’s as if Sahib is asking: what happens when the places that matter to me, where I express myself, are destroyed? What is left for me, for us? Who decides which spaces can survive, who decides what communities are worth preserving, who decides where bodies get to exist?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI don’t think it all works. The recording of Suella Braverman hatefully talking about the migrant crisis that you listen to while looking out at the sea is a bit on the nose, and the little dotty images of the horizon that line one wall don’t really add a huge amount.But for the most part, Sahib is brilliant, with an incredible knack for crushingly intense minimalist atmospherics. He’s been one of the most interesting artists working in this country for more than a decade now, and a big institutional show like this feels long overdue.Prem Sahib: Chamberis at De La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArtInstallationExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake Iseo | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: Smaller and less visited than Como and Garda, Lake Iseo harbours a gorgeous car-free island ideal for easy-going cycling and sightseeing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Smaller and less visited than Como and Garda, Lake Iseo harbours a gorgeous car-free island ideal for easy-going cycling and sightseeing
Content: Monte Isola on Iseo Lake with Carzano village on shore.Photograph: Simone Polattini/AlamyView image in fullscreenMonte Isola on Iseo Lake with Carzano village on shore.Photograph: Simone Polattini/AlamyItaly holidaysA lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake IseoSmaller and less visited than Como and Garda, Lake Iseo harbours a gorgeous car-free island ideal for easy-going cycling and sightseeingSuzy PopeMon 12 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 03.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRust red and burnt sienna speckle the green mountain rising from Lake Iseo. Golden autumn sunlight shimmers on the water. Monte Isola, Italy’s largest lake island, is a peak of sheer cliffs and dense forest, dotted with old fishing hamlets and hillside villages, each as pretty as the terraced villas of Lake Como and Garda, but with far fewer visitors. I arrive at the small port town of Peschiera Maraglio – where striped wooden boats jut from the water like the gondolas of Venice – on a ferry from Sulzano, a five-minute hop across the water.“Only three people on the island are allowed to own a car: the priest, the doctor and the mayor,” says Chiara, my tour guide from Brescia. Residents can zip up and down the steep island roads on mopeds, and a small fleet of van-sized buses trundle around throughout the day, but nearly all cars are forbidden and visitors have to explore on foot or bike.Even bikes are banned from boats at the weekend. Not that it matters: the harbour front is lined with bike rentals (from €4 an hour for a standard bike). I’m normally a nervous cyclist, but car-free roads raise my confidence. Plus, most other visitors have the telltale front-wheel wobble of novice riders. This isn’t the place for Lycra and personal bests; the smooth-as-silk, quiet roads are for slow pedalling, and neck swivelling to take in another gorgeous view of Lake Iseo.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of Lake Iseo with Monte IsolaThe circular lakeside route winds past olive groves tumbling to the shore. I thought I’d need base layers and gloves this far into autumn, but I’m in shorts and a T-shirt and already working up a sweat in 24C sunshine. I pedal through the lakeside hamlet of Sensole in the island’s south-west and stop in Menzino, just along the shore. There’s a cafe-bar catering to cyclists, so I fuel up with an espressoconlake view.double quotation markThe south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyardsThe view from the western side of the island is somewhat marred by a huge concrete factory on the mainland, so I keep my head down on the pedal to Siviano, the island’s capital. The shambling streets are sleepy; the stacked skyline of orange, lemon and magnolia villas is punctuated by the looming facade of Santi Faustino e Giovita church and a medieval stone tower. Monte Isola has been inhabited since the Roman era. Venetian rule in the 15th and 16th centuries left the main towns resembling those on Garda and Como: hillside terraces of wooden-shuttered pastel villas. In the late 18th century, Monte Isola found its main industry: net making. AtRetificio La Rete Srl, a small shop and net factoryat Siviano’s port, fishing nets have been handwoven for centuries, along with nets for basketball hoops, football goals, shopping bags and hammocks.At the northern tip of the island, I get the best views of Lake Iseo’s craggiest mountains. The south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against gently undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyards. The north is where jagged peaks scrape the sky, plummeting to the emerald-green lake water. Just off the shore, a speck of an island (Isola di Loreto) is topped with a grand, castle-like building, which Chiara says is privately owned. A flotilla of kayakers from Marone make their way towards the private dock, slipping across the glass-still water.In Carzano, I pause to admire thepink-and-white facade of San Giovanni Battista church, before cycling along the more functional stretch of road along the eastern shore. The traffic-free spell is broken by an old Fiat Punto, apologetically crawling along the road. Maybe the driver is the doctor or priest.double quotation markThe steep trail to the top begins with the cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forestI complete my circle back in Peschiera Maraglio, where a late lunch of lake fish awaits atLa Foresta restaurant. To begin, pickled tench so vinegary it makes my mouth water and a chub carpaccio that tastes like fresh lake water; followed by the island staple of dried, saltedsardinason grilled polenta. “Sardinais not a sardine; it’s actually a type of shad fish,” Chiara explains. “In the middle ages, when Monte Isola had to pay tax to Venice, they didn’t understand how money worked, so they paid in saltedsardinasinstead.”View image in fullscreenFish drying in Peschiera Maraglio, Lago d’Iseo.Photograph: Matthias Scholz/AlamyAs the last ferries leave for the evening, it feels as if I have Peschiera Maraglio to myself. Accommodation is private holiday apartments or restaurants with rooms. AtDecio, a modern bistro dominates the ground floor, with a handful of sleek bedrooms above. The glass front shows off an uninterrupted lake view and the room is bathed in orange light at sunset. I spend the evening perched on a stool outsideL’Isola dei Sapori, a no-frills alfresco spot where sparkling franciacorta wine is perfectly chilled, and snacks of local salami, olives and fish dishes combine for a light dinner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMake tracks: 8 of the UK’s best walking and cycling trails on former railway linesRead moreThe next day, I forgo my bike and lace up my hiking boots. The steep trail to the top of the island begins with the enclosed cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forest. I pocket a particularly beefy conker, unable to resist the childhood urge for a blinder. My legs start to burn against the gradient – the trail is 450 metres of climbing. Rocks and twisting roots burst through the forest path and there’s a sheer drop to one side, but the glimpses of Lake Iseo between the trees are worth every wheeze.View image in fullscreenSantuario della Madonna della Ceriola chapel on the island of Monte Isola in Lake Iseo.Photograph: Image Professionals/AlamyAfter an hour, the trees thin out and I emerge atSantuario della Madonna della Ceriola. The striking white sanctuary was built in the 13th century, on the remains of a pagan temple and early Christian chapels. A vast golden altar and detailed frescoes adorn the interior, but it’s the panoramic view outside that really makes the hike worthwhile. The ferry to Sulzano is a toy boat, leaving a white tail of wake.From up high, I see that autumn colours are already creeping into the forest. I wipe the sweat from my eyes. This view is only going to get prettier as the season evolves, and the prize conkers are yet to fall.The trip was arranged byVisit Brescia.Bike rentalstartsat €4an hour.The ferryfrom Sulzano to MonteIsola is€2.60each way.Trainsrun from Brescia to Sulzanofrom€4.10. title: Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri | Food | The Guardian
description: A spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauce
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauce
Content: Gurdeep Loyal’s Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenGurdeep Loyal’s Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.Quick and easyFoodGurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheriA spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauceGurdeep LoyalMon 12 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBiber salçasıis a Turkish paste made from concentrated cooked red peppers and salt. It comes in two varieties:acı(spicy) andtatlı(sweet). The hotter version adds a deep, umami heat to cumin-spiced lamb in this pasta recipe, which in Turkey is known asmarkana. Traditionally, markana is served with garlicky yoghurt and a generous drizzle of chilli butter enlivened with pul biber and sumac. With flavours this loud, it’s best to use a large pasta shape such as paccheri, because its cavernous middles can hold satisfying morsels of the filling.Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheriPrep10 minCook25 minServes41tbsp olive oil1 large red onion, peeled and dicedFine salt500g lamb mince2tsp cumin seeds, crushed6 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed4tbsp acı biber salçası(hot Turkish pepper paste)3tbsp tomato puree1tsp dried mintSugar400g paccheri200g natural yoghurtFinely grated zest and juice of 1 large unwaxed lemon50g unsalted butter1tsp pul biber or chilli flakes1tsp sumac15g fresh dill, leaves finely choppedPour the olive oil into a wide, deep frying pan, then add the onion and a quarter-teaspoon of salt, and saute for four minutes. Add the lamb mince, cumin and four of the crushed garlic cloves, and cook for six to seven minutes, until the meat is just beginning to brown.Add the hot pepper paste, tomato puree, dried mint, a teaspoon of fine salt and a generous pinch of sugar, and cook for two minutes. Pour in 250ml water, turn down the heat to medium-low and simmer gently for 10 minutes.Meanwhile, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions, then drain.In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the remaining two crushed garlic cloves and the lemon zest.Melt the butter in a small frying pan and cook for three to four minutes, until it just begins to tint brown. Stir in the pul biber and sumac, then take off the heat.Stir most of the lemon juice and most of the dill into the lamb sauce, then add the drained pasta and mix well to coat. Swirl over the garlic yoghurt, followed by the sumac butter, garnish with more dill and another squeeze of lemon, and serve straight from the pan.Flavour Heroes: 15 Modern Pantry Ingredients to Amplify Your Cooking, by Gurdeep Loyal, is published by Quadrille at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodQuick and easyTurkish food and drinkLambMeatPastaMain courseHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Calum Franklin’s recipes for balti paratha pie with spicy green chutney | Indian food and drink | The Guardian
description: A pleasingly proper curry-filled pie with a zingy chutney to go with it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A pleasingly proper curry-filled pie with a zingy chutney to go with it
Content: Calum Franklin’s balti paratha pie with spicy green chutney.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.View image in fullscreenCalum Franklin’s balti paratha pie with spicy green chutney.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.Indian food and drinkCalum Franklin’s recipes for balti paratha pie with spicy green chutneyA pleasingly proper curry-filled pie with a zingy chutney to go with itCalum FranklinMon 12 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is one of my all-time favourite pies, pie born out of the Midlands. While studying at University College Birmingham, the now head of department at the college of food there, Lewis Walker, and I were in digs together and regularly ended up in very late-night balti houses after big nights out. These pies remind me of that really special time. It wasn’t much before my university days when balti cooking emerged in 1970s Birmingham, apparently created as a way to appease the British palate of the time. Its roots are in Pakistani-Kashmiri cooking and the base of the curry always has to contain tomatoes, onions, peppers and chillies, although variations can be built on those foundations. They’re a wonderful celebration of multicultural Britain.Balti pieEnjoyed on football terraces across the nation, thefirst balti pieis thought to have been served at Walsall football club in 1997, and they are now sold at more than 70 football grounds throughout the UK. There is a version of the balti pie that not many know (or have even considered) outside the UK, but it is the stuff of dreams: thebalti pie barm, or whole balti pie inside a soft bread roll. Don’t knock it until you’ve tried it. You will need a nonstick 12-hole muffin tray.Prep15 minChill15 minCook2 hrServes46 chicken thighs on the boneFine table salt1tsp medium curry powder1tsp garam masala½tsp ground turmeric½tsp chilli powder½tsp ground cumin½tsp ground cinnamon70g butter1 red onion, peeled and finely chopped1 green pepper, deseeded and cut into small cubes1 garlic clove, peeled and chopped2cm pieceginger, peeled and chopped400g tin chopped tomatoes1tsp tomato puree200ml chicken stock1 heapedtbsp cornflourZest and juice of 1 lime10g fresh coriander, roughly chopped16 frozen roti paratha1 egg yolk, strained and beaten with 1 tsp water, for egg washing1 pinch each nigella seeds and fennel seeds, for toppingHeat the oven to 210C (190C fan)//415F/gas 6½. Put the chicken thighs in a roasting tray, season with a pinch of salt, and roast for 25 minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool.Lower the oven to 205C (185C fan)//gas 6. Scatter all the ground spices over a sheet of foil, then put the foil in the oven and toast the spices for 10 minutes. Turn off the oven.Meanwhile, melt 50g of the butter in a wide-based pan. Add the red onion, green pepper, garlic and ginger, and cook on a low heat until softened.Add the toasted spices, cook for a minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, tomato puree and stock. Bring everything to a simmer on a medium heat, then reduce the sauce by half and turn off the heat.When cool enough to handle, strip the meat off the chicken bones and chop it into small nuggets.In a small bowl, mix a tablespoon of cold water into the cornflour to make a slurry, then stir that into the sauce. Stirring continuously, bring the sauce gently back to a simmer. Add the chopped chicken, mix well, then add the lime zest and juice. Taste to check the seasoning, and add a little salt, if need be. Fold through the chopped coriander, leave to cool to room temperature, then chill in the fridge.Use the rest of the butter to grease eight holes in the muffin tin. Take the paratha out of the freezer and, working swiftly, roll out eight of them to about 11cm. Line each greased hole in the muffin tin with a rolled-out paratha and fill three-quarters of the way with the balti mix. Lightly brush the exposed paratha with a little water, then use the remaining paratha to close the pies, gently crimping the edges together; don’t worry about being too neat – I like to give them a rustic look. Chill the pies in the fridge for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Using a sharp knife, cut a small hole in the top of each pie, lightly brush the tops with a thin coating of egg wash, then scatter with the nigella and fennel seeds. Bake for 30 minutes, then serve hot with the green chutney below for dippingSpicy green chutneyView image in fullscreenCalum Franklin’s spicy green chutney.A fresh yet heady dressing that is so easy to make. It complements the balti pies superbly.Prep15 minMakes150ml1 garlic clove, peeled2cm piece ginger, peeled1 green chilli½tsp cumin seeds, lightly toastedJuice of ½ lemon60g fresh coriander, leaves picked40g fresh mint, leaves picked1 pinch fine table saltIn a blender, blitz the garlic, ginger, chilli, cumin, lemon juice and four tablespoons of water, until smooth. Add the coriander and mint leaves and a pinch of salt, then blend again, until smooth. Store in an airtight container in the fridge, where the chutney will keep for up to a week.These recipes are edited extracts from The Modern Pie Maker: A Mouth-Watering Journey Around Britain in Eighty Recipes, by Calum Franklin, published by Bloomsbury at £26.
